title: Radionuclide geochemistry and radiological implications of deep-sea ferromanganese crusts from the Rio Grande Rise
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Muhammad Bin Hassan, Paulo Sergio Cardoso da Silva, Christian Millo, Luigi Jovane, Frederico Antonio Genezini, Gabriel Bertolini, Fábio V. Sussa, Marco A. Stanojev Pereira, Carina Ulsen
abstract: Ferromanganese (Fe-Mn) crusts are hydrogenetic marine deposits that incorporate naturally occurring radionuclides during their formation, making them valuable archives of marine geochemical processes. This study investigates the distribution of radionuclides, 222Rn emanation, and radiological properties of 15 Fe-Mn crust samples from the Rio Grande Rise (RGR), South Atlantic Ocean, spanning water depths of 650-5218 m. The analyzed crusts include hydrogenetic, phosphatized, and ironstone types and are compared with published data for polymetallic nodules. Gamma-ray spectrometry and neutron activation analysis were used to determine the activity concentrations of 238U, 232Th, 228Ra, 228Th, 226Ra, 210Pb, and 40K. Radon emanation was measured under open- and closed-system conditions to characterize radon accumulation and release from Fe-Mn crusts. Calculated external effective doses remained below 1 mSv y−1, indicating minimal radiological risk during routine handling, transport, and storage. Water-depth-dependent variations in 232Th, 228Ra, 228Th, and 222Rn reflect the combined influence of particle reactivity, radionuclide solubility, parent radionuclide availability, and crust porosity. Due to its strong particle reactivity, 232Th preferentially accumulates in porous hydrogenetic crusts, whereas phosphatization reduces porosity by replacing Fe-Mn oxyhydroxides with carbonate fluorapatite, thereby limiting radionuclide transport and radon release. Short-lived radionuclides (228Ra and 228Th) and 222Rn emanation were higher in porous hydrogenetic crusts, consistent with the availability of their parent radionuclides and enhanced pore connectivity. Neutron tomography revealed differences in internal porosity among crust types, supporting the interpretation that phosphatization limits 222Rn mobility by sealing pore networks. The integration of geochemical, radiometric, and structural analyses provides new insights into the links between Fe-Mn crust formation, alteration, and radionuclide behavior.

title: Geochemical characteristics of the Mid-Eocene organic-rich carbonates from northern Jordan: Insights into warm climate and anoxia impacts on organic carbon accumulation
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Mohammed Hail Hakimi, Mohammad Alqudah, Khairul Azlan Mustapha, Baleid Ali Hatem, Waqas Naseem, Alok Kumar, S.M. Talha Qadri, Aref Lashin
abstract: Organic-rich carbonates of the Mid-Eocene Wadi Shallala Formation (WSF) in northern Jordan were studied using organic geochemical and elemental analyses, along with microscopic observations to evaluate the past climate and redox conditions, as well as their role in controlling organic carbon accumulation. The WSF samples are characterized by elevated organic matter (OM) and sulfur, reaching maximum values of 6.53 wt % and 3.20 wt %, respectively, indicating marine, anoxic-to-euxinic conditions that promote effective OM preservation during deposition. Redox-sensitive proxies support this interpretation, particularly low Pr/Ph ratios (<1) and higher abundances of vanadium (V) and Uranium (U) than Nickel (Ni) and Thorium (Th), with V/Ni and U/Th ratios reaching 3.07 and 13.24, respectively. The biomarkers also indicate mainly marine (i.e., planktonic-bacterial) OM, reflecting hydrogen-rich kerogen as the original OM during deposition of the WSF sediments. The predominance of marine-derived OM is evidenced by the abundance of alginite, including telalginite and lamalginite, together with diverse assemblages of marine organisms. The oxygen isotope (δ18O) and organic carbon isotope (δ13C) data, together with paleoclimatic indicators, further suggest an increase in temperatures during the warm-water climatic conditions associated with the Mid-Eocene event, intensifying subaerial weathering and enhancing the influx of nutrients and then promoting greater organic production by marine photosynthetic organisms in the photic zone. The elevated warm-water climate of the Mid-Eocene event was associated with anoxic conditions, confirming its strong impact on OM preservation and accumulation during deposition.

title: Travertine spring hydrogeochemistry as a guide to buried Au–Cu mineralization in the Dehaj–Sardouiyeh metallogenic zone, Bam–Rayen district, SE Iran
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Jamal Fereydoni Sarvestani, Abbas Bahroudi, Kaveh Pazand, Faramarz Doulati Ardejani
abstract: Travertine springs in the Bam–Rayen region exhibit exceptionally high concentrations of large-ion lithophile elements (LILE), including Cs (240–4900 μg/L), Li (1500–5700 μg/L), and Rb (600–3900 μg/L), as well as anomalous enrichments of chalcophile elements such as As (290–52000 μg/L), Mo (3.6–47 μg/L), Te (0.05–0.34 μg/L), Tl (0.07–16.5 μg/L), Se (2.5–570 μg/L), and Sb (1.3–43.6 μg/L). In addition, one spring sample contains detectable gold (Au = 0.11 μg/L). Although the source of these anomalies remains unclear, the widespread Au and Au–Cu mineralizations in the area suggest a potential link between elevated elemental concentrations and water–rock interactions in mineralized zones. Hydrochemical (Physicochemical parameters) and hydrogeochemical analyses of major ions (Ca2+, Na+, Mg2+, K+, Cl−, HCO3 −, SO4 2−) and trace elements (LILEs and chalcophile elements) suggest that spring waters interact directly with sulfide-bearing mineralization zones. This interaction facilitates the dissolution of trace-element–rich minerals and their subsequent transport to the surface. Moreover, the passage of groundwater through alteration zones associated with Au–Cu mineralization (notably potassic and phyllic types), coupled with the presence of phyllosilicate minerals such as sericite, illite, and muscovite, enhances the mobility of LILEs (Cs, Li, Rb). These elements substitute for K in the crystal lattice of alteration minerals and are subsequently released into circulating waters. Similarly, chalcophile elements (As, Sb, Se, Te, Tl) are introduced into spring waters through the leaching of sulfide veins. Overall, these findings emphasize the significance of travertine spring geochemistry as an indicator of hidden mineralization at depth.

title: Helium and carbon isotopic systematics of hot spring gases at the intersection of the Nantinghe and Longling–Lancang fault zones, southeast Tibetan Plateau: Tracing volatile migration and the seismogenic environment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Qilin Li, Ciping Zhao, Hua Ran, Xiang Zhang, Can You, Zihan Tai
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive geochemical dataset of gas compositions and He–C isotopic data for 36 hot spring sites at the intersection of the Nantinghe Fault Zone (NTHF) and Longling–Lancang Fault Zone (LLF), which is a key tectonic junction on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau. Air-corrected 3He/4He ratios (Rc/Ra) range from 0.02 to 0.49 Ra, indicating dominantly crustal He; mantle-derived He contributes 1%–5% and is higher in the NTHF Western Branch Zone than in the Eastern Branch Zone. CO2 is derived from carbonate dissolution, while CH4 has mixed origins. The NTHF Western Branch Zone is controlled by the deep LLF, Neogene Yingpan volcanism, and high-permeability faults, yielding higher mantle He and CO2 fluxes. In contrast, the NTHF Eastern Branch Zone is affected by radiogenic 4He from the Lincang granite batholith and calcite precipitation, and is dominated by crustal fluids. The transition zone between high and low deep fluid fluxes aligns with the boundary of geophysical anomalies, and the epicentres of historical M ≥ 7.0 earthquakes are located precisely along this boundary, suggesting deep fluids influence seismicity. Deep fluid migration is controlled by fault architecture and may influence the seismogenic environment through fluid overpressure and fault weakening. Comparable geophysical signatures and fluid activity imply a high potential for large earthquakes along the northern segment of the NTHF.

title: Mantle CO 2 degassing and carbon dynamics in a volcanic aquifer: δ 13 C evidence and Python-coded PhreeQC quantification for the Jimma area, Ethiopia
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Wagari Mosisa Kitessa, Sisay Kebede Balcha, Lelisa Regea Mengistu, Sebilewongel Milargh, Milkesa Kelbessa Kebbe
abstract: Quantifying mantle CO2 degassing in volcanic aquifers is difficult because δ13C signatures are non-unique and modified by degassing, carbonate reactions, water-rock interaction, and mixing. This study integrates δ13C-DIC (n = 51), major-ion chemistry, and Python-PhreeQC modeling to investigate carbon sources in the Jimma volcanic aquifer, Ethiopia. Deep wells DW8 and DW9 show δ13C values (−3.8‰, −3.5‰) within the mantle CO2 range, supported by high HCO3 − (732-874 mg/L), Na-HCO3 type, high pH (7.5-8.6), and near-ambient temperatures (≤28.5°C). Springs (−12.5‰ to −9.5‰) and urban wells (−13.5‰ to −11.8‰) reflect biogenic and sewage-derived carbon. A multi-endmember mixing model estimates mantle-like contributions of 65% (95% CI: 52-78%) for DW8 and 82% (68-90%) for DW9, though these are indicative rather than precise. PhreeQC degassing simulations show CO2 loss (pCO2: 0.32 → 0.00032 atm) increases pH from 6.47 to 8.22 and drives calcite supersaturation, but Rayleigh modeling (ε ≈ −1‰) confirms degassing alone cannot produce observed δ13C enrichment, suggesting a mantle-like component. Three vertical zones are identified: shallow biogenic ( 150 m). Volcanic aquifers may conduit deep carbon, with implications for rift carbon budgets and groundwater sustainability, though interpretation remains indirect without noble gas or direct CO2 measurements.

title: Challenges in identifying groundwater salinization processes in a coastal aquifer affected by multiple salinity sources
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Lamine Boumaiza, Randy L. Stotler, Romain Chesnaux, Mohamed El-Gettafi, Bernhard Mayer, Christoph Schüth, Shaun K. Frape, Matthew I. Leybourne, Karen H. Johannesson, Frédéric Huneau, Neus Otero, Orfan Shouakar‐Stash, Christine Stumpp
abstract: Despite the variety of environmental tracers that can be used for tracing salinity sources, their interpretation can be complicated in specific contexts where many sources can overlap. This study integrates major ions with a range of isotope tracers (i.e., δ 18OH2O, δ 2HH2O, δ 11B, δ 37Cl, and 87Sr/86Sr) to identify salinity sources in a Mediterranean coastal area, historically impacted by the Messinian Salinity Crisis (MSC), where multiple contributors beyond modern seawater are possible. By comparing δ 18OH2O to δ 2HH2O values, groundwater chemistry is shown to be influenced by three endmembers, i.e., the Mediterranean Sea, surface water recharge, and deep groundwater that interacted with Messinian units (DGIMU). This finding is consistent with observations from plots of δ 18OH2O-Cl, Cl-Br/Cl, and Cl-87Sr/86Sr, which reveal that most groundwaters fall within the expected domain of the proposed endmembers. The relative influence of each endmember is supported by mass-balance mixing models, which indicate that groundwater with a composition like DGIMU is the major contributor of salinity. The plot B-δ 11B does not provide a clear boron source determination but suggests potential marine boron contributions along with likely anthropogenic boron contributions. The 87Sr/86Sr values (0.709021 to 0.709129) are less radiogenic than modern Mediterranean Sea water, supporting potential mixing of groundwater with terrestrial surface waters having lower 87Sr/86Sr values. The observed overall decrease in Br/Cl with increasing Cl concentrations suggests salinization via dissolution of halite. This is supported by (i) the groundwater δ 37Cl range (−0.6 to +1.2‰), which is consistent with dissolved Cl in groundwater that has interacted with halite deposits; (ii) the strong correlation of Cl with Na concentrations suggesting halite dissolution; and (iii) the calculated negative saturation indices with respect of halite. The measured 87Sr/86Sr values suggest dissolution of the underlying late MSC-salt units. Therefore, groundwater salinity in the study area cannot be explained by seawater intrusion alone, rather it appears to be the result of mixing of shallow groundwater with groundwater that interacted with the late underlying MSC salt units.

title: Occurrence and geochemical controls of manganese, arsenic, and iron in groundwater in Alberta, Canada
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Isabel Plata, Pauline Humez, Raphaël Bondu, Cynthia McClain, Bernhard Mayer
abstract: Groundwater quality in Alberta, Canada, is influenced by geogenic constituents such as manganese (Mn), arsenic (As), and iron (Fe), which can pose health risks when present above drinking water standards. This study investigates the geochemical controls on Mn, As, and Fe occurrence and mobility using over 10,600 groundwater samples (depths <250 m) for Mn and Fe, and 1700 samples for As. Guideline exceedances were observed in 18% of samples for Mn, 11% for As, and 21% for Fe (aesthetic objective). Elevated concentrations in bedrock units were most common in marine and transitional formations, where exceedance frequencies surpassed 20% for all three elements. In surficial sediment aquifers, Mn and As concentrations exceeded drinking water guidelines in 48% and 22% of the samples, respectively, while the Fe aesthetic objective was exceeded in 46% of the samples, highlighting a potential risk to untreated groundwater users and demonstrating the impact of regional lithology on aqueous geochemistry. Post-oxic conditions, characterized by nitrate depletion, exhibited the highest median concentrations of Mn, As, and Fe. Reductive dissolution of Fe(III) oxides facilitates the release of Fe and As, with As primarily occurring as arsenite [As(III)], a more mobile and toxic species. Arsenic mobility was further enhanced under alkaline, Na-HCO3-rich conditions. Manganese release was linked to both oxide and carbonate dissolution under suboxic to anoxic conditions. Overall, redox zonation and aquifer mineralogy strongly control Mn, As, and Fe distributions in groundwater. These findings support improved groundwater resource management in sedimentary basin settings.

title: Soil–plant transfer and organ-specific partitioning of trace elements (Mn, Zn and Mo) in irrigated soils
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Avazbek Turdaliev, Evgeny Lodygin, Iskandar Musaev, Mashkhura Khaydarova, Validjan Isakov, Zokirjon Isomiddinov
abstract: Irrigation is a major driver of soil transformation in arid agroecosystems and can influence trace-element partitioning and soil–plant transfer. This study investigated the behavior of Mn, Zn, and Mo in the soil–grapevine system of the Northern Fergana region (Uzbekistan) along a gradient of irrigation-induced pedogenic development, including newly developed, newly irrigated, and long-term irrigated Calcisols. Total element concentrations in soils and grapevine organs (leaves, stems, and berries) were determined by instrumental neutron activation analysis. Soil–plant transfer was evaluated using biological absorption coefficients (BAC), barrier function indices (BFI), and selectivity accumulation indices (SAI), while principal component analysis (PCA) was used to identify patterns of element partitioning among plant organs. Soil concentrations of Mn and Zn were higher in the long-term irrigated site than in the newly irrigated site, whereas Mo showed a different pattern across the irrigation-history categories. These differences represent integrated responses of the contrasting irrigation-history and cultivar–site combinations rather than an independently quantified effect of irrigation duration. However, higher soil concentrations were not accompanied by proportional increases in berry concentrations. All studied elements exhibited a consistent distribution pattern, with the highest concentrations in leaves, intermediate concentrations in stems, and the lowest concentrations in berries. BAC values for berries remained low for all elements, indicating limited transfer from soil to harvested products. High BFI values indicated pronounced differences in trace-element concentrations between leaves and berries, consistent with restricted accumulation in reproductive organs. Zinc showed preferential accumulation in plant tissues, whereas Mn was characterized by stronger physiological regulation and Mo displayed intermediate behavior. PCA revealed a clear organ-related structure in the trace-element concentration data. The results indicate that trace-element partitioning in the studied irrigated viticultural systems reflects the combined influence of soil geochemical conditions and plant-mediated processes. The observed organ-specific partitioning was associated with substantially lower Mn, Zn, and Mo concentrations in grape berries than in vegetative organs, despite differences in total soil concentrations.

title: Geospatial prediction of potentially toxic elements in urban dust and associated health risks using machine learning at the watershed scale
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Rodrigo Rodríguez, Diana Meza-Figueroa, Agustin Robles-Morua, José Tuxpan-Vargas, Bhaskar Sen-Gupta, Nadia Martínez-Villegas
abstract: In urban environments, multiple pollution sources and environmental factors lead to complex spatial patterns of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in urban dust that conventional interpolation methods may not capture. This study integrated Random Forest modeling, deterministic and Monte Carlo health risk assessments, and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA) at the watershed scale (n = 12) to predict concentrations of Zn, As, Pb, Cu, Fe, and Sr in fine urban dust (<20 μm) and assess associated health risks in a city of 1.2 million inhabitants in central Mexico. The Random Forest model achieved high predictive performance (R2 = 0.90–0.98, nMAE <20.5%, nRMSE <29.1%) and identified proximity to a zinc refinery, industrial zones, main streets, and flood-prone areas as key predictors of PTE distribution. Predicted mean concentrations were 4058 mg/kg for Zn, 80 mg/kg for As, 306 mg/kg for Pb, 479 mg/kg for Cu, 51,877 mg/kg for Fe, and 253 mg/kg for Sr. Deterministic risk assessment, verified through Monte Carlo simulation, revealed that children face elevated non-carcinogenic risks (THI = 5.9 ± 2.7) and carcinogenic risks (TCR = 1.6 × 10−3) exceeding acceptable thresholds across the entire city, while adults showed localized risks (THI = 0.6 ± 0.3) near industrial facilities. HCA identified two priority watersheds (C3 and C5) with significantly higher PTE concentrations and health risks (p < 0.05), where approximately 60,000 residents live. This study advances our understanding of the spatial distribution and risk of PTEs in urban dust at the watershed scale, and the factors driving them, using machine learning.

title: Source apportionment and multi-dimensional driving mechanism of soil potentially toxic elements in the high-background alpine mining area
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Zihao Fan, Jiang Xiao, Liuyuan Jin, Tongyang Zhao, Shiming Yang, Zihan Yang, Yangshuang Wang, Yunhui Zhang
abstract: Soils are fundamental to environmental quality, and elevated concentrations of potentially toxic elements (PTEs) in surface soils pose growing risks to ecosystem health. This study used multiple complementary methods to quantify sources and identify key drivers of eight PTEs in 264 surface soil samples from the West Kunlun Mountains, Xinjiang. Overall, soil PTE concentrations across the study area were largely consistent with the national soil background values of China. As, Ni, and Cd exhibited the highest variability (coefficient of variation, CV > 0.6). Relative to these background values, only Cd showed slight enrichment (enrichment factor EF = 1.37), whereas As, Cd, Ni, and Pb displayed localized hotspots. Self-Organizing Mapping (SOM) and Principal Component Analysis-Absolute Principal Component Score-Multiple Linear Regression (PCA-APCS-MLR) identified four potential source groups based on element associations. Integrating these results with driving factor identification from Geo-detector model (GDM) and Random Forest (RF), which revealed the relative importance of natural versus anthropogenic controls on element distribution, the four sources were quantified as follows: a traffic-agriculture-residential mixed anthropogenic source (16.68%; Pb, As, Cd), a lithology- and relief-dominated natural source with weak traffic influence (21.19%; Cr, Ni), a coal mining-atmospheric deposition source (15.41%; Hg), and a precipitation-driven natural source (30.44%; Cu, Zn). GDM and RF further showed that individual factors explained limited variance, whereas two-factor interactions induced strong nonlinear enhancement. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Model (PLS-SEM) further demonstrated that anthropogenic factors exerted a significant direct inhibitory effect on PTE accumulation, while socioeconomic, climatic, and environmental factors mediated indirect suppression. Collectively, these results underscore the primacy of natural controls in establishing regional PTE baselines and the spatially confined nature of anthropogenic perturbations, providing a robust, quantitative framework for targeted soil risk management in heterogeneous mountainous regions.

title: Experimental study on the contribution of microbial-induced carbonate precipitation to carbon sequestration in soil from the northern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Lingjie Huang, Xuelin Li, Shuang Li, Xuefen Sheng, Xinyuan Guo, Baitang Li, Ruoyu Hu, Fuchun Li
abstract: Soil inorganic carbon (SIC) plays a critical role in global carbon cycling; however, the contribution of microbial-induced carbonate minerals (CMs) to the SIC pool remains poorly explored. There is no definitive method for distinguishing between microbial-induced and chemical CMs in soil nor a calculation of the ratio between the two. To fill this gap, a soil profile at a depth of 110 cm, located in the alpine grassland of the northern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP), was examined. Incubation experiments were conducted using mixed microbes isolated from soil. Our analysis encompassed vertical variation along the profile in soil organic carbon (SOC), SIC, and Ca2+, as well as the carbon isotopic composition (δ13C) of CMs, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), and SOC. X-ray diffraction and field-emission scanning electron microscopy equipped with energy-dispersive analysis were used to characterise the CMs in the soil. The close negative correlation between microbial biomass and δ13CCMs in both soil samples and incubation experiments suggests that soil microorganisms actively participate in CM formation. To quantify the proportion of microbial-induced CMs in soil, we established an empirical relationship between δ13Ccalcite and δ13CCO2(g) through incubation experimencts. This relationship allowed us to estimate the δ13C of the microbial-induced CMs (δ13CMCMs) using the δ13CCO2(g). Thereby, the calculated average δ13CCO2(g) for the upper soil layer was −36.2‰, corresponding to an estimated δ13CMCMs value of −26.5‰. Based on the above δ13CCMs, the estimated proportion of microbial-induced CMs in the total CM content is calculated, ranging from 43.7% to 4.0% with depth. Consequently, microbial-induced CMs are estimated to contribute approximately 20.2% to the SIC pool within the upper 1-m soil profile at Laohugou. These findings provide a novel framework for quantifying the contribution of microbially induced carbonate minerals to SIC sequestration using carbon isotopes. They highlight a pathway for transferring soil-derived CO2 into relatively stable inorganic carbon pools, with implications for understanding carbon cycling under changing environmental conditions.

title: Returned concrete as a new sustainable feedstock for enhanced weathering: Carbon dioxide removal potential and methodological recommendations
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Rémi Rateau, Ruadhán Magee, Frank McDermott, Maurice Bryson
abstract: Returned concrete is a cumbersome by-product generated by the ready-mix concrete industry. A new potentially sustainable market for the estimated 42 ± 19 Mt yr−1 of limestone-rich crushed returned concrete produced globally is its deployment as a pH-adjusting enhanced weathering feedstock for carbon dioxide removal in agricultural soils. However, its variable mineralogical composition presents methodological challenges that are not addressed by existing protocols and carbon credit registries. Based on literature review and limited but new observations at concrete plants, a model-based tiered methodological approach is proposed to address these challenges. Our methodology is based on measurements of bicarbonate in soil water, assuming that the bicarbonate originates entirely from calcite weathering, coupled with a calculation of additional carbonation-driven CO2 uptake that takes account of the potential and realized carbonation of hydrated cement paste in concrete at the post-milling stage. With the simple Tier 1 approach, a stochastically modelled carbonation uptake value of 0.032 ± 0.007 (1σ) t CO2 t−1 returned concrete spread is suggested, which should be added to enhanced weathering-derived carbon dioxide removal calculated in the field using a soil water-based approach. In cases where more complete local data are available, Tier 2 methods are suggested for improved accuracy. The methodology described here estimates carbonation-driven carbon dioxide removal that is additional, as it takes into account the CO2 removal that occurred during storage of the returned concrete before milling and also subtracts the counterfactual removal that would have occurred had the returned concrete remained un-milled and used as buried road base aggregate.

title: Geochemical controls on natural arsenic variability in Arctic tundra soils: Implications for regional geochemical baselines and environmental assessment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Evgeny Lodygin
abstract: Reliable regional geochemical baseline values are essential for distinguishing natural variability in trace elements from anthropogenic pollution, particularly in Arctic environments where pedogenic processes create pronounced spatial heterogeneity. However, information on the natural distribution of arsenic (As) in tundra soils of the European Russian Arctic remains limited. This study examined As concentrations in representative background soils of the Vorkuta district (Komi Republic, Russia) to identify the main factors controlling its distribution and establish regional geochemical baseline values for environmental assessment. A total of 280 soil samples representing ten WRB soil groups and their genetic horizons were analyzed for total As content, as well as for selected physicochemical properties. Statistical evaluation included Spearman correlation analysis, principal component analysis (PCA), and calculation of the upper 95% confidence limit (UCL95%) for individual soil groups. Arsenic concentrations varied significantly between soil types and horizons, reflecting substantial pedogenic and geochemical variability in soils without identified local anthropogenic sources. The lowest mean concentrations were observed in sandy Podzols, while loamy hydromorphic and cryogenic soils consistently had higher values. The PCA analysis revealed that the main factors influencing arsenic distribution differ between organic and mineral horizons. In organic horizons, As variability was primarily associated with soil pH, whereas organic carbon represented a separate source of variability. In mineral horizons, As concentrations were primarily associated with the fine mineral fraction and Fe2O3 and Al2O3 contents. These contrasting relationships explain the pronounced vertical differentiation of arsenic in tundra soil profiles. Calculated UCL95% values also differed substantially between soil groups, indicating that a single regional background concentration cannot adequately reflect the natural geochemical variability of Arctic tundra soils. The results indicate that regional geochemical baseline values should be established separately for major soil groups and genetic horizons. The proposed baseline values provide a scientifically sound basis for environmental assessment and geochemical mapping in the European Russian Arctic and can serve as a guide for long-term monitoring of trace element behavior in permafrost-affected landscapes.

title: Primary mineral assemblage controls cation release and carbonation pathways in shallow basaltic reservoirs
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Lizi Liao, Yijun Zheng, Shichen Duan, Tian Liang, Rong Xue, Yongchun Fan, Zhiqiang Yu, Ping'an Peng
abstract: Shallow basaltic formations are promising reservoirs for geological CO2 storage by mineral carbonation, yet the role of primary mineral assemblage in controlling cation release and carbonation pathways under shallow-burial conditions remains poorly constrained. We conducted 60-day batch CO2–H2O–basalt experiments at 30 °C and 2 MPa on six basalts from the Leizhou Peninsula, South China, spanning altered, alkaline, transitional and tholeiitic lithologies. Time-resolved fluid chemistry was combined with mineralogical, spectroscopic and thermal characterization of reacted solids and of the precipitates recovered from the filtrates. Cation release varied systematically with mineral assemblage. Peak dissolved Ca followed the ordering of modal pyroxene abundance, ranging from 29 to 195 mg/L, whereas plagioclase and olivine abundances gave no comparable ordering. Transitional basalts exhibited the lowest molar (Ca + Mg)/Si release ratios and approached amorphous-silica saturation only after Day 30, too late to explain their low Ca fluxes. The montmorillonite-rich altered basalt released anomalously high Mg (149 mg/L) decoupled from Si; extraction experiments and thermal analysis indicate that exchangeable Mg and dissolution of pre-existing magnesite together account for no more than one quarter of this inventory, and that most mobilized Mg remained in solution rather than being converted to carbonate. Carbonate precipitates recovered from filtrates formed after depressurization and storage, and cannot be interpreted as in situ mineralization. Primary mineral assemblage, rather than bulk oxide composition, therefore controls not only cation release but also cation partitioning among aqueous and solid sinks (e.g., incorporation into Fe-(oxy)hydroxides versus carbonate phases), and recovered fluids require analytical-purpose-specific preservation.

title: 40-kyr of environmental history of the southeastern sector of paleolake Cuitzeo, central-western Mexico: Insights from abiotic and biotic proxies
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Nayeli Pérez-Rodríguez, Juan Morales, Isabel Israde-Alcántara, Gabriela Domínguez-Vázquez, Miguel Cervantes-Solano, Avto Goguitchaichvili, Francisco Bautista
abstract: We present a multiproxy reconstruction of environmental changes recorded in the southeastern sector of Lake Cuitzeo (central-western Mexico) over the last ∼40 kyr. Our study integrates abiotic (major-element geochemistry, rock-magnetic parameters, pH, and electrical conductivity) and biotic proxies (diatoms and pollen) from a ∼10 m-long sedimentary core (Cz-07). This multiproxy approach provides a robust framework for identifying variations in terrigenous input, redox conditions, nutrient availability, carbonate precipitation, and hydrological balance, as well as the response of local vegetation to climate fluctuations. Comparing the Cz-07 record with previous data from a depocenter core reveals some spatial differences in the lake's sensitivity to environmental changes. The sequence indicates generally low lake levels between ∼42 and ∼26.5 kyr BP, followed by pronounced environmental variability during the Last Glacial Maximum, including a marked dry episode at its onset. Enhanced runoff and predominantly oxic conditions characterize the interval from ∼17.5 to ∼11 kyr BP, encompassing the Bølling–Allerød and Younger Dryas events. During the early-to-middle Holocene (∼11.7–5 kyr BP), a progressive shift toward arid conditions is evidenced by increased carbonate precipitation, higher salinity, and reduced runoff. The most severe drought occurred during the middle Holocene, causing a substantial contraction of the lake's southeastern sector. This arid phase aligns with middle Holocene drying trends reported in other lacustrine records across central Mexico.

title: Beyond expert weighting: A data-knowledge driven COBRAC-Fuzzy RAWEC framework for mineral prospectivity mapping
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Mahnaz Mahboobi, Homayoon Katibeh, Yousef Bahrami, Amin Beiranvand Pour
abstract: The inherent subjectivity of expert-driven weighting schemes remains a major limitation in mineral prospectivity mapping, often introducing cognitive bias and reducing predictive reliability in geologically complex environments. This study presents a novel, data- and knowledge-driven multi-criteria decision-making framework that integrates COBRAC (Comparisons Between Ranked Criteria) and Fuzzy RAWEC (Fuzzy Ranking of Alternatives with Weights of Criteria) for mineral prospectivity mapping, which, to the best of our knowledge, represents the first application of these methods to mineral exploration. COBRAC objectively derives internally consistent weights for criteria and subcriteria directly from Prediction-Area (P-A) performance and mineral occurrence frequencies, reducing subjective weighting bias while capturing nonlinear and non-monotonic relationships between evidential intensity and mineralization probability that conventional expert-based weighting schemes often overlook. Fuzzy RAWEC incorporates uncertainty through statistically derived triangular fuzzy numbers and a deviation from reference ranking mechanism, supporting false-positive reduction, mitigating rank reversal, and generating more stable suitability rankings under heterogeneous exploration conditions. The framework was applied to porphyry copper prospectivity mapping in the Shahr-e-Babak district of the Kerman Copper Metallogenic Belt, Iran, using seven evidential layers comprising UHK (UMAP-Hypergraph-Kmeans) geochemical anomalies, volcanic lithologies, phyllic, argillic, propylitic, and FeO/OH alteration zones, as well as fault structures. These layers were standardized using a logistic transformation and classified using the fractal C-A model. The proposed CFR framework achieved the highest prediction rate (82%), outperforming the robust BWM-ARAS (78%) and conventional AHP-TOPSIS (72%) models. This performance hierarchy (CFR > BWM-ARAS > AHP-TOPSIS) was demonstrated by the P-A analysis and corroborated by the success-rate curves, supporting the comparative effectiveness of CFR within this study area. A key advantage of the proposed approach lies in its data-driven weighting strategy, which objectively captures non-monotonic relationships between evidential intensity and mineralization probability. In several cases, intermediate anomaly classes exhibited higher P-A rates, and consequently greater predictive significance, than extreme classes. This characteristic enables CFR to accommodate spatially complex patterns and statistically dispersed extreme values without assuming a strictly linear relationship between evidence intensity and mineral occurrence. The proposed framework provides an objective, uncertainty-aware, and reproducible alternative to conventional Multiple-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) approaches, enhancing exploration targeting in the study area while offering a potentially transferable methodology for mineral prospectivity mapping in other geological settings.

title: Effects of low-molecular-weight organic acids on phosphate release from partially oxidized vivianite
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 212 Author(s): Qian Wang, Peng Zhang, Zhang Wen
abstract: Vivianite dissolution and precipitation play important roles in regulating phosphate (PO4-P) dynamics in subsurface environments. However, under redox-dynamic conditions, vivianite is readily oxidized to form partially oxidized vivianite, which exhibited a reduced dissolution rate. Despite its environmental significance, the influence of co-existing low-molecular-weight organic acids (LMWOAs) on the release of PO4-P from partially oxidized vivianite remains poorly understood. In this study, PO4-P release from partially oxidized vivianite (10 g/L) was systematically investigated in the presence and absence of LMWOAs. The results showed that LMWOAs significantly enhanced PO4-P release across a broad pH range (pH 5–9). For instance, in the absence of LMWOAs, the cumulative dissolved PO4-P concentration reached 0.11 mM within 10 h at pH 7, whereas the presence of LMWOAs increased PO4-P release by a factor of 2.3–6.5. The enhancement of PO4-P release strongly depended on the type and concentration of LMWOAs, solution pH and the oxidation extent of vivianite. Enhancement effects increased with higher stability constants of LMWOAs toward Fe2+ and Fe3+ and with a higher Fe(II) fraction in vivianite, but decreased with increasing solution pH. The LMWOA-induced enhancement of PO4-P release was mainly attributed to ligand complexation, which lowered the energy barrier for mineral dissolution and inhibited secondary precipitation reactions between phosphate and iron. These findings provide new insights into PO4-P dynamics in redox-dynamic environments and suggest an alternative strategy for enhancing PO4-P availability from vivianite in agricultural soils.

title: TLM-0 and TLH-0: Development of Lunar Maria and Highlands Simulants and Their Evaluation Through Figures of Merit and Multivariate Analysis
description: Publication date: Available online 4 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): F. Alberquilla, G. Gorla, K. Fernández-Cosials, J. Alonso-Azcárate, I. Martínez-Arkarazo, J. Aramendia, J.M. Madariaga, J. Abella-Larraz, C. Aguilar-Borasteros
abstract: Two new general-purpose lunar regolith simulants were developed to represent the main geological terranes of the Moon, namely TLM-0 (low-Ti mare) and TLH-0 (anorthositic highlands), both engineered from terrestrial source materials to reproduce key physical, mechanical, mineralogical, and geochemical properties of lunar soils. Comprehensive characterization, including particle size distribution, morphology, bulk density, shear strength, magnetic susceptibility, X-ray diffraction (XRD), μ-EDXRF, Raman microscopy, and ICP-MS indicates that TLH-0 exhibits a feldspathic composition enriched in Al2O3 and CaO with plagioclase-dominated mineralogy, whereas TLM-0 displays a more mafic signature characterized by higher FeO, MgO, and TiO2. During their evaluation, significant limitations were identified in establishing robust sample-to-sample comparisons with Apollo datasets, primarily due to heterogeneous analytical methodologies, incomplete or inconsistently reported particle size data, and the absence of standardized, fully integrated databases, all of which introduce uncertainty in simulant validation and hinder direct intercomparison across studies. Within this context, fidelity assessment using the Figure of Merit (FoM) framework yields mean values of 89 for TLH-0 and 91 for TLM-0, placing both among the highest-performing simulants within their respective domains, while complementary principal component analysis (PCA) on compositional data demonstrates that both materials remain embedded within the multivariate compositional structure defined by Apollo samples and plot closest to highlands and low-Ti mare reference fields. These results highlight the importance of combining univariate and multivariate approaches to achieve a more robust and comprehensive framework for simulant validation.

title: Potentially toxic elements in urban dust and soil at the San Ysidro and Otay Mesa border crossings: Identification of sources, lung bioaccessibility, and health risk assessment in Tijuana (México)
description: Publication date: Available online 4 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Marisol Juárez-Reyes, Claudio Inguaggiato, Benedetto Schiavo, Diana Meza-Figueroa, Bodo Weber, Belem González-Grijalva
abstract: Tijuana is linked to the USA through two land ports of entry: San Ysidro and Otay Mesa. Persistent congestion at both crossings promotes the accumulation and resuspension of fine particles enriched in potentially toxic elements (PTEs). This study evaluates the geochemical characteristics, sources, and health risk assessment of PTEs in <20 μm urban dust and soil from Tijuana, by integrating elemental concentrations, particle characterization by SEM-EDS, and lung bioaccessibility in artificial lysosomal fluid (ALF). Moreover, selected samples were further examined in the <10 μm fraction. Moderate to high contamination of Cr, Ni, Cu, Zn, Mo, Cd, Sb, and Pb, based on the geoaccumulation index (Igeo), was observed at the ports of entry, while V, Mn, and As displayed lower levels with dominant geogenic contributions. Elemental ratios (Mo/Pb vs Ba/Pb) identified a traffic-derived particle origin as a major contributor to PTE enrichment. Lead isotopes indicated mixing between geogenic and anthropogenic sources, including traffic sources. Approximately 85% of analyzed particles were <5 μm (74.5-95.3%) across samples, with 36.7-53.1% within the 1.0-2.5 μm range. The results of SEM-EDS analysis showed abundant particles containing Pb, Ba, Cu, Sb, Zn, and Cr, with morphologies consistent with brake wear, tire and metallic abrasion, and urban paint. The most bioaccessible elements (Ni, Cu, Zn, Sb, and Pb) included several of the main contaminants identified in the samples. The health risk assessment identified children as the group of concern, with non-carcinogenic risk exceeding safe levels and a carcinogenic risk higher than in adults; the inhalation risk based on the ALF-bioaccessible fraction was lower than that based on total concentrations.

title: Mechanisms of Iodine Enrichment in Groundwater Mediated by Bacterial Sulfate Reduction under Varying Salinity Conditions
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Zhenwei Sun, Mengdi Li, Haiming Li, Sihui Su, Cuixia Zhang, Xiaodong Zhang
abstract: Elevated iodine in groundwater poses dual threats to drinking water safety and ecological security. Microbial-mediated processes, particularly bacterial sulfate reduction (BSR), are recognized as pivotal yet poorly constrained drivers of iodine migration and transformation in aquifers. This study investigates the mechanisms by which BSR regulates iodine accumulation in groundwater under variable hydrochemical conditions, focusing on the iodine-rich saline aquifers of the Tianjin coastal area. A laboratory simulation system was constructed to elucidate the synergistic effects of salinity (as TDS) and initial sulfate concentration on BSR and its consequent impact on aqueous iodine dynamics. The findings reveal that salinity and sulfate exert joint control over BSR activity. While high sulfate concentrations accelerate the process, elevated salinity partially inhibits the metabolic activity of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB). The most rapid BSR rate was observed under high-sulfate, low-salinity conditions. Iodine concentration variation was tightly coupled to SRB growth phases. During the lag and logarithmic growth phases (0-12 days), iodine levels decreased primarily due to stabilization onto organic matter. Subsequently, in the active growth phase (12-36 days), enhanced BSR alkalinized the water and drove iodine enrichment through multiple interconnected mechanisms: the degradation of iodine-adsorbing organic matter, sulfide (S2−)-induced reductive dissolution of iodine-bearing iron minerals, and competitive adsorption from microbially generated bicarbonate (HCO3 −). In high-iodine systems, HCO3 − competition dominated, whereas in low-iodine systems, S2--mediated reductive release was more significant. During the decay phase (36-48 days), iodine concentrations stabilized as BSR weakened. The overall iodine enrichment efficiency followed the order: high sulfate/low salinity > high sulfate/high salinity > low sulfate/high salinity > low sulfate/low salinity. This demonstrates that the promoting effect of a robust BSR process on iodine release outweighs the inhibitory effect of salinity. In summary, SRB can significantly enhance iodine mobility via organic degradation, mineral reduction, and competitive anion exchange. This research establishes that between sulfate availability and salinity critically regulates BSR-mediated iodine enrichment, providing a mechanistic framework for predicting iodine fate in complex groundwater systems.

title: Selective separation and recovery of rare earth elements using adsorbents for urban mining: Design of functional groups, porous materials, and desorption strategies
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Young Gun Ko
abstract: The accelerating deployment of advanced electronics, electric vehicles, and renewable energy systems has intensified global demand for rare earth elements (REEs), while conventional mining faces escalating environmental and geopolitical constraints. Urban mining has therefore emerged as a strategic secondary resource, yet its highly complex and dilute leachates impose formidable challenges for selective REE recovery. Among available technologies, adsorbent-based processes offer unique advantages in terms of tunable selectivity, operational simplicity, and reusability. Although ion-imprinted and ligand-functionalized adsorbents can preferentially bind specific REEs under controlled conditions, sufficiently high REE-to-REE selectivity remains difficult to achieve in realistic multicomponent leachates containing chemically similar lanthanides and large excesses of competing species. Consequently, practical REE fractionation is unlikely to rely on a single adsorbent alone. This review therefore proposes an integrated strategy that combines adsorbents with complementary selectivity profiles and hierarchical porous structures in sequential adsorption and desorption stages.

title: Stable isotope evidence for hydrogeological differences on plant water-source use and water-use efficiency across karst and non-karst settings
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Jing Ning, Hui Yang, Jianhua Cao, Fen Huang, Shengnan Ning
abstract: Karst and non-karst landscapes differ fundamentally in subsurface structure, soil development, and water storage, yet how lithological contrasts are associated with plant water use and water-use efficiency (WUE) remains insufficiently quantified. Here, we combined stable isotopes of hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon (δD, δ18O and δ13C) with meteorological monitoring, soil-water observations, and leaf nutrient measurements to investigate seasonal water-source partitioning and δ13C-derived WUE across adjacent sandstone non-karst and dolomite-karst settings in a subtropical catchment in Southwest China. IsoSource mixing analysis showed that soil water was the dominant estimated source for the sampled Machilus grijsii Hance and Castanopsis hystrix J.D.Hooker individuals at the non-karst site during both sampling periods. At the karst sites, the two sampled tree-form Loropetalum chinense (R.Br.) Oliver individuals showed high estimated contributions from precipitation during the dry-season campaign and increased groundwater contributions during the rainy-season campaign, whereas the sampled shrub-form individual relied more consistently on soil water. δ13C-derived WUE differed among the sampled site-plant groups, with higher values in the non-karst setting and lower values in the karst shrub group. Across the sampled groups, WUE was positively associated with leaf C and N and negatively associated with leaf P. These results indicate that contrasting hydrogeological settings are associated with distinct plant water-source patterns and carbon-water relations. The combined isotope approach provides a useful framework for linking subsurface water availability with plant water use and nutrient status in heterogeneous karst landscapes.

title: Differential development mechanisms of marine–continental transitional coal-bearing source rocks in the Xihu Sag: Evidence from multi-factor controls
description: Publication date: Available online 2 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Ruilin Xu, Hua Wang, Jiancheng Tang, Fei Ding, Lianfu Mei, Yongchao Lu, Jiaren Ye, Qiang Cao, Guanyu Ouyang, Zhiyao Zhang
abstract: Understanding how localized tectono-sedimentary factors regulate organic matter (OM) enrichment despite a broadly uniform regional background remains insufficiently constrained in marine–continental transitional settings. The Xihu Sag provides an ideal case for addressing this issue because its adjacent slope belts illustrate how localized depositional dynamics drive the differential development of coal-bearing source rocks. Integrating organic and inorganic geochemistry with palynology, we investigated the Eocene Baoshi (E2bs) and Pinghu (E2p) formations across three slope belts. Regionally, a cooling–drying paleoclimate drove marine regression from the E2bs to the E2p, with tidal-flat and delta expansion improving source-rock quality and promoting coal seam development. However, spatial heterogeneity was mainly controlled by local tectono-sedimentary factors superimposed on this regional trend. In the northern Hangzhou Slope Belt, a topographically restricted bay affected by intense clastic dilution suppressed OM enrichment, yielding low total organic carbon (TOC; avg. 0.67%). Conversely, the central Pinghu Slope Belt developed stacked thin coal seams and high-quality source rocks (avg. TOC 4.06%) in a tidal-flat setting characterized by dysoxic to oxic water-column conditions and localized waterlogged, oxygen-limited preservation within peat-forming wetlands. In the southern Tiantai Slope Belt, positioned near the entrance of marine incursion, a well-circulated, oxic littoral to shallow-marine setting increased oxygen exposure and reduced OM preservation efficiency, yielding moderate source-rock quality (avg. TOC 1.86%). This study highlights how local tectonic paleogeomorphology organizes accommodation, sediment routing, and OM burial processes, providing a valuable tectono-facies conceptual framework for understanding source-rock heterogeneity in analogous marine–continental transitional settings.

title: Inter-simulator reactive-transport modelling of CO 2 trapping mechanisms in the UK Bunter Sandstone Formation
description: Publication date: Available online 2 November 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Shahryar Rashidi, Seyed Shariatipour
abstract: Reliable predictions of subsurface CO2 behavior is critical for the safe deployment of geological CO2 storage. The Bunter Sandstone Formation is a prospective storage reservoir in the UK. However, uncertainties remain regarding geochemical reactions between its rock-forming minerals and CO2-saturated brine and the consistency of long-term storage predictions across reactive-transport simulators. This study investigates mineral trapping and associated geochemical evolution over 3,000 years of CO2 storage in the Bunter Sandstone Formation. Two reactive-transport simulators, CMG and TOUGHREACT, are used to evaluate inter-simulator variability in storage predictions under harmonized modelling conditions. Despite efforts to ensure methodological consistency, the simulators produce systematic but interpretable differences due to their distinct treatments of relative permeability hysteresis and CO2 dissolution. TOUGHREACT predicts a broader CO2 plume beneath the caprock, whereas CMG predicts greater pressure build-up near the injection zone. TOUGHREACT reports over 80% structural trapping at well shut-in, compared with approximately 50% in CMG. Despite these differences, both simulators predict that mineral trapping reaches approximately 4% by the end of the simulation period. They also indicate mineral reactions confined to the near-well region, suggesting limited formation-scale geochemical alteration. Calcite acts as the primary buffering mineral during injection. However, the continued dissolution of abundant k-feldspar dominates post-injection buffering, highlighting the need to examine its spatial distribution given the potential impacts on long-term rock integrity. Overall, the results demonstrate the importance of assessing long-term geochemical evolution and interpreting storage predictions within a practical uncertainty envelope defined by inter-simulator outcomes, thereby improving confidence in geological CO2 storage assessments.
