description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Shan-Shan Yang, Jian Wang, Derek A. Wyman, Wei Dan, Qiang Wang, Gong-Jian Tang
abstract: A-type granites are commonly considered to crystallize from high-temperature (>900 °C) melts. Yet almost no classical A-type granites have been identified in the Himalayan-Tibetan orogen. Here we investigate a rare Miocene A-type granitoid association from the East Pamir to West Kunlun, northwestern Tibetan Plateau, comprising syenite, syenitic granite, monzogranite and granite porphyry. They show typical A-type geochemical affinities, e.g., high alkali contents (K2O + Na2O > 7.2 wt%) and elevated 10,000 × Ga/Al ratios (mostly 2.1–6.6). Syenites and syenitic granites contain Fe-rich aegirine-augite, whereas biotite in granite porphyries is F-rich (up to 6.2 wt%). However, they differ from classical A-type granites: some are magnesian; most have high Sr (> 250 ppm) and Ba (> 500 ppm), significant REE fractionation [(La/Yb)N = 7–228], low HREE abundances, insignificant Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu* = 0.51–1.36), and relatively low emplacement temperatures (mostly <850 °C). We therefore propose that they represent a distinctive group of non-classical A-type granites. The syenite–syenitic granite and monzogranite–granite porphyry suites formed by fractional crystallization of mantle-derived magmas and melting of thickened lower-crustal sources, respectively. The rarity of classical A-type granites and the occurrence of these distinctive analogues in the Himalayan–Tibetan collisional orogen reflect the combined and interacting effects of a cold mantle, thick crust, and fertile crustal sources. Similar distinctive A-type granitoids may have been overlooked in other collisional orogens in Earth's history, where recognition relies mainly on classical high-temperature and ferroan A-type characteristics. Their identification provides a comprehensive model for understanding A-type magmatism and geodynamic evolution in collisional orogens.

title: The Moon's mantle, as recorded by olivine in Apollo 17 dunite 72415
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): E.S. Jennings, H. Downes, K.K. Bhanot, D. Cooper
abstract: Several samples of lunar material have been claimed to represent deep olivine-rich cumulates derived from crystallisation of the lunar magma ocean (LMO). These samples should contain an important direct record of lunar mantle composition and key insights into the Moon's formation history. We present new measurements of olivine and metal grains from the Apollo 17 dunite sample 72415, including zoning profiles, maps and high-precision minor element data. The data highlight a high degree of inter- and intra-grain compositional homogeneity, suggesting a prolonged cooling history following crystallisation. We identified a polycrystalline clast that is internally unbrecciated and shows a high degree of textural equilibrium; olivines in this clast have a higher Ti content than other olivines, which may relate to mantle redox heterogeneity. Generally, all olivines in 72415 have low CaO contents and compositions that, apart from NiO, are similar to olivines found in terrestrial mantle xenoliths. These characteristics, alongside their symplectites that record a garnet+olivine stoichiometry, make a strong case for 72415 being mantle-derived, specifically from the earlier and deeper layers of the LMO. However, accepting this interpretation raises some interesting questions. Firstly, 72415's olivine composition is not easily reconciled with high-Ni olivines in a Chang'e-6 soil sample that have previously been interpreted as being mantle-derived, suggesting a different origin for the two groups. Secondly, we show that the very low NiO (0.012 wt%) paired with the low Ni/Co of approximately 1.6 of olivines from dunite 72415 cannot be explained by core formation and equilibrium crystallisation alone. Even if all of the Ni in the rare small metal grains in 72415 was diffusively transferred from the olivines, the olivine prior to equilibration with metal had only a slightly higher Ni/Co of 2.5, which still cannot be explained by core formation. Assuming an Earth-mantle-like bulk Moon, we demonstrate that additional differentiation processes beyond just core formation are required to further deplete Ni in the LMO, such as the fractional crystallisation of olivine. Even then, it is difficult to deplete Ni to the extent required by the olivine compositions, suggesting perhaps that a further process occurred such as the segregation of iron sulfide in the LMO. Alternatively, the bulk Moon is depleted in Ni relative to bulk silicate Earth, but not other refractory elements, which is difficult to reconcile with our current understanding of the Earth-Moon system.

title: First-principles study of hydrated and hydrolyzed Nd(III) adsorption on kaolinite (001) and 00 1 ¯ surfaces
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Yingzi Xia, Shanqi Liu, Huiquan Tian, Yongbing Li, Shuping Yin, Jianming Liu
abstract: Ion-adsorption deposits (IADs) are important sources of heavy and selected light rare earth elements (REEs), yet the adsorption mechanisms of hydrated and hydrolyzed Nd(III) on clay-mineral surfaces remain incompletely resolved. Structural refinement of adsorbed Nd by extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) is challenging because the Nd L3-edge region is susceptible to interference from nearby Ce and Pr absorption edges. In this study, first-principles calculations were performed to investigate the adsorption of [Nd(H2O)9]3+ and [Nd(OH)(H2O)8]2+ on the (001) and ( 00 1 ¯ ) basal surfaces of kaolinite. Optimized isolated complexes show that nine-coordination represents the saturated first hydration shell of Nd3+. Upon adsorption, [Nd(H2O)9]3+ remains outer-sphere on both basal surfaces. Partial dehydration occurs on the (001) surface, whereas the dehydration behavior on the 00 1 ¯ surface depends on the adsorption geometry. For [Nd(OH)(H2O)8]2+, adsorption remains outer-sphere on the (001) surface without dehydration. On the 00 1 ¯ surface, the adsorption mode of [Nd(OH)(H2O)8]2+ is influenced by the Nd–OOH bond orientation, with a toward-surface orientation leading to partial dehydration and inner-sphere complexation. Electronic-structure analyses reveal localized interfacial charge redistribution on the (001) surface, pronounced Si-O framework polarization on the 00 1 ¯ surface, and more pronounced overlap between Nd-d and surface O-p states in the inner-sphere complex. DFT + U tests for [Nd(H2O)9]3+ indicate no substantial changes in adsorption geometries or net interfacial charge redistribution. These results indicate that Nd hydrolysis, Nd–OOH bond orientation, and basal-surface chemistry jointly influence the adsorption mode of Nd on kaolinite, providing molecular-level constraints on pH-dependent light REE retention in IADs.

title: Turbidite-associated pyritization in deep-sea sediments: Geochemical insights from the Bengal Fan
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Xiangyu Chen, Jingrui Li, Yu Gu, Xin Chang, Xuefa Shi, Shengfa Liu, Xiting Liu
abstract: Marine microbial sulfate reduction (MSR) is the principal process driving authigenic pyrite formation in marine sediments, yet the influence of episodic turbidite deposition on pyritization and early diagenetic sulfur cycling remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated a turbidite-bearing core (BOB-91) and a hemipelagic reference core (BOB-4) from the western Bengal Fan by integrating sedimentological observations, bulk-sediment geochemistry, reactive iron speciation, pyrite sulfur isotopes, and in situ pyrite trace-element analyses. Two turbidite intervals in BOB-91 are distinguished from adjacent hemipelagic sediments by abrupt grain-size coarsening followed by fining-upward trends, prominent XRD peaks of quartz and albite, and higher Fe/Al, Ti/Al, and K/Al ratios. Compared with adjacent hemipelagic sediments, the turbidites contain more nitric-acid-extractable iron (FeHNO3), lower contents of dithionite- and oxalate-extractable iron (FeD and FeO), a modestly higher mean degree of pyritization (DOP = 0.034 versus 0.023), and lower δ34Spy values. These changes are consistent with more efficient conversion of reactive iron into pyrite and larger apparent sulfur-isotope offsets between seawater sulfate and sedimentary pyrite within the turbidites. Turbidite-hosted pyrite is generally enriched in Mg and Mo and depleted in Cr relative to pyrite in adjacent hemipelagic sediments. This trace-element pattern records distinct pyrite-forming conditions within the turbidite intervals, but does not independently resolve the relative contributions of organoclastic sulfate reduction (OSR) and sulfate-driven anaerobic oxidation of methane (SD-AOM). In addition, FeHR/FeT and MoEF/UEF relationships do not indicate a persistent shift toward strongly reducing bottom-water conditions. Taken together, these observations suggest that turbidite deposition reorganized local early diagenetic reaction–transport conditions, rather than causing a sustained change in bottom-water redox state, and was associated with more efficient pyritization. These findings highlight the importance of depositional processes and sedimentary facies in regulating pyrite formation and interpreting sulfur cycling in deep-sea sediments.

title: Determination of ferrous iron in biotite by EPMA using the flank method: development of a mineral-specific calibration
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Shahed Shahrestani, Ioan V. Sanislav, Yang Liu, Kevin Blake, Avish Kumar, Shane Askew
abstract: The oxidation state of iron in biotite provides key information on redox conditions, magma evolution, and fluid–rock interactions in igneous, metamorphic, and hydrothermal systems, yet routine determination of Fe2+ and Fe3+ by electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) remains difficult. This study presents a biotite-specific calibration of the flank method for estimating Fe2+ from Fe Lβ/Lα intensity ratios. Rather than defining flank positions from garnet end-members, as in the conventional approach, flank positions were established directly from biotite spectra, exploiting the comparatively narrow Fe3+/ΣFe range of biotite to achieve more consistent spectral behaviour. Twelve biotite samples spanning a wide range of total iron content (8.29–22.61 wt% ΣFeO) were analysed by EPMA and independently characterised by wet chemistry to calibrate and test the method. A simple linear regression of Fe2+ against Lβ/Lα produced a strong correlation with wet-chemistry values (R2 = 0.95, average error 0.47 wt%), and incorporating total iron (ΣFe) into a multiple regression model improved the prediction of Fe2+/ΣFe, accounting for matrix-dependent effects associated with total Fe concentration. Leave-one-out cross-validation was applied to evaluate the performance of both models, and independent validation against a well-characterised reference biotite (LP-6) yielded Fe2+ estimates within 0.4–0.6 wt% of the reported composition. These results demonstrate that mineral-specific calibration of the flank method, combined with controlled instrumental conditions, offers a practical, and in-situ alternative to Mössbauer spectroscopy or synchrotron XANES for constraining Fe2+/Fe3+ in biotite, with potential application to other Fe-bearing silicates and to broader petrogenetic, ore-deposit, and metamorphic studies in which iron oxidation state provides information on mineral-forming conditions.

title: The Sutrakar trachydacite: volcanology, 40 Ar/ 39 Ar systematics and petrogenesis of a crystal-rich silicic flood lava in the western Deccan Traps, India
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Arunodaya Shekhar, B. Astha, Hetu Sheth, Hijas Hameed, Anmol Naik, Waliur Rahaman, Ghulam Rabbani, Hugo K.H. Olierook, Fred Jourdan, Christopher L. Kirkland
abstract: The 16-km-long Sutrakar flow, in the western Deccan Traps, is a fissure-fed, crystal-rich, silicic flood lava with an original volume > 4.8 km3. It contains abundant phenocrysts and glomerocrysts of plagioclase (andesine), and minor augite and Fe–Ti oxides, in a glass-rich groundmass with oligoclase, anorthoclase and sanidine microlites. Its composition is mainly trachydacite, less commonly rhyolite or trachyte, due to slightly variable phenocryst contents; an altered vitrophyric variety is a dacite. Most samples are metaluminous. Phenocryst cores yield crystallisation temperatures of 1123–1089 °C (± 35 °C, 1σ, clinopyroxene) and 1071–1021 °C (± 12 °C, 1σ, plagioclase) at 1 kbar pressure. Fe-Ti oxides in the vitrophyre and a trachydacite yield T-fO2 conditions on or above the nickel‑nickel oxide buffer, indicating interaction with oxidising fluids. Plagioclase 40Ar/39Ar step-heating spectra for two trachydacites show low-temperature 40Ar* loss and high-temperature excess 40Ar and do not yield a geologically meaningful age; existing geochronological data for the underlying Jawhar Formation basalts indicate the Sutrakar flow to be younger than ∼66.0 Ma. The flow shows enrichments in the light rare earth elements (LaN/LuN = 9.41–14.9), negative Nb-Ta, Sr, Eu, P, Ti anomalies and Pb peaks in multielement patterns, and high (87Sr/86Sr)t ratios (0.71854–0.72814) and very low εNdt values (−21.7 to −23.2). The geochemical data, combined with Magma Chamber Simulator (MCS) and Energy-Constrained Assimilation and Fractional Crystallisation (EC-AFC) modelling, show that the Sutrakar silicic magma originated by advanced fractional crystallisation of Jawhar Formation basalts with ∼20–30% assimilation of ancient granitic basement crust.

title: Redistribution of iron isotopes during serpentinization: Insights from peridotites of Troodos Ophiolite, Cyprus
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Kun Xu, Yanhong Chen, Yaoling Niu, Meng Duan, Xiaohong Wang, Hongmei Gong, Yong Wu
abstract: Serpentinization redistributes iron (Fe) among secondary minerals and drives significant Fe isotope fractionation, yet the role of Fe3+-bearing serpentine in this process remains poorly constrained. We investigated serpentinized harzburgites and dunite from the Troodos Ophiolite, Cyprus, integrating petrography, mineral chemistry, Raman spectroscopy, Fe isotope analyses, and thermodynamic reaction-path modeling. Bulk-rock samples exhibit limited Fe isotope variation (δ56Fe = −0.06 ± 0.03‰ to 0.00 ± 0.03‰, 2SD), indicating that serpentinization has negligible effect on the bulk Fe isotope composition of peridotites. In contrast, serpentine separates display divergent Fe isotope trends relative to coexisting olivine between two protolith types. Serpentine from harzburgites yields δ56Fe values similar to or heavier than coexisting olivine (Δ56FeSrp-Ol = −0.01‰ to +0.10‰, differences exceeding the analytical uncertainty of 0.03‰ for all but one sample), whereas serpentine separated from dunite is slightly lighter than olivine (Δ56FeS rp-Ol = −0.04‰). This contrasting fractionation pattern indicates that Fe isotope redistribution during serpentinization is primarily governed by the assemblage of secondary Fe-bearing minerals and the initial protolith composition. Petrographic observations, mineral compositional data, and thermodynamic modeling collectively constrain the moderate to intense serpentinization of harzburgite to low-temperature (< 200 °C), high water/rock ratio conditions that favor crystallization of Fe3+-bearing lizardite but limited magnetite production. Under this condition, lizardite with preferential incorporation of heavy Fe isotopes results in higher δ56Fe values in serpentines than in olivine. In contrast, secondary sulfides may act as a potential reservoir for light Fe isotopes, consistent with the extremely low δ56Fe value of −1.08 ± 0.02‰ (2SD, measured in one sample). By comparison, magnetite-dominated serpentinization partitions heavy Fe into magnetite, leaving serpentine with comparatively light Fe isotopes. Our findings demonstrate that Fe isotope redistribution during serpentinization depends not only on magnetite formation, as previously recognized, but also on the occurrence of Fe3+-bearing serpentine under low-temperature, high-fluid-flux regimes. Given that serpentine is the primary mineral dominating the Fe budget in these rocks, while sulfides have a negligible effect, Fe3+-bearing serpentine thus constitutes a critical yet underappreciated endmember for global Fe cycling linked to seafloor alteration. Because of unavoidable impurities in mineral separates and the lack of comprehensive data on coexisting sulfide and magnetite, further in-situ Fe isotope and valence state analyses are warranted to provide microscale constraints.

title: Triple oxygen isotope insights into the HIMU source
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): J. Cameron Adams, James W. Dottin, Daniel E. Ibarra, Matthew G. Jackson, Jon Woodhead
abstract: Geochemical analyses of oceanic hotspot lavas exhibit chemical heterogeneity that is interpreted as the expression of a chemically heterogenous mantle that was established through partial melting and crustal recycling. The diversity of mantle sources is often observed among the concentrations and isotopic compositions of trace lithophile and siderophile elements. However, oxygen (O), among the most abundant elements on Earth, exhibits minimal isotopic variability across the full spectrum of geochemical heterogeneity expressed by oceanic hotspot lavas. The homogeneity of O isotopes among ocean island lavas is difficult to reconcile with the proposed proportions of recycled crustal materials and suggests that either not yet constrained magmatic processes or sampling biases are at play. Recent advances in mass spectrometry now allow for the high precision measurement of 17O/16O which, when combined with the traditional measurement of 18O/16O, may provide additional insight into the magmatic processing of O throughout Earth's tectonic history, beyond confirming depleted versus enriched recycled crustal components in plume lavas. This study reports δ18O and Δ′17O (Δ′17O = δ′17O − λ × δ′18O, where λ = 0.528) in olivine and clinopyroxene separated from nine Mangaia basalt samples. Mangaia is an oceanic island (Macdonald hotspot) and a type locality for the high-μ (μ = 238U/204Pb, HIMU) mantle component which offers the opportunity to evaluate the potential advantages of 17O/16O measurements in geochemically extreme plume lavas. The data reveal considerable isotopic variability. The δ18O values range from +2.38‰ to +6.31‰ (± 0.352, 2σ) and Δ′17O values range from −0.041‰ to −0.085‰ (± 0.008, 2σ). Some Δ′17O values are distinct from estimates of the bulk convecting upper mantle (−0.052‰). The δ18O values of likely co-genetic olivine and clinopyroxene pairs indicate that the olivine and clinopyroxene are not in isotopic equilibrium. There is also inverse co-variation in δ18O and Δ′17O observed. Together the data are reconciled as an interplay between two isotopically unusual O mantle reservoirs: one that fingerprints a composition established through early mixing of a recycled crust component (e.g., altered oceanic crust) in the deep mantle and another (e.g., a sub-continental lithospheric mantle component) subsequently introduced at shallower depths, possibly during crystallization. Ultimately, this work shows that mantle plume lavas are not homogenous with respect to oxygen isotopes when measured on individual mineral phases and that the additional measurement of 17O/16O is valuable for constraining the source of recycled materials within a single plume system and identifying processes involved in the plumes' chemical evolution.

title: Experimental investigation of the reaction between sediment-derived supercritical fluid and mantle peridotite
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Zhaohui Yu, Wan-Cai Li, Quanyou Liu, Huaiwei Ni
abstract: Slab-derived supercritical fluids serve as important agents for material transport in deep subduction zones. However, the mechanisms and products of the reaction between supercritical fluid and mantle peridotite remain poorly constrained. In this study, we experimentally investigated the reaction between a peridotite (PERD, specifically spinel lherzolite) and a supercritical fluid (SCF) containing 50 wt% solute (devolatilised global subducting sediment) under hot wedge condition. Using a double-capsule technique, an SCF was first synthesised in an inner Ag capsule at 3.0 GPa and 1000 °C; the temperature was then raised to 1200 °C to melt the Ag capsule and to allow SCF–PERD reaction. The quenched liquids and residual mineral assemblages were characterised by EPMA and LA-ICP-MS. With an increasing SCF:PERD mass ratio from 1:15 to 2:1, the liquid evolved from a hydrous basaltic melt to a hydrous boninitic (high-Mg andesitic) composition, and the residual mineral assemblage changed from Opx + Cpx + Ol + Grt + Amp to Ol + Opx, and ultimately to Ol. Comparison with the starting materials reveals that the hot SCF leached a range of components including MgO, FeO, and CaO from the peridotite, in contrast to melt–peridotite reactions, which instead introduce felsic components and produce pyroxenite. In addition, the basaltic melts formed through the interaction of SCF and peridotite contained lower levels of Na2O, K2O and Al2O3. More unique to SCF–peridotite reaction is that high-Mg andesitic magmas, such as those from the Mariana Arc or the Kamchatka Arc, could be generated by a substantial flux of SCF into the mantle wedge.

title: Sulfur isotope evidence for shale recycling in pyroxenites from the Beni Bousera orogenic massif (Morocco); insights on the HIMU mantle endmember
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Jabrane Labidi, Jean-Pierre Lorand, Pierre Cartigny, Fatima El Atrassi
abstract: The recycling of surface materials into the mantle shapes the chemical diversity of oceanic basalts. The Beni Bousera orogenic massif (Morocco) provides a unique window into these processes, exposing a great diversity of mantle pyroxenites, including samples formed from the recycling of lower oceanic crust. This massif hosts especially rare graphite-bearing pyroxenites, with evidence that graphite was once diamond. Here we present sulfur isotope compositions (δ34S, Δ33S, Δ36S) of graphite-free and graphite-bearing pyroxenites from Beni Bousera. Graphite-free pyroxenites preserve near-zero sulfur isotope signatures with low sulfur contents (∼300 ppm), similar to MORB. In contrast, graphite-bearing pyroxenites exhibit fractionated isotopic signatures, with δ34S ∼ −3.5‰, Δ33S ∼ +0.065‰ and Δ36S ∼ −0.45‰. Those are associated with extreme sulfur enrichment, up to 5600 ppm. Mass balance calculations indicate that these signatures reflect the addition of ∼5% black shale to an igneous oceanic crust protolith. The Δ36S/Δ33S systematics and the magnitude of Δ33S anomalies suggest the recycled shale is of post-Archean age. The sulfur isotope signatures documented in Beni Bousera are similar to those observed in basalts from the Mangaia HIMU plume. We propose that partial melting of shale-hybridized pyroxenites, analogous to those at Beni Bousera, generates metasomatic melts that transfer carbon and sulfur with fractionated isotope signatures to plume sources. The radiogenic lead isotope composition of Mangaia, however, remains consistent with the classical model of slab devolatilization and U/Pb fractionation during subduction. Our mechanism reconciles the classical HIMU model with the growing evidence for carbon and sulfur enrichment in the Mangaia HIMU mantle source.

title: Controls on Rb enrichment during granitic magma–hydrothermal evolution: Constraints from fluid–melt partitioning at 850 °C and 200 MPa
description: Publication date: 20 December 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 726 Author(s): Jianping Li, Jinsheng Han, Xia Hu, Xingcheng Liu, Huayong Chen
abstract: Rubidium (Rb) enrichment in granites and granitic pegmatites commonly reaches several thousand to tens of thousands of μg/g, far exceeding average crustal abundances, yet the relative roles of magmatic differentiation and fluid exsolution in generating such enrichment remain poorly constrained. Here, we experimentally determined Rb and Cl partitioning between hydrous granitic melts and supercritical Cl-bearing aqueous fluids over a range of melt and fluid compositions at 850 °C and 200 MPa, and integrated the partitioning results with Rayleigh-type modelling to track the coupled evolution of fluid chlorinity and Rb extraction efficiency during progressive magma crystallization. Rb fluid–melt partitioning is controlled primarily by fluid chlorinity rather than by melt composition, with fluid–melt partition coefficients for Rb increasing systematically from 0.3 to 1.2 as fluid chlorinity rises from ∼1 to 4 mol/kg H₂O, consistent with increasingly important RbCl complexing in saline fluids. However, comparison with previous in situ measurements indicates that the absolute magnitude of D Rb f / m at the highest chlorinity varies among experimental systems and should be interpreted cautiously. Combining Cl partitioning data, the modelling results indicate that the chlorinity of exsolved fluids rapidly decreases and stabilizes near ∼1 mol/kg H₂O (∼ 5 wt% NaCleq.) during crystallization, largely independent of initial melt H₂O content, melt composition, or initial fluid chlorinity. Under these conditions, fluid–melt partition coefficients for Rb converge rapidly to ∼0.3, causing magmatic fluids to extract only a minor fraction (<10% at 99% crystallization) of the total magmatic Rb budget even in initially saline systems. In contrast, residual melts continuously concentrate Rb to ore-forming levels during advanced crystallization. These results demonstrate that extreme Rb enrichment in granite systems is controlled primarily by prolonged magmatic differentiation, whereas magmatic fluid exsolution is generally inefficient for Rb concentration.

title: Corrigendum to “Investigating pressure effects of Ti and Zr partitioning into zircon, quartz, and rutile at crustal temperatures” [Chem. Geol. 673 (2025) 122518]

title: A multi-isotopic study to constrain groundwater geochemistry - case study of a quaternary sand and gravel aquifer in Cardiff, UK
description: Publication date: Available online 4 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Zhe Dong, Katharine Hendry, David Boon, Ashley Patton, Jamie Lewis, Hong Chin Ng, Fiona Whitaker, Tong Wang, Xiaoning Liu, Tom Kibblewhite
abstract: Chemical alteration of groundwaters has implications for elemental fluxes into rivers, estuaries and coastal oceans. Individual isotope systems offer strong process constraints, while integrating multiple isotopes adds complementary insight that reveals the complexity of coupled geochemical processes. Here, we use multiple stable isotopic systems to investigate the physical and chemical controls on groundwater composition in a Quaternary sand and gravel coastal aquifer from Cardiff, UK. Stable isotopic compositions of silicon (Si), magnesium (Mg), and strontium (Sr), along with radiogenic Sr isotopes reveal significant impacts of anthropogenic interventions on the groundwater system, particularly the construction of a barrage and groundwater extraction. The saltier coastal groundwaters likely reflect contributions from saline estuarine/seawater-derived water and/or localized seepage from the underlying Triassic bedrock. This influx of saline water, combined with reducing conditions, has facilitated calcite precipitation that has removed substantial amounts of dissolved calcium (Ca) from the groundwater. The mechanisms controlling dissolved silicon (DSi) dynamics in the groundwater are complex. In coastal regions, silica precipitation predominantly influences DSi concentrations and isotopic composition, whereas vegetation uptake is the primary control on DSi concentrations and isotopic signatures in inland groundwaters. These findings are crucial for understanding the intricate interplay between natural processes and human interventions in shaping groundwater geochemistry, offering valuable insights for managing coastal water resources and mitigating anthropogenic impacts. By providing a multi-isotopic framework for investigating groundwater systems, this study provides a clearer perspective on the factors controlling modern and palaeo groundwater chemistry and can aid in predicting solute fluxes from groundwater to the ocean.

title: Experimental diagenetic transformation of biogenic aragonite to calcite in sulfate and/or phosphate-bearing fluids
description: Publication date: Available online 2 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Amalia Jiménez, Joel Marcelo Coronel, José Manuel Astilleros
abstract: The transformation of biogenic aragonite to calcite in phosphate or phosphate-sulfate bearing fluids was investigated through hydrothermal experiments at 60–80 °C up to 90 days. A phosphate-only system (BF) and a phosphate-sulfate system (BFS) were characterized by XRD, FTIR, and aqueous geochemical analyses supported by PHREEQC modelling. In both series, the reaction proceeded via an interface-coupled dissolution–precipitation mechanism, producing a two-stage sequence: hydroxylapatite (HAp) precipitation followed by calcite, consistent with the higher supersaturation of the fluid with respect to HAp. Variations in unit cell parameters are consistent with incorporation of HPO₄2− into HAp and oxyanions into secondary calcite. The contraction of the HAp c-axis and the decrease in dissolved sulfate (11.3% at 90 days), which may involve surface adsorption, are consistent with SO₄2− incorporation into the HAp lattice. Although dissolved P removal was similar in both series, calcite formed earlier and more extensively in BFS system (>83 vs. <30 wt% at 90 days), a difference not explained by the bulk saturation with respect to calcite. We hypothesize an indirect effect of sulfate, through the HAp intermediate and the Ca budget of the system, rather than a direct effect on calcite nucleation. Dissolved phosphate modifies the aragonite-to-calcite reaction pathway by introducing HAp as a reactive intermediate whose non-stoichiometric crystal chemistry may couple mineral replacement kinetics to fluid composition. Carbonate phosphatization may alter primary geochemical signatures in diagenetically altered carbonates from phosphate-rich environments and carbonate-to-apatite replacement is a potential pathway for P sequestration during carbonate diagenesis.

title: A two-population lattice strain model for H + -coupled REE incorporation in zircon: calibration, detection threshold, and implications for LREE anomalies
description: Publication date: Available online 2 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Ioan V. Sanislav, Mabrouk Sami
abstract: The classical single-site lattice strain model fails systematically for light and middle rare earth elements (LREE and MREE) in zircons from hydrous, phosphorus-undersaturated magmatic systems, predicting concentrations one to three orders of magnitude below observed values. We develop a two-population model in which the bulk partition coefficient is the mole-fraction-weighted sum of contributions from the ideal ZrO8 site and a second, enlarged site generated by REE3+–H+ coupled substitution. Both sites are parameterised by independent Brice parabolas; the fractional occupancy of the defect site, fd, follows a Langmuir saturation function of water content with half-saturation constant H0 = 422 ppm. Initial calibration of defect-site parameters against the 32 published SIMS spot analyses of Vema Fracture Zone oceanic gabbro zircons reported by De Hoog et al. (2014) gives an unconstrained Nd/Lu optimum of r 0 REE − H = 0.9916 Å, EREE–H = 592.1 GPa, D 0 REE − H = 344.5 (RMSE = 0.154 log10 units), whereas physically constrained weighted global optimisation, within-grain REE-pattern inversion, and DFT-consistent modest site expansion together indicate a preferred effective defect radius near 0.984 Å with an admissible envelope of ~0.975–0.993 Å. Forward modelling defines a detection threshold in temperature–[H2O] space below which the defect-site signal is unresolvable from geological noise, requiring [H2O]zrc > ~30–80 ppm depending on temperature. The model predicts that in hydrous, P-undersaturated systems the REE3+–H+ mechanism alone can produce Lazrc exceeding 0.1 ppm through genuine lattice incorporation, demonstrating that a fixed La threshold is not a universal inclusion-free criterion but depends on temperature, water content, and melt La concentration. The charge-balance ratio f d CB = (REY–P)/REY, recoverable from routine LA-ICP-MS data without water measurement, provides an independent estimate of defect-site occupancy and correlates with water-based estimates where the REE3+–H+ mechanism is active, thereby providing a quantitative test of mechanism activation across natural systems. The model is applicable specifically to P-undersaturated, hydrous, low-temperature magmatic systems where the REE3+–H+ mechanism has been independently confirmed by FTIR spectroscopy and charge-balance analysis.

title: Nd-Hf isotopes of clinopyroxene-orthopyroxene couples to decipher geochemical heterogeneity in depleted peridotites (Alpine-Apennine ophiolites)
description: Publication date: Available online 2 November 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): C. Ferrando, V. Basch, G. Borghini, F. Genske, A. Stracke, E. Rampone
abstract: The geochemical heterogeneity of the mantle beneath mid-ocean ridges is documented by the variable radiogenic isotope ratios of abyssal peridotites and basalts. Incompatible element-depleted peridotites also occur in ophiolites of variable ages world-wide. The time when peridotites in ophiolite massifs last melted constrains the evolution of the paleo-ocean basin they originate from. Yet, estimating the ages of peridotites in ophiolite massifs becomes significantly more complicated if the strong geochemical heterogeneity documented in present-day abyssal peridotites also characterizes the ancient mantle of ophiolite massifs. Here, we apply a challenging approach, analysing the NdHf isotopic composition of coupled clinopyroxene and orthopyroxene within single samples to calculate dates for the last melting and melt-rock interaction events in peridotites from the Internal Liguride and Monte Maggiore ophiolites of the Alpine Tethys Ocean. This approach avoids the use of a theoretical average ‘Depleted Mantle’. The time of magmatic processes inferred from the new pyroxenes NdHf isotope data ranges from Late Triassic to Middle Jurassic, contemporaneous to the opening and maturing of the Alpine Tethys Oceanic basin. The NdHf isotope ratios of pyroxene couples in peridotites and pyroxenites indicate that MORB-like (on average εNdi 7.5 ± 2.5 and εHfi from 13 ± 4) to slightly more melt-depleted peridotites (on average εNdi 14 ± 3 and εHfi from 19.5 ± 3.5) coexisted in the subridge mantle of the Alpine Tethys Ocean. Finding remnants of peridotites which were variably melt-depleted prior to the embryonic opening of the Alpine Tethys Ocean (Internal Liguride) agrees well with the ubiquitous isotopic heterogeneity of peridotites from modern mid-ocean ridges, which indicates they have melted once, or several times, before recent processing under modern mid-ocean ridges.

title: Rodingites as archives of Ca-Mg-Fe metasomatism and trace element mobility: constraints from Mount Orliakas (Pindos Ophiolite, Greece)
description: Publication date: Available online 31 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): L. Tsiarsioti, C. Karkalis, A. Sideridis, H. Tsikos, P. Mason, P. Petrounias, P. Pomonis, A. Rogkala, P. Koutsovitis
abstract: Rodingites serve as critical archives of fluid-rock interaction in mafic-ultramafic complexes. In the Mount Orliakas massif (Pindos Ophiolite, Greece), rodingitization of gabbronoritic protoliths occurred through distinct multi-stage Ca-metasomatism within serpentinized ultramafics. Notably, the dykes preserve nearly unaltered gabbroic cores, providing a direct reference for quantifying metasomatic fluxes without relying on extrapolated protolith compositions. Stage-1 (~370 °C, 3–5 kbar) formed prehnite and grossular, while Stage-2 (~300 °C, final exhumation) developed (hydro)andradite, Ti-rich garnet, and vesuvianite. Geochemical trends reveal a two-stage fluid evolution: initial Ca-enrichment coupled with Si, Mg, and Fe depletion (Stage-1), followed by distinct Mg and Fe enrichment in advanced Stage-2 rodingites. This reversal marks a shift to Mg-Fe-rich fluids driven by extensive interaction with surrounding serpentinizing ultramafics. Alkali depletion reflects plagioclase replacement by garnet. Trace elements show early REE depletion and late re-enrichment; Th, Ta, Nb, Cr, and Ni were depleted, while Zr was enriched. Highly mobile elements (Ba, Pb, Cs, U, As) were largely removed. Notably, Ti was immobile in shallow Group-A but mobilized at depth in Group-B rodingites, while Nb and Y showed inverse enrichment, reflecting pressure-dependent fluid mobility. Thermodynamic modeling results (PERPLE_X) validate the P-T path, constraining the Stage-1 to Stage-2 transition as a shift towards oxidizing, low-CO₂, Fe-Mg-rich fluids. These findings highlight rodingitization as a key process in element mobility within mafic-ultramafic complexes, controlled by protolith depth, redox conditions, and evolving fluid composition.

title: The geochemistry of uraniferous hyalite from Zacatecas, Mexico: Implications for the origin, timing, and deposition of Electric Opal
description: Publication date: Available online 30 October 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Bozana Pasic, John Mavrogenes, Ian S. Williams, Dominique Tanner, Peter K.M. Megaw
abstract: Green, daylight-luminescent hyalite from Zacatecas is a rare form of opal containing elevated concentrations of uranium. Through combined in situ isotopic and trace element analyses we investigated the process of uranium sequestration by opal to determine hyalite depositional conditions. Trace element analyses revealed a near perfect 1:1 correlation between uranium and calcium, which we attribute to “trapping” of calcium-uranyl carbonate complexes. Oxygen isotopic analyses and modelling estimate depositional temperatures of between ~23 °C and ~ 64 °C, respectively. Uranium‑lead dating of zoned hyalite indicates three principal generations of growth at 14.2 ± 0.69 Ma, 11.7 ± 0.8 Ma and 9.2 ± 0.7 Ma. Electric Opal was probably deposited from silica supersaturated, alkaline, groundwater-dominated fluids under confined lateral flow, making formation of Electric Opal a product of late volcanic or post-volcanic processes.

title: Preference-conditioned feature selection for interpretable multi-objective water-system operating policies
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Guang Yang, Matteo Giuliani, Zengchuan Dong, Pan Liu, Bin Xu, Andrea Castelletti
abstract: The operation of water resources is inherently complex, necessitating the reconciliation of competing objectives, the coordination of interconnected infrastructures, and adherence to various regulations and stakeholder perspectives. Multi-objective optimization methods have emerged as powerful tools for addressing these complexities by enabling decision-makers to balance conflicting goals. The effectiveness of these methods is contingent upon the input variables utilized in water resource operation models. However, decision-makers often find it challenging to understand how different input variables impact optimization performance regarding different objectives, thereby reducing the interpretability of these models and impeding their practical application in real-world contexts. In this regard, the careful selection of input variables can enhance both the efficacy and interpretability of multi-objective water resource operations. This paper assesses the significance of various input variables in water system operation models under differing decision-making preferences and extracts the most relevant information to alleviate conflicts among competing objectives. The approach is demonstrated on the GERD-Merowe-HAD reservoir system within the Nile River Basin, where the primary functions are hydropower generation and irrigation water supply at a strategic monthly planning scale. The framework is designed to support strategic policy design and input-variable screening, rather than to generate real-time gate-release schedules. A systematic feature selection framework that integrates Recursive Feature Elimination with Evolutionary Multi-Objective Direct Policy Search is employed to analyze the importance of various input variables in multi-reservoir operation. By linking input variable importance evaluations with multi-objective reservoir operation performance, we identify compact input formulations for operational policies tailored to specific decision-making preferences. The findings indicate that using selected input variables can mitigate conflicts between hydropower generation and irrigation water supply in the Nile River Basin, particularly when a lower irrigation deficit is desired. Furthermore, customizing reservoir operation policies with input variables chosen based on decision-making preferences can enhance the performance of the relevant objectives. The selected reduced-input policies also improve the trade-off performance relative to conventional input formulations, indicating that compact input sets can reduce policy complexity without sacrificing system performance. This proposed framework holds promise for improving the interpretability of machine-learning-based operational policies for water resource systems and fostering a stronger connection between these complex systems and their human operators. The transferable contribution is the feature-selection workflow itself; the specific selected variables should be re-evaluated for each reservoir system according to local objectives, constraints, available information, and decision scale.

title: Relative roles of spatial resolution and temporal coverage in basin-average SMAP soil moisture assimilation over the Mekong River basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Sebastian R.O. Marshall, Duc Tran, Binh Quang Nguyen, Manh-Hung Le, Bin Fang, Hesham Elhaddad, John Eylander, Sameh A. Kantoush, John D. Bolten, Venkataraman Lakshmi
abstract: Satellite soil moisture offers a basin-wide constraint on the water state of large monsoon basins, where ground networks are sparse and cloud interrupts optical and thermal observation. Downscaled Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) products add spatial detail but inherit that cloud dependence, raising the question of how resolution and temporal coverage each contribute to assimilation. This study examined it over the Mekong River Basin using 9 km, 1 km, and 400 m products from 2015 to 2024. A 200-member ensemble Kalman filter assimilated each product as a basin-average composite, isolating temporal sampling, while a separate coupled experiment updated soil storage in the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) and evaluated discharge at five gauges against a matched control. Assimilation reduced discrepancies with each assimilated input by 58.9–60.6%, the 9 km product retaining the smallest residual under common error settings. Imposing the finer products’ schedules on the 9 km record left shared-day scores within sampling uncertainty but raised full-calendar error by 0.0036 and 0.0048 m3/m3, because the omitted 8.3% and 11.7% of days contributed 35.8% and 44.3% of squared error. Product-specific error calibration reversed the ranking, showing that coverage alone did not determine it. Within SWAT, 1 km assimilation produced the largest discharge gains, resolved at the two downstream gauges, raising Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency at Kratié from 0.621 to 0.706 as monsoon storage bounds converted proposed water additions into a net removal that reduced surface runoff and groundwater flow. Agreement with assimilated observations and hydrological benefit therefore ranked the products differently.

title: Accuracy comparison of classic bedload transport formulas in the Yangtze River
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Zhongwu Jin, Ke Hu, Wenqi Li, Jinyou Lu, Lixia Sun, Qianting Liang, Yihui Xiao
abstract: Most classic bedload transport formulas were calibrated using flume experiments or field data collected from small- and medium-sized rivers, leaving their applicability to large rivers uncertain. This study compared ten widely used formulas using 1,618 field measurements from seven hydrological stations along the Yangtze River mainstem during 1973–2023. A qualitative–quantitative framework combined distributional diagnosis of transport-rate frequency patterns with three log-scale metrics: interval compliance rate, systematic log-bias, and log-scale root mean square error. These metrics were integrated using an entropy-weighted composite accuracy index. Hydro-sedimentary conditions varied markedly: the upper Yangtze had confined channels with narrow, deep cross-sections, higher velocities despite lower discharges, and coarser, more heterogeneous bedload, whereas the Zhicheng–Hankou reach was dominated by uniform sand bedload. The recommended formulas were Schoklitsch for Cuntan, Recking for Fengjie, Meyer-Peter and Müller for Yichang and Zhicheng, Bagnold for Shashi, and Wong and Parker for Jianli and Hankou. These results indicate that different formulas are suited to different ranges of hydro-sedimentary conditions along the Yangtze River. Across fluvial geomorphic settings, recommendations varied most among mountainous rivers because of flow–sediment variability and the limited suitability of classic formulas under heterogeneous conditions, whereas formulas performing well in transitional and alluvial reaches showed more consistent performance and greater transferability. Structural analysis indicated that fixed coefficients and exponents and deterministic incipient-motion thresholds constrain formula adaptability. Formula selection in large rivers should therefore jointly consider hydro-sedimentary characteristics, fluvial geomorphic setting, and intrinsic formula structure.

title: Investigating subirrigation, seasonal variability and hydrogeological control in a salinized shallow aquifer-aquitard system
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Chiara Sbarbati, Mattia Gaiolini, Abram Ofori, Micòl Mastrocicco, Massimo Marchesi, Vincenzo Piscopo, Nicolò Colombani
abstract: This study investigates the seasonal hydrogeochemical evolution and persistent hydrogeological controls in a salinized shallow aquifer-aquitard system located in a reclaimed coastal lowland. The study focuses on two adjacent agricultural field plots with contrasting hydrostratigraphic settings. Major ions, stable isotopes, and redox-sensitive species were integrated to identify the processes controlling groundwater composition and their seasonal evolution. The key findings include: (i) groundwater salinization primarily reflects inherited paleo-marine salinity preserved within low-permeability Holocene sediments; (ii) subirrigation produces a temporary and spatially variable dilution of groundwater, without substantially altering the composition of the saline groundwater end member or causing systematic mobilization of dissolved trace elements, indicating that the effects of subirrigation are largely transient; (iii) the deep saline groundwater component is controlled by processes operating over timescales much longer than the seasonal recharge cycle. Persistent reducing conditions within the peat-rich groundwater domain promote ammonium accumulation, while sulphur isotope compositions suggest differences in sulphur cycling between the two groundwater domains, reflecting differences in groundwater evolution under reducing conditions. Methane isotope data are consistent with microbially produced methane in the deeper peat-rich sequence. The results show that the hydrogeochemistry of the aquifer-aquitard system is governed by the interaction between inherited salinity, peat-rich sediments and redox-driven biogeochemical processes. These processes must be considered, for example, when attempting to mitigate the salinization of this aquifer-aquitard system through subirrigation practices; moreover, the findings here identified can be transferred to similar alluvial deltaic environments around the world.

title: Riparian freshwater lenses adjacent to curved rivers: morphology and controls
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Hongrong Zong, Huiqiang Wu, Wenyu Xu, Kai Lu, Jiaxin Chen, Chunhui Lu
abstract: Freshwater lenses can persist in saline floodplain aquifers adjacent to gaining rivers, yet existing research has largely examined them in cross section and has not systematically addressed the role of river planform geometry. This study provides the first systematic assessment of how river planform geometry modifies riparian freshwater lens morphology under gaining river conditions. Riverbank traces are represented using sine-generated curves with varying deflection angles. Three-dimensional variable-density groundwater flow and solute transport simulations are then conducted to examine freshwater–saltwater distributions in these idealized planforms. The results show that freshwater lenses extend farther inland near convex banks than near concave banks. Riverbank curvature redirects upper freshwater toward convex sectors, whereas deeper mixed and saline groundwater flows toward concave sectors. This redistribution contributes to the greater lens extent near convex banks. When valley wavelength is fixed, increasing sinuosity enlarges the lens, with freshwater storage increasing by a factor of 7.65 as the deflection angle increases from 0° to 105°. However, when channel length is fixed, freshwater storage initially rises and then declines as sinuosity increases. Stronger saline groundwater discharge compresses the lens toward the river, where its morphology is more constrained by local bank curvature. These findings highlight the need to consider river planform geometry when assessing freshwater storage in saline riparian aquifers, as spatial variability in freshwater availability may otherwise be underestimated.

title: Effects of a shallow landslide on headwater storage and drainage functions: a comparison of subsurface saturation before and after a 2016 landslide in northeastern Taiwan
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Wei-Li Liang
abstract: Shallow landslides reshape the surfaces of headwater catchments, yet their hydrological effects are generally interpreted based on observations of shallow soil layers rather than the soil–bedrock interface. To our knowledge, no continuous record at this interface has spanned a complete natural shallow landslide event at the same site. This study compared subsurface saturation before and after a typhoon-induced shallow landslide in a steep forested headwater catchment in northeastern Taiwan. Pore water pressure (ψ) at the soil–bedrock interface was monitored at 60 points at 10-min resolution for > 2-year periods before and after the landslide. Saturation frequency classification, join count statistics, event-based saturation analysis, and recession-rate analysis were conducted. After the landslide, the number of perennially saturated points increased from 18 to 23, and the saturated zone expanded within the landslide area. Saturated points were spatially clustered in both periods, and the clustering extended to a larger spatial scale after the landslide. However, the mean ψ of the most frequently saturated group decreased from 27.0 to 18.5 cmH2O, and in perennially saturated groups the maximum saturation amount per point decreased. Median recession rates increased by 0.68 and 0.93 cmH2O/day in the intermediate- and high-pressure zones, respectively. Site-scale relationships between rainfall and saturation appeared unchanged, because opposing changes inside and outside the landslide boundary offset each other. These changes plausibly reflected subsurface loosening and fissuring, as inferred from changes in soil depths and surface displacement. Thus, the saturated zone expanded but weakened. Both the storage and regulation functions at the soil–bedrock interface declined, whereas lower and shorter-lived pore water pressures suggest hydrologic conditions that were less favorable for renewed failure.

title: Cropland and population exposure to extreme precipitation events in Central Asia under future climate change
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Tao Li, Fengjiao Song, Andrée De Cock, Jiayu Bao, Philippe De Maeyer, Ting Wang, Diwen Dong, Ye Yuan, Xiaoran Huang, Tao Yu, Naibi Sulei, Anming Bao, Peter Goethals
abstract: Central Asia (CA) is experiencing rapid warming and an intensifying hydrological cycle, with important implications for extreme precipitation events (EPEs). However, future changes in cropland and population exposure to EPEs remain insufficiently quantified in this climate-sensitive dryland region. Here, we projected changes in EPE characteristics and associated cropland and population exposure across CA using daily precipitation simulations from five bias-adjusted ISIMIP3b global climate models under SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5. The historical period 1995–2014 was used as the reference, and future changes were assessed for 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, and 2081–2100. The results show increasing extreme precipitation amount, frequency, intensity, and spatial extent toward the end of the century, particularly under SSP5-8.5 and in high-mountain regions. Under SSP5-8.5, cropland exposure increases by 46.4% from 2021 to 2040 to 2081–2100, with cumulative exposure of approximately 190.7 ± 73.7 million km2-days during 2021–2100. Under SSP3-7.0, population exposure increases by 97.2% between the first and last future periods, with cumulative exposure reaching approximately 47.12 ± 18.8 billion person-days during 2021–2100. Exposure hotspots are mainly located in northern Kazakhstan and the tri-border region of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Signed decomposition shows that climatic changes dominate most increases in cropland exposure, particularly under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5, whereas the drivers of population exposure vary strongly among socioeconomic pathways, with demographic changes either reinforcing or offsetting climate-driven exposure changes. These findings highlight increasing exposure of Central Asian populations and croplands to future extreme precipitation and suggest the importance of strengthened flood management, agricultural drainage, early-warning systems, and climate-resilient land-use planning.

title: A hydrological comparability framework for hydropower potential assessment: evidence from China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Ning Xu, Peifang Leng, Qiuying Zhang, Zhipin Ai, Gang Chen, Fadong Li
abstract: Hydropower outputs depend on water availability, hydraulic head, conversion assumptions and the operating rules or constraints applied. Meaningful comparison of reported values requires identifying the specific quantity being assessed and the methodological, spatial, temporal, and operational conditions under which each value was derived. This structured critical review examines 100 China-focused, benchmark, and conceptual studies, linking 362 terminology records and 358 quantitative-output records from 73 papers. Differences in assessment objects, hydrological baselines, spatial aggregation, and operation and feasibility constraints explain why similar terms or units can describe distinct quantities. Source studies illustrate how runoff timing, storage, turbine releases, and ecological requirements enter resource, generation, and risk assessments. The framework connects author terminology, assessment objects, conditioning layers, and metric families to a question-specific comparison procedure. Users align the required quantities and reference conditions, distinguish deliberately varied conditions, and identify the permitted interpretation. Numerical comparison requires compatible quantities and reference bases. Design differences may constrain interpretation, whereas incompatible quantities or missing essential information may preclude meaningful numerical comparison. Contextual values retain their background role and attribution. A conditional reporting table and five-item checklist specify the information needed to apply the procedure in hydrological assessment, basin and cascade planning, and reservoir management.

title: High and variable nitrous oxide emissions from human-impacted lentic freshwaters
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Mingliang Jiang, Qitao Xiao, Lei Hong, Yuhang Liu, Xingyu Jiang, Cheng Hu, Ligang Xu
abstract: Inland waters are important but poorly constrained sources of atmospheric nitrous oxide (N2O). Lentic freshwaters including lakes and reservoirs represent key components of inland waters and serve as critical hotspots for nitrogen cycle, yet how anthropogenic disturbances drive their N2O dynamic variability remains unclear. To address this knowledge gap, systematic field measurements in three lakes and one reservoir in China’s eastern plain with intensive anthropogenic activity were conducted to characterize the dynamic variability of N2O emissions and disentangle the key environmental drivers. Results found dissolved N2O concentrations showed uniform vertical distribution but distinct seasonal and spatial variability. These water bodies acted as significant and variable N2O emissions sources, with the emissions flux ranging from 0.25 to 69.27 µmol m−2 d-1 (mean value 7.98 ± 9.12 µmol m−2 d-1). The N2O emissions exhibited strong seasonality, peaking (hot moments) in warm seasons (spring and summer), and N2O emissions of warm seasons were 3.8 times those in cold seasons (autumn and winter). Hot moments of N2O emissions were likely linked to temperature and precipitation-derived hydrological regimes. Inflow-affected zones were hot spots of N2O emissions, with emissions about twice those of pelagic zones (12.47 versus 5.76 µmol m−2 d-1). While regulating factors differed among water bodies and zones, anthropogenic-derived nutrient loadings and associated environment change substantially promoted N2O production and emissions, particularly in inflow-affected zones. Our findings likely deepen insights into N2O biogeochemistry in lentic freshwaters under anthropogenic disturbances and underscore the need to account for waterbody heterogeneity in aquatic N2O emissions estimate.

title: Quantifying and interpreting annual and daily slopes between actual and potential evapotranspiration by land cover type
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Meredith Reitz
abstract: In the water cycle, the lion’s share of precipitation transforms into evapotranspiration (ET), which is the water converted to water vapor through evaporation and plant transpiration. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) characterizes the atmospheric demand for water. Both ET and PET are driven to first order by radiative forcing, but the manner and extent to which ET and PET affect each other is unclear. Many hydrologic models assume that a rise in PET induces a rise in ET, whereas in complementary theory a rise in PET is caused by a decrease in ET. Here we use data from the conterminous U.S. to test the competing conceptual frameworks for the relationship between ET and PET by partially controlling for the influence of radiative forcing. We observe negative correlations between annual ET and PET, consistent with the feedback described by complementary theory. At the daily timescale, we observe the sign and magnitude of the slope between ET and PET to vary with time of year and landscape type, with values that are not well explained by either theory. The varying slopes are consistent with observed differences in vegetation response to atmospheric demand, and may indicate that plants have adapted to their typical water availability conditions with varying transpiration responses to PET. The results indicate an opportunity to improve the accuracy of current methods of estimating ET from PET by including these dynamics.

title: Layered heterogeneity with subsurface dams controls nitrate fate and denitrification in tidally-influenced coastal aquifers
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Maochun Liu, Jina Yin, Chunhui Lu, Frank T.-C. Tsai
abstract: Stratified heterogeneity is known to substantially alter groundwater flow and saltwater-freshwater mixing in coastal aquifers, but its effects on nitrate ( N O 3 - ) fate and denitrification under tidal forcing remain poorly understood, particularly when subsurface dams add hydrogeological complexity. Elucidating these effects is critical for evaluating nitrate attenuation prior to submarine discharge, yet their function as biogeochemical reactors has received little attention. The study combines laboratory experiments with numerical models coupling variable-density flow and reactive transport to investigate how a low-permeability layer (LPL) modulates flow patterns, mixing, nitrate transformation, and solute exchange across the aquifer-ocean interface. Results reveal that the permeability contrasts between the LPL and adjacent sediments induce irregular saltwater advancement and markedly delay upstream saltwater retreat. Due to suppressed seawater circulation downstream of the dam, particle travel time is nearly twofold longer. Denitrification hotspots are found near the margin of the upper saline plume (USP) and its adjacent LPL, where oxygen depletion allows residual dissolved organic carbon (DOC) to mix with N O 3 - entering the aquifer, forming N O 3 - -depleted and N2-enriched zones. Compared to homogeneous settings, the LPL expands denitrification zones and promotes nitrate removal, reducing maximum absolute nitrate flux by approximately 50% and nearly doubling maximum absolute N2 flux, demonstrating that physical retention and biogeochemical transformation are coupled. Sensitivity analyses identify three distinct but interacting controls on nitrate attenuation: residence time, reactant mixing, and DOC decomposition kinetics. These findings provide a new conceptual framework that reframes the LPL as a key control on biogeochemical processes in heterogeneous coastal aquifers.

title: Effects of droughts and warm months on phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations in surface waters globally
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Duncan J. Graham, Arthur H.W. Beusen, Marc F.P. Bierkens, Michelle T.H. van Vliet
abstract: Phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N) concentrations in surface waters are substantially affected by droughts and warm months. However, previous studies of phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations under these hydro-climatic extremes are limited to a small number of regions, mainly in parts of North America, Europe and Australia. Here we perform the first global-scale analysis of phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations in surface waters under droughts, warm months and compound drought-warm months for the period 1980–2010. To achieve this, we developed an approach to downscale existing simulation data of total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) concentrations from annual to monthly level with machine learning at 0.5 × 0.5 degree resolution. The results indicate generally mixed responses in phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations under drought, with some regions showing increases in the concentrations of phosphorus and nitrogen due to drought and others showing decreases. Additionally, the results show more consistent increases in phosphorus (P) concentrations during warm months (average change: +21%) and compound drought-warm months (average change: +10%), which was mainly attributed to less dilution during periods of low flow and high temperature. Furthermore, there is a general decrease in the N:P ratio observed globally during warm months (average change: −11%). The results from this study provide a broader understanding of the effects of droughts and warm months on phosphorus and nitrogen in surface waters compared to previous local-scale studies. Furthermore, the results highlight the significant changes in phosphorus and nitrogen ratios during droughts and warm months, which may significantly influence freshwater ecosystem health worldwide.

title: HydroFlow: A robust and lightweight network for river surface velocimetry on edge devices via semi-supervised learning
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Jicheng Wang, Hongliang Wang, Xiaoting Guo, Yayu Liang, Yuxuan Liao
abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-based image velocimetry is a key advancement in hydrological monitoring, offering non-contact measurement and high spatiotemporal resolution. However, deploying existing deep learning optical flow algorithms in real-world field conditions faces two main challenges: the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, and the “synthetic-to-real” domain shift. High-precision models like RAFT are computationally intensive, hindering real-time performance on resource-constrained edge devices, and are vulnerable to environmental disturbances such as glare and shadows. To address these challenges, this paper proposes HydroFlow, a lightweight, interference-robust optical flow network tailored for edge computing. Based on the NeuFlow V2 architecture, HydroFlow integrates enhancement modules: Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) and Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) to prioritize water motion features, while the Texture-Gated Correlation (TGC) module and Confidence-aware Residual Update (CRU) mechanism reduce outliers caused by noise. Additionally, a RealFlow-EM-based semi-supervised strategy is used to generate confidence-filtered pseudo-labels for unlabeled real-river imagery, thereby supporting synthetic-to-real adaptation without requiring dense optical-flow annotations. Experimental results show that HydroFlow achieves a model-only inference speed of 34 FPS on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, with MAPE values of 8.32% and 8.40% under challenging shadow and glare conditions, respectively, outperforming the comparison methods. This work provides an efficient and robust candidate network for future real-time edge deployment in river-velocity monitoring under complex environmental conditions.

title: Marked thermal heterogeneity within a small mountain stream network and its response to climate warming
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Luca Bonacina, Valeria Mezzanotte, Riccardo Fornaroli
abstract: Water temperature is a key driver of aquatic ecosystems, yet thermal heterogeneity across river networks at fine spatiotemporal scales remains poorly understood. This study investigates the thermal regime of five mid-altitude streams (500–1400 m a.s.l.) in the Serio River catchment (Orobic Alps, Northern Italy), influenced by contrasting water sources (snowmelt/stormwater vs. groundwater) and hydrological modifications (reservoirs), and evaluates how thermal patterns may change under future climate warming scenarios. Sub-daily temperature monitoring at 16 sites over 2017–2022 enabled the characterization of multiple aspects of the stream thermal regime: magnitude, variability, range, frequency, timing, and duration of thermal events, and catchment-scale thermal heterogeneity in relation to environmental drivers. Watercourses exhibited distinct thermal responses associated with lithology, hydrology, and reservoirs: siliceous, unregulated streams were thermally reactive, closely tracking air temperature, whereas groundwater-fed and reservoir-regulated streams were thermally buffered and less sensitive to warming. Catchment-scale thermal heterogeneity was pronounced (3.6 °C in annual means and up to 8.7 °C across maxima), comparable to that of alpine systems influenced by glaciers, and is projected to change under climate warming. The fine-scale variability of thermal habitats within a small area highlighted the importance of understanding thermal dynamics for interpreting ecological patterns and guiding conservation strategies.

title: Enhancing lake dissolved oxygen retrieval by integrating process-based model with machine learning: maximizing the utility of multi-source monitoring data
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Xuemei Pan, Qixin Lin, Gang Li, Xinfa Xu, Zhangjun Liu, Jingqiao Mao
abstract: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is critical for lake ecosystem health. Although satellite remote sensing (RS) coupled with machine learning (ML) has emerged as an effective approach for DO monitoring, the stringent requirement for temporal synchronization between in-situ measurements and satellite overpasses often limits the availability of viable training samples. This scarcity significantly constrains both the retrieval accuracy and the generalizability of ML models. To address this issue, this study proposes a novel framework integrating a Process-Based (PB) model with ML algorithms for lake DO retrieval. Within this framework, the PB model assimilates multi-source data of diverse types and varying frequencies to generate high-frequency simulated DO. These simulations serve as substitutes for in-situ measurements to augment “DO–surface reflectance” training pairs, thereby promoting the utilization of ground monitoring data and RS imagery to enhance ML model training. Taking Poyang Lake as a case study, we constructed ML training datasets by pairing RS surface reflectance with three distinct DO data configurations: in-situ measurements only, PB-simulated DO data only, and a hybrid of both. The retrieval performance of six ML algorithms was evaluated across these configurations using rigorous spatial and temporal cross-validation comprising 72 independent scenarios. Results indicate that the PB model achieves high-frequency DO simulations with satisfactory accuracy, with R2 ranging from 0.63 to 0.92 across seven stations. Furthermore, augmenting training samples with PB-simulated data significantly improved the retrieval performance across all ML models. Under the hybrid training sets configuration, the six ML models achieving a mean R2 of 0.40 across 21 spatial cross-validation scenarios and 0.52 across 3 temporal cross-validation scenarios, significantly outperforming traditional methods relying solely on limited in-situ measurements (mean R2 of 0.26 and 0.17, respectively). The proposed framework effectively fuses multi-source heterogeneous monitoring data and maximizes historical RS imagery usage, providing a novel technical pathway for high-precision water quality retrieval in inland lakes, especially under data-scarce conditions.

title: Short-term predictability of groundwater electrical conductivity and water level in a coastal aquifer considering antecedent states and external forcing
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Fuwei Yang, Fan Yang, Xiaonong Hu, Chuanshun Zhi, Guangwei Wu, Wenwen Bi, Yulong Dong
abstract: Groundwater electrical conductivity (EC) and groundwater level (GWL) in coastal aquifers respond to both antecedent groundwater conditions and external forcing, but their short-term predictability and the contribution of these information sources remain uncertain. Using automated monitoring records from the southern coast of Laizhou Bay, we developed a daily prediction framework combining data quality control, time-lagged correlation analysis, five data-driven models, a persistence benchmark, and grouped-input ablation. Rainfall- and tide-related responses showed weak but spatially heterogeneous lagged associations; the 24-h mean tidal level showed the clearest associations with GWL at several wells, whereas EC responses were more variable. The persistence benchmark produced lower eight-well mean errors than all five data-driven models, with mean RMSE values of 0.460 mS/cm for EC and 0.081 m for GWL, showing that antecedent groundwater states account for a large part of one-day-ahead predictability. Among the data-driven models, SVR gave the strongest integrated EC performance, while GWL performance depended on the evaluation metric. Ablation experiments showed that antecedent target states contained substantial predictive information, whereas the added value of rainfall and tidal inputs varied with prediction target and model architecture. Short-term predictability in this coastal aquifer depended strongly on groundwater-state persistence, while the added information from external forcing varied among locations and model architectures.

title: Hydrogeological controls on seasonal groundwater level dynamics across Greece: A national-scale assessment integrating monitoring data, earth observation, and interpretable machine learning (2013–2022)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Evangelos Tziritis, Miltiadis Iatrou, Christos Drougas, Spyridon Tasoglou, George Arampatzis
abstract: Groundwater monitoring networks typically provide broad spatial coverage but sparse and irregular temporal observations, which limit their direct use for operational groundwater status assessment. Mediterranean groundwater systems are subject to strong seasonal contrasts between winter recharge and summer abstraction, yet national-scale assessments resolving how aquifer type modulates this signal remain scarce. We analyzed 22,281 quality-controlled groundwater level records from 2,477 monitoring wells across the 14 River Basin Districts of Greece (2013 to 2022), drawn from the WISE database of the European Environment Agency, combining stratified non-parametric statistics with an interpretable XGBoost classification framework for screening of deeper-than-normal groundwater conditions. Seasonal dynamics differed systematically by aquifer type (Kruskal-Wallis H = 32.37, p = 9.34 × 10−8). Porous aquifers showed the smallest seasonal amplitude (σ = 5.36 m) and the strongest coupling with root-zone soil moisture (Spearman ρ = +0.228), consistent with diffuse vertical Darcian recharge. Karstic aquifers exhibited intermediate amplitude (σ = 6.42 m) with a marked elevation gradient in dry-season drawdown, from + 0.79 m at low elevation to + 2.83 m above 300 m, reflecting dual-porosity behaviour in upland carbonate massifs. Fractured-rock aquifers displayed the largest amplitude (σ = 6.83 m) and effectively no soil-moisture coupling (ρ = +0.020), consistent with preferential recharge bypassing the soil column. The divergence in soil-moisture sensitivity between porous and fractured systems is the clearest statistical contrast in the dataset and is consistent with a difference in dominant recharge pathway, although the observational design does not allow that mechanism to be established directly. Within porous aquifers, sites combining high cropland cover and high vegetation vigour showed net summer recovery (Δh = − 0.42 m, Mann-Whitney p = 2.79 × 10−3), a signal consistent with irrigation return flow that was statistically absent in karstic and fractured systems (p > 0.3). Among wells with continuous records over 2018 to 2022, 61.7% showed net decline and 100 wells (6.8%) showed persistent drawdown above 2 m per measurement interval, concentrated in Thessaly and the Messara plain; with only five annual values and irregular observation intervals, these are reported as short-period changes among repeatedly monitored wells rather than as national depletion trends. A station-standardized XGBoost classifier achieved ROC AUC = 0.695 on an independent 2021 to 2022 test set, with SHAP attribution identifying seasonal phase, antecedent soil moisture, annual precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration as the leading physically coherent predictors. The findings support consideration of aquifer-type-stratified reference conditions within the Water Framework Directive and provide a quantitative basis for prioritising monitoring investments in karstic and fractured-rock systems.

title: Socioeconomic-driven spatiotemporal dynamics of urban flood resilience at the agglomeration scale under shared socioeconomic pathways
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Jiaxuan Zheng, Xiaoying Zhao, Guoru Huang
abstract: Investigating the spatiotemporal evolution of urban flood resilience (UFR) serves as a theoretical foundation to enhance future UFR amid evolving flood challenges. However, current discussions on this topic remain insufficient, especially in terms of isolating the impacts of socioeconomic development on UFR. These hinder a faster and clearer translation of actionable, policy-relevant insights into practical enhancement strategies. This study aims to clarify the socioeconomic-driven spatiotemporal evolution of UFR in the Pearl River Delta. Comparisons were conducted between the current and future periods regarding the patterns and values of UFR across the study area, as well as the spatial directionality and heterogeneity of low-UFR regions. Suggestions for future resilience-based flood risk management were proposed. The findings suggest that the coverage of low-UFR areas increases in future periods. Future socioeconomic development does not substantially change the overall spatial pattern of UFR. The effects of socioeconomic development on the spatial distribution of UFR are nonlinear and stage-dependent. Highly urbanized areas play a dominant role in shaping low-resilience spatial patterns. Enhancing UFR should prioritize improvements in the highly urbanized areas, with Dongguan City as the principal target. Resilience planning should consider the dominant expansion axis of low-resilience areas in each urban region, which is predominantly east–west in the Pearl River Delta. Implementation of UFR measures is more likely to yield tangible results by the end of the mid-future.

title: Groundwater flow in vertically heterogeneous unconfined aquifers with spatially varying boundary heads: A Girinskii–Lambert analytical framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part B Author(s): Ali Mahdavi
