OGPAT establishes analytic outlet-state identification as a transferable operator principle for short-range forecasting under human-impact domain shift.

title: Drone–based camera discharge derived from the entropy–based probability concept and image velocimetry algorithms
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Duncan B. Morel, Christopher A. Kirk, John W. Fulton, Frank L. Engel, Carl J. Legleiter, Brandon T. Forbes, Noah Eno, Matthew J. Nicotra, Matthew C. Gyves, Robert R. Lotspeich, Heather R. Best
abstract: In June and August 2023, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) conducted small Uncrewed Aircraft System (sUAS or drone) flights at five streamgages in the Upper Colorado River Basin, Colorado, USA. The objectives of this research were (1) compare maximum surface velocities and discharges derived from Space-time Image Velocimetry (STIV) and Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and (2) evaluate drone-based camera algorithms that rely on the entropy-based probability concept and mid-section method relative to standard discharge measurements. To evaluate the scalability and transferability of the methods, river reaches were selected with varying top widths, depths, and discharges and colocated with existing USGS streamgages. Percent errors between drone-based camera algorithms and hydroacoustic measurements were substantially smaller for large rivers such as the Colorado River, Colorado when compared to small rivers such as the Blue River, Colorado. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test suggests there was no difference between the discharges generated by STIV and PIV algorithms and hydroacoustic measurements. This implies that, if the appropriate algorithms are properly parameterized, drone-based camera discharges are consistent with standard discharge measurements when siting is conducted appropriately.

title: Stage-dependent responses of shallow groundwater salinization under multiple coupled drivers: multi-period hydrochemical evidence and mechanistic insights from a coastal gold mining area
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Chang Lu, Bo Zhang, Fangying Dong, Xiang Jiang, Zhenzhou Sun, Rongxin Zhao, Huiyong Yin, Tianyuan Zheng
abstract: Coastal shallow groundwater is a key medium for maintaining ecological security and supporting the sustainable use of water resources in coastal regions. However, it is prone to salinization and water quality deterioration under the combined effects of climate change and human activities, while its stage-dependent responses under different background conditions remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated a typical coastal gold mining area in the Jiaodong Peninsula using multi-period regional hydrochemical data, source apportionment, and major-ion relationships to identify the dominant salinization processes and their stage-dependent responses. Groundwater solutes were jointly controlled by five key end members: coastal saline input, evaporative salinization, mining disturbance related water–rock interactions, agricultural and domestic inputs, and natural carbonate weathering. The study period was divided into three stages with distinct hydrochemical responses. Climate change regulated recharge intensity and hydrological conditions, thereby controlling the expression of coastal saline sources and anthropogenic disturbances. Enhanced recharge during wet conditions promoted dilution, leaching, and solute redistribution, whereas relatively dry conditions intensified evaporative concentration, coastal saline influence, and the hydrochemical expression of mining and agricultural inputs. Based on multiple lines of evidence, three stage-dependent salinization response modes were identified: a natural background-controlled mode, a climate-buffered mode, and a multi-factor coupled driving-dominated mode. These modes reveal the stage dependent transition of the system from buffered regulation to enhanced multi source driving. The proposed framework provides new systematic insights for stage-specific salinization risk identification and groundwater monitoring and management in coastal mining areas.

title: Wildfire disturbance during extreme drought reshapes groundwater dissolved inorganic carbon export pattern in a subtropical karst trough valley
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Chenpeng Hu, Sibo Zeng, Yan Yang, Lidan Lei, Lei Liu, Xuyang Liu, Mingyang Li, Xinhe Huang, Yonghao Tang
abstract: Hydrochemical processes in karst system are highly sensitive to climate extremes because of rapid surface–subsurface connectivity. However, the effects of extreme drought and drought-associated wildfire on carbon cycling in these systems remain poorly understood. Here, we use nine-year records (2017–2025) of groundwater hydrochemistry, δ13C of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), discharge-based DIC fluxes, and remote-sensing vegetation indices from the Longtan karst trough valley, Southwest China, to evaluate the impacts of hydroclimatic variability, vegetation dynamics, extreme drought, and wildfire on groundwater DIC pattern. We found the increasing precipitation and vegetation recovery promoted carbonate dissolution during the relatively humid period (2017–2021), resulting in higher DIC concentrations and more negative δ13CDIC values. DIC and δ13CDIC exhibited clear seasonal patterns associated with vegetation dynamics. In 2022, however, an extreme drought compounded by wildfire abruptly disrupted these trends, which revealed by a random forest model and a comparision framework of LSTM-RF predictions. Fire-induced vegetation loss, together with drought-related declines in soil moisture and groundwater recharge, weakened carbonate weathering and reduced DIC and Ca2+ concentrations. After the wildfire, DIC fluxes decreased by 90.88 %, respectively, mainly because of sharply reduced groundwater discharge. These findings show that extreme events can strongly disrupt DIC export from karst systems and should be explicitly incorporated into future karst system carbon cycling models.

title: New insight into the biogeochemical fingerprint of nitrate: linking chemical weathering and carbon cycling to groundwater discharge
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Shen Qu, Zhongli Wang, Le Qiao, Wei Bao, Lijuan Hu, Wengeng Cao, Limin Duan, Xiaomin Liu, Ruihong Yu
abstract: Anthropogenic nitrate enrichment reshapes biogeochemical cycling, yet its role in linking chemical weathering and carbon cycling during groundwater discharge across lake and river basins remains poorly understood. Here, multi–isotopic tracers (δ15N, δ18Onitrate, 222Rn), 16S rRNA data, and a corrected forward model are integrated to quantify nitrate sources, groundwater discharge processes, and weathering-related CO2 consumption, and to explore microbial associations with nitrogen and carbon cycling. Results show nitrate primarily originates from sewage/manure (45.8%–57.4%), soil nitrogen (17.4%–30.7%) and fertilizer (18.4%–19.2%). Groundwater discharge rates range from (3.4 ± 3.3) × 104 m3/d to (1.2 ± 1.8) × 105 m3/d, transporting 106–107 g/d nitrate to surface water. Nitrification dominates nitrogen transformations, releasing H⁺ that accelerates carbonate and silicate weathering, with average CO2 consumption rates of 0.1 × 105 mol/km2/yr and 0.6 × 105 mol/km2/yr, respectively. Elevated nitrate was associated with reduced net CO2 consumption and a potential theoretical shift from a CO2 sink toward a CO2 source. Microbial community composition was associated with nitrogen and inorganic carbon variables, while PICRUSt2 predictions suggested potential links between nitrification-related functions and autotrophic carbon fixation. This study highlights nitrate as a potentially important biogeochemical linkage agent linking nitrogen cycling, chemical weathering, and carbon dynamics, providing insights for water quality protection and carbon sink assessment in groundwater-dependent ecosystems.

title: An integrated assessment of groundwater controls on streamflow and ecosystem functioning in the Guarani aquifer outcrop zone
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): José Gescilam S.M. Uchôa, José A.C. Ayllon, Daniel P. Abrahão, Luis E. Bertotto, Alan Reis, Davi Gasparini F. Cunha, Juliano J. Corbi, Jamil A.A. Anache, Edson C. Wendland
abstract: Groundwater–surface water interactions sustain river ecosystems and regulate biogeochemical processes. However, despite growing interest in hyporheic zone functioning, interdisciplinary assessments remain scarce in tropical regions. Here, we present a scalable interdisciplinary framework to evaluate groundwater influences on streamflow and ecosystem functioning at the reach scale in the Guarani Aquifer System (GAS) outcrop area, São Paulo, Brazil. The approach combines (i) temperature as a natural tracer of groundwater discharge, (ii) physicochemical and nutrient analyses, (iii) macroinvertebrates as bioindicators, and (iv) cotton-strip assays to estimate organic matter decomposition. Two years of quarterly monitoring were conducted across three creek reaches (S1, S2, and S3) with contrasting degrees of groundwater connectivity. The reach with stronger groundwater influence (S2) exhibited significantly lower thermal variability than the upstream (S1) and downstream (S3) reaches, whereas no significant differences in phase lag were detected. Nutrient concentrations showed contrasting longitudinal patterns between S1–S2 and S2–S3, particularly for NH4 +-N. Furthermore, S2 had the highest macroinvertebrate diversity, and the highest organic-matter decomposition rates, with a significant difference between S2 and S1, whereas biofilm respiration was higher in S3. The overall consistency among indicators suggests that river-aquifer interactions not only sustain streamflow but also regulate relevant biological communities, ecosystem functions and biogeochemical processes. Although spatially limited relative to the overall extent of the GAS, its outcrop areas are critical recharge zones and particularly susceptible to anthropogenic contamination. The proposed approach may be adapted to other local creeks in GAS outcrop area, or tropical regions with similar climate and hydrological conditions.

title: From static susceptibility mapping to rainfall-driven spatiotemporal urban flood prediction: a joint susceptibility–depth learning framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Thuan Thanh Le, Tuong Quang Vo, Jongho Kim
abstract: Urban flood prediction has traditionally relied on static susceptibility mapping or single-output inundation estimation, limiting its ability to represent rainfall-driven flood evolution under varying spatial conditions. This study proposes HydroX-Risk, a hybrid rainfall-driven spatiotemporal deep learning framework for the joint prediction of urban flood susceptibility and inundation depth. The proposed architecture integrates a CBAM-enhanced convolutional spatial encoder with a hybrid TCN-Transformer rainfall module within a unified multitask learning framework. Using an event-based dataset for Seoul from 2010 to 2024, HydroX-Risk achieved strong predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.89, an AUC of 0.95, and an F1-score of 0.88 for flood susceptibility classification, together with an MAE of 0.08 m and an RMSE of 0.15 m for inundation depth estimation. Comparative experiments demonstrated improved performance relative to both the spatial-only baseline (HydroX-Risk-S) and the univariate framework (HydroX-Risk-U), highlighting the added value of rainfall-driven temporal modeling and bivariate multitask learning. The framework advances urban flood prediction from static susceptibility mapping toward rainfall-driven spatiotemporal modeling by jointly modeling temporal rainfall forcing and spatial flood susceptibility to learn rainfall-conditioned flood responses. Bayesian optimization and SHAP analyses further enhanced model robustness and interpretability. SHAP analyses revealed heterogeneous contributions of rainfall and spatial predictors to the predicted flood responses and showed that identical rainfall forcing can be associated with substantially different predictions depending on local spatial conditions. Dominant local predictors, including DTRiver, DTDrainage, DTRoad, and Aspect, highlighted the importance of local river proximity, drainage configuration, road proximity, and terrain orientation in the model predictions. Overall, HydroX-Risk advances urban flood prediction toward interpretable rainfall-driven spatiotemporal flood modeling under evolving storm conditions.

title: Representing canopy interception in a distributed snow model to improve snow accumulation and melt timing
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yijing Liu, J. Michelle Hu, Alvaro Robledano, S. McKenzie Skiles
abstract: Seasonal snowmelt is a vital water resource for downstream populations and supports ecological processes in the mountainous Western United States. In subalpine forests, snow interception by tree canopies strongly influences snow accumulation, snow duration, and runoff timing. However, canopy interception has not been incorporated into the widely used, process-based distributed snow energy balance model, iSnobal. To address this gap, we integrated multiple forest canopy snow processes into iSnobal. To assess the version of iSnobal with canopy processes, it was run over five water years in the East River Watershed, a mountainous, partially forested basin in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Across model runs, 50–150 mm of snowfall, equivalent to 10% − 30% of cumulative snowfall, was intercepted annually. Within the canopy, melt dominated snow loss, while wind-driven unloading was limited and elevation-dependent. Relative to baseline runs, snow depths were decreased (mean 0.09–0.11 m) and snow cover duration was shortened (7–16 days) due to delayed snow onset and faster snow depletion. The model was assessed against lidar-mapped snow depth, which showed that accounting for interception improved model performance, with 39.4% to 57.3% of pixels exhibiting better agreement and reduced errors, especially during late melt (May and June). Random forest analysis identified intercepted snowfall, snow onset date, leaf area index, cumulative snowfall, and aspect as primary controls on snow depth differences between default iSnobal and its canopy-enabled version. This study emphasizes the importance of accounting for forest canopy processes in snow models and provides a basis for more reliable snowmelt inputs to water supply forecasting in snow-dominated forested regions.

title: Deciphering leakage in cut-off walls-aquifer dual domain system using tracer breakthrough analysis
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yunzhao Zhang, Huaxiang Yan, Hamid Rajabi, Samad Sabbaghi, Hongqiang Dou, Qiao Wang
abstract: Cut-off walls are commonly used as engineering barriers to prevent contaminant transport by reducing groundwater seepage. However, the development of fractures and cracks in the cut-off wall under wet-dry cycles and chemical erosion can create preferential flow paths, significantly compromise the effectiveness of the cut-off walls. A cut-off wall aquifer dual domain analytical model is consequently developed to investigate the potential leakage of the barrier system by interpreting the breakthrough curve (BTC) of tracers. A conservative tracer experiment in the sandbox validates the proposed solution. The effects of cut-off wall thickness (B), hydraulic head (hw ), and fracture aperture (bf ) on BTC characteristics were systematically analyzed. The leakage of cut-off wall due to the development of fractures and cracks alters the BTC of tracer, advancing the transit time (ta ) and peak arrival time (tp ) by 98.3% and 98.6%, respectively. Under non-leakage conditions, increasing the cut-off wall thickness delays tracer transport, whereas under leakage conditions, preferential flow through fractures diminishes the influence of wall thickness on leakage resistance. By integrating the peak breakthrough concentration (Cp ), flow velocity (vc ), the Péclet number (Pe )-dimensionless time (Tv ) relationship, and the Tv -bf relationship, a multi-stage leakage identification framework was proposed. The framework enables leakage detection, barrier-integrity assessment, and quantitative characterization of preferential flow pathways using tracer-monitoring data, providing a theoretical basis for long-term performance evaluation of cut-off walls.

title: A public-data-driven framework for urban flood modelling and credibility assessment under detailed-data scarcity
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yubin Zhang, Xiaojuan Zhao, Tianyu Feng, Yixuan Zhang, Pingping Luo
abstract: Urban flood modelling in data-scarce cities is limited by the absence of high-resolution hydraulic terrain, drainage-network maps, inlet records, calibrated parameters, and systematic flood observations. This study proposes a public-data-driven framework for planning-level flood-prone pattern diagnosis under detailed-data scarcity. The framework combines Urban Hydraulic Surface Model (UHSM) reconstruction, road-based generalized drainage-network inference, storage-conserving 1D-2D surface-drainage coupling, capacity-matched equivalent drainage comparison, sensitivity analysis, and Data-Driven Spatial Credibility (DDSC) assessment using screened public evidence. In Xiaozhai, Xi’an, the comparison included a static terrain proxy and four dynamic configurations representing raw public terrain, UHSM reconstruction, equivalent drainage, and explicit 1D-2D drainage coupling. A second case in Zhengzhou was used to examine whether the same workflow could be reproduced in another city. Results show that UHSM reconstruction reduced scattered shallow ponding produced by the raw public DEM and generated more hydraulically interpretable flood-prone patterns. Equivalent drainage mainly acted as a local surface-water removal term, whereas explicit drainage coupling partitioned captured water into surcharge return flow, outfall export, and temporary pipe storage under closed water balance. Public-evidence assessment showed that high evidence hit rates alone are insufficient because sparse and road-biased evidence may also be matched by overly broad model support. Combining evidence agreement, evidence-to-model distance, model-support extent, and sensitivity diagnostics provided a more cautious credibility assessment. The Zhengzhou case demonstrated methodological portability, but not predictive validation of the synthetic drainage network. The proposed framework provides a reproducible approach for preliminary urban flood screening and model-structure diagnosis where detailed drainage and validation data are unavailable.

title: Accounting for the unaccounted: a new framework for incorporating farm social diversity in micro-regional water budgets
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): C. Hemingway, C. Aubron, R. Chitra-Tarak, M. Vigne, G. Boulet, M. Sekhar, L. Ruiz
abstract: Aquifer overexploitation in irrigated regions calls for better water-flow quantification, yet existing methods are data-intensive and often overlook farmers’ social diversity. We propose a framework representing water flows in small regions while accounting for farm social diversity, distinguishing groundwater users and non-users. We introduce the Blue Water Potential (BWP) indicator, using a simplified soil water balance at plot and farm levels and a mixed-methods archetype village approach to aggregate water flows. We applied this framework to a semi-arid region of southern India, examining how BWP differs across farm typologies and between the 1950s and 2022, and how contributions of these farm types combine to determine village BWP in each period. Results show that, at the plot scale, BWP varies widely depending on land use. At the farm level, all production systems had positive BWP in the 1950s; in 2022, irrigating farmers show largely negative BWP, while those growing mainly rainfed crops and pastoralists maintain positive BWP. At the village level, negative BWP of a minority of wealthy irrigators is balanced by positive BWP of poorer rainfed farmers and pastoralists. By accounting for farmers’ social diversity, our framework reveals contrasting roles in groundwater dynamics and introduces the concepts of ‘blue water consumers’—groundwater-dependent farmers—and ‘blue water producers’—rainfed and pastoral farmers whose land uses contribute to groundwater recharge—highlighting how the former rely on the hydrological contributions of the latter. This approach represents groundwater-related interdependencies between social groups, supporting equitable groundwater governance, scenario planning, and management.

title: Synergy of policymaking and water storage variations in global transboundary basins
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Roniki Anjaneyulu, Abhishek
abstract: Water and war are increasingly interconnected issues. Transboundary river basins, which cover nearly half of Earth’s land surface and account for about 60% of global river discharge, play a critical role in global ecological, economic, and social systems. However, there is a lack of comprehensive analysis of terrestrial water storage (TWS) change and how individual countries influence changes in these basins, particularly in the context of climate change and anthropogenic activities. Understanding the movement of basin water is also important for equitable resource distribution among nations. This study examines 22 years of TWS anomalies (TWSA) dynamics, analyzing country-wise contributions to TWSA trends and the impacts of climate change and human activities. We also employ a spatially weighted centroid approach to track the mass movement of water storage and discuss the implications of relevant policies and laws on transboundary water resources. Results show groundwater storage (GWS) constitutes > 50% of the TWSA in 27 basins. Notably, 17 basins exhibit significant decreasing TWSA trends. The movement of TWSA and precipitation centroids is concordant in 9 basins, discordant in 21, with 15 basins experiencing lower water contestations and another 15 facing potential transboundary water contestations. Overall, in 18 basins, anthropogenic factors account for a larger share than climate change in the observed TWSA. The findings provide crucial insights for researchers, stakeholders, and policymakers by highlighting key laws, organizations, agreements, and policies related to water allocations, data sharing, strategic plans for sustainable groundwater recharge, and fostering discussions on dispute resolution.

title: Bidirectional concentration–discharge analysis reveals source–sink shifts and contrasting nutrient transport processes in regulated plain-river networks
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Xiaoyu Jiang, Xuan Huang, Dongli She, Yongqiu Xia
abstract: Concentration–discharge (c-Q) relationships are fundamental for understanding watershed nutrient transport, yet traditional unidirectional frameworks fail in regulated plain-river networks with frequent flow reversals. To address this issue, a bidirectional c-Q hysteresis framework that references concentration responses against “discharge valleys” during backflow was developed to decouple nutrient dynamics under complex hydrodynamic conditions. We applied this framework to the Caoqiao River, a major tributary of Lake Taihu, using three-year high-frequency monitoring data of ammonia nitrogen and total phosphorus (May 2022 to April 2025, 4-hour intervals) from three sites along the river–lake gradient. The findings revealed that backflow exerted a limited influence on reverse nutrient loads, accounting for only 0.71–3.81% of the net loads, as well as on long-term c-Q relationships, with consistent trends observed during both lakeward-flow and backflow periods. However, although annual loads remained low during backflow periods and long-term relationships were consistent across both periods, differences were evident at the event scale in this study. At the event scale, backflow triggered pronounced source–sink shifts, producing transport mechanisms contrasting with those observed during lakeward-flow events. Ammonia nitrogen (NH3-N) and total nitrogen (TN) predominantly exhibited clockwise hysteresis (up to 33.3% and 29.0% of events, respectively), as dilution by cleaner lake water delayed the arrival of external nutrient inputs. Total phosphorus (TP) frequently showed counterclockwise hysteresis (up to 31.3% of events), with backflow-induced disturbance promoting the early release of particulate phosphorus from sediments.

title: A 5-year assessment of radar quantitative precipitation estimates during the cool season over the Midwest and Eastern United States
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Brian C. Filipiak, Brendan Raykoff, Matthew Sinchi, Diego Cerrai, Marina Astitha
abstract: Wintertime precipitation measurements present challenges as changes in precipitation phase and sub-freezing temperatures can impact the quality of observations from different types of precipitation gauges. Weather radars have a different set of challenges from gauges that include beam blockage, changes in scanning volume size, and application of the most appropriate radar reflectivity to rain rate relationship. Gridded quantitative precipitation estimates (QPEs) from weather radars are commonly used to assess numerical weather model precipitation forecasts or initiate hydrologic modeling, but during the wintertime, concerns over the quality of the QPEs raise questions of when they can be used. Here, two gridded radar-derived, gauge-corrected QPE products, Stage IV and MRMS, were compared to 85 ASOS stations with weighing precipitation gauges, the standard gauge for measuring winter precipitation, across the Great Lakes, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast United States during five cool seasons. The products were compared over 1-, 6-, and 24-hour QPE accumulations, divided spatially by NWS River Forecast Center, and by observed precipitation phase. The results from this work indicated that Stage IV was statistically closer to in-situ observations compared to MRMS over all accumulation periods. However, the efficacy of the products varied spatially with Stage IV having pronounced regional differences due to its processing procedure. While assessing the impact of precipitation phase, MRMS performed better for liquid precipitation, whereas Stage IV was better for mixed or frozen precipitation. End users can use these results to select the most appropriate QPE radar product depending on the applications related to cool season precipitation.

title: Seasonal reorganization of vertical partitioning in microbial carbon fixation in a high-altitude saline lake
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yixuan Han, Xiaoyan Li, Fangzhong Shi, Guangrong Hu, Xin Liu, Zhigang Wang, Rui Wang, Jingjing Wu, Wenhao Zhang, Yishu Meng
abstract: Microbial carbon fixation links dissolved inorganic carbon assimilation with carbon cycling in aquatic ecosystems, yet how seasonal environmental gradients reorganize carbon fixation through the water column remains poorly understood in high-altitude saline lakes. Here, we quantified seasonal and vertical variations in light-dependent carbon fixation (LCF) and dark carbon fixation (DCF) by integrating carbon fixation rates with physicochemical variables, microbial community composition, and C-, N-, and S-cycling functional potentials throughout an annual cycle in Qinghai Lake (QHL). Microbial carbon fixation exhibited four distinct seasonal vertical configurations, with LCF dominating during summer stratification and DCF contributing proportionally more under winter ice cover. The transition depth between LCF and DCF shoaled progressively from approximately 16.7 m in summer to 10.2 m in autumn and 5.4 m in winter before disappearing during spring mixing, demonstrating seasonal reorganization of the vertical partitioning of microbial carbon fixation. These seasonal patterns were explained more consistently by microbial functional potential than by taxonomic composition, with Calvin-Benson-Bassham (CBB) cycle genes prevailing under favorable light conditions and alternative carbon assimilation together with coupled nitrogen and sulfur metabolism becoming more important under low-light conditions. Together, these findings show that seasonal environmental gradients reorganize the vertical partitioning of microbial carbon fixation primarily through shifts in microbial metabolic potential, providing a process-based understanding of microbial carbon assimilation in high-altitude saline lakes.

title: Relating precipitation extremes to streamflow peaks using percentile-based correspondence and interpretable machine learning
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Tongtiegang Zhao, Xiaodong Li
abstract: The extent to which precipitation extremes translate into streamflow peaks is a critical part of the rainfall-runoff relationship. This paper focuses on the extent to which the upper 90th percentile precipitation extremes correspond to streamflow peaks above different percentiles. Specifically, precipitation extremes are paired with streamflow peaks by searching for event-specific discharge maxima and estimating empirical percentiles; the percentile-based correspondence is calculated as the hit rate to quantify the proportion of paired streamflow peaks above different percentile levels; furthermore, random forest models coupled with analyses based on SHapley Additive exPlanations are used to diagnose the effects of catchment attributes on the correspondence by accounting for feature importance and interaction effects. A case study is devised for the dataset of Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies across the continental United States. The results show that the median proportions of paired streamflow peaks exceeding the 80th, 90th and 95th percentiles are about 70%, 57% and 45%, respectively. For the upper 90th percentile streamflow peaks, the random forest model identifies the snow fraction as the dominant attribute, with its negative impacts shaped by its interaction with mean elevation. Among catchments with the highest 20% of snow fraction, the median hit rates remain 0.53 below 500 m and 0.57 between 500 and 1000 m, but drop to 0.14 above 1000 m. After constraining the snow fraction-elevation interactions, the five leading catchment attributes shift to mean high-flow duration, longitude, mean precipitation, streamflow elasticity and silt fraction. Overall, the results inform the interpretation of catchment-specific precipitation extremes for streamflow forecasting and flood warning.

title: Integrating deep learning into distributed hydrological modeling with physical constraints: unified streamflow prediction and reanalysis-supervised soil moisture representation over South Korea
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Dong-Gi Lee, Gyu-Ho Noh, Kuk-Hyun Ahn
abstract: Deep learning models have improved hydrological prediction, but their application to distributed modeling remains limited by weak physical consistency and the frequent separation of runoff generation from river routing. Here, we develop a physically constrained distributed Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework that jointly simulates reanalysis-supervised grid-scale soil moisture, runoff generation, and downstream streamflow through an end-to-end D8-based routing scheme. The framework incorporates soft constraints representing water balance, precipitation-based water availability, potential evapotranspiration limits, and soil moisture bounds. We evaluated the framework across South Korea using daily meteorological forcing, streamflow observations from 21 gauging stations, and a reanalysis-based soil moisture for 964 grid cells during 2005–2024. Temporal, spatial, and spatiotemporal validation experiments were conducted to assess predictive performance and transferability. The physically constrained model retained comparable performance at temporally held-out observations while providing its clearest benefits in ungauged basins. It achieved the highest median streamflow Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) under both the spatial validation (0.690 and 0.721) and spatiotemporal validation (0.688 and 0.640). These values exceeded those of the corresponding unconstrained distributed model by 0.049–0.080 for NSE and 0.089–0.162 for KGE. The learned internal responses satisfied the imposed bounds and exhibited hydrologically coherent changes in timing, persistence, and sensitivity to antecedent wetness, although they should not be interpreted as independently validated physical fluxes. The results indicate that soft hydrological constraints can improve streamflow transferability across ungauged basins, even when they do not uniformly improve all prediction targets or evaluation settings.

title: Coupling effects of vegetation and crack on soil climate resilience: insights from electrical conductivity monitoring
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Jun-Zheng Zhang, Chao-Sheng Tang, André Revil, Dong-Wei Wang, Yu Zhang, Chang Sun, Jin-Jian Xu
abstract: Clayey soils are widespread on Earth’s surface and exhibit variable mechanical and hydraulic properties that are sensitive to climate conditions. Although vegetation covers can protect clayey soils from climate change, drought-induced desiccation cracks in clayey soils are inevitable, significantly altering their hydraulic behavior. Characterizing the coupling effects of vegetation covers and desiccation cracks on the climate resilience of clayey soil is therefore an important topic. This study develops a framework using electrical conductivity for investigating the dynamics of soil moisture content in shallow clayey soils during the yearly cycle. Five electrical profiles were set on the slope surface with and without vegetation covers, including a refined profile on cracked soils for conductivity tomography. The soil temperature modeling and petrophysical relationship between electrical conductivity and volumetric water content help to reconstruct the moisture dynamics in shallow layers. Results indicated that vegetation covers can improve soil climate resilience by reducing soil temperature fluctuations in spring, maintaining the soil moisture in summer, and inhibiting soil freezing in winter. Under the coupling effects of cracks and vegetation, infiltration and evaporation in shallow soils vary with weather conditions. This study emphasizes the significance of non-invasive and distributed monitoring of clayey soils on the Earth’s surface, offering an innovative framework for evaluating the climate resilience of these soils under climate change.

title: Climate change restructures extreme-event memory and hydroclimatic regime persistence across Africa
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Nickson Tibangayuka, Wenxi Liao, Deogratias M.M. Mulungu
abstract: Climate extremes are intensifying globally, yet their most consequential impacts emerge from temporal clustering and regime persistence rather than isolated events. Here, we demonstrate that climate change systematically restructures extreme-event memory (i.e., the time-dependent influence of past extremes on future hydroclimatic states) across Africa. We develop an event-conditioned probabilities framework and apply it to observations (1985–2024) and climate model projections (2041–2080). We reveal that the dominant 6-month memory timescale strengthens in semi-arid regions but weakens in humid tropics, creating opposing regional responses in hydroclimatic predictability. We found that climate change induces asymmetric regime shifts, making dry states more persistent while wet states more transient. These shifts bias the hydroclimatic regime toward more prolonged droughts. The projected hydroclimatic changes remain robust across emission scenarios, indicating restructuring that is independent of mitigation ambitions. Our findings show that climate change not only makes extreme events more intense but also fundamentally alters how climate systems retain memory of past events. These results have important implications for planning and forecasting in an increasingly uncertain climate.

title: Runoff regime-aware mixture of experts (RR-MoE) for interpretable and robust streamflow prediction
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Lin Yan, Junran Yang, Junming Shao, Xiufeng Wu, Jiangyu Dai, Guoqing Wang, Peilu Tang, Qinli Yang
abstract: Accurate streamflow prediction is challenged by the heterogeneity of hydrological processes across different flow regimes. Most deep learning–based models rely on globally shared parameters and optimize overall prediction errors, implicitly assuming homogeneous runoff generation behavior. This often leads to parameter interference between low-flow and high-flow conditions, reduced sensitivity to extreme events, and limited interpretability. To address this issue, this study proposes a Runoff Regime-Aware Mixture of Experts framework (RR-MoE), which enables implicit, data-driven identification of hydrological regimes and decoupled parameterization across regimes. The framework integrates convolutional feature extraction and sequence modeling with a sparse top-k gating mechanism, which dynamically partitions basin states and routes hydro-meteorological inputs to specialized expert subnetworks. This divide-and-conquer architecture effectively mitigates cross-regime competition and improves the representation of both low-flow and high-flow dynamics. The framework is evaluated in the upper reaches of Tiaoxi River basin. Results demonstrate that RR-MoE consistently outperforms benchmark models (CNN-LSTM, CNN-GRU, EA-LSTM, and RR-MoE (GRU)), achieving a Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of up to 0.919 and improving extreme-flow prediction. Furthermore, the learned expert specialization aligns with physically meaningful runoff regimes, indicating that the model captures regime-dependent hydrological behaviors and enhances structural interpretability. This study offers a promising direction for improving predictive performance and interpretability under non-stationary hydrological conditions.

title: Comprehensive risk assessment of snowmelt-runoff and storm-runoff flood disasters in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Haiting Zhang, Min Xu, Shichang Kang, Xingdong Li
abstract: Global warming and the increasing frequency of extreme weather events have led to an increase in flood incidents. Assessing flood risk is of great significance for disaster prevention and reduction. This study aims to propose a novel framework for flood disaster risk assessment in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Firstly, considering the flood risk indicators of snowmelt runoff and storm runoff related to geographical environment, climatic conditions, and social development, a comprehensive assessment indicator system was developed. Secondly, flood risk was evaluated by combining Analytical Network Process (ANP) with an and the objective weighting framework based on Genetic Algorithm (GA). Finally, the relationships between different risk indicators and flood risk were analyzed using the explainable machine learning model (XGBoost-SHAP). The results indicated that the spatial distribution of flood disaster risks in the CPEC presented an obvious distribution pattern along river networks, mainly distributed in N.W.F.P., Islamabad, Punjab, and Sindh. Approximately 21.05% of the area experienced a dual high risk of snowmelt-runoff and storm-runoff floods. High- and very high-risk areas of snowmelt runoff flood and storm runoff flood accounted for 21.60% and 20.27% of the total area, respectively. In most areas of the CPEC, landuse/cover, rivernetworkdensity, elevation, and slope were the main positive contribution indicators of snowmelt-runoff and storm-runoff floods. Multi-year average maximum 3-day cumulative snowmelt runoff mainly affected snowmelt runoff flood in mountainous areas, while that for storm runoff and multi-year average temperature dominated the storm runoff flood in northern Pakistan. This study explores the distribution of flood risk and disaster-influencing factors, which is crucial for the CPEC to develop relevant and effective risk mitigation policies.

title: Spatial heterogeneity and attribution analysis of urban flood risk throughout the full lifecycle: insights from a safety-economy-environment framework and an interpretable MCDM-XGBoost-GWRF model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Hao Jia, Danyang Di, Zhuo Chen, Zhaoyang Zhang, Meiqin Qi, Jie Li
abstract: Driven by climate change and rapid urbanization, urban flood risks exhibit significant multidimensionality, non-linearity, and spatial heterogeneity. To address these complexities, this study uses Jiaozuo, a mid-sized inland city located in a plain–mountain transition zone, as a case study and constructs an integrated risk assessment system incorporating the safety-economy-environment framework. A flood risk index is established using a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) model that combines the Monte Carlo-based entropy weight method (MCEWM) with the VlseKriterijumska Optimizacija I Kompromisno Resenje (VIKOR) method. Furthermore, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and geographically weighted random forest (GWRF) are adopted to parse global driving mechanisms and local spatial heterogeneity. The results indicate that: (1) Flood risk exhibits a “high center, low periphery” mono-centric decay pattern. (2) Socio-economic exposure and drainage capacity are primary global drivers, with drainage capacity, population density, and impervious surface ratio making the highest contributions. (3) Driving mechanisms are distinct across risk levels: high-risk areas are dominated by the coupling of hazard intensity and population exposure; medium-risk areas are governed by topography; and low-risk areas rely on ecological regulation. (4) GWRF revealed pronounced spatial heterogeneity in adaptive capacity and surface-environment effects and provided a more refined representation of localized flood-risk patterns than MCDM and XGBoost. Local high-risk areas were primarily associated with low-lying terrain, constrained drainage conditions, and concentrated socio-economic activities. The proposed synergistic framework systematically constructs a complete causal analysis, providing a scientific basis for optimizing urban flood control strategies.

title: Decomposition, quantification and reduction of hydrological modelling uncertainty across multiple climate zones
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yuhao Wang, Zhanling Li, Yingtao Ye, Xiaoyan Zhai, Zhanjie Li
abstract: Hydrological simulations are subject to substantial uncertainties arising from factors such as meteorological forcing, model structure, and parameter selection. Yet the uncertainty contributions from the factors and targeted uncertainty reduction strategies especially across different climate zones remain insufficiently understood. To address this limitation, we investigated 12 watersheds across three major climate zones in China using the lumped conceptual hydrological model WASMOD-E. A new framework was developed to evaluate model applicability, quantify simulation uncertainty, decompose the uncertainty contributions of meteorological products, model structures, and model parameters using MANOVA, and further propose targeted uncertainty reduction strategies. The results showed that: (1) the WASMOD-E model exhibited good applicability across the study areas, with better simulation performance in the northwestern arid zone (NAZ) and the Tibetan Plateau zone (TPZ); However, the NAZ has the largest simulation uncertainty according to the evaluation indicators, and the TPZ has the smallest uncertainty. (2) meteorological products were the primary uncertainty contributor in the NAZ and TPZ, model structures contributed most in the the Eastern Monsoon Zone (EMZ), and model parameters contributed marginally in all study areas; (3) the proposed dynamic quantile weighting and adaptive Bayesian model averaging strategies were proved to be effective in enhancing simulation accuracy and reducing the uncertainties arising from meteorological products and model structural variations, providing a flexible and practical solution for uncertainty reduction under changing hydrometeorological and model structural conditions. By clarifying the patterns governing the hydrological uncertainties across the climate zones, this study provides new insights for improving hydrological models and enhancing hydrological simulation forecasting capabilities.

title: Mechanistic shifts in seasonal precipitation isotope variability across China’s monsoon–westerlies transition zone
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Wenqing Han, Zhaowei Jing, Xiaoyi Shi, Feng Jiang, Tao Pu, Yanlong Kong, Shaoyong Wang, Shijin Wang, Shengjie Wang
abstract: Understanding the drivers of precipitation δ18O (δ18Op) across China remains a long-standing challenge because of complex interactions between the monsoon systems and the westerlies. Using a seasonal decomposition approach, our results indicate a sandwich-like spatial configuration of the dominant controls on seasonal δ18Op variability. The monsoon-dominated southeastern region and the westerly-dominated northwestern region are governed mainly by seasonal shifts in remote oceanic moisture sources. In contrast, the monsoon-westerlies transition zone is controlled primarily by moisture transport processes. Furthermore, the transport-dominated belt shifts seasonally with the monsoon. This migration shows that the spatial influence of moisture transport on δ18Op is not fixed. This migration pattern suggests a potential mechanism by which spatially distributed paleoclimate isotope records may reflect past changes in the spatial extent of monsoon influence, providing a new perspective for investigating East Asian paleoclimate archives.

title: Global patterns of reservoir normal water storage capacities estimated by statistical and machine learning models
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Ping Liu, Li Tang, XiaoHui Sun
abstract: Reservoir water storages are increasingly recognized as important tools for adapting to water-related hazards under climate change, particularly through their normal water storage (NWS). However, a critical data gap on regarding global reservoir NWS hinders our understanding of their spatial patterns and impacts on water management. This study aims to bridge this data gap by estimating the NWS for 7250 global reservoirs using an ensemble approach that includes linear regression, machine learning, and satellite-based methods. We train and evaluate these models based on a representative sample of 801 reservoirs with reported NWS data and multiple static attributes. Among the evaluated methods, the Gradient Boosted Decision Trees model utilizing various reservoir features performed best (achieving a coefficient of determination of 0.95 and a mean absolute percentage error of 12%), and was subsequently selected to estimate the NWS for unrecorded reservoirs. Our analysis of the global reservoir NWS ratio (NWSR) at individual, basin, and national scales reveals significant spatial variations, with a global mean NWSR of 72%. The distribution of NWSRs varies considerably across different reservoir groups categorized by physical size, primary purpose, and climatic region. At the national and basin scales, the USA, Canada, China, Russia, and Brazil, along with the Yenisey, Nile, Mississippi, Parana, and Yangtze basins, account for substantial portions of the global NWS capacity. The developed dataset and the analyzed spatial patterns provide vital empirical inputs for water resource management, large-scale hydrological modeling, and climate change adaptation, ultimately supporting effective planning for sustainable freshwater supplies.

title: Machine learning-enhanced joint inversion of GNSS, InSAR, and GRACE for terrestrial water storage reconstruction in the Three Gorges reservoir region
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Liangke Huang, Tianci Feng, Tengxu Zhang, Lin He, Lilong Liu, Yu Xia, Wenhao Wu, Peng Yuan, Peijie Zhu, Xiaohan Guo
abstract: Accurately quantifying terrestrial water storage (TWS) dynamics is essential for understanding regional hydrological processes, especially in areas with complex topography and intense human interventions. However, monitoring TWS at sub-basin scales remains challenging due to the coarse resolution of satellite gravimetry (GRACE/GFO) and the spatial sparsity or baseline absence of ground/radar geodetic measurements. To overcome this, we propose a physics-constrained and data-driven joint inversion framework to reconstruct TWS at 0 . 5 ° resolution in the Three Gorges Region (TGR). An Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBML) model, driven by hydrometeorological variables, is employed to downscale discrete GNSS and InSAR deformations into a spatially continuous displacement field. These spatially enhanced constraints are subsequently fused with GRACE data via Green’s function theory and ABIC-based adaptive weighting. A closed-loop simulation demonstrates that this three-source inversion significantly outperforms single-source estimates, reducing the average Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) to 26.92 m m . Monte Carlo analysis further reveals a 45.6 % reduction in spatial uncertainty. Independent external assessment using ERA5-Land indicates consistent temporal water storage variations (r = 0.723, p < 0.001), while comparison with GLDAS yields a spatial correlation coefficient of 0.757. Importantly, after removing seasonal cycles and correcting for autocorrelation, a significant positive correlation with precipitation is identified at a one-month lag (r = 0.532, p_corr < 0.001), and the framework successfully captures the transient mass surge triggered by the 2020 summer extreme flood. Furthermore, reservoir-scale spatial masking quantitatively verifies the “anti-seasonal” mass transfer driven by the Three Gorges Dam regulation, revealing a negative correlation (r = −0.503) between mainstream Equivalent Water Height (EWH) and dam water levels. These findings demonstrate that the proposed framework can reliably resolve both natural and anthropogenic water storage signals at regional scales.

title: Runoff fingerprinting reveals transitions in urban underpass flooding from local surface-runoff convergence to sewer-network feedbacks
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Guangxue Luan, Fuqiang Wang, Jingming Hou, Honglin Xiao, Chen Yang, Qingqing Qi, Songlin Yang, Guanghui Wu
abstract: Urban underpasses are recurrent hotspots of pluvial flooding, yet the changing roles of local surface–runoff convergence and sewer-network feedbacks in shaping ponding remain poorly understood. This study developed a conservative rainfall–runoff fingerprinting module and embedded it in an existing high-resolution hydrodynamic model that dynamically and bidirectionally couples two-dimensional surface flow with one-dimensional sewer hydraulics, establishing a source-pathway-response diagnostic framework. The framework was applied to four flood-prone underpasses (P1–P4) in Changzhi, China, under seven 2-h design storms with return periods of 1–100 years. The simulations revealed nonlinear and site-specific changes in ponding dynamics. As rainfall intensity increased, ponding changed from a short-lived, first-peak-dominated response to a delayed, second-peak-dominated process; the second ponding peak first exceeded the first in the tested 5-, 2-, 100-, and 5-year scenarios at P1–P4, respectively. The maximum lag relative to the rainfall peak reached 155 min, and the maximum inter-site differences in peak timing reached 140 min. Runoff fingerprinting revealed that early ponding primarily resulted from near-source surface runoff exceeding inlet-capture capacity. Delayed accumulation flooding was triggered when sewer surcharge and node overflow converted the drainage network from a conveyance pathway into an additional water source. Downstream backwater further amplified the second peak and delayed recession. These processes produced three flooding patterns in the simulated cases: surface-runoff-driven local ponding, node-overflow-driven compound flooding, and downstream-backwater-modulated flooding. The findings demonstrate that similar ponding responses can arise from different combinations of runoff supply and drainage constraints. By linking time-varying source contributions to transport pathways and hydraulic controls, the framework provides a basis for interpreting underpass flooding mechanisms and identifying site-specific forecasting and mitigation priorities.

title: Uncertainty in streamflow simulation performance arising from precipitation inputs and hydrological models under different flow regimes and catchment conditions
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yongjing Wan, Jie Chen, Daiyuan Li, Jingjing Sun, Yuanlin Qiu, Mingming Wang, Shihua Zhang
abstract: Hydrological simulations are inherently affected by uncertainties arising from precipitation inputs and hydrological models. The relative importance of those uncertainty sources across different flow regimes and catchment conditions remains poorly understood. This study used six gridded daily precipitation datasets to force five widely applied conceptual hydrological models over 379 catchments in China. Nine performance metrics were used to represent different flow regimes, and a two-way analysis of variance method (ANOVA) was applied to quantify the relative contributions of those uncertainty sources to streamflow simulation performances. Results show substantial discrepancies in precipitation magnitude among those datasets, while model calibrations partially compensate for these biases. Attributions of hydrological simulation uncertainties exhibit flow-regime dependence. For metrics represented to high-flow performances, the contribution associated with hydrological model choice is dominant, which accounts for approximately 40–80% of total uncertainty. In contrast, the primary contribution shifts to precipitation input for metrics of low flow performances, explaining 40–70% of the total uncertainty. For metrics of the mid-flow performances, precipitation inputs, hydrological models, and their interaction contribute comparably to total uncertainty. Moreover, uncertainty in hydrological simulation performance is significantly related to catchment characteristics with larger uncertainty in smaller and more arid catchments. In terms of relative contribution, the contribution associated with precipitation forcing choice increases with mean slope and runoff coefficient but decreases with catchment area and aridity index, whereas the contribution associated with hydrological model choice decreases with mean slope and elevation. The contribution associated with the interaction increases with mean elevation, catchment area, and elongation ratio, but decreases with runoff coefficient. This study provides new insights into the flow-regime dependence and catchment-related variability of uncertainty in hydrological simulation performance and offers guidance for selecting modeling strategies.

title: Responses of heavy metal concentrations and partitioning to water-source-associated suspended sediment gradients in a Tibetan Plateau river
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Wang Danyang, Tang Xianqiang, Liu Han, Li Rui
abstract: Heavy metals threaten fragile high-altitude river ecosystems, yet how variations in the water sources feeding river and associated suspended sediment influence riverine metal concentrations and dissolved-particulate partitioning remains poorly understood. To address this, we conducted in situ sampling in Duoma River on the Tibetan Plateau during the flood and pre-flood seasons. Across both seasons, Concentrations of Cu, As, Pb, and Zn were 6.0-11.8, 2.4-4.8, 2.7-2.8, and 25.9-289.9 μg/L, respectively. Suspended sediment concentrations followed a consistent gradient among water-source types (spring-fed < wetland-fed < mixed-source < glacier/snowmelt-fed), spanning 6.7-14,907 mg/L, whereas Fe/Mn oxide contents in suspended sediment showed the opposite gradient. These contrasts in sediment concentration and composition were associated with marked differences in metal concentrations and partitioning among water source types. Dissolved metal concentrations, metal concentrations per unit mass, and particle-water distribution coefficients were generally higher in spring- and wetland-fed waters, while glacier/snowmelt-fed and mixed-source waters had higher particulate metal concentrations per unit volume of water and generally higher particulate fractions. Differences among metals in their affinity for particles further shaped how these sediment contrasts were expressed in metal occurrence. Pb had the highest particulate fraction and distribution coefficient and As the lowest.

title: Complex behavior of an urban green infrastructure imaged using time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography and time-series clustering
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Alexis Luzy, Adrien Dimech, François Duhaime, Janie Masse-Dufresne, Jean-Sébastien Dubé, Rose-Anne Farley, Rémi Clément, Maxime Paradis
abstract: Urban green infrastructure (GI) is increasingly being implemented to manage stormwater, promote infiltration, and limit loads on drainage networks. However, their design still relies largely on large-scale hydrological performance, with limited attention to site-specific hydrogeological processes. Key mechanisms governing infiltration, solute transport, and seasonal dynamics remain poorly understood, especially in cold-climate cities using de-icing salts, which may threaten buried infrastructure, contribute to groundwater salinization, and degrade receiving ecosystems. Field observations are needed to improve understanding of these processes. This study presents one year of monitoring of water and chloride dynamics around an instrumented GI using high-resolution cross-borehole time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (TL-ERT) at a roadside site in Laval, Quebec, Canada. Automated geoelectrical monitoring was conducted between October 2024 and November 2025 with four surveys per day, using commercial and open-source hardware. The geophysical approach was complemented by hydrogeological monitoring (water levels and sensors). A time-series clustering method was applied to the inverted dataset to identify distinct temporal behaviors of subsurface units. Results indicate infiltration linked to winter rainfall and spring snowmelt. Seasonal conductivity variations in winter and spring are interpreted as being largely influenced by pore-water conductivity associated with de-icing salt mobilization, while late summer and autumn changes are more consistent with VWC-driven responses. Overall, combining cross-borehole TL-ERT, time-series clustering, and hydrogeological instrumentation provides detailed insight into seasonal water and solute movement in small-scale, heterogeneous urban environments, where point monitoring is often limited. This approach is well suited for studying urban GI, while remaining dependent on auxiliary measurements for process attribution.

title: Coupling water balance and vegetation carbon dynamics in a parsimonious global hydrologic model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Guta Wakbulcho Abeshu, Hong-Yi Li, L. Ruby Leung
abstract: Understanding ecohydrological responses to environmental change requires parsimonious models that can represent interactions between water balance and vegetation carbon uptake. Simple conceptual hydrologic models efficiently simulate runoff and evapotranspiration, but they usually lack dynamic vegetation representation. We extend the abcd monthly water-balance model to simulate coupled water-carbon dynamics by integrating the Horton Index framework with a two-parameter Gross Primary Productivity-Evapotranspiration (GPP-ET) functional relationship. The resulting eight-parameter framework is calibrated using observation-constrained runoff and GPP, while ET is withheld from the calibration objective and evaluated independently. Using GSWP3-W5E5 forcing, FLUXCOM-X BASE GPP and ET, and GRUN-ensemble runoff over 235 global basins, we calibrate the model for 2001-2014 and evaluate it independently for 2015-2019. During validation, the model reproduces GPP robustly, with a median Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) of 0.746 and positive KGE in 94.9% of basins. ET performance is also broadly positive despite not being directly calibrated, with a median validation KGE of 0.675 and positive KGE in 86.8% of basins. Runoff skill is moderate and more heterogeneous, with a median validation KGE of 0.593 and positive KGE in 89.8% of basins. Seasonal-cycle and anomaly analyses show that the model strongly captures the climatological timing of GPP and ET while retaining meaningful anomaly skill after removing the mean annual cycle. The calibrated coupling parameters λ , β , and α exhibit geographically organized patterns consistent with their physically interpretable roles in evaporative partitioning and water-carbon coupling, while β and α remain effective model-scale rather than intrinsic physiological coefficients. These results show that a parsimonious monthly hydrologic model can be extended to diagnose first-order coupled water-carbon dynamics while retaining interpretable structure and computational efficiency.

title: Process-based modeling of managed aquifer recharge in a hillslope-valley system under two contrasting climatic regimes
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Xinying Ling, Menberu B. Meles, Scott A. Bradford, Hoori Ajami
abstract: Managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is increasingly used to enhance groundwater storage, yet its effectiveness has mainly been studied in flat agricultural and flood-plain areas, not hillslope regions. In this study, we investigated groundwater dynamics in response to pumping and MAR in an idealized hillslope-valley system under two contrasting climatic regimes based on Modesto (244 mm yr⁻1) and Camino (941 mm yr⁻1), California. A physically-based, fully coupled MIKE SHE model was developed to simulate coupled overland flow, unsaturated-zone, and groundwater flow. Long-term simulations were conducted to establish dynamic equilibrium under natural (undeveloped) conditions, followed by pumping and MAR scenarios (injection wells, surface MAR-release, and surface MAR-hold) to evaluate groundwater responses to different management strategies. The subsurface storage reached dynamic equilibrium within 180 years (dry climate) and 140 years (wet climate) under natural climate forcing conditions. Human-impacted scenarios required additional time for subsurface storage adjustment (90–130 years under dry conditions and 30–70 years under wet conditions). Pumping near the river had a negligible influence on groundwater levels but reduced streamflow, whereas pumping in the valley and especially the hillslope led to extensive cones of depression due to differences in aquifer response time and groundwater storage, respectively. Under the simulated conditions, hillslope MAR produced a faster groundwater response due to larger hydraulic gradients and increased lateral flow, while MAR in valley and floodplain regions was limited by groundwater travel times and surface water interactions, respectively. The short-term groundwater responses varied systematically among MAR approaches. Injection wells produced rapid, localized groundwater mounding; surface MAR application with runoff release caused small mounding due to runoff losses; and surface MAR with ponding generated higher groundwater mounding due to prolonged ponding. Hillslope MAR further enhanced recoverable storage in the valley. This is particularly important in overexploited valley aquifers. MAR effectiveness should be assessed over decadal to centennial timescales, as short-term assessments can substantially overestimate sustainable groundwater recovery. These findings provide a process-based framework for evaluating long-term MAR performance and designing sustainable groundwater extraction and recharge strategies.

title: Hydrodynamic regulation of microbial coupling between nitrate reduction and carbon fixation in a karst conduit–fissure aquifer
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Danni Zhu, Haiping Lu, Yi Li, Lihua Niu, Changsong Zhou, Shengzhang Zou
abstract: Hydrodynamic contrasts between conduit and fissure domains may regulate nitrate (NO3 −) attenuation and carbon (C) transformation in karst aquifers, but the microbial mechanisms linking these processes remain poorly understood. Herein, the coupled C and nitrogen (N) cycling were investigated using stable isotope analysis, 15N-tracer incubations, and metagenomic sequencing in a typical karst conduit–fissure system. In conduit water (CW) with high flow velocity (mean: 665 m d−1), TN, NO3 −, and DIC decreased significantly, whereas DOC, δ15N–NO3 −, and δ13CDIC increased synchronously. Such coordinated changes were not observed in fissure water (FW) with low flow velocity (mean: 205 m d−1). 15N-tracer incubations showed that dissimilatory nitrate reduction (denitrification and DNRA) rates were higher in CW and positively correlated with δ13CDIC and DOC. These observations collectively indicated stronger coupling between NO3 − reduction and microbial C transformation in CW. Metagenomic co-occurrence networks further revealed pathway-specific associations between NO3 − reduction and microbial C fixation in CW, with dissimilatory nitrate reduction linked to the rTCA cycle and assimilatory nitrate reduction associated with the CBB cycle. Genome-scale metabolic modeling suggested that NO3 − reduction in CW was mainly associated with heterotrophic nitrate-reducing taxa, such as Tabrizicola and Sediminibacterium, and was potentially supported by metabolite cross-feeding from autotrophic carbon-fixing taxa, including Limnohabitans and Prosthecobacter. In contrast, NO3 − reduction in FW appeared to be driven predominantly by autotrophic nitrate-reducing bacteria with significantly lower metabolic connectivity. Groundwater flow velocity indirectly regulated the coupled NO3 − reduction and C fixation by enhancing microbial network connectivity and metabolic cooperation among functional guilds. These findings advance our understanding of NO3 − pollution mitigation and subsurface C fixation in karst aquifers.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution and drivers of compound dry-hot and wet-hot events in a changing climate
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Chao Wang, Fanli Sun, Shuzhe Huang, Wei Wang
abstract: Compound dry-hot events (CDHEs) and compound wet-hot events (CWHEs) are two contrasting types of compound heat extremes with different impacts. However, their global evolution and changes under climate change, as well as their attribution to thermal and precipitation factors, remain insufficiently compared within a consistent framework. This study assesses CDHEs and CWHEs from 1961 to 2100 using multi-model CMIP6 simulations under the historical period and four SSP scenarios. We analyze changes in several indicators and use a copula-based return-period decomposition to separate the effects of hot conditions, precipitation anomalies, and their dependence structure. Diagnostic land-atmosphere analyses using vapor pressure deficit, relative humidity, and soil moisture are conducted to explore associated physical pathways. Results show that both CDHEs and CWHEs have intensified since the 1990s, but with distinct spatial patterns. CDHEs increase more strongly in arid and semi-arid regions, whereas CWHEs intensify more rapidly in humid climatic zones and high-latitude regions. Future projections indicate continued increases in compound heat risks under all SSPs, especially under high-emission scenarios. By the late 21st century, CWHEs are projected to become increasingly dominant, with faster increases in severity and duration than CDHEs. The decomposition analysis shows that hot conditions are the dominant driver, and the diagnostic analysis further identifies vapor pressure deficit as the most consistent predictor associated with both event types. These findings highlight the growing importance of wet-heat hazards and provide a basis for differentiated adaptation strategies under continued warming.

title: Occurrence-rate nonstationarity alters design rainfall return levels: A decomposed Poisson-GPD analysis across contrasting hydroclimatic regimes
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Shubham Dixit, Kamlesh K. Pandey
abstract: Climate-informed rainfall frequency analysis increasingly informs design rainfall estimation. Atmospheric processes favoring extreme rainfall occurrence may differ from those amplifying event magnitude, yet peaks-over-threshold (POT) models often treat occurrence as stationary while modeling nonstationary (NS) severity. Because POT return levels (RL) depend jointly on occurrence and excess magnitude, this choice can alter design estimates. We evaluated whether separating occurrence and severity changes return levels using daily rainfall at 15 climatically contrasting Indian locations. Occurrence and severity covariates were screened separately and used in Poisson occurrence and GPD severity models to compare stationary, NS-occurrence-only, NS-severity-only, and full NS-occurrence-severity formulations. Models allowing occurrence to vary received more support than stationary and severity-only formulations and reduced unexplained variability in exceedance counts. Nonstationary return levels were defined using fitted monthly occurrence and severity conditions over the evaluation period. Over 2001–2022, adding occurrence nonstationarity to the severity-only model lowered RL at 8 stations and raised it at 7. At Indore and Panaji, full occurrence-severity formulation also avoided implausibly large severity-only return levels, showing that occurrence modeling can affect magnitude and plausibility. Because nonstationary return levels depend on climatic conditions, sensitivity to alternative evaluation periods was examined. Occurrence covariates remained informative beyond seasonality, particularly for moisture transport, whereas severity covariates showed varied associations with thermodynamic, dynamic, and teleconnection-related variables. Overall, separating occurrence and severity showed that changes in exceedance frequency can materially influence design return levels and improve process interpretation of nonstationary rainfall-frequency estimates. Sensitivity checks consistently supported occurrence nonstationarity, although return-level effects were sometimes specification-dependent.

title: Effects of water depth and exit width on bottleneck evacuation dynamics under flood conditions
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Xintong Li, Chenglin Guo, Jun Zhang, Weiguo Song
abstract: Floods pose a growing threat to urban safety, particularly in buildings and underground infrastructures where evacuation often depends on pedestrian movement through bottleneck exits. Although previous studies have shown that floodwater reduces pedestrian mobility, its effects on bottleneck capacity, flow organization, and congestion dynamics remain insufficiently understood. This study presents the first systematic investigation of pedestrian evacuation through bottlenecks across four water-depth conditions (0, 0.35, 0.60, and 0.90 m) and exit widths ranging from 0.5 to 1.9 m. Increasing exit width improves evacuation efficiency under all conditions, whereas the average specific flow under flooded conditions is approximately 36% lower than that under no-water conditions. In contrast, differences in specific flow among the three flooded conditions are relatively small. Flooded conditions increase time headway and delay the transition from intermittent to continuous flow. Using an average burst size of 〈 s 〉 ⩾ 2 pedestrians as the criterion, the critical exit width for the onset of continuous flow increases from 0.9 m under no-water conditions to 1.3 m under flooded conditions. By comparison, distance headway is less sensitive to water depth, indicating that pedestrians primarily adapt to water resistance by reducing speed rather than compressing interpersonal spacing. Greater water depth enlarges the upstream high-density region and intensifies congestion. Stopping time decreases with increasing exit width and approaches zero at the critical width associated with the onset of continuous flow. These findings provide empirical evidence for incorporating flood-induced mobility constraints into pedestrian evacuation models and improving flood-risk assessment and evacuation planning in buildings and underground infrastructures.

title: A knowledge-guided machine learning framework for reconstructing climate-driven subsurface water dynamics from time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Weiyu Guo, Hang Chen
abstract: Understanding and anticipating climate-driven subsurface water dynamics is essential for assessing water availability and ecosystem function, yet it remains challenging in heterogeneous mountain environments. Time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (TL-ERT) provides spatially distributed observations of subsurface change but has been used mainly to monitor subsurface change rather than to model its evolution. Here, we develop a knowledge-guided machine learning framework to reconstruct the spatiotemporal evolution of subsurface resistivity from daily meteorological forcing and continuous TL-ERT observations on a monitored hillslope. Before training, the TL-ERT data were corrected to a common reference temperature to remove the direct temperature dependence of resistivity, allowing temporal resistivity changes to be interpreted as a proxy for subsurface water-content change. Three neural architectures were evaluated within a shared recursive framework using structured loss terms that preserve reconstruction accuracy, local spatial structure, and coherent temporal variation. All models reproduced the dominant seasonal patterns, and the PredRNN-based architecture performed best, with an RMSE of 9.5 Ω·m over held-out test windows. Under rolling recursive reconstruction without subsequent ground-truth resistivity observations, the framework maintained seasonally coherent trajectories within the observed record. Under a + 4 °C warming scenario, the simulated temperature-corrected resistivity showed earlier shallow spring decreases about 12% and slight shallow summer increases, with weaker responses at depth. Through a water-content conversion, these changes are consistent with earlier spring wetting and shallow summer drying. These results provide a site-specific proof of concept that continuous TL-ERT observations combined with knowledge-guided machine learning can reconstruct the seasonal evolution of subsurface resistivity within the observed record and support scenario-based hydrologic interpretation.

title: Sensitivity of mountain riverine air–water CO 2 exchange estimates to elevation decompression and localized atmospheric CO 2 variability
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Xue Qiao, Hui Liu, Weiyang Xiao, Wenbin Hu, Hailiang Song, Yue Ding, Zhongjun Xu, Jie Du, Ya Tang
abstract: Mountain rivers act as critical CO2 outgassing hotspots in the global carbon cycle. However, conventional air–water CO2 exchange estimates often rely on static atmospheric CO2 boundary conditions, which introduces potential uncertainties in topographically complex regions. Integrating multi-site spatial surveys across an 1,100 m elevation gradient and a one-year high-frequency in-situ monitoring campaign at a site in the subalpine Jiuzhaigou karst catchment, we decouple the independent effects of physical topography and micro-meteorology on riverine CO2 evasion. First, altitude-driven barometric decompression steepens the air–water CO2 partial pressure gradient. While atmospheric CO2 calculations do not universally assume standard sea-level pressure, failing to apply site-specific local barometric corrections can alter each site’s mean riverine CO2 exchange rate by up to 23.2 mmol m−2 h−1, with the absolute magnitudes dependent on local turbulence. Independently, localized atmospheric CO2 pooling dynamically shifts the instantaneous air–water gradient. This pooling occurs not only at night but also during the daytime, driven by local microclimate, biological processes, and human activities. Second, despite substantial daytime photosynthetic CO2 drawdowns, the karst waters maintain continuous year-round outgassing. This persistent supersaturation is predominantly sustained by massive, continuous external groundwater and soil dissolved inorganic carbon inputs that consistently exceed evasion and assimilation rates.
