Ultimately, while boundary simplifications do not significantly impact annual cumulative CO2 emissions (0.02%−11% deviation), integrating dynamic barometric corrections and localized atmospheric CO2 monitoring is essential for accurately resolving high-frequency instantaneous outgassing kinetics in complex terrains.

title: Canal-mediated water redistribution and ecohydrological responses in an arid inland oasis: Evidence from stable isotopes and remote sensing
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Rui Li, Zhijie Zheng, Guofeng Zhu, Xinyue Wang, Jiangwei Yang, Yuxin Miao, Yani Gun
abstract: Irrigation canals are a defining feature of managed water systems in arid oasis regions, yet their effects on hydrological and ecological processes remain poorly constrained. Here, we combine multi-year stable hydrogen and oxygen isotope observations with isotope-based evaporation modeling, Bayesian plant water-source analysis and satellite remote sensing to examine canal-mediated water redistribution in the Minqin Oasis, Northwest China. Canal-water δ18O and δ2H became progressively enriched among five fixed sampling sites located 5–100 km downstream of the reservoir outlet, while d-excess generally decreased, providing consistent evidence of evaporative modification during conveyance. Isotope-based mass-balance calculations for April–October 2019–2022 indicated that monthly cumulative evaporation losses ranged from 1.14% to 14.54%, with a mean of 5.11 ± 3.66%. Mean loss increased to 8.20% during June–August. Comparative isotope analyses revealed partial overlap among canal water, groundwater and soil water, indicating local hydrological connectivity between surface and subsurface water stores, although the direction and magnitude of water exchange could not be quantified. Soil-water and xylem-water isotopes, together with MixSIAR estimates, showed that poplars in artificial canal-side shelterbelts used more shallow and intermediate soil water during the middle growing season and relied more strongly on deep soil water and groundwater during the early and late growing season. At the downstream Qingtu Lake terminal region, satellite observations showed pronounced lake re-expansion following the initiation of ecological water conveyance (EWC) in 2010. After adjustment for precipitation, temperature and potential evapotranspiration, the regional mean annual maximum NDVI trend accelerated significantly after 2011. Associations between lake area and NDVI were concentrated within the lake boundary and the adjacent 0–5 km zone, indicating that vegetation responses were spatially localized around the replenished terminal lake. These findings show that canal systems influence arid-oasis water cycling through seasonal evaporation and local interactions among surface water, soil water, groundwater and vegetation, while terminal-region ecological changes are closely linked to managed water delivery. This underscores the need to account for conveyance losses and local water redistribution in ecological water planning and dryland irrigation management under increasing aridity.

title: Precipitation isotope baseline for India: regional patterns, process controls, and applications
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Harsh Oza, Virendra Padhya, Akash Ganguly, Amit Pandey, Swagatika Chakra, R.D. Deshpande
abstract: Precipitation isotopes (δ18O, δ2H, and d-excess) record moisture transport, rainout, recycling, source-region effects, and sub-cloud evaporation, but India lacks a unified isotope framework across its major hydroclimatic regimes. We present the most comprehensive precipitation-isotope baseline for India to date, using 1,485 monthly amount-weighted records from 61 stations across nine Köppen-Geiger climate classes. The Indian Meteoric Water Line is δ2H = (7.52 ± 0.04) δ18O + (7.20 ± 0.22), with R2 = 0.968, and falls below the Global Meteoric Water Line, indicating widespread secondary evaporative modification of rainfall. Seasonal analyses show that isotope controls shift through the annual cycle. Pre-monsoon rainfall shows the strongest sub-cloud evaporation signal, with the lowest seasonal meteoric-water-line slope, highest dew-point depression, enriched δ18O, and reduced d-excess. During the southwest monsoon, δ18O becomes spatially organized by moisture transport, rainout, and orography, including a significant west-east peninsular depletion gradient from the Arabian Sea margin across the Deccan interior toward the Bay of Bengal coast. Post-monsoon rainfall remains widely depleted but shows variable d-excess, indicating mixed influence from residual monsoon moisture, recycling, altered moisture sources, and local evaporation. Linear mixed-effects models reveal strong tracer asymmetry. Fixed effects, including season and monthly meteorological anomalies, explain 31.9% of δ18O variance but only 10.4% of d-excess variance. Thus, δ18O primarily tracks large-scale monsoon moisture transport, whereas d-excess retains stronger source, recycling, sub-cloud, and event-scale information. This baseline supports recharge assessment, paleoclimate interpretation, and isotope-enabled model evaluation across India.

title: Bivariate regional frequency analysis of extreme rainfall depth and intensity: comparing annual maxima and r-Largest approaches with simulated annealing regionalization across South Korea
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Adisa Hammed Akinsoji, Qudus Adeyi, Rahmon Abiodun Salau, Deepak Chaulagain, Kyung Sook Choi
abstract: Extreme rainfall in South Korea has intensified under recent climate variability, yet national infrastructure design standards still rely on univariate analyses of pre-2000 data that treat rainfall depth and intensity as independent, understating joint flood risk. This study addresses that gap with a bivariate regional frequency analysis (BRFA) of multi-duration extreme rainfall, jointly modeling event depth and mean intensity across accumulation durations of 6, 12, 24, and 48 h using 41 years of hourly records from 61 KMA ASOS stations. Two sampling approaches are compared: annual maxima (AMx) with residual-based decorrelation, and r-Largest, retaining the five largest IETD-separated monsoon events per year without decorrelation. Simulated Annealing optimization of the bivariate L-comoments H1 statistic delineated six homogeneous regions (H1 = 0.105–0.916, all satisfying H1 < 1.0) pooling 2,501 station-years. GUM dominated AMx marginal selection at 6–12 h and PE3 at 24–48 h; PE3 and Exponential dominated r-Largest. The Gaussian copula prevailed under AMx (54.2%); Frank (41.7%), and GUM (25.0%) prevailed under r-Largest. Critically, exponential back-transformation in the AMx decorrelation procedure amplifies intensity estimation errors (per-site NSE = −97.5), while r-Largest yields physically realistic intensity estimates (RMSE 2–16 mm h−1). Regional 100-year depth quantiles of 160–233 mm at 6 h and 271–372 mm at 24 h exceed the current Korean national standards by 15–25%, warranting revisions to design standards for agricultural drainage and hydraulic infrastructure.

title: Predicting drought dynamics and high-standard farmland suitability in Shanxi Province using a GAT-based multi-model framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Yongheng Shen, Azhar Ali Laghari, Qingxia Guo, Junzhe Zhang, Yalin Wang, Yanli Shen, Zhenghao Liu, Da Fang, Bheel Chander Kumar
abstract: Climate-induced drought evolution substantially impacts cropland patterns, but conventional downscaling and simulation methods limit prediction accuracy. Taking the semi-arid Shanxi Province in Northern China as the study area, this research proposes a hybrid Delta-MLs downscaling method and introduces Graph Attention Networks (GAT) to predict two directionally consistent drought indices, the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI-D) and the Temperature Vegetation Dryness Index (TVDI-D). The Meteorological Drought and Surface Response-Cropland Resilience (MDSR-CR) framework is then applied to assess municipal-level high-standard farmland (HSF) suitability. Results show that: (1) hybrid models (Delta-KNN and Delta-XGBoost) outperform single methods in correcting meteorological and hydrological variables, with KNN appearing to better preserve spatial patterns than XGBoost; (2) SPEI-D drought will intensify across all scenarios, especially under SSP585, with changes mainly related to topography and vegetation, while TVDI-D drought shows the greatest variability under SSP370 and the least under SSP245, primarily associated with the combined effects of natural and anthropogenic factors; (3) a structural mismatch exists between HSF-suitable areas and the distribution of cultivated land resources across cities, highlighting the need for differentiated construction strategies. This study demonstrates that integrating remote sensing and intelligent modeling offers a promising framework for drought assessment and agricultural suitability, providing insights for climate-resilient farmland planning.

title: Analytical stochastic framework for coupled heat and moisture transfer in permafrost active layers with hydraulic parameter and thermal conductivity heterogeneity during seasonal thawing
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Ching-Min Chang, Chuen-Fa Ni, Chi-Ping Lin, I-Hsien Lee, Wei-Cheng Lo
abstract: As climate change accelerates Arctic and alpine warming, accurately simulating coupled heat and moisture transfer during seasonal thawing is essential for predicting permafrost degradation and its hydrological impacts. However, deterministic models generally neglect the effects of natural spatial variability in soil hydraulic and thermal properties on thermo-hydrological responses. This study therefore develops a stochastic framework for coupled heat and moisture transfer in heterogeneous permafrost active layers during seasonal thawing. The formulation explicitly incorporates the spatial variability of saturated hydraulic conductivity and thermal conductivity and derives analytical expressions in the Fourier spectral domain for the temperature semivariogram, heat-flux semivariogram, and variance of capillary pressure head. Closed-form solutions are obtained for the case in which the random fields of the natural logarithms of saturated hydraulic conductivity and thermal conductivity are characterized by hole-type exponential covariance functions. The analytical solutions show that the perturbation fields for temperature, heat flux, and capillary pressure exhibit nonstationary spatial variability, despite the assumption of second-order stationarity in log-hydraulic and −thermal property perturbation fields. The results are also used to analyze the influence of key parameters in coupled stochastic heat and moisture transfer models on the spatial variability of coupled thermo-hydrological responses. The proposed framework provides a physically based means of quantifying uncertainty propagation from heterogeneous soil properties to coupled heat and moisture transfer, thereby improving the understanding of active-layer dynamics and providing a theoretical basis for uncertainty analysis and stochastic parameterization in permafrost hydrological models.

title: Seasonal shift from phosphorus retention to remobilization along an aquaculture pond–sediment–groundwater pathway in a monsoon-influenced shallow lake margin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Saier Chen, Teng Ma, Zhijia Zeng, Ting Jiang, Liuzhu Chen
abstract: Pond-based aquaculture is an important source of phosphorus (P) to adjacent shallow lakes, and previous studies have mainly examined P dynamics at the pond sediment–water interface or along surface-water pathways. In monsoon-influenced lake margins, pond-water leakage may carry aquaculture-derived P through underlying sediments into shallow groundwater, yet how seasonal hydrological connectivity and sediment Fe/P reactions regulate P retention, remobilization, and potential lakeward transfer remains poorly understood. We combined wet- and dry-season field surveys in an aquaculture-affected margin of Honghu Lake, China, with a sequential wet-to-dry column experiment to examine how the balance between P retention and export changes along this pathway as boundary conditions shift from pond-water leakage to groundwater throughflow. Field observations showed an apparent inconsistency between groundwater redox indicators and soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) concentrations: SRP was lower in the relatively reducing wet season but higher in the relatively oxidizing dry season. In the column experiment, the sediment strongly attenuated SRP from simulated P-rich pond water (0.86–0.99 mg·L−1), with cumulative net SRP retention reaching 93.35 mg·m−2 and Fe-bound P (Fe–P) enrichment. After switching to simulated low-P, more mineralized groundwater influent (0.27 mg·L−1 SRP), the wet-stage-conditioned sediment shifted to net SRP export, and the cumulative net SRP balance declined by 85.34 mg·m−2 from the wet-stage endpoint, accompanied by Fe–P depletion and an increased Fe(II)/Fe(III) ratio, consistent with selective remobilization of previously retained sediment P. Together, the column responses and the more favorable dry-season groundwater–lake hydraulic conditions suggest a seasonal reorganization of functional connectivity within the aquaculture pond–sediment–groundwater–lake continuum: wet-season pond-water leakage favored temporary retention of incoming P within the pond–sediment segment, whereas dry-season remobilization coincided with greater potential for lakeward P export. Management should therefore consider aquaculture-derived P inputs, seasonal hydrological connectivity, and the stability of retained sediment P.

title: Changes in the annual cycle of shallow subarctic groundwater regimes over 50 years
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Pietari Pöykkö, Mira Tammelin, Anna-Kaisa Ronkanen, Lauri Ahopelto, Pekka M. Rossi
abstract: Seasonal groundwater level regimes are exposed to climate change, with implications for drought and flood risks, water supply, agriculture, and ecosystems. Changes in the intra-annual groundwater fluctuations are accentuated in quickly responding shallow aquifers found worldwide, but particularly in subarctic regions, where the cold winter season attenuates infiltration and evaporation. To identify the types of subarctic groundwater regimes and their responses to the changing climate, 50-year groundwater level data from 52 monitoring stations throughout Finland were analyzed. This was done by partitioning around medians (PAM) clustering of Pearson correlations and a principal component analysis (PCA) of normalized monthly values. Four distinct regimes were identified, mostly following the southwest–northeast temperature and snow condition gradients. The migration of regimes towards the colder northeastern regions could be seen between the clustering periods of 1975–1999 and 2000–2024. This migration manifested as rising winter levels and lowering summer levels, in addition to changing seasonality timing, such as the spring recharge peak advancing by an average of half a month and by up to two months. Furthermore, seasonal groundwater level responses were seen to depend on the projected surface area of the aquifer, as comparatively larger aquifers among the studied 0.1– 41 km2 scale showed a lagged regime. The results suggest that the selected approach effectively captures the spatially evolving conditions. They also highlight the importance of long-term monitoring for effective decision-making and preparedness for shortages in water availability in the changing climate.

title: Soil temperature governs deep soil water infiltration in alpine meadows on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Jie Li, Qiaoyan Chen, Junna Feng, Bo Fan, Yangong Du, Licong Dai, Ruiyu Fu, Xiaowei Guo
abstract: Deep soil water infiltration is a critical process linking surface water inputs with deeper soil water storage and potential groundwater recharge, yet its seasonal dynamics and controls remain poorly understood in alpine meadows of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. Based on growing-season (May–September) observations from 2017 to 2023, this study quantified seasonal variations in deep soil water infiltration and identified controlling factors using an XGBoost machine-learning model combined with SHAP (Shapley additive explanations). We found deep infiltration showed pronounced seasonal variability and was not directly synchronized with precipitation patterns. During the growing season, cumulative evapotranspiration (361.7 mm) slightly exceeded cumulative precipitation (344.7 mm), suggesting that all rainfall was consumed by evapotranspiration rather than contributing directly to deep recharge. Among the examined variables, soil temperature (ST) was identified as the most important predictor of deep infiltration, accounting for 33.3% of the total SHAP-based importance, followed by air temperature (T; 29.5%) and volumetric soil moisture (VSM; 15.3%), which accounted for nearly 80% of the total SHAP-based importance, whereas precipitation and evapotranspiration display relatively limited contributions. Notably, ST exhibited a distinct nonlinear threshold effect, i.e. lower soil temperatures enhanced deep infiltration, but substantially reduced when ST exceeded approximately 9.2 ∼ 9.6 °C. Besides, deep infiltration was also significantly negatively correlated with aboveground biomass (P < 0.01), suggesting that enhanced plant water use during the peak growing season may restrict downward water movement. Meanwhile, plant water-use analysis showed that dominant alpine meadow species mainly relied on 0–40 cm soil water, with limited use of deeper soil water, which further explain the enhanced root-zone water consumption and reduces deep recharge during growing season. These findings suggested that soil thermal conditions and vegetation jointly regulate deep infiltration by altering soil water availability, and vertical water transfer. Our study provided new insight for improving process-based hydrological models and assessing the vulnerability of alpine meadow water cycling under future warming scenarios.

title: An adaptive Picard-SBFEM-level set formulation for three-dimensional saturated-unsaturated seepage flow analysis and free-surface tracking
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 681, Part A Author(s): Chuhao Huang, Jun Liu, Fuming Wang, Chengchao Guo, Lei Gan, Wenbin Ye, Binghan Xue, Gao Lin
abstract: This study presents a semi-analytical numerical framework for three-dimensional steady saturated–unsaturated seepage analysis with free-surface tracking. The proposed method integrates the scaled boundary finite element method, an adaptive linearized Picard iteration scheme, and a level-set method into a unified formulation. The nonlinear Richards equation with pressure-head-dependent hydraulic conductivity is solved using a coefficient-frozen Picard strategy, while the unknown free surface is implicitly represented by a level-set function and corrected until both the hydraulic and kinematic conditions are satisfied. Five three-dimensional examples comprising 16 cases are investigated, covering spatially varying permeability, zoned heterogeneous media, non-uniform boundary conditions, complex geometries, confined seepage fields, and internal defects. The computed phreatic surfaces, total head distributions, pressure head distributions, and local seepage patterns agree well with the corresponding reference solutions, thereby validating the accuracy and reliability of the proposed method. Computational efficiency is further assessed using the global degrees of freedom (DOFs), matrix-assembly time, nonlinear-iteration time, peak memory usage, and total wall-clock time rather than the element count alone. For five representative cases, the proposed method reduces the global DOFs by 52.8%∼87.1%, the total matrix-assembly time by 15.5%∼32.4%, the average nonlinear-iteration time by 12.0%∼27.6%, and the peak memory usage by 31.7%∼44.3%. The corresponding total computational time is reduced by 28.0%∼58.3% relative to the reference models. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately and efficiently solve complex three-dimensional saturated–unsaturated seepage problems while maintaining stable convergence and reliable free-surface tracking.

title: Experimental characterisation of supersonic steam ejectors for geothermal applications: An analytical model comparison
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Ximena Guardia, Christine Groves, Hugo Quinteros, Nursanty Banjarnahor, Yonatan Afework Tesfahunegn, Gudrun Saevarsdottir, Maria Gudjonsdottir
abstract: An ejector is a passive device that utilises a high-pressure primary stream to draw in low-pressure secondary fluid, thereby mixing the two into a single intermediate-pressure stream. While geothermal facilities typically implement ejectors for extracting non-condensable gases from condensers, academic literature has not reported the successful use of supersonic ejectors to induce geothermal fluid from low-pressure wells. This paper presents the results of experiments used to characterise supersonic steam ejectors for geothermal applications and compares them against an analytical design framework. It examines how the ratio of the Constant Area Mixing Section (CAMS) area to the primary nozzle throat area, known as the area ratio (AR), and the distance from the nozzle exit position (NXP) to the entrance of the constant pressure mixing section, affect the entrainment ratio (ER) and the gained pressure (GP). The area ratio (AR) significantly influenced operational efficiency across the prototype geometries, with AR=4.2 yielding the highest entrainment ratio (ER) among the tested configurations. Finally, ejectors with positive NXP, and those closer to the CAMS, exhibit the highest entrainment ratios and pressure gains.

title: Hydrogeochemical evolution and recharge of carbonate geothermal systems in intermountain basins: Multi-isotope constraints and implications for sustainable management, Taiyuan Basin, Northern China
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Zhanqiang Chen, Liuzhu Chen, Teng Ma, Chenfeng He, Xin Zhang, Shuai Shen, Liangliang Zhang, Xiancang Wu
abstract: Carbonate geothermal systems in intermountain basins host substantial low-to-medium temperature resources, yet their hydrogeochemical evolution, recharge and renewal capacity remain incompletely understood owing to the structural complexity of basin-bounding fault systems. Taking the Taiyuan Basin, northern China, as a representative case, this study integrates hydrogeochemistry with a multi-isotope suite (δD, δ18O, 87Sr/86Sr, δ34S-SO4, δ18O-SO4, 3H, 14C) to investigate the origin, chemical evolution, mixing, and renewal capacity of carbonate geothermal fluids. Hydrochemical facies evolve from Ca·Mg–HCO3·SO4 to Ca–SO4 type along the flow path, driven by carbonate and evaporite dissolution coupled with dedolomitization. The sulfate–water oxygen isotope geothermometer yields basin-center reservoir temperatures of 75–88 °C, corresponding to circulation depths of 2495–2993 m. Silica-based temperatures converge with sulfate–water oxygen isotope temperatures at sites of minimal cold-water mixing, providing independent validation. Stable isotopes confirm a meteoric origin with Late Pleistocene recharge at elevations ≥1400 m in the Xishan and Dongshan Mountains. Cold-water mixing ratios (f_δD) increase systematically from the basin center (<10%) toward the mountain margins (up to ∼75.2%) and are corroborated by Sr isotopes. Vogel-corrected 14C ages place basin-center geothermal waters at ∼18,000–20,000 a, with renewal rates of 0.001–0.002%/a. The renewal-rate gradient mirrors f_δD, showing that apparent renewability is dominated by cold-water admixture rather than intrinsic recharge flux. A 16-year rise in f_δD at a Xishan-margin well (A-XT13/B-XT17) suggests progressive cold-water encroachment. These findings support a “recharge–circulation–evolution–mixing–discharge” conceptual model in which basin-bounding faults govern deep circulation while intrabasinal faults create local vertical connectivity, offering a transferable framework for renewability assessment and sustainable management of carbonate geothermal systems in intermountain basins.

title: Thermo-hydraulic behaviour of energy pile in chalk: First experimental characterisation and field-scale performance assessment under unsaturated conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): M’hammed Taghlaoui, Hussein Mroueh, Diana Salciarini
abstract: Energy piles—foundation elements that simultaneously provide structural support and exchange heat with the ground—offer a direct response to the growing heating and cooling demands of north-western Europe, where chalk is the primary bearing stratum for pile foundations. Despite the widespread occurrence of chalk and its frequently unsaturated state, its coupled thermo-hydraulic behaviour has not yet been characterised as a host medium for energy piles: existing estimates of chalk thermal conductivity correspond to discrete saturation states rather than to a continuous conductivity–saturation relationship established experimentally, representing a gap in geothermal foundation design. This study addresses that gap by delivering the first chalk-specific experimental dataset, constitutive framework, and validated numerical model for energy pile performance in unsaturated chalk. Thermal conductivity was measured on intact chalk specimens using a transient needle-probe across controlled degrees of saturation, and the data were used to calibrate a thermal conductivity function. A fully coupled thermo-hydraulic formulation was implemented in the finite-element framework COMSOL Multiphysics and verified against two independent benchmarks: a field thermal response test on an energy pile in saturated clayey sand and a laboratory model energy-pile test in unsaturated sand. The validated model was then applied to a three-dimensional field-scale energy pile in three chalk formations, and compared with representative sand, silt and clay, to examine the effect of saturation on thermal performance under a seasonal heating–cooling cycle. For the investigated configuration, increasing GWT depth from 0 to 29 m reduces the end-of-extraction heat rate by 6.1%, 8.8% and 11.9% for Estreux, Château-Landon and Seaford chalk, respectively, compared with 3.6% for clay, 8.6% for silt and 26.0% for sand. At 29 m, the chalk cases retain 159.4–169.9 W m − 1 , compared with 135.5 W m − 1 for sand. This crossover highlights the potential of water-retentive chalk under deep groundwater conditions, subject to the adopted material properties and modelling conditions.

title: How selecting representative training sites and features can improve machine learning models of hydrothermal resource favorability
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Pascal D. Caraccioli, Stanley P. Mordensky, Jacob Deangelo, Erick R. Burns, John J. Lipor
abstract: Fundamental challenges for improving supervised machine learning (ML) models for predicting geothermal resources include: 1) available training data being mostly positive (e.g., hot springs or operating power plants), so negative training sites must be selected, and in particular, negative training sites must represent the full range of conditions where no resources exist; and 2) input features potentially containing signals of several geologic processes, some of which may not be directly informative for modeling the availability of geothermal resources. We consider the artificial neural network (ANN) developed by the Nevada Machine Learning project (NVML), propose new selection strategies for negatives, and use signal separation to enhance the information content of input features. Using these strategies, we develop ML models using arguably simpler algorithmic approaches (Logistic Regression and eXtreme Gradient Boosting [i.e., XGBoost]) and compare the new results with the original ANN results. In particular, we evaluate the influence of selection strategy for negative training sites by comparing two training strategies: 1) using the original negative sites defined by NVML (NVML negatives); and 2) randomly selecting negatives from outside ellipsoids defined by NVML as having favorable structural settings, under the assumption that areas far from favorable settings are likely negative. Next, we explore the added value of splitting the topography input feature into two features to separate signals into regional elevation trend and local relative elevation, under the assumption that regional trends are correlated to regional geology (e.g., crustal thickness) and that local relative elevation (e.g., basin and range topography) is correlated to local geology (e.g., faulting). All new models using logistic regression and XGBoost were run 60 times each using Monte Carlo cross-validation to evaluate predictive uncertainty. Models using the randomly selected negatives outperform models using the negatives selected for the NVML ANN; models using XGBoost outperform models using logistic regression; and models using separated elevation features outperform models using the original elevation data. The results showing improved performance with random sampling of negatives demonstrates the value of sampling the entire input feature space when fitting a model (i.e., providing the ML workflow with all types of negatives and positives). The results showing improved performance with separated topography demonstrates that ML models cannot always find important patterns when they are obscured by larger trends, so feature engineering that enhances these patterns can be beneficial.

title: Effect of thermal treatment on the fracture characteristics of tight sandstone under monotonic and triangular incremental hydraulic fracturing
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Pankaj Rawat, Narendra Kumar Samadhiya
abstract: This study investigates the effects of thermal treatment (heating followed by water quenching) on the fracture characteristics of sandstone samples subjected to two hydraulic fracturing schemes: monotonic loading and triangular incremental loading. Sandstone specimens were thermally treated at temperatures ranging from 25 °C to 500 °C to replicate the thermal-shock damage and microcrack network induced when cold working fluid contacts hot reservoir rock, and then fractured under a constant deviatoric stress of 25 MPa with a confining pressure of 10 MPa. The experimental program involves breakdown pressure determination, Brazilian tensile strength measurements, and detailed fracture morphology analysis using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and X-ray computed tomography (μ-XCT). Results indicate that increasing temperature significantly reduces both breakdown pressure and tensile strength, with triangular incremental loading consistently yielding lower breakdown pressures than monotonic loading, attributed to enhanced secondary crack propagation. SEM imaging revealed that thermal treatment induces extensive microcracking, with intergranular fractures dominating under triangular incremental loading and a combination of intergranular and intragranular fractures observed under monotonic conditions. Fracture width in thermally treated tight sandstone decreases up to 200 °C from microcrack nucleation, then increases beyond 300 °C due to thermal softening and grain expansion. Monotonic loading produces wider fractures than triangular incremental loading at each temperature. Tortuosity, width of the process zone, and the fractal dimension of the fracture network increase with rising temperature, reflecting greater complexity. μ-XCT analysis corroborated these findings by demonstrating that triangular incremental loading produces more intricate and tortuous fracture networks than monotonic loading. These results underscore the role of thermal treatment and loading methodology in governing fracture propagation in tight sandstone reservoirs.

title: Thermal conductivity of partially saturated controlled low strength material made with by-products
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Ba Huu Dinh, Tan Manh Do, Young-sang Kim, Hai Viet Vo
abstract: Controlled low-strength material (CLSM) has commonly been defined as a material that compacts and levels itself. However, when CLSM has high enough thermal conductivity, it can serve effectively as a thermal transfer medium (i.e., thermal grout) in geothermal systems owing to its superior flow characteristics and minimal shrinkage properties. This study aims to assess the thermal conductivity of partially saturated CLSM incorporating various by-products. Material costs and CO2 emissions of CLSM made with by-products from this study were also performed and compared to conventional thermal grout. In this investigation, natural sand was entirely substituted with pond ash, while conventional Portland cement and other alternative cementless binders are used in the production of CLSM. The initial phase involved evaluating general properties of the CLSM mixtures, including flowability tests, bleeding tests, setting time tests, and compressive strength tests - followed by thermal conductivity analyses of the specimens using a thermal needle probe at several levels of partial saturation. The results indicated that most CLSM mixtures conformed to ACI 229R specifications, whereas Mixes 14, 15, 16, 20, and 21 were classified as nonconforming because of flowability, bleeding, or initial setting-time criteria. Furthermore, the findings from feature importance analysis revealed that thermal conductivity is significantly dependent on the degree of saturation. Finally, thermal conductivity prediction models for CLSM were developed utilizing normalization and machine learning approaches. It is believed that this study can provide a better understanding of thermal conductivity in partially saturated CLSM made with by-products, which are well-known for their lower cost, cleaner, and more sustainable production.

title: A novel integrated workflow for deep geothermal reservoir characterization using core data, optimized coupled petrophysical–seismic modeling, and machine learning: A case study from the SW Paris Basin, France
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Joshua Pwavodi, Camille Maurel, Aurelien Bordenave, Alexandre Stopin, Alexandre Ortiz, Agathe Faure, Eric Lasseur, Laurent Beccaletto, Justine Briais, Benoit Issautier, Stephane Marc, Nicolas Maubec, Laure Capar, Pavel Didenko, Kirill Siraev, Shervin Rasoulzadeh, Amit Singh, Ali Moradi Tehrani
abstract: The Paris Basin hosts one of the longest-operating deep geothermal systems in Europe, with approximately 50 geothermal doublets exploiting the Middle Jurassic Dogger carbonate and Lower Cretaceous Albian siliciclastic aquifers and supplying nearly 2 TWh of renewable heat annually. Despite extensive geological and geophysical investigations, predicting reservoir facies, heterogeneity, and transmissivity remains highly uncertain. This study presents a physics-guided, multi-scale workflow that integrates petrophysics, rock physics, seismic inversion, and stochastic reservoir modeling to characterize the Dogger, Oxfordian, and Triassic geothermal reservoirs of the Paris Basin. The workflow combines four components: (i) estimation of mineral volumes and total porosity ( ϕ total ) using a hybrid statistical–machine learning approach calibrated with X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements; (ii) joint Monte Carlo inversion of water saturation ( S w ) and formation water resistivity ( R w ) under petrophysical constraints; (iii) generation of a rock-physics-guided synthetic pseudo-well catalogue and corresponding pre-stack Zoeppritz angle gathers, in which XRD-calibrated mineral end-members and petrophysically consistent elastic trends impose physical structure absent from a purely data-driven training set; and (iv) convolutional neural network (CNN) prediction of clay volume ( V clay ), total porosity, and effective porosity ( ϕ eff ) from pre-stack seismic data, pretrained on this synthetic catalogue and fine-tuned via transfer learning on seven real wells. Three additional wells, excluded from transfer learning, were reserved for semi-blind validation. At the calibration wells, R 2 ranges from 0.858 to 0.985 across the three properties, with normalized mean-square error (NMSE) of 1.8%–18.0% and root-mean-square error (RMSE) below 0.043. At the semi-blind wells, performance varies with local well-to-seismic tie quality: one well reproduces calibration-level statistics ( R 2 > 0.92 , NMSE < 10%), while the other two show progressively degraded performance ( R 2 as low as 0.41, NMSE up to 113%), consistent with documented tie-quality issues at those locations rather than a general failure to generalize. The predicted properties reproduce major depositional trends, including Oxfordian lateral continuity and Dogger reservoir compartmentalization, without explicit stratigraphic conditioning. Effective porosity predicted along 1,990 km of interpreted 2D seismic profiles was then integrated into stochastic three-dimensional reservoir modeling, generating 100 equiprobable realizations that represent reservoir heterogeneity and uncertainty while remaining consistent with well observations and regional seismic trends.

title: Defining the operating and utilization envelope of a marginal geothermal well: integrated thermo-hydraulic and geochemical assessment of OW-927A, Olkaria Domes, Kenya–Manuscript Draft
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Maureen N. Ambunya, Chris Wambua, Willis Ambusso, Ivanka Orozova-Bekkevold
abstract: Marginal geothermal ells are commonly defined as wells that do not meet the pressure, enthalpy, phase, or flow requirements for conventional steam-based power generation. Marginality is, however, use-dependent, and wells unsuitable for electricity generation may still support controlled heat recovery. This study develops an integrated thermo-hydraulic and geochemical framework to define the operating and utilization envelope of OW-927A in the Olkaria Domes field, Kenya, using static and flowing pressure-temperature logs, stepped-discharge tests, shut-in pressure build-up analysis and surface geochemistry. Four stable discharge states yielded total mass flow rates of 29.15–122.46 t/h, enthalpies of 838–884 kJ/kg and steam fractions of 0.09 0.12. Flowing logs indicate a hot, liquid-dominated, multi-feed system in which most phase change occurs in the upper wellbore. The interpreted flashing depth was approximately 930 m for the 8-inch discharge state and 850 m for the 6-inch state; relative to the production-casing shoe at approximately 910 m, only the 8-inch state met the base-case hydraulic-stability criterion. Pressure build-up showed approximately 7.3 bar of recovery but no unambiguous radial-flow plateau, indicating moderate pressure support and limited near-well transmissivity rather than strong high rate deliverability. Geochemical results show ascent-related modification, persistent amorphous-silica undersaturation and increasing calcite-scaling risk during flashing and carbon-dioxide loss. Gross thermal power at discharge ranged from about 7.2 to 29.6 MW. The base-case feasible operating envelope is confined to wellhead pressures of approximately 4.0–4.35 bar(a), total mass flow rates of 90–122 t/h, discharge enthalpies of 871–884 kJ/kg and steam fractions of 0.09–0.11. OW-927A is therefore unsuitable for conventional steam-led power generation but remains technically suitable for controlled direct heat recovery. Cascade utilization is preferred where staged heat recovery is feasible, whereas binary conversion remains conditional on sustained flow, chemistry control, surface design and project economics. The framework is transferable to geothermal fields containing wells with comparable thermo-hydraulic and geochemical characteristics

title: Identifying geothermal prospectivity zones in the Fergana Valley through lineament density and land surface temperature anomalies
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Arya Pradipta, Izzul Qudsi, Sherzod Allaev, Daffa Arrofi
abstract: Uzbekistan possesses substantial yet largely underutilized geothermal resources, with an estimated geothermal potential that exceeds its hydrocarbon resources. However, geothermal exploration in this country remains limited due to the data scarcity of detailed subsurface data and the high cost of conventional exploration methods. This study presents a regional-scale geothermal prospectivity assessment in the Fergana Valley using remote sensing and Geographic Information System (GIS)-based techniques. A lineament density map derived from Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) and land surface temperature (LST) anomalies extracted from Landsat 8 were integrated using fuzzy logic to identify areas favorable for geothermal exploration. The resulting prospectivity map was further constrained by the distribution of granitic rocks to delineate geothermal exploration target zones. Results indicate that zones of high lineament density and elevated LST anomalies are primarily concentrated within the Chatkal Range, particularly in the southeastern part, where a total of eleven geothermal exploration target zones were identified. The prospectivity model was evaluated using a prediction rate curve (PRC). The area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.74 indicates acceptable predictive performance and a reasonable level of agreement between the prospectivity model and the observed heat flow. These findings demonstrate that the integration of lineament density, LST anomalies and lithological information provides a transparent, low-cost, and transferable workflow built on openly available data for geothermal prospectivity assessment in data-limited areas, particularly in the intramontane regions of Central Asia.

title: Temporal changes in seismic response of the Tres Vírgenes geothermal field (Mexico) from HVSR: Reservoir-scale variability and depth sensitivity
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): José Antonio Martínez-González, Martín Cárdenas-Soto, Martín Carlos Vidal-García
abstract: We analyze more than seven years of continuous ambient seismic noise recorded at the Tres Vírgenes geothermal field (Mexico) to investigate temporal changes in reservoir-scale seismic response using horizontal-to-vertical spectral ratios (HVSR). Daily H/V amplitudes were evaluated at representative frequencies for seven stations with the highest temporal continuity and compared quantitatively with water-injection rates and local seismicity. Network-scale correlations were weak and did not remain robust after accounting for temporal dependence, while objectively defined external perturbations did not, as a group, produce immediate H/V changes larger than those observed during matched non-event periods. Nevertheless, individual episodes exhibited coherent immediate or delayed responses, indicating substantial temporal and spatial heterogeneity across the field. To investigate the physical origin of selected spectral changes, H/V curves from August 2010 and January 2013 at station TV01 were inverted using a geologically constrained one-dimensional model. The preferred model families indicate approximately 21% lower S-wave velocity in the fractured granodioritic unit and approximately 5% lower S-wave velocity in the overlying sandstone unit for January 2013 relative to August 2010, although the inversion remains inherently non-unique. Frequency-dependent sensitivity kernels show that the low-frequency mode near 0.08 Hz is primarily sensitive to deeper crystalline portions of the model, whereas sensitivity progressively shifts toward intermediate and shallow units at higher frequencies. These results show that long-term HVSR monitoring may provide complementary information on temporal changes in fractured geothermal systems when interpreted together with independent operational, seismicity, geological, and geophysical constraints, but the response is episodic, spatially variable, and should not be interpreted as a deterministic proxy for injection, seismicity, or reservoir stress or as a stand-alone operational diagnostic.

title: Integrated geophysical characterization of multiscale subsurface structures in the Joban area, Japan: implications for possible deep-to-shallow fluid migration
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Kyosuke Okamoto, Yusuke Yamaya, Toshihiro Uchida, Yasuaki Murata, Naoki Aoyagi, Takuya Ishibashi, Yota Suzuki, Norihiro Watanabe, Hiroshi Asanuma, Kaoru Jin, Chisato Konishi
abstract: The 2011 Fukushima Hamadori earthquake (MJMA 7.0) triggered widespread groundwater discharge and groundwater-level changes in the Joban area, northeastern Japan. Geochemical studies have suggested that thermal groundwater in the Joban area contains contributions from deep-seated fluids possibly related to subduction processes. However, the subsurface structures that may facilitate fluid migration between deep crustal levels and shallow groundwater systems remain poorly understood. To investigate the structural framework potentially relevant to fluid migration, we integrated microseismic monitoring, microtremor surveys, gravity surveys, and magnetotelluric (MT) surveys in the southern part of Iwaki City, where groundwater discharge has continued for more than a decade after the earthquake. Microtremor and gravity surveys consistently revealed basement geometry and fault-related structural discontinuities, defining a complex fault system that segments the shallow basement. MT imaging revealed low-resistivity structures extending from depths of approximately 10 km toward shallower levels beneath and around major faults. Recent microseismicity was detected mainly at depths of 2 – 6 km, with a few deeper events overlapping part of the region where the 2011 seismic swarm occurred. Regional seismic tomography showed relatively high Vp/Vs ratios in the broader region containing the recent hypocenters. The spatial relationships among fault-related structures, low-resistivity structures, and seismicity are consistent with a possible structural relationship between deep crustal processes and the shallow thermal-groundwater system associated with the persistent surface discharge after the 2011 Fukushima Hamadori earthquake.

title: Strength prediction and feature interpretation of granite after high temperature based on Stacking ensemble learning
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Zhongwen Wang, Zishuang Han, Meilu Yu, Zhiyuan Li, Mingming Ren, Yao Niu, Cheng Fang
abstract: In deep rock engineering, temperature is an important factor affecting the strength of rock, which can cause the internal thermal effect of rock, lead to structural strengthening or deterioration, and then produce thermal strengthening / deterioration of strength. In order to achieve rapid and accurate prediction of granite strength after high temperature, this paper uses BPNN, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, AdaBoost-CART, SVR and KNN seven machine learning models as candidate base learners to construct Stacking integrated prediction model, in order to improve the accuracy and stability of granite strength prediction after high temperature. The results show that the machine learning method can describe the nonlinear relationship between the strength of granite after high temperature and multiple factors. The BPNN+XGBoost+AdaBoost-CART combination has the highest integral R 2(0.9558), which is better than the single base learner. The RMSE, MAE and MAPE of the ensemble model are 21.628 MPa, 14.307 MPa and 8.781%, respectively, and the R 2 on independent external data is 0.8823, which further reflects its external generalization ability. Kernel SHAP analysis shows that when the Stacking model predicts strength, different strength levels will be distinguished according to the mechanical boundary and loading conditions, and further combined with the heat treatment process and rock state information for correction. In addition, the supporting GUI tools provide a convenient operation interface for strength prediction and result visualization. The research results can provide data-driven methods and application references for the strength evaluation of granite after high temperature and related deep rock engineering analysis.

title: Fluid composition controls on reaction pathways and pore structure evolution in CO 2 -enhanced granitic geothermal reservoirs
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Binbin Gao, Yanlong Kong, Tianming Huang, Zhonghe Pang, Yiman Li
abstract: The chemistry of circulating fluid is critical for the long-term sustainability of CO2-Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS). This study investigates the effects of Na+- and K+-dominated fluid chemistries on fluid–rock reaction pathways and the associated pore-structure and permeability evolution of granite at 200 °C and 25 MPa over 5 days. The objective is to clarify the cation-specific controls of monovalent cations on mineral dissolution–precipitation processes under representative EGS conditions. Results show that plagioclase hydrolysis was the predominant geochemical reaction, accompanied by the precipitation of diaspore and minor kaolinite. High Na+ concentrations inhibited plagioclase hydrolysis, while K+ suppressed the dissolution of orthoclase and biotite, consistent with a common-ion effect. The dissolution of the more reactive andesine initiated an interface-coupled dissolution–precipitation process, generating a local interfacial environment with an elevated Al/Si molar ratio that favored diaspore precipitation and inhibited kaolinite nucleation. Mineral dissolution predominantly increased porosity and shifted pore sizes toward larger diameters. Estimated permeability showed an overall increase after reaction, although the magnitude of permeability change differed between the two theoretical models. These findings demonstrate that fluid composition plays a pivotal role in mineral reaction pathways and pore-structure evolution in granitic CO2-EGS reservoirs, providing a basis for assessing fluid-chemistry management in EGS operations.

title: Tracer-constrained stochastic reservoir characterization of limited heat exchange volume in the Gonghe geothermal reservoir, China
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Guilin Zhu, Qingda Feng, Donglin Liu, Wenqiang Zhao, Runsheng Ma, Linyou Zhang, Zhihui Deng, Zhaoxuan Niu
abstract: A conservative tracer test was conducted at the Gonghe Enhanced Geothermal System (EGS) demonstration site to evaluate inter-well connectivity in a hydraulically stimulated granitic reservoir. Breakthrough curve analysis reveals two preferential transport pathways between the injection well GH02 and the production well GH01, with strongly contrasting parameter identifiability caused by pronounced flow channelization and incomplete tracer recovery. To address the high-dimensional and non-unique nature of tracer-based reservoir characterization under field conditions, a two-stage stochastic inversion framework combining large-scale Monte Carlo screening and block-updated Metropolis–Hastings refinement was applied. The inversion results consistently indicate the presence of a localized preferential flow corridor connecting the two wells, while most of the surrounding reservoir contributes little to the tracer transport observed during the test. Heat transfer simulations constrained by the inferred porosity structure indicate that fluid circulation and heat extraction are dominated by localized preferential flow zones, while large portions of the surrounding reservoir regions with lower effective porosity remain weakly swept by the circulating fluid. As a result, only a limited fraction of the available thermal energy can be effectively extracted, leading to inefficient resource utilization and accelerated thermal decline of the actively connected flow pathways.

title: Integrated thermo-economic analysis of repurposed hydrocarbon wells for closed-loop coaxial geothermal systems in South Texas
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Billel Sennaoui, Khaled Enab, Carlos Mendez, Ayman Samak, Mohamed Khaled
abstract: The global push to decarbonize energy systems and reduce fossil fuel dependence has renewed interest in geothermal energy as a clean, dispatchable thermal resource. Converting depleted oil and gas wells into geothermal heat extractors is among the most economically viable deployment strategies, eliminating the drilling cost barrier, which accounts for 50–60% of total geothermal project expenditures. This study presents a fully integrated thermo-economic framework for repurposing vertical and horizontal hydrocarbon wells in South Texas into closed-loop coaxial systems for direct-use applications. Unlike prior studies that treat thermal performance and economic evaluation separately, this work couples transient thermal-hydraulic wellbore simulation with project-level economic modeling to directly link subsurface heat extraction to financial viability metrics. Two formations were investigated: the Lobo Sand Member (vertical well, 3.3 km TVD, 140.9 °C BHT) and the Eagle Ford Shale (L-shaped horizontal well, 3.5 km TVD, 178.28 °C BHT). A total of 70 simulation scenarios systematically varied mass flow rate, injection temperature, formation thermal conductivity, and lateral length. Thermal outputs, outlet temperature, and net thermal power were directly integrated into an economic model assessing Levelized Cost of Heat (LCOH), Net Present Value (NPV), and Internal Rate of Return (IRR) to define economically optimal operating windows. Results show the vertical configuration reaches an operational optimum near 23 kg/s, after which thermal breakthrough causes a decline in performance, while the horizontal l-shaped well delivers over three times the thermal power and an LCOH of $42/MWh versus $95/MWh at the vertical optimum. An increase in injection temperature was found to reduce the value of the project, particularly in the less efficient vertical system, where LCOH increased by over $40/MWh. Conversely, higher formation thermal conductivity proved to be a powerful screening criterion, as it substantially reduced LCOH in both systems by approximately $50–60/MWh in the vertical case and $25/MWh in the horizontal case. Furthermore, the analysis strongly demonstrates that while a higher bottom-hole temperature contributes a moderate 27–30% to thermal performance, the lateral extension of a horizontal well is the dominant factor, yielding a remarkable 121–127% improvement in thermal output. This finding provides crucial guidance for the future selection and design of geothermal projects from repurposed oil and gas wells, illustrating the superior potential of horizontal drilling infrastructure

title: Hydrogeological genetic pattern of the carbonate geothermal reservoir within the anticline folds in view of hydrogeochemical evolution and regional hydraulic connections
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Yongli Guo, Fajia Chen, Zhang Wen, Cheng Zhang, Qiong Xiao
abstract: The hydrogeological genetic pattern of the carbonate geothermal reservoir within anticline folds represents a significant research topic in both geothermics and karstology. This study integrated environmental tracers with the anticlinal structures to elucidate the hydrochemical evolution and potential regional flow pathways of geothermal waters. From the Wentangxia anticline (WTXA) (northwest) to Taozidang anticline (TZDA) (southeast), the karstification degree decreased, while the estimated geothermal circulation depth increased, from which it can be inferred that geothermal water flows from northwest to southeast. Along the geothermal water flow direction, the average circulation depths ranged from 2580 m to 3627 m, while the average temperatures varied between 71 °C and 92 °C. In sequence, hydrochemical types identified along the recharge zone, runoff zone, and discharge zone were HCO3·SO4 Ca, SO4 Ca, and either SO4 Ca or SO4 Ca·Mg, SO4 2– and Sr initially increased and then decreased, while HCO3 – exhibited an opposite trend. The stable 87Sr/86Sr ratio, along with elevated δ13CDIC and δ34SSO4 values in geothermal water, and the observed correlations among HCO3 –, Sr, Ca2+, and SO4 2–, indicated that the hydrochemical evolution is primarily driven by the dissolution of carbonates and gypsum, whereas sulfate reduction occurred secondarily in an anoxic environment influenced by overlying coal-bearing strata. The hydrogeological genetic pattern of geothermal reservoir was constructed by integrating geological background conditions, spatial karstification degree, regional geothermal water flow field, and hydrogeochemical evolution. These findings validate the use of hydrochemical tracers in indicating hydrogeological functions of carbonate geothermal reservoir and provide insights for promoting the sustainable development of geothermal resources.

title: Optimizing EGS stimulation diagnostics: Quantifying hydro-mechanical decoupling and fracture closure dynamics using distributed strain sensing at Utah FORGE
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Yizhao Wang, Tingxue Jiang, Bing Hou
abstract: Accurate characterization of fracture closure dynamics is critical for stimulation optimization in Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS). This study quantifies hydro-mechanical decoupling during post-shut-in closure using synchronized distributed strain sensing (DSS) and pressure diagnostics in four Utah FORGE stages (4, 5, 8, and 9). Our primary objective is to determine whether mechanical closure ( T m e c h ) systematically precedes hydraulic closure ( T h y d ), to quantify decoupling magnitude and variability, and to evaluate whether HMCS can provide physically interpretable closure-stiffness signatures. Mechanical closure is identified from strain-rate decay and hydraulic closure from G-function derivative behavior with manual quality control for complex stages. All stages show T m e c h < T h y d , with decoupling factors of 1.8–3.9 and lag times of 3.4–8.9 min. We further apply a Hydro-Mechanical Closure Stiffness (HMCS) framework based on phase-wise secant stiffness, revealing stage-dependent stiffening behavior and a distinct screen-out signature in Stage 9. This work contributes a reproducible field workflow for DSS-based mechanical closure picking, integrated hydro-mechanical timing diagnostics, and practical HMCS interpretation guidance. Because the dataset is limited (n = 4), conclusions are interpreted as exploratory and mechanistic rather than statistically definitive.

title: Linking geothermal reservoir and lithium distribution: A handheld spectroscopy approach on deep wells in the Upper Rhine Graben
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Jeanne Vidal, Manaarii Salmon, N’Zé Emmanuel Traoré, Fabien Baron, Patricia Patrier, Baptiste Dazas, Lisa Operto
abstract: The Upper Rhine Graben (URG) hosts a deep geothermal system characterized by fluid circulation within fractured reservoirs at the sedimentary-basement interface. This study investigates cuttings from two deep geothermal wells in the Strasbourg area to assess how reservoir heterogeneity and hydrothermal circulation influence alteration and lithium distribution. Cuttings collected below 3.8 km true vertical depth cover lithologies from the Buntsandstein sandstones to the Carboniferous granitic basement. Reservoir characterization was performed using handheld SWIR (Short-Wave Infrared) and LIBS (Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy) spectrometers as rapid screening tools, complemented by laboratory analyses, to characterise alteration and lithium zonation at the well scale. The results reveal strong heterogeneity in fracture-related alteration patterns and lithium-enriched fluid circulations in the reservoir. Lithium-enriched geothermal brines, with concentrations up to ∼200 ppm, are interpreted to circulate preferentially along fault and fracture networks, promoting sustained fluid–rock interactions. Variations in lithium content correlate with distinct alteration facies, highlighting the role of clay minerals and carbonates during hydrothermal circulation. These findings support a conceptual geothermal model in which structurally controlled fluid flow governs lithium-bearing brine circulation in the URG, with implications for geothermal projects targeting the co-extraction of heat and lithium.

title: Electrically responsive wellbore cement for integrity monitoring: coupled electromechanical behavior of graphene-modified cement systems
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Ali Ettehadi, Mileva Radonjic, Loic Bethel Dje, Omar A. Hamdy, Jonny Rutqvist, Hunjoo P. Lee
abstract: Wellbore cement provides zonal isolation and structural integrity in subsurface energy systems but offers limited capability for continuous integrity monitoring. This study evaluates the self-sensing potential of field-representative API Class H wellbore cement containing 0.3, 0.5, and 1.0 wt% graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), prepared using practical slurry formulations and industry-standard mixing procedures. Electrical resistance was characterized over 1 Hz–10 kHz, followed by coupled unconfined compressive strength (UCS)–electrical resistance monitoring under saturated conditions and post-failure microstructural characterization. GNP incorporation generally reduced electrical resistance relative to neat cement, although the relative conductivity of the GNP-modified formulations varied with frequency, demonstrating that the concentration–conductivity relationship was not strictly monotonic. Under compressive loading, the 0.5 wt% powder-GNP specimen reached the highest UCS of 3885.1 psi, compared with 1499.6 psi for neat cement. The tested GNP-modified specimens also exhibited earlier electrical deviations relative to mechanical failure. Electromechanical warning times were 262 s for neat cement, 909 s for 0.3 wt% powder GNP, 570 s for 0.5 wt% powder GNP, and 1581 s for 0.5 wt% liquid GNP. The liquid-dispersed specimen therefore exhibited the longest warning interval and sustained electrical evolution throughout progressive deformation and post-peak degradation. These results demonstrate the feasibility of combining structural performance with intrinsic electrical sensing in practical wellbore-cement formulations. The study establishes an engineering framework for electrically responsive wellbore cement intended for geothermal, carbon-storage, hydrogen-storage, and long-term well-integrity monitoring applications.

title: Modelling wellbore scaling in geothermal systems using a coupled hydrodynamic–geochemical simulator
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): O.E. Melnik, J.D. Blundy
abstract: Flow in geothermal wells is characterised by strong variations in pressure ( P ), temperature ( T ), and flow velocity ( V ). These changes can drive the fluid into supersaturation with respect to specific mineral phases, leading to scale deposition on pipe walls. Scale growth modifies the pressure–temperature distribution inside the well and progressively alters scale thickness and mineralogy. Increased hydraulic resistance reduces the flow rate, thereby lowering the efficiency of heat extraction (Gunnarsson and Arnórsson, 2005; Zarrouk et al., 2014). We develop a multi-feed-zone, transient wellbore scaling simulator that uniquely integrates, within a single openly available framework, (1) transient two-phase wellbore flow, (2) multi-mineral equilibrium and kinetic geochemistry through a coupling to PHREEQC, and (3) the feedback of scale growth on conduit geometry and wall roughness. This enables the coupled spatio-temporal evolution of scale thickness, mineralogy, and wellhead conditions to be simulated for a specified feed-zone chemistry, mineral assemblage, set of deposition rates, and production protocol. Applied to Krafla well KJ-9, the model reproduces the calcite scale location inferred from caliper logs. Simulations of the simultaneous deposition of calcite, anhydrite and quartz yield scale compositions that are zoned in both the vertical and radial directions.

title: Experimental Study on Transient Hydraulic and Heat Transfer Characteristics of Granite Fractures under Thermo-Hydro-Mechanical-Chemical Coupling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Guan Rong, Ruotao Liu, Qinyan Qiu, Huqi Zhang, Bowen Li
abstract: The hydraulic and heat transfer evolution of granite fractures under thermo-hydro-mechano-chemical coupling represent a pivotal challenge for the sustainable and stable operation of Enhanced Geothermal Systems. In this study, transient fracture flow and heat transfer experiments were conducted under high-temperature and high-pressure conditions. Concurrently, an analytical model for the average fracture surface temperature was developed to achieve a quantitative characterization of the hydraulic and thermal characteristics. The results indicate that normal stress reduced the equivalent hydraulic aperture by 4∼6 µm, dominating the macroscopic closure of the fracture. Meanwhile, it triggered pressure solution and micro-fracturing, which macroscopically smoothed the surface-as evidenced by a 0.1∼0.4 decrease in the Joint Roughness Coefficient while enhancing its microscopic complexity. Under elevated temperatures, the concentrations of N a + , K + , and C a 2 + escalated rapidly to 1.2∼1.6 mmol/L within the first 8 hours, accompanied by a pH rebound from weakly acidic back to neutral, reflecting distinct mineral dissolution and chemical buffering mechanisms. An increased flow rate enhanced the local roughness via hydraulic erosion, whereas the acidic injectate intensified mineral dissolution along with secondary precipitation, ultimately driving the microscopic remodeling of local apertures. Multi-scale analysis demonstrates that high temperatures and chemical activation mitigated the mesoscopic thermal resistance through localized preferential dissolution. Conversely, hydraulic and mechanical constraints locked the hydraulic aperture, resulting in a distinct decoupling between thermal and hydraulic performances. This study elucidates the co-evolutionary mechanisms of fractures under THMC coupling, providing a rigorous quantitative framework for heat transfer prediction and engineering optimization in geothermal reservoirs.

title: Curie point depth (CPD) and thermal anomaly of the Rukwa Rift Basin, SW Tanzania from aeromagnetic data
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Obeid Saitabau Lemna
abstract: Curie point depth (CPD) variations across the Rukwa Rift Basin, southwestern Tanzania, were estimated from aeromagnetic data using 2D radially averaged power spectrum analysis. The results reveal pronounced lateral variations in CPD, ranging from 14 km and 33 km, corresponding to estimated surface heat flow values of 51 - 119 mWm-2. A NW – SE trending zone of shallow CPD ( 69 mWm-2) is observed in the southern part of the Rukwa Rift Basin, indicating elevated geothermal gradients and surface temperatures. In contrast, deeper CPD values (26 - 33 km) and lower heat flow (51 – 69 mWm-2) characterise the adjacent Precambrian basement and the northwestern margin of the basin. These spatial variations are interpreted to reflect spatial differences in crustal thermal structure and the degree of regional thermal demagnetisation, potentially associated with asthenospheric upwelling during crustal and lithospheric extension. The observed thermal anomalies in the southern Rukwa Rift Basin may be linked with inherited lithospheric heterogeneities, including pre-existing basement fabrics that could have acted as preferential pathways for upward migration of hot fluids from the lower lithosphere. If such controls are present, the resulting thermal perturbations may have contributed to localised thermal weakening and strain localisation during rift development. These findings provide new insights into the thermal structure and geodynamic evolution of the Rukwa Rift Basin and suggest that inherited lithospheric heterogeneities may have influenced the spatial distribution of thermal anomalies and the evolution of this segment of the western branch of the East African Rift System, however, further geological and geophysical evidence is required to substantiate this interpretation.

title: Temperature and velocity dependent drift-flux model for gas–liquid flow in geothermal systems
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Adolph Bravo, Erlend Straume, Samuel Scott, Andri Stefánsson
abstract: Multiphase gas–liquid flow governs mass and energy transport in geothermal reservoirs, wellbores, and surface facilities. Because direct resolution of interfacial fluid dynamics is generally impractical, simplified approaches such as drift-flux formulations are widely used to predict fluid-phase behavior including phase slip and void fraction. However, most commonly used correlations were developed for air–water and oil–gas systems under near-ambient conditions, introducing uncertainty in their applicability to geothermal environments where fluid properties vary strongly with temperature. In this study, the performance of widely used drift-flux correlations was evaluated using 421 measurements obtained from water–N2 and water–NaCl–N2 experiments conducted in the Geothermal-Flowloop (GFL) at the University of Iceland under conditions of 20–180 °C and 1–20 barg. Void fraction was determined by gamma densitometry, and the results were compared with predictions from classical drift-flux formulations. At ambient temperatures (20–30 °C), the existing models reproduced the measurements well, and comparison with two independent flow-loop datasets confirmed the consistency of the data. However, all major correlations progressively overpredict void fraction with increasing temperature and total superficial velocity, indicating that important temperature- and flow-dependent effects are not adequately represented. To address these deficiencies, a modified drift-flux model was developed from the Zuber–Findlay framework. Analysis of the experimental data showed that phase slip increases systematically with decreasing liquid viscosity and increasing superficial velocity. Accordingly, the classical drift-velocity expression was reformulated using normalized liquid viscosity and total superficial velocity, and a transition function was additionally introduced to extend applicability across different flow regimes. The resulting formulation substantially improves agreement with experimental observations across the full range of temperatures, flow velocities, and void fractions, reducing systematic void-fraction overestimation, lowering RMSE from 0.20 to 0.05 at 180 °C, and reproducing the observed thermal and flow-rate trends. The results demonstrate that explicit incorporation of temperature-dependent fluid properties and flow-dependent slip behavior is important for accurate multiphase flow modelling in geothermal systems and provide an extended drift-flux framework applicable to high-temperature gas–liquid flows.

title: Heat transfer performance of HDD‑installed horizontal ground heat exchangers: influence of subsurface stratigraphic structure under low-groundwater-flow conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Koutaro Tsubaki, Retsu Harada
abstract: Horizontal ground heat exchangers (GHEs) installed using the Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD) method offer a cost‑effective alternative to vertical systems in regions with fragile geological formations such as Japan. When placed within permeable aquifer layers, these systems may benefit from groundwater‑induced convective heat transfer; however, the actual influence of groundwater flow on horizontally installed GHEs remains insufficiently understood. This study experimentally investigates the heat transfer performance of two HDD‑installed horizontal GHEs of different lengths under both heating and cooling conditions in Saga City, Japan. The subsurface at the installation depth consists of alternating clay and coarse sand layers, and a nearby boring survey indicates that the heat exchangers traverse the boundary between these strata. Measured heat transfer rates were compared with theoretical predictions based on the Kelvin line‑source model to estimate the effective thermal conductivity of the surrounding soil. The north heat exchanger exhibited thermal conductivities of 1.0–1.2 W/(m·K), whereas the south exchanger showed higher values of 1.6–2.9 W/(m·K), reflecting strong geological heterogeneity along the horizontal installation path. Analysis of Nusselt and Fourier numbers revealed no clear enhancement due to groundwater flow, consistent with previously reported low groundwater velocities in the region. These findings indicate that subsurface stratigraphic heterogeneity plays a dominant role in the thermal performance of horizontal GHEs, while the influence of groundwater flow remains limited under low-velocity conditions. The results provide practical guidance for the design and installation of HDD-based horizontal ground heat exchangers in heterogeneous subsurface environments.

title: Preliminary observations from a decameter-scale field test of fracture thermal energy storage: Initial and induced in-situ stress and its impact on fluid flow
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Leon Hibbard, Dana Sirota, Matthew Ingraham, Joseph Pope, Taylor Myers, Jeffrey Burghardt
abstract: We present preliminary data, results, and analysis from the first decameter-scale test of fracture thermal energy storage. The test took place at the Sanford Underground Research Facility 1250 m underground in an amphibolite test bed comprising five boreholes connected by a stimulated fracture network. The system was “charged” by injecting hot water in the central borehole while producing from the others, and subsequently “discharged” by injecting ambient temperature in the peripheral boreholes while producing from the center borehole. During the charging phase more than 60% of the injected water was recovered but during the discharging phase recovery rates were less than 10%. Significant compressive stress heterogeneity on the fracture network (> 4 MPa difference) existed between boreholes before hot water injection and was exacerbated (up to ∼ 9 MPa) during hot water injection. We observed a strong correlation between the compressive stress gradient on the fracture network and the injection impedance between boreholes. Our results suggest that adding thermal energy to our system induced poroelastic and thermoelastic effects that exacerbated existing compressive stress heterogeneity on the fracture network. This, in turn, guided fluid flow away from the areas of highest compressive stress (near the center borehole) towards areas of lower compressive stress.

title: The delineation of low- to medium-temperature geothermal prospectivity zones in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, using GIS-based Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP)
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Emi Prasetyawati Umar, Agung Harijoko, Agung Setianto, Dikdik Risdianto, Dudi Hermawan
abstract: Geothermal potential of South Sulawesi is partly associated with old volcanic rocks aged ∼6.5–0.6 Ma but the distribution of prospective zones and geological controls of fluid circulation is insufficiently determined. Previous studies mostly depended on geological and geochemical observations with limited attention to geophysical datasets and a particular focus on magneto-telluric data which hindered reliable geothermal prospectivity mapping in old volcanic settings. Therefore, this study aimed to apply geospatial multi-criteria decision framework developed through Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) to delineate prospectivity zones for low- to medium-temperature geothermal resources. AHP weights were derived from multi-expert judgement to represent geological uncertainty and improve prospectivity classification reliability. The focus was on eight geoscientific parameters which included reservoir temperature, active manifestation type, volcanism, lineament density, lithology, gravity anomaly, hydrothermal alteration, and land surface temperature (LST). Prospectivity map reported that very low, low, and moderate classes covered 40.57%, 14.18%, and 26.77% while high and very high only had 18.05% and 0.43%, respectively. The high-to-very-high prospectivity zones recorded spatial correspondence with major structural lineaments, old volcanic units, active geothermal manifestations, thermal anomalies, hydrothermal alteration zones, and gravity anomaly patterns despite the limited coverage. The validation process conducted using receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) subsequently produced 86.8% which reflected robust predictive performance of the model. This study provided a practical framework for prioritizing prospectivity zones for further exploration and sustainable geothermal development in South Sulawesi.

title: Fracture characteristics of layered rock during supercritical carbon dioxide fracturing: an experimental and thermal–hydraulic–mechanical–damage numerical study
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Geothermics, Volume 143 Author(s): Guan Rong, Qinyan Qiu, Huqi Zhang, Ruichen Luo, Zuhao Lyu
abstract: Rock heterogeneity and structural anisotropy exert significant influences on fracture propagation during reservoir stimulation. Focusing on layered sandstone, this study conducted supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO₂) fracturing experiments under different stress ratios and bedding angles and developed a coupled thermal–hydraulic–mechanical–damage (THMD) model incorporating the pressure- and temperature-dependent thermophysical properties of CO₂.
