The monotonic BNN attains R2 = 0.877 and RMSE = 1.33 °C, and the gradient-band BNN produces physically consistent geothermal gradients (≈0.014–0.018 °C/m), aligning with regional heat-flow constraints. Both physics-guided models deliver near-ideal uncertainty calibration (≈97–99% prediction-interval coverage) and eliminate nonphysical deep-zone oscillations. Independent validation against the Grado-1 well confirms agreement within ±1 °C across the full 100–1200 m profile. The proposed framework enables extrapolation-robust and uncertainty-aware 3D geothermal mapping, providing a transferable approach for geothermal resource assessment in data-limited subsurface systems.

title: Curie-point depth, geothermal gradient and near-surface heat flow estimation from spectral analysis of aeromagnetic data over Natron Rift Basin, Tanzania
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Neema Bernad Mjami, Obeid Saitabau Lemna, Cuthbert Kimambo, Sarah Ayeng’o, Ivanka Orozova-Bekkevold
abstract: The Natron Rift Basin (NRB) in northeastern Tanzania, situated within the eastern branch of the East African Rift System (EARS), is among the country's promising geothermal prospects and has been designated as a priority development area. However, research into its geothermal potential remains limited despite active geothermal manifestations and favourable tectonic features, including faults, fractures, hot springs and volcanoes. Specifically, localized investigations of the geothermal gradient and near-surface heat flow have not yet been carried out. This study aims to estimate the Curie-Point Depth (CPD) within the NRB using spectral analysis of aeromagnetic data, focusing on the area bounded by latitudes 2° S - 3.6°S and longitudes 35.2° - 36.8°E. The estimated CPD ranges from 12 to 18 km below ground level. These CPD estimates were used to constrain the geothermal gradient and near-surface heat flow in the area. The calculated geothermal gradient and heat flow range from 31 to 46.5 °C/km and 77.6 to 116.3 mW/m², respectively. The results indicate a widespread distribution of low- to medium-temperature geothermal resources in the NRB. A potential high-enthalpy heat source was identified beneath the volcanic belt to the south of Lake Natron. This study presents the first regional scale maps of geothermal gradient and heat flow in the NRB, with an approximate spatial resolution of 44 km between data points. The results are spatially coherent with major structural and volcanic features of the EARS in the study area. These findings improve the understanding of the NRB deep thermal structures and can be used to identify priority areas that may warrant further investigation for future geothermal exploration.

title: Synergistic effects of epoxy/PTFE/CNT hybrid nanocomposite coating against silica scaling and corrosion under varying geothermal flow conditions
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Yurian Ariandi Andrameda, Khasani, Kusmono, Hendra Ardi Kurniawan, Herdian Ardi Febrianto, Kadek Wahyudi, Zaky Ahmad Aditya, Shad Abdelmoumen Serroune
abstract: This study presents the development of a multifunctional epoxy/polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)/carbon nanotube (CNT) hybrid nanocomposite coating designed to simultaneously mitigate localized corrosion and silica scaling in geothermal environments. Morphological and surface property evaluations identified an optimal formulation (Epoxy/PTFE40/CNT0.8) that successfully balances surface hydrophobicity (water contact angle of 139°) with enhanced adhesion strength (8.68 MPa), avoiding the nanoparticle agglomeration observed at excessive filler loadings. Thermal analysis demonstrated that the integrated CNT network acts as a physical diffusion barrier, modifying the matrix degradation into a stabilized two-stage process capable of withstanding continuous exposure up to 150 °C. Electrochemically, the optimized composite established a highly tortuous barrier against corrosive Cl⁻ ions, achieving a charge transfer resistance of 882.9 Ω·cm² (47% above neat epoxy), a corrosion protection efficiency of 94.05%, and a minimal corrosion rate of 0.0098 mm/year. Furthermore, the tailored micro/nano-topography formed by PTFE particles and CNT networks successfully prevented the mechanical interlocking of mineral deposits, delivering peak silica scaling reductions of 65.08% under Upstream (near-wellhead) brine conditions and maintaining a 50.92% mitigation efficiency under Downstream (near-pond) supersaturation conditions. Ultimately, this synergistic hybrid coating offers an effective and scalable strategy for simultaneously combating the dual threats of scaling and corrosion, extending the operational lifespan of geothermal infrastructure.

title: 2D magnetotelluric inversion and 3D resistivity visualization for geothermal system characterization: A case study of Mount Parakasak
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Eko Minarto, Fatony Zepanya
abstract: Mount Parakasak in Banten hosts promising yet underexplored geothermal resources. This study integrates two-dimensional magnetotelluric (MT) and time-domain electromagnetic (TDEM) surveys to delineate subsurface resistivity structures and characterize the geothermal system. Thirty-six MT soundings, corrected for static shift using TDEM data, were inverted to generate 2D resistivity sections. These sections were subsequently interpolated to construct a three-dimensional resistivity visualization constrained by geological and geochemical datasets. The results identify a conductive clay cap (∼100 Ω·m) overlying an upflow zone near the Kaipohan manifestation, corresponding to estimated reservoir temperatures of 240–260 °C. The Batukuwung hot spring defines an outflow zone with temperatures of 52–75 °C. The integrated interpretation indicates an active geothermal system and identifies promising drilling targets at approximately 1500 m depth. These findings provide a robust framework for geothermal exploration and resource assessment, supporting future geothermal development in Banten Province.

title: Imaging the resistivity structure of Nage Geothermal System, Flores Island, Indonesia through 3-D magnetotelluric inversion incorporating the sea effect
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Maryadi Maryadi, Asep Sugianto, Iqbal Takodama, After Helfert Pasaribu, Yan Mark, Supriyanto Supriyanto, Hideki Mizunaga
abstract: The geothermal potential of Flores Island, Indonesia, is significant but structurally complex, requiring advanced geophysical imaging to delineate active hydrothermal systems. However, in such island-arc settings, some magnetotelluric (MT) inversion attempts still neglect the influence of the highly conductive surrounding seawater, thereby generating artificial deep conductive anomalies that can lead to costly misinterpretations of geothermal features. In this study, a three-dimensional (3-D) MT inversion of the Nage geothermal system is presented, which is based on full-impedance data from 82 stations. The model domain explicitly incorporates regional bathymetry and the seawater body to account for the sea effect. The results delineate a massive conductive clay cap beneath the high-temperature FW fumarole, identifying it as the primary hydrothermal upflow zone. A distinct, shallower geothermal reservoir was also identified between the Keli (APK) and Nage (APN) hot spring complexes, which appears to be hydrologically partitioned from the primary upflow by an NE-SW-oriented fault that acts as a structural permeability barrier between the complexes. Furthermore, the model detects a deep resistive body, interpreted as older intrusive rock, beneath the Nage caldera. These findings yield a refined conceptual model of the Nage geothermal field and demonstrate that explicitly modeling the sea effect is crucial to preventing the misinterpretation of deep reservoir structures in coastal volcanic environments.

title: Thermomechanical Response of Weathered Granite Soils Surrounding Energy Geostructures under Cyclic Thermal Loading
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Hanh Nguyen-Cong, Ba Huu Dinh, Ju-Won Ryu, Gyeong-O Kang, Young-Sang Kim
abstract: Understanding the thermomechanical behaviors of geomaterials is crucial for ensuring the successful design and long-term performance of energy geostructures. This study investigated the response of an undisturbed, low-plasticity weathered granite soil (WGS) from Gwangju, Korea, a saprolitic soil derived from regional granite that behaves as a transitional soil between sands and clays, under cyclic thermal loading. A modified temperature-controlled oedometer was used to subject both normally consolidated (NC) and overconsolidated (OC) states to multiple-cycle drained heating (60 °C) and cooling (20 °C) tests at different preconsolidation pressures. The experimental results indicated that the NC-WGS exhibited irreversible thermal consolidation under a single thermal cycle, whereas the heavily OC-WGS primarily exhibited reversible thermo-elastic expansion. In addition, the magnitude of NC-WGS thermal consolidation was strongly stress-dependent, with the maximum volumetric strain during the first heating phase decreasing from 0.404 % at 240 kPa to 0.134 % at 640 kPa. Multiple thermal cyclic loadings produced accumulated consolidation in NC with rapidly diminishing incremental strain (thermal hardening-type stabilization), reaching 0.915 % and 0.825 % after three cycles at 240 kPa and 320 kPa, respectively, and 1.015 % after eight cycles at 640 kPa. In contrast, OC responses became nearly repeatable from the second cycle onward with negligible additional plastic strain. Even under repeated cycling, the low-plasticity WGS (plasticity index of 2.6 %) exhibits markedly lower thermally induced volumetric strain than high-plasticity clays, supporting long-term serviceability and structural safety throughout cyclic thermal operation in energy geostructures.

title: Enhancing identification of geothermal prospection in Yingshan geothermal field using machine learning and thermal infrared remote sensing
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Xin Zhang, Zhentao Hong, Xianjun Xie, Yanxin Wang, Qiang Liu, Haijin Xu, Xiao Wang, Tianyu Ren, Peisong Dong
abstract: Improving the accuracy of land surface temperature (LST) retrieval from thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing and inverting the properties of subsurface geothermal reservoirs remain significant challenges. This has particularly constrained the integration of TIR remote sensing with other exploration methodologies, such as geochemical surveys. To address this issue, we derived thermal infrared information from Landsat 8 and MODIS data, with Sentinel-2 and SRTM data providing auxiliary optical and topographic features in the Yingshan geothermal field. Subsequently, we adopted the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model to perform spatial downscaling of LST. By establishing the optimal feature combination for temperature retrieval, we achieved high-precision surface temperature inversion and compared its performance with the traditional bilinear interpolation and DisTrad models. In parallel, we developed a processing workflow for altered mineral identification based on ASTER and Landsat 8 reflectance data. Finally, we conducted a comprehensive analysis integrating the downscaled LST, thermally altered minerals, and in-situ geochemical data including soil gas Rn, Hg, and geothermal gradient (GTG), to improve the accuracy of geothermal prospect targeting. The results show that the XGBoost model significantly enhanced the detail richness of the LST map, increasing the entropy value from 3.13 to 3.30, which outperforms the results of bilinear interpolation (3.12) and the DisTrad model (3.14). Validation against in-situ surface temperature measurements shows that the XGBoost model achieved a mean bias error (MBE) of -0.492 ± 0.2 °C and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.39 ± 0.0702 °C, which are significantly better than the results of the DisTrad model (MBE = 0.539 ± 0.2 °C; RMSE = 2.77 ± 0.0387 °C) and bilinear interpolation (MBE = 0.625 ± 0.2 °C; RMSE = 2.98 ± 0.0418 °C). Furthermore, the P-P plot analysis indicates that the XGBoost model significantly improved the identification accuracy for both the relatively high-temperature geothermal fields and the low-temperature vegetation-covered areas. Our TIR remote sensing analysis identified four types of hydrothermal alteration: propylitic, argillization, biotitization, and sericitization, all of which were validated by field investigations. In the focal research area, we identified five high-temperature anomalies, along with their corresponding thermally altered mineral anomalies. The results indicate that the geothermal reservoirs in the anomaly zones are dominated by medium-acidic and medium-low temperature environments. Moreover, through comprehensive integration with soil gas Rn, Hg, and geothermal gradient (GTG), we classified the thermal anomalies into three distinct types with complete quantitative signatures: (1) Type 1 (geothermal fields): showed LST anomalies of 23.3 ± 1.12–24.6 ± 1.22 °C, with the presence of surface hydrothermal alteration minerals, paired with elevated Hg and GTG; (2) Type 2 (hidden faults): had normal LST, with no detectable hydrothermal alteration minerals, but pronounced Rn anomalies; (3) Type 3 (heat island/conductive zones): exhibited extreme LST fluctuations, with no detectable hydrothermal alteration minerals, paired with elevated GTGs but weak geochemical anomalies. This classification result suggests that downscaled LST, when integrated with soil gas Rn, Hg, geothermal gradient, and structural information, can assist in distinguishing known geothermal fields from potential concealed structural or conductive zones. The XGBoost-based downscaling method, combined with hydrothermal altered mineral identification, can significantly improve the accuracy of geothermal exploration targeting, analyze the genesis of geothermal distribution at the initial exploration stage, and substantially reduce the cost of geothermal system exploration.

title: Thermal diffusivity and transient thermal response of the Sabatini volcanic succession: insights from the shallow geothermal field at the ENEA-Casaccia Research Centre (Roma, Italy)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Anna Carmela Violante, Marco Proposito, Giambattista Guidi, Simona De Iuliis
abstract: Understanding transient heat transfer in heterogeneous volcanic formations improves the design of shallow geothermal energy systems (SGES). However, the thermal behaviour of stratified volcanic successions remains poorly constrained due to lithological variability, porosity contrasts, and groundwater driven heat transport. This study investigates the thermal diffusivity and thermal response of the Sabatini volcanic succession (Central Italy) using laboratory measurements, in situ thermal tests and Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) monitoring at the ENEA-Casaccia shallow geothermal field. Thermal conductivity (λ), bulk density (ρ), and specific heat capacity (cp) were determined along a borehole and used to derive thermal diffusivity (α). DTS monitoring enabled characterised transient thermal evolution along the borehole. Thermal diffusivity values range from 4.2 × 10⁻⁷ to 7.1 × 10⁻⁷ m²/s. Highest values are associated with lava and sandy tuffs, whereas the lowest occur in fine-grained, clay-rich deposits. DTS monitoring during a 12 h thermal stimulation test revealed depth-dependent heterogeneity and contrasting cooling behaviours among lithologies. Saturated lava units showed rapid heat uptake and dissipation, while fine-grained tuffs and sandy silts retained thermal anomalies for up to 48 h, indicating higher thermal inertia and heat storage capacity. Results demonstrate that lithology, porosity and saturation control transient thermal behaviour in volcanic successions.

title: Entraining low-pressure geothermal fluid for power generation using a supersonic ejector: A case study from Theistareykir power plant
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Ximena Guardia, Egill Juliusson, Karl Emil Sveinsson, Hilmar Einarsson, Gudrun Saevarsdottir, Yonatan Afework Tesfahunegn, Maria Sigridur Gudjonsdottir
abstract: An ejector is a device without moving parts that uses a high-pressure fluid to entrain fluid from a low-pressure source, thereby mixing them to create a single flow at an intermediate pressure. Such a device was designed for geothermal power plant conditions by Reykjavik University and tested at the Theistareykir Geothermal Power Plant in Iceland, in collaboration with Landsvirkjun Power Company, in November 2024. The system used high-pressure saturated steam from well ThG-11 to draw in a lower-pressure, two-phase mixture (with a 20% steam quality) from well ThG-15. The ejector was designed using an analytical model to handle a primary steam flow of up to 2.90 kg/s, and it was tested across a wide range of operating conditions. During the tests, the pressure of the primary fluid (from well ThG-11) varied from 8.5 to 28.5 bar g , while the pressure of the secondary fluid (from well ThG-15) ranged from 1.8 to 9.1 bar g . The ejector successfully entrained the secondary flow when the pressure difference between the primary and secondary fluids ranged from 9.9 to 26.3 bar. The highest entrainment ratio (ER), defined as the secondary-to-primary mass flow ratio, across the entire data set was 0.38. This occurred at a primary fluid mass flow rate of 2.76 kg/s and a pressure of 28.5 bar g , with a secondary fluid mass flow rate of 1.05 kg/s at 6.6 bar g . At the ejector outlet, the mixed flow pressure was 9.9 bar g , representing a 3.4 bar pressure gain relative to the entrained secondary fluid. The exergy analysis for this peak condition revealed an additional exergy rate of 269.17 kW. This represents a 9.1% increase in the total useful energy delivered from this pair of wells at the testing conditions. Scaling to the full capacity of both wells suggests a potential additional exergy rate of 1.65 to 1.96 MW for the power plant, based on the stable experimental operating range. The analytical model used to design the ejector showed good agreement with the measured data for the primary fluid but poor agreement for the secondary fluid, particularly in times of low or no entrainment and when the secondary fluid pressure did not have stable conditions. Overall, these results are promising for future applications of ejectors in connecting high- and low-pressure geothermal wells.

title: Effects of reservoir permeability heterogeneity on the size of solute and thermal protection zone around a geothermal reinjection well in a porous reservoir, Hungary
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Bence Molnár, Daniele Pedretti, István Garaguly, Gábor Varga, Judit Mádl‑Szőnyi, Attila Galsa
abstract: Sustainable groundwater management requires accurate delineation of a protection zone (PZ) around wells. While PZ has been widely studied for solute protection zone (SPZ) of drinking water wells, the growing use of geothermal applications requires also the delineation of both solute and thermal protection zone (TPZ). In this study, the effects of reservoir heterogeneity on SPZ and TPZ size were investigated using numerical simulations around a deep geothermal reinjection well, where reservoir heterogeneity was studied by stochastic permeability distributions. In the first part of the study, synthetic simulations were performed to highlight the importance of the scientific question, where the role of the permeability heterogeneity scale, and the thermal retardation were examined. The SPZ and TPZ size was characterized by monitoring the evolving position of the solute and thermal front. In the main part, the theoretical findings were applied to a real geothermal project in Hungary, proposing a novel workflow where the heterogeneity scale was derived from seismic attributes and geophysical logs. The results show that the SPZ and TPZ size increases with the heterogeneity scale, indicating that a larger protection zone is needed, although the effect of heterogeneity decreases over time. Heterogeneity has significant effect on the TPZ extension especially on small time scale, so its investigation in heat transport cannot be neglected despite greater heat diffusion. The probability maps of SPZ and TPZ areas illustrate well the uncertainty caused by reservoir heterogeneity. Finally, results highlight that TPZ cannot be directly rescaled from SPZ because of the time-varying difference between apparent and effective thermal retardation.

title: Wet and dry faults at thrust fronts as indicators of paleofluid flow in the carbonates of the Geneva Basin (Switzerland, France)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): G.L. Cardello, M. Lupi, E. Carminati, C. Doglioni, M. Sartori, E. Samankassou, M. Meyer
abstract: Thrust fronts are common targets for geothermal exploration in foreland basins because they contain fractured reservoirs made of a floor thrust and a frontal anticline, eventually crossed by high-angle transfer faults, and minor thrust splays. Although regional fluid flow is also controlled by petrophysical properties and the geothermal gradient, the tectonic contribution is best understood through outcrop analogs. We investigate tectonic controls on paleo-circulation across the carbonate-rich thrust front systems surrounding Geneva to better understand present-day hydrothermal pathways. Structural mapping and mesostructural analysis identify high-angle “wet” (mineralized) and “dry” (non-mineralized) faults, revealing where paleofluids circulated and sealed voids. Fault geometry defines a hierarchical network. First-order faults (>2.5 km long), mainly NW-oriented tear faults, accommodated thrust front curvature and acted as primary conduits for mineralizing fluids, except where E-W and WNW faults intercept the thrust front. Second-order faults, which are 0.4–2.5 km long, are less continuous and rarely mineralized. This suggests limited fluid migration in such gregarious faults. The fabric of mineralizations ranges from syn-kinematic slickenfibers to post-kinematic vadose cements, depending on fault orientation, kinematics, offset, and segmentation. The presence of rebrecciated fabrics and multiple generations of syn-thrusting veins and polygenetic calcite in NW-striking faults at thrust fronts suggests that these faults represent fossil examples of transient builds-up of paleofluid overpressure and deformation. Conversely, W- to WNW-tear faults mostly represent alternated pressure-solution and discrete faulting. These findings provide a framework for identifying permeable zones in carbonate thrust fronts, offering practical guidance for assessing geothermal exploration in deformed foreland basins.

title: Temperature field and assessment methodology for a low-medium temperature geothermal field: 3D geological-geophysical modeling in the Xiong'an Area, Northern China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Na Peng, Yihao Wu, Hanqing Qiao, Jiangtao Han
abstract: Mid-low temperature hydrothermal systems are widely distributed in continental intraplate basins, and accurately characterizing their deep thermal structures is crucial for understanding regional geothermal genesis. As a typical intraplate field, the Xiong'an Area in North China possesses significant deep potential. However, previous studies focused on localized assessments of isolated shallow fields, lacking regional 3D simulations based on fine structural constraints, which restricts the understanding of deep heat transfer mechanisms.In this study, we integrated three deep seismic reflection profiles, one magnetotelluric (MT) profile, regional geological, and well-log data to construct a high-resolution 3D geological-geophysical model. Constrained by petrophysical data, we employed a Multi-source data integration approach to solve the 3D steady-state heat conduction equation, achieving high-precision geothermal simulation down to 5 km depth, validated by measured well temperatures.Our results reveal significant spatial differentiation in the regional thermal structure, primarily controlled by varying "caprock-reservoir" configurations. The northern region (e.g., Rongcheng and Niutuozhen fields) exhibits a "thin caprock-shallow reservoir" pattern ( 3 km). The 3D model indicates the southern deep system possesses a significantly higher geothermal gradient, forming a promising target for deep exploration. Furthermore, we identify a concealed deep geothermal prospect near the Raoyang depression. This study delineates reliable exploration targets and provides a universally applicable framework for modeling Multi-source data integration in intraplate geothermal systems.

title: Field demonstration and integrated productivity-economics assessment of multi-lateral geothermal wells enabled by directional steel shot drilling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Paromita Deb, Andreas Reinicke, Jan Jette Blangé, Morteza Esmailpour, Carlo Guarnieri Calo’ Carducci, Martin O. Saar
abstract: This study explores the potential of multi-lateral slim-hole drilling to enhance reservoir access and connectivity in fractured geothermal reservoirs. At the core of this work is Directional Steel Shot Drilling (DSSD), a technology that combines conventional mechanical drilling with the erosive action of pressure-accelerated steel shots. This approach enables the cost-effective construction of multi-directional boreholes from a single wellbore. The DSSD technology was piloted at the VersuchsStollen Hagerbach underground research facility in Switzerland. The test site provides access to fractured hard rock formations under realistic stress and pore-fluid pressure conditions. Two horizontal wellbores, each 125 m long, were drilled. Rates of penetration (ROP) increased up to 2–5 times depending on the steel shot concentration in the drilling mud. Controlled building rates under steering (∼ 3.8–6.6°/30 m) and stable trajectories under non-steering conditions (∼ 0.3° /30 m) were achieved. The pilot demonstrated several key aspects: straightforward retrofitting of DSSD on conventional drill rigs, effectiveness of the steering concept, efficient transportation of steel shots in the mud, and the resulting enhanced bit performance in hard rock. To assess field-scale implications, reservoir simulations and a techno-economic assessment were performed using a fractured carbonate reservoir case. A set of 1000 geological realizations was generated to capture uncertainty in permeability distribution. These models were used to evaluate thermal energy production for 20 years, employing single-, dual-, and triple-lateral well architectures. Median results indicated that adding a second lateral boosts production by 45 – 50%, while a third lateral leads to an additional 25 – 30% gain. The techno-economic evaluation shows corresponding reductions in the levelized cost of heat by ∼20% when moving from single- to dual-lateral configurations, and by a further ∼25% when a third lateral is added. Similarly, the specific capital cost declines by ∼24% from single to dual laterals and by an additional 16% for triple laterals. Results remain conditional on assumptions of geology, well design, economics, and scalability to greater depth.

title: A GIS-based geothermal heat cost index (GHCI) map for efficient energy planning in Europe
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Younes Noorollahi, Steffen Nielsen, Bernd Moller, Amir Naseri
abstract: In the present society, sustainable energy system development is a vitally important issue receives considerable attention. Central district heating systems supported by renewable energy sources would play an essential role in future energy systems. Geothermal energy, as a renewable energy source, can provide a reliable baseload energy supply for direct uses of heat, such as space heating. For future energy system planning the economic feasibility of such a geothermal district heating system is very important for its viability among other available renewable and nonrenewable energy resources. In this regard, the Levelized Cost of probable hydrothermal geothermal resources of European countries is evaluated using a modified GIS-based GEOPHIRES code. The cost of geothermal heat varies over a wide range according to the many local and global parameters that are affecting the produced heat cost. The results show that, for the resources at a depth of 1000 m the geothermal heat can be provided by 3.7–18 USD/GJ. Furthermore, for deeper geothermal resources (a depth of 2000 m) the heat can be provided at a lower cost and it is more widely available in most of the countries with a cost of 3.4-17 USD/GJ around Europe.

title: Comprehensive characterization of drill core, and geochemical alteration pathways of drill core from the Humu’ula groundwater research project, Hawaii, USA: II. Keamuku maneuver area
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Pooja Sheevam, Wendy M. Calvin, Eric Haskins, Thomas Bristow
abstract: In 2013–2015, two deep wells, PTA-2 and KMA-1, were drilled in the Humu‘ula Saddle region of Hawai‘i for groundwater and geothermal exploration as part of a broader effort to understand the geological history and resource potential of subsurface environments on the island of Hawai‘i. This study focuses on the alteration mineralogy of the KMA-1 drill hole, complementing similar investigations conducted on PTA-2. Mineralogical analysis of KMA-1 involved a multi-scale characterization of aqueous alteration using bulk and high-resolution visible and short-wave infrared (VIS-SWIR) and long-wave infrared (LWIR) spectral imaging, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray fluorescence (XRF). Several types of secondary phases, including alunite, jarosite, secondary hematite, and smectites, were identified. This study shows distinct zones of alteration interspersed with largely unaltered sections and that alteration is not progressive with depth. Field surveys showed widespread alteration and abundant sulfates, while high-resolution techniques like XRD and XRF detected smaller quantities in bulk rock. This discrepancy suggests that spectroscopic methods are highly sensitive to strongly absorbing, albeit minor, mineral phases. Sulfates are not correlated with confined groundwater units suggesting possible fumarole systems buried over time or acid-steam alteration during post-shield volcanic phases. This study contributes to ongoing efforts to characterize the mineralization associated with geothermal and groundwater systems in the Hawaiian subsurface, providing further insight into hydrothermal processes and alteration pathways.

title: Uncertainty quantification under data worth for the Delft campus geothermal project
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Yuan Chen, Guillaume Rongier, James Robert Mullins, Denis Voskov, Alexandros Daniilidis
abstract: Low-enthalpy geothermal doublets for direct-use heating are highly sensitive to subsurface heterogeneity and operational uncertainty. This study quantifies these uncertainties for the Delft campus geothermal system using an integrated workflow that couples geological modeling with GPU-accelerated, high-spatial-resolution reservoir simulation. Ensembles of three-dimensional regional-scale facies models of the Delft Sandstone Member, with and without conditioning to Geothermie Delft (GTD) well data, were generated using object-based modeling and sequential indicator simulation. Porosity was modeled by sequential Gaussian simulation, and permeability was derived from a nuclear magnetic resonance-based porosity–permeability correlation calibrated to GTD well data, yielding higher permeability than core-based correlations for porosity below 15%. Lorenz coefficients indicate strong variability in property distributions, resulting in a wide spread of production temperatures. In total, 2000 geological realizations were simulated over 50 years using the GPU-enabled open-source Delft Advanced Research Terra Simulator (open-DARTS) under maximum and 2025-demand production schemes. Conditioning to GTD wells adds considerable data worth by constraining uncertainty in production well bottom-hole temperature (BHT) and pressure (BHP), while keeping injection pressure within Dutch regulatory limits. SIS models exhibit greater temperature and pressure variability than OBM models due to lower sand-body continuity. Despite large 80% confidence intervals, P50 production temperatures remain comparable for conditioned models. Distance-based generalized sensitivity analysis identifies net-to-gross ratio and the porosity–permeability correlation as dominant controls on thermal response. The 2025-demand scheme delays cold-front propagation. Results demonstrate that ensemble-based, GPU-accelerated high-spatial-resolution simulations enable robust and efficient uncertainty quantification for direct-use geothermal systems, highlighting the importance of well conditioning and reservoir heterogeneity characterization in constraining thermal responses.

title: Thermal structure and geothermal potential of the onshore Gippsland basin inferred from 3D conductive heat flow modelling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Belay Gulte Mino, Graeme Beardsmore, Mark A McLean
abstract: Understanding spatial and depth-dependent variations in thermal conductivity is essential for accurate geothermal modelling in sedimentary basins. This study investigates the thermal structure and geothermal potential of the onshore Gippsland Basin, southeastern Australia, by integrating published thermal-property datasets with 3D steady-state conductive modelling using the open-source Underworld3 framework. Lithology-dependent mean thermal conductivity values for the Latrobe Valley Subgroup were derived from borehole lithological proportions and ranged from 0.56 to 1.21 W/m·K, reflecting strong lateral heterogeneity associated with variable coal content. The thermal model incorporates spatially variable land surface temperature (LST), interval temperature logs, bottom-hole temperature data, and laterally varying basal temperatures extrapolated using one-dimensional conductive heat flow models and interpolated across the basin. Model results predict surface temperatures ranging from approximately 11.54 to 20.68°C and laterally variable basal temperatures of approximately 120 to 256°C at 5,000 m depth, reflecting the combined influence of thermal conductivity, heat flow, and surface temperature variability. Temperatures at the top of the Cenozoic-aged geothermal source rock range from approximately 14 to 65°C, indicating favourable conditions for low-enthalpy geothermal applications. Model constraining against borehole temperature data demonstrates good agreement between measured and modelled thermal profiles. Volumetric heat-in-place calculations indicate that the Cenozoic-aged geothermal source contains maximum values of approximately 31 exajoules (EJ) of stored thermal energy. These results highlight the importance of incorporating spatially variable thermal conductivity and non-uniform basal boundary conditions into geothermal models and provide a refined framework for geothermal assessment in the onshore Gippsland Basin and other coal-bearing sedimentary basins.

title: Mapping hydrothermally altered minerals using Landsat-8 satellite data, along bambam-billiri-kaltingo axis, in Upper Benue Trough, Northeastern Nigeria
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Bello Yusuf Idi, Mukaila Abdullahi
abstract: The Northeastern Nigerian Upper Benue trough is characterized by hydrothermal and geothermal manifestation features. In this work, the hydrothermally altered mineral deposits are mapped as a reconnaissance survey of the most feasible regions for geothermal energy and oxide mineral exploration in the trough. Bands 2, 4, 5, 6 and 2, 5, 6, 8 of the Landsat-8 OLI are respectively used to highlight iron-oxide and clay/hydroxide-bearing minerals. Band-ratio composites are used to map the relative spatial distribution of the alteration zones. The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is been used to identify the desired spectral bands for Crosta analysis. Based on the eigenvector loadings of the PC components, PCA bands with the highest eigenvalue loadings of the opposite signs are used to map the spatial distribution of iron-oxide and clay/hydroxyl minerals. The plot of delineated zones of hydrothermal alteration indicates the occurrence of iron oxide predominantly within the Keri-Keri Formation in the Northwestern region of the area. The clay and hydroxyl‑bearing minerals occur mostly within the alluvium sediment of the Bima Formation in the Southern region of the area. The work is a guide for geothermal and hydrothermally altered solid mineral explorations.

title: Characteristics and constitutive model of segmented damage and fracture in granite under thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) condition
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 142 Author(s): Luping Cheng, Chun Wang, Yi Tan, Hao Li, Zonghong Zhou, Yumeng Ren, Juanjuan Li, Taihao Cui
abstract: Rock damage induced by uneven heating, stress, and water supply (three-uneven) from exothermic minerals and geothermal exploitation remains a critical challenge. Four controlling factors (heating temperature, immersion water temperature, heated section height ratio, and heating-immersion water cycle times) were used to simulate the three-uneven conditions. Cyclic heating-immersion water and segmented heat treatment mechanical tests were conducted on granite. Additionally, the concept of "segmented damage" is introduced to describe regionally differentiated physicochemical damage. Results show four stages in axial stress-strain curves: upward concave, linear, nonlinear post-peak, and downward rebound. The first two stages are significantly influenced by the four factors. Both compressive strength and elastic modulus decrease with increasing four factors, and the dominant failure mode is compression shear. The heating boundary is a tensile stress concentration zone, revealing tensile crack initiation. A smaller heated section height ratio causes more severe fracturing in the unheated section, and vice versa. Positioned acoustic emission method reveals crack initiation from tensile thermal damage at the heating interface, and damage fractures morphologies (V-shaped, Y-shaped, single inclined planes). Damage evolution exhibits phased characteristics similar to biological population growth: slow accumulation, accelerated development, and stabilization. Based on this, a damage variable for granite under THM conditions is defined using biological population growth theory, and a segmented damage constitutive model is established. Theoretical curves match experimental data, showing the model effectively describes and predicts pre-peak mechanical behavior and strength characteristics under THM conditions, especially in the compaction and elastic stages.

title: Environmental performance of land use change in the Brazilian Pampa Biome: Integrating emergy and life cycle-based carbon assessment
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1056 Author(s): Caroline Conteratto, Alexandre Meyer, Gabrielli do Carmo Martinelli de Souza, Edson Talamini, Clandio Favarini Ruviaro
abstract: Land use change in the Brazilian Pampa biome, marked by the rapid conversion of native grasslands into soybean and rice fields, has raised urgent concerns about environmental sustainability. This study provides a novel integrated assessment of the environmental performance of both traditional livestock systems and modern crop-livestock configurations by combining Life Cycle Assessment and Emergy Evaluation. Over a four-year production period, Life Cycle Assessment was used to quantify greenhouse gas emissions, which were then incorporated into the emergy framework by estimating the additional ecosystem services required for atmospheric emission dilution. Key indicators such as transformity, specific emergy, and emergy-based indices (Emergy Renewability, %R; Emergy Yield Ratio, EYR; Emergy Investment Ratio, EIR; Environmental Loading Ratio, ELR; e Emergy Unsustainability Index, EUI) were applied. Results show that native grassland systems demonstrated superior emergy efficiency, higher reliance on renewable resources, and lower environmental loading. In contrast, integrated systems, particularly those based on rice and soybean, exhibited greater emissions higher entropy, and increased dependence on non-renewable inputs, largely due to irrigation and agrochemical use. A high-yield rice monoculture stood out as an exception in emergy efficiency. These findings highlight the environmental trade-offs associated with agricultural intensification in the Pampa and underscore the importance of integrated assessments to inform sustainable land use strategies and public policies.

title: Integrating machine learning and remote sensing for comprehensive drought modeling in Louisiana, USA
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1056 Author(s): Mizbah Ahmed Sresto, Xuelian Meng, Basant Awasthi, Sharmin Siddika, Sourav Saha, Sanjoy Roy, A.H.M. Mainul Islam, Tanvir Hossain, Zuhayr Shahid Ishmam, Sanzida Rahman Setu, Md Nabid Hashar
abstract: Drought poses significant risks to ecosystems, agriculture, water resources, and society. Among U.S. states, Louisiana experiences severe droughts, as shown by an extreme drought in 2023 that severely affected agricultural and hydrological systems across the region. Although the US Drought Monitor and the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) provide weekly and monthly drought maps, the results often aggregate large areas and lack the spatial detail needed for local-scale assessments. To address this limitation, this research developed an ensemble machine learning (EML) framework integrating Landsat 8 OLI data and environmental variables to assess and map drought vulnerability at a 30-m spatial scale across Louisiana. Training data for ML models were prepared from ground-based monitoring and government sources and were split into 80% training and 20% testing datasets. Initially, four ML models: Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM) were tested. By ensembling the best-performing ML models in different combinations, the stacking ensemble XGB + ANN, with a linear regression meta-learner, achieved the highest test R2 (0.94) for drought prediction. For regional cross-validation, this research used 25 km spatial blocks to evaluate model performance, and the XGB + ANN ensemble produced better results, with R2 = 0.85 and RMSE = 9.57. Findings suggest that the southwestern, southcentral, and southeastern parts of Louisiana experience high drought intensity. About 40% of Louisiana is exposed to high and extreme drought conditions, with woody wetlands (23.2%), evergreen forests (20.3%), and cultivated crops (14.8%) as the most drought-exposed land cover types. Along with providing critical drought insights for Louisiana, this study delivers a high-resolution drought assessment framework, offering state and local agencies and agricultural and water resource management industries a low-cost, data-driven system for effective drought monitoring and management.

title: Multi-decadal evolution of trace metal contamination and hydrologically-driven arsenic enrichment in Eğirdir Lake (Türkiye): a 71-year sentinel case study of a shrinking Mediterranean freshwater ecosystem
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1056 Author(s): Şehnaz Şener, Erhan Şener, Cafer Bulut, Dilek Fidan
abstract: Eğirdir Lake, Türkiye's second-largest freshwater lake and a major drinking-water source for Isparta Province, fell below its regulatory minimum operating level (914.62 m) to 913.98 m in October 2024, the first such breach in a 62-year record. We combined wet-season (April) and dry-season (October) campaigns in 2023–2024 at eight stations with water-quality data dating back to 1953 and monthly hydrological records (1962–2024). Ten trace metals were determined by ICP-MS; water quality was evaluated with pollution indices, and health risks with deterministic and probabilistic USEPA models. A lake-wide mass balance applied to seasonally matched campaigns separated the hydrological concentration effect from net source–sink behaviour. Arsenic enrichment was hydrologically driven on seasonal and interannual time scales: autumn concentrations were 2.0–2.7 times those in spring, exceeded the WHO guideline (10 μg/L) in 12 of 16 samples, and between 2023 and 2024 followed the volume loss within uncertainty. This enrichment did not accumulate over the long term. Despite a volume loss of about 40% since 2009, spring arsenic fell from 13.0 μg/L (48 stations, 44 exceeding the guideline) to 5.6–7.2 μg/L (one exceedance in 16 samples), implying net removal of at least 45–57%. The seasonal rise exceeds what volume change can explain, pointing to a low-water source, hypothesized to be release from sediments. Cadmium, which reached 253 μg/L in 1984, is now largely below detection, a water-column decline of more than 97%. Assuming use of untreated lake water, dry-season arsenic yields adult carcinogenic risks up to 4.7 × 10−4 and child hazard quotients up to 5.7; in the probabilistic analysis, the dry-season probability of exceeding 10−4 was 75% for adults, and that of HQ > 1 was 93% for children. In open freshwater lakes, shrinkage may intensify seasonal arsenic peaks without long-term accumulation, so monitoring and drinking-water treatment should target the low-water season.

title: Indoor pesticide contamination in household and preschool buildings near small agricultural fields
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Tomaz Langenbach, Máize M. Campos, Lúcia Helena P. Bastos, Angélica Castanheira de Oliveira, Maria Helena W.M. Cardoso, João Pedro P. Brandão, Gabriel R. Kandrikg, Ricardo Q. Aucélio, Tácio M.P. de Campos
abstract: It is well known that facilities near agricultural fields are exposed to pesticide drift. However, little data are available in the current literature on indoor pesticide contamination in such settings, particularly for small agricultural sites. In this context, this work presents a study of airborne pesticide pollution across various buildings in the mountainous region of Rio de Janeiro State, both outdoors and indoors. The methodological approach used polyurethane traps: active ones, which allow immediate adsorption of pesticides to measure air-residue concentrations, and passive ones, which only provide insight into the types of pesticides to which the site has been exposed over time. Extraction was performed using methanol in an ultrasonic bath, followed by chromatographic (UPLC-MS/MS) analysis. Results showed a higher number of pesticide molecules indoors than outdoors, reflecting the accumulation of residues from years ago that adsorbed to various surfaces and are later released as volatile “off-gasses”. Control houses in non-agricultural areas are contaminated with home and garden insecticides. Alternatives to reduce exposure and minimise the risk of hazardous effects from inhalation and skin contamination in humans are discussed.

title: Soil nitrogen availability as a metabolic switch between microbial autotrophy–heterotrophy balance and soil carbon sequestration
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Sudeshna Bhattacharjya, Namrata Pal, Asha Sahu, M.C. Manna, A.B. Singh, Dhiraj Kumar, Mahendra Prasad
abstract: One potentially significant but poorly understood process in terrestrial carbon cycling is soil microbial autotrophy. We investigated how soil nitrogen (N) availability regulates the balance between microbial autotrophic and heterotrophic pathways controlling soil carbon (C) dynamics across contrasting land use systems (grassland, horticulture, agroforestry, and natural forest) in central India. RuBisCO enzyme activity and cbbL gene abundance were used to measure microbial autotrophic activity, whereas extracellular enzyme activities, microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE), and glomalin-related soil protein (GRSP) were used to measure heterotrophic processes. Soil N availability appeared to be a major regulator of microbial autotrophic C-fixation capability, which varied consistently across land use systems. RuBisCO activity was found to be mostly predicted by total and mineral N, suggesting that microbial carbon fixation is facilitated by nitrogen availability. Conversely, greater specific oxidative enzyme activity has been linked to lower soil N availability, indicating a shift toward heterotrophic decomposition pathways. The microbial CUE was highest in grassland soils, while the autotrophic C-fixation potential was highest in agroforestry systems. Autotrophic C-fixation potential, nitrate-N, and total GRSP were found to be significant indicators differentiating land use systems by canonical discriminant analysis. Our results reveal that microbial autotrophy is a nitrogen-regulated ecological mechanism that shapes soil carbon sequestration rather than a minor auxiliary pathway. We propose RuBisCO and specific activity of phenol oxidase as robust ecological indicators of soil carbon sequestration potential across land use systems.

title: Shotgun metagenomic surveillance of airport wastewater reveals microbial community restructuring and persistence of antimicrobial-resistance determinants after treatment
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Roberta Magnano San Lio, Maria Clara La Rosa, Andrea Maugeri, Martina Barchitta, Antonella Agodi
abstract: Airport wastewater has emerged as a valuable matrix for wastewater-based epidemiology, providing insights into microbial circulation and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among highly mobile populations. However, the effects of wastewater treatment on the microbial community structure and resistome of airport wastewater have not been comprehensively characterized. Here, we present the first comprehensive metagenomic assessment of paired influent and effluent airport wastewater, enabling characterization of treatment-induced changes in microbial community composition and antimicrobial resistance determinants. Paired influent and effluent wastewater samples were collected from the wastewater treatment plant serving Catania–Fontanarossa Airport (Sicily, Italy). Wastewater treatment significantly reduced microbial richness and induced a consistent shift in community composition, as demonstrated by paired beta-diversity analyses. Proteobacteria became the dominant phylum after treatment, whereas Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes markedly declined. Differential abundance analyses showed enrichment of treatment-associated taxa, including Thauera, Aliiarcobacter and Pseudomonas, accompanied by depletion of gut-associated genera such as Bacteroides, Prevotella and Alistipes. Qualitative resistome profiling indicated partial reduction of several ARG classes but persistence of clinically relevant resistance determinants, particularly those associated with beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides and sulphonamides. Functional profiling indicated treatment-associated metabolic restructuring; however, no functional features remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. Overall, these findings demonstrate that airport wastewater treatment acts as an ecological filter that substantially restructures microbial communities without completely eliminating antimicrobial resistance signatures. Shotgun metagenomic surveillance of airport wastewater may therefore provide valuable complementary information for monitoring AMR dissemination and microbial dynamics within a One Health framework.

title: From targeted to broad detection: How probe-based hybrid capture enhances antibiotic resistance detection in wastewater
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Laura A.E. Van Poelvoorde, Andrea Gobbo, Stefan Hoffman, Cristina Garcia-Graells, Veronik Hutse, Sigrid C.J. De Keersmaecker, Kevin Vanneste, Pieter-Jan Ceyssens, Koenraad Van Hoorde, Marie-Alice Fraiture, Nancy H.C.J. Roosens
abstract: Wastewater-based surveillance has emerged as a promising approach for population-level monitoring of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) beyond clinical settings. Although digital PCR and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) enable sensitive detection and quantification of predefined ARGs, their limited multiplexing restricts the number of targets analysed in a single assay. In contrast, shotgun metagenomics offers broad resistome coverage but may have limited sensitivity for low-abundance targets in complex matrices. Probe-based hybrid capture combines targeted enrichment of thousands of ARGs with high-throughput sequencing and may enhance sensitivity while retaining broad coverage and sequence-level resolution. However, its performance relative to ddPCR and shotgun metagenomics has not yet been evaluated using the same wastewater samples. Therefore, we compared ddPCR, shotgun metagenomics and probe-based hybrid capture using eight influent samples from one wastewater treatment plant. Samples were selected from a longitudinal dataset to cover contrasting ARG abundance profiles. Eight predefined targets were quantified by ddPCR to compare target detection and relative abundance patterns. Shotgun metagenomics described the resistome but detected intermediate- and low-abundance ARGs less consistently. Under the conditions tested, probe-based hybrid capture detected more ARGs per sample and improved recovery of targets poorly represented in the shotgun metagenomic data. Probe-based hybrid capture abundances were positively correlated with ddPCR concentrations for some targets. These results indicate concordance in relative abundance patterns for selected targets, rather than agreement in absolute concentrations. Probe-based hybrid capture may complement ddPCR and shotgun metagenomics for wastewater AMR surveillance when both broad ARG coverage and sensitive detection are required. However, the findings are based on a small, deliberately selected sample set from a single wastewater treatment plant. Further evaluation using larger, independently selected datasets from different treatment plants, geographical settings and wastewater matrices is needed to determine the robustness and applicability of the approach for routine surveillance.

title: Early post-emission particle decay dynamics of E -cigarette aerosols under controlled conditions
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Kaitlyn A. Hunter, Stephanie Jacoby, Nahin Ferdousi-Rokib, Akua Asa-Awuku
abstract: Thirdhand smoke consists of residual pollutants that remain on indoor surfaces after smoking or vaping and may contribute to later exposure through desorption and gas-particle-surface partitioning. However, the early post-emission aerosol dynamics that precede and may contribute to residue formation remain poorly characterized for electronic cigarettes. Here, we quantify particle-number decay following a single controlled electronic-cigarette puff in a controlled small-volume chamber under defined airflow and surface conditions. Particle concentrations showed a consistent two-stage decay pattern: a shorter initial decline, potentially driven by airborne removal and surface deposition, followed by a long-tail post-emission particle-decay phase potentially influenced by surface-related and gas-particle processes. Across triplicate experiments, the tested surface configurations produced no consistent change in the fitted decay parameters, whereas increased airflow accelerated particle clearance. These results characterize the early post-emission behavior of electronic-cigarette aerosols and establish a quantitative baseline for processes that may contribute to subsequent thirdhand residue formation.

title: Hybrid geostatistical and machine learning framework for spatial prediction of natural radionuclides along the Kerala coast
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): R. Akhil, V. Vineethkumar, G. Jayapal, K.P. Shimod, V. Prakash
abstract: Kerala's coastline region is known across the world as a High Background Radiation Area (HBRA) because of the large amounts of placer deposits that include monazite. In order to precisely map radioactive concentrations throughout a 512 km coastal corridor, this study creates a proven hybrid approach that combines gamma spectrometry, geostatistics, and machine learning. Activity concentrations for 232 Th, 226 Ra and 40 K were determined by aggregating 88 individual samples into 18 representative stations using a high-density strategy. A near-perfect positive correlation (r = 0.982) was observed between 232Th and 40K, while 226Ra also exhibited a strong positive correlation (r = 0.917) with 232Th, indicating the co-occurrence of these radionuclides in the monazite-bearing beach sands. The Forest-based Regression model functioned as a spatial prediction model accurately simulating non-linear deposition patterns, while Empirical Bayesian Kriging (EBK) effectively represented spatial uncertainty. A significance value of p = 0.152 was obtained from validation using Paired-Samples T-testing, demonstrating that projected values are showed no statistically significant difference between measured and predicted values (paired t-test, p = 0.152). In the Neendakara-Chavara sector, where Radium Equivalent Activity (Raeq) peaks at 12,809.85 Bq kg−1, our study finds important hotspots. In geomorphologically active coastal regions, the study provides an affordable, potentially applicable framework for similar coastal environments for focused radiation protection measures and environmental monitoring.

title: Multi-seasonal assessment of soil contamination and metal mobility following the Jagersfontein tailings storage facility failure event in South Africa
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): P.S. Rossouw, Marc Humphries
abstract: The failure of the Jagersfontein tailing storage facility (TSF) in South Africa on 11 September 2022 released ~5.8 million m3 of kimberlite tailings into a semi-arid wetland, representing one of the largest such spillages in history. This study investigates the chemical evolution of the deposited tailings and their impact on soil geochemistry over three seasons (18 months). Geochemical and statistical analyses identified two broad elemental groupings: Group 1 elements (B, Na, Mg, Cr, Mo, Co, and Ni) were primarily introduced into the landscape by the tailings, whereas Group 2 elements (V, Mn, Cu, Zn, As, Sn, Cd and U) were mainly enriched through landscape-driven processes, particularly groundwater discharge, and material redistribution during flood events. Sodium migrated rapidly through the soil profile, contaminating soils down to bedrock, and showed no signs of recovery even where surface tailings had been removed. In contrast, Mg, Cr, Co and Ni migrated primarily via colloidal-facilitated transport, resulting in the progressive enrichment of the upper soil horizons. The tailings' sodic and metal-laden nature is particularly problematic in an environment naturally enriched in Na, B, As and Mo. Chemical mass transfer analyses indicate that pedogenic processes are unlikely to reverse contamination within ecologically meaningful timescales. Immediate remediation, including tailings removal, is recommended to mitigate long-term environmental and health impacts. Overall, the findings demonstrate that environmental impacts extend far beyond surface contamination, revealing complex subsurface enrichment pathways that offer new insights into contaminant behaviour following large-scale tailing failures in dryland environments.

title: A 4000-year record of parallel collapse in the ecological niche of Black Sea top predators
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Magie Aiken, Paul Szpak, Morgan L. McCarthy, Jennifer Routledge, Daniela Bănaru, Krishna Das, Elena Gladilina, Pavel Gol'din, Morten Tange Olsen
abstract: Marine ecosystems face multifaceted threats stemming from historical overexploitation and environmental degradation. Despite existing research, there are notable gaps in understanding the long-term dietary dynamics of marine organisms in the context of anthropogenic impacts. To address these gaps, we utilized stable isotope analysis as a proxy for dietary niche and examined changes in the Black Sea over a 4000-year period, focusing on ancient and contemporary samples from cetaceans (Phocoena phocoena, Delphinus delphis, Tursiops truncatus) and fish (Scophthalmus maximus). Among the ancient samples, the isotopic data from all four species revealed a wide and generally overlapping average dietary niche. In contrast, contemporary cetacean and fish samples exhibited niche compression, indicative of a fundamental shift in the Black Sea marine ecosystem from Antiquity to the present day. Our analyses provide ecologically significant temporal perspectives, shedding light on critical trends and changes essential for conservation efforts aimed at addressing contemporary ecological challenges in degraded marine systems.

title: Microplastics as vectors and reservoirs of pharmaceuticals and drugs of abuse: experimental evidence, mechanistic predictions and analytical challenges
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Cinzia Citti, Francesca Vezzalini, Elena Ferri, Cristian Caprari, Giuseppe Gigli, Giuseppe Cannazza
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly investigated as particulate phases capable of interacting with emerging organic contaminants in aquatic environments. This review critically evaluates experimental evidence for pharmaceutical-MP interactions and distinguishes it from mechanistic extrapolation for drugs of abuse, for which direct sorption data remain largely unavailable. Environmental occurrence data for drugs of abuse are used to establish environmental relevance and prioritize target analytes rather than as evidence of sorption onto MPs. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of physicochemical speciation, including pH-dependent lipophilicity (logD), ionization equilibria, and the evolution of polymer surfaces, in governing contaminant-particle interactions. Experimental evidence indicates that sorption onto MPs cannot be described solely by hydrophobic partitioning (logKow), but involves coupled mechanisms, including electrostatic interactions, aging-induced surface oxidation, and biofilm-mediated processes. For drugs of abuse and new psychoactive substances, current knowledge is mainly limited to environmental occurrence and physicochemical properties, which can support testable mechanistic hypotheses but not quantitative predictions. Predictive models remain poorly constrained, particularly because of the scarcity of pH-dependent plastic-water partition coefficients (Kpw) for ionizable compounds. From an analytical perspective, the integration of microplastic sampling with LC-HRMS-based workflows introduces significant methodological challenges. Sampling artifacts, extraction-induced redistribution, matrix effects in electrospray ionization, adduct formation, in-source fragmentation, and variability in identification confidence levels in non-target analysis directly affect data interpretation. The lack of harmonized QA/QC protocols further limits comparability across studies. Progress toward a dynamic and quantitative framework requires controlled sorption and desorption experiments with HRMS, standardized reporting, and models that account for chemical speciation. This combined approach is essential for robust exposure assessment and for testing mechanistic predictions for ionizable contaminants, particularly drugs of abuse.

title: Strategic phosphorus recovery clusters in Europe: Linking geospatial resource availability with thermochemical recovery potential
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Lukas Thomae-Pohl, Matthias Rapf, Ayumi Schober, Christian Schmidberger, Markus Reinmöller, Patrick Braeutigam
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is an essential, non-substitutional resource, yet Europe's supply of elemental P (P4) - classified as critical raw material – remains highly vulnerable. This study assesses whether Europe's secondary organic P resources can support centralized P4 recovery by linking demand, resource availability, spatial distribution and thermochemical recovery potential. European P4 demand was estimated at 34.7 kt(P4)/a from foreign trade statistics for 2017–2022. Sewage sludge alone contains an estimated 190.9–220 kt(P)/a across the EU-27 and the United Kingdom, demonstrating that resource availability exceeds current demand but is spatially distributed. Geospatial clustering identified nine phosphorus resource centers (PRCs) containing 19.5% of the European sewage-sludge-derived P4 potential, while 80.5% remains distributed outside these hotspots. The PRCs differed substantially in plant size and feedstock distribution, highlighting spatial aggregation, not P availability, as a key constraint for centralized recovery. Highest P-flux Ruhr-area PRC was subsequently evaluated using a METSIM-based FlashPhos digital twin. Co-processing sewage sludge with Category 1 meat-and-bone meal (MBM) reduced the Fe:P ratio and increased the modeled P4 recovery from 73.42% to 78.09%, corresponding to a potential output of up to 5350 t(P4)/a, or 16.5% of European demand. MBM co-processing provided an additional gross economic contribution of 4.02–5.25 million€/a through increased P4 production and avoided CaO expenditure. The results demonstrate that Europe possesses sufficient secondary P resources to substantially exceed current P4 demand, but their decentralized distribution makes spatial aggregation a principal constraint. High-density PRCs combined with complementary feedstocks therefore represent promising targets for future site-specific logistical, techno-economic and experimental assessment of centralized P4 recovery.

title: Pesticide-driven bacterial adaptation: biodegradation pathways and co-selection of antibiotic resistance
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Ibrahima Sow, Cheikh Sokhna, Georges Diatta, Jean-Marc Rolain, Seydina M. Diene
abstract: The intensive use and misuse of pesticides has increased the chemical pressure exerted on soil microbiomes. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the global pesticide used in agriculture in 2023 reached 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients, highlighting the magnitude of environmental exposure. Soil bacteria can adapt to pesticide contamination through catabolic pathways encoded by chromosomal genes and/or mobile genetic elements (MGEs), enabling pesticide transformation and sometimes supporting bioremediation. In parallel, a growing body of evidence indicates that non-antibiotic chemicals including herbicides and insecticides can contribute to the emergence and persistence of antibiotic resistance through co-selection. Mechanisms include cross-resistance mediated by multidrug efflux pumps and permeability changes, stress-induced responses and enhanced horizontal gene transfer (HGT) that facilitates the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and MGEs in environmental ecosystems including soil, water and others. In this review, we summarise current knowledge on biodegradation pathways, genetic determinants and documented evidence linked to antibiotic resistance for five selected pesticide case studies: glyphosate, atrazine, cypermethrin, chlorpyrifos and paraquat. We identify where evidence is strongest (e.g., herbicide-associated AMR outcomes) and where major gaps remain, particularly regarding causal attribution under environmentally realistic concentrations and the frequency of ARG co-localisation with catabolic loci. We further propose an explicit mechanistic framework in which biodegradation and antibiotic resistance are examined as potentially interconnected components of bacterial adaptation, connected by a shared mobilome, a shared efflux and stress-response, the reactive intermediates of incomplete catabolism, and nutrient-driven community restructuring.

title: Using performance reference compounds to assess diffusion kinetics of peeper passive samplers to measure the availability of inorganics
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Florent F. Risacher, Jason Conder, Brent G. Pautler, Gunther Rosen
abstract: Dialysis passive samplers (peepers) are often used to measure inorganics in sediment porewater and water. Reverse tracers, added to peepers before their deployment, can be used to estimate the degree to which the peeper has equilibrated with the aqueous matrix via the use of diffusion modeling to predict equilibrium concentrations of non-equilibrated target analytes. Despite the availability of the tracer approach and potential benefits to peeper applications, reverse tracers are not frequently applied due to a lack of clear methods and few practical demonstrations of the approach. This paper evaluated and demonstrated the application of a lithium bromide reverse tracer in peepers via measuring the kinetics of metals analytes and lithium in peepers in water under laboratory conditions. Laboratory results with metal-spiked water indicated that Li tracer data could be used to predict equilibrium concentrations of target metals in water to within 20% accuracy if the deployment time when the tracer achieved at least 50% to 75% equilibrium. A field demonstration of peepers deployed in surface sediment and surface water for 10 days indicated 90% measured equilibration for the tracer and predicted equilibration of 70% to 90% for target metals. This data indicated deployment time periods as short as 4 to 7 days could provide a reasonable estimate of equilibrium concentrations of the metal target analytes using the diffusion modeling approach. Longer peeper deployment periods are likely to result in tracer equilibration above 90% such that the modeling is unnecessary. For more compact and/or finer-grained sediments with lower diffusivity, it is recommended to deploy peepers for approximately 14 to 21 days or longer. Regardless of the deployment time or peeper design, it is recommended to measure a tracer so that the relative level of peeper equilibration can be measured in sediment or surface water field deployments.

title: Changes in the fire resilience of black pine in response to Mediterranean climate variability over the past 300 years
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Bulle I. Alberto, Justin Badeau, Aurèle Baretje, Frédéric Guibal, Jean-Christophe Domec, Christopher Carcaillet
abstract: Elucidating the resilience of trees to wildfires remains a critical issue for forest conservation. The potential changes in tree resilience over time in response to the combined changes in fire regime and climate remain unknown. We hypothesised that tree resilience was influenced by mean fire-return intervals (MFI) and by their interactions with atmospheric conditions over the past 300 years, particularly during drought and hot years. This hypothesis was tested by analyzing tree-ring widths following past fires, using growth during fire-free periods as baseline, and atmospheric values (annual and seasonal temperature and precipitation, drought index and CO2 concentration). The study focused on black pine (Pinus nigra) as a model species to investigate long-term ecological responses to fires in natural forests of Corsica, a western Mediterranean island. The study is based on 180 cross-dated black pines from four Corsican mountain sites. 54 fires were recorded between 1719 CE and 2012 CE. Four contrasted periods, defined according to MFI and atmospheric records are used to assess the black pine responses to fire events, MFI period, and climate. The fire resistance and resilience of trees have gradually declined since about 1850, independently of the MFI and increased atmospheric CO₂ levels. Post-fire radial growth recovery lengthened over time, indicating a decline in resistance. Concurrently, tree-ring responded more positively to precipitation and negatively to drought intensity. In isolation, fire does not compromise tree resilience. But the combined effects of drought and wildfires thus threaten black pines by shrinking their resilience mainly since 1971, which underscores the increasing vulnerability of this Mediterranean tree to fire in an increasingly dry climate.

title: The use of biochar in agricultural soils: Impacts on vineyard productivity and the potential for carbon capture and sequestration
description: Publication date: 10 November 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1055 Author(s): Leonel J.R. Nunes
abstract: Background Viticulture is increasingly exposed to water deficit, heat and soil degradation, prompting interest in biochar as a soil amendment that may simultaneously improve productivity and sequester carbon. Methods This integrative review used a documented Scopus search (June 2026), targeted searches (September 2026), explicit eligibility criteria and a PRISMA-style flow diagram. All vineyard field trials were tabulated, meta-analyses were reported with effect and sample sizes, and each conclusion was graded by level of evidence. Results Significant yield gains were confined to three Tuscan vineyards amended with the same 500 °C orchard-pruning biochar on acidic to neutral, carbon-poor, non-irrigated soils (+16% to +67% per harvest, persisting ten years after application), and eight site-level comparisons, six in humid-temperate, cool or calcareous-alkaline settings, showed no significant yield response, whereas increases in soil water and topsoil organic carbon were more consistent. The most robust climate outcome is the persistence of the biochar carbon (inert fraction unchanged after 15 years, 65–89% remaining after 100 years), whereas N2O and CH4 reductions are not robust at field scale and remain undetected in vineyards. The previously cited 7.5 Mg CO2-eq ha-1 yr-1, the mean of all soil‑carbon practices in vineyards, rests on very few biochar observations, whereas a single 16.5 t ha-1 (dry) application stores 31–42 Mg CO2-eq ha-1 over 100 years before life-cycle emissions. Without a yield response, the break-even carbon price for biochar costing €200–500 t-1 is €90–243 per t CO2-eq, against a carbon-removal index of €135 (2026), and a single application requires 22–48 years of a vineyard's own prunings. Conclusions Carbon storage in the biochar itself is well supported, agronomic benefits are demonstrated only for a narrow pedoclimatic domain and require independent replication, and greenhouse-gas co-benefits, long-term microbial effects, economic viability and large-scale carbon farming remain plausible but poorly documented or speculative.

title: Early diagenetic Mo-S isotope and trace metal systematics in organic-rich marine sediments
description: Publication date: 1 December 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 434 Author(s): Ricardo D. Monedero-Contreras, Carolina Rosca, Francisca Martínez-Ruiz, Antonio Delgado-Huertas, Martin Wille, Stephan König
abstract: Molybdenum (Mo) isotope compositions have been widely applied as a paleoredox proxy to reconstruct past ocean deoxygenation, particularly from organic-rich sediments such as sapropels and Black Shales. Yet the extent to which early diagenetic processes influence Mo primary redox signals (concentration and isotope composition) remains insufficiently constrained. Here, we present high-resolution molybdenum (Mo) and sulfur (S) isotope compositions, as well as trace metal concentrations, to assess the influence of postdepositional processes, including redoxcline migration and mineral phase cycling on sedimentary Mo isotope records in a deep marine setting, precisely sapropel S1 from ODP Site 969 (Mediterranean Ridge). At this site, sapropel S1 provides an ideal natural laboratory as it exhibits: (i) a complete redox sequence from oxic/suboxic to anoxic and sulfidic conditions; (ii) evidence of early diagenetic modification; and (iii) a distinct triple-peak Mo concentration pattern, each deriving from specific syndepositional and postdepositional redox processes. The oxygen-depleted organic-rich and sulfide-rich intervals exhibit light Mo isotope compositions (expressed as δ98Mo relative to NIST-3134 + 0.25‰) ranging from −0.52‰ to as low as −1.63‰, as well as light S isotope compositions below −35‰ (expressed as δ34S relative to Vienna Canyon Diablo Troilite standard). These δ98Mo values are lighter than expected for organic- and sulfide-rich sediments and likely reflect additional early burial diagenetic fractionation driven by non-quantitative Mo thiolation and Mn redox cycling under weakly sulfidic conditions. The enrichment of Mn- and Fe-oxyhydroxide-associated trace elements (e.g., Co, Ni, Tl, and Cu) at or above the oxidation front, together with U enrichment beneath organic-rich sediments, supports a multistage redox-diagenetic framework involving Mn–Fe oxide cycling, sulfide mineralization, and element redistribution across dynamic redox boundaries. The coupled Mo–S isotope systematics further constrain variations in sulfide availability and sulfur cycling. It shows how incomplete Mo thiolation can modify the dissolved Mo pool, whereas S reflects a sustained sulfate supply under open-system sulfidic diagenesis. Together, these results show that the Mo isotope record of sapropel S1 at ODP Site 969 is a diagenetically integrated signal rather than a direct archive of depositional redox conditions, illustrating how primary signatures can be remodeled across dynamic redox boundaries.
