Net N2O consumption in the hypolimnia of both basins was accompanied by isotopic shifts toward lighter δ15Nbulk and δ15Nβ values, contrary to trends observed in pure cultures. These inverse apparent isotope effects suggest concurrent N2O production during net consumption. Using a simplified box-model (i.e., isotope mass balance) approach, we estimated that 5–17% of the consumed N2O needed to be replaced by simultaneous N2O production in order to match the observed in situ δ15Nbulk-N2O data. Our findings highlight the complexity of N2O cycling in lake systems and reveal that isotopic overprinting from simultaneous N2O production and consumption can obscure traditional isotope-based interpretations. At the same time, they underscore the value of stable isotopes in disentangling N2O production and consumption mechanisms.

title: Porewater nitrate isotope dynamics in selected benthic habitats: Modulation by sediment reactivity and process coupling via nitrite
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 433 Author(s): Alessandra Mazzoli, Peter Reichert, Cameron M. Callbeck, Claudia Frey, Paul M. Magyar, Tim J. Paulus, Donald E. Canfield, Sergei Katsev, Jakob Zopfi, Moritz F. Lehmann
abstract: Denitrification is the primary pathway for fixed nitrogen (N) removal from aquatic systems. Its occurrence in sediments is promoted by suboxic conditions, high organic matter reactivity, sharp redox transitions, and the co-occurrence of multiple N-transformation processes. Benthic denitrification can be investigated through natural abundance nitrate N and oxygen (O) isotope ratio measurements to trace nitrate reduction and related N-transformation processes within the sediment. Yet, while the biological and apparent (i.e., in the overlying water) isotope effects for nitrate reduction, εDen, have been widely investigated, the controls on their expression at the sediment porewater level remain underexplored, particularly in lacustrine systems. Additionally, it is unclear how simultaneously occurring N-cycle processes may modify the resulting nitrate isotope signatures. Since apparent εDen values are commonly used to estimate benthic denitrification, it is also crucial to identify how these processes affect their expression. Here, we measured nitrate isotope ratios in sediment porewaters from multiple lacustrine and marine settings and quantified denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium, and anammox rates using 15N-tracer incubations. We further employed a novel diagenetic N isotope model to estimate εDen under different sedimentary reactivity and redox conditions. In most investigated environments, Rayleigh-derived N and O isotope effects are strongly reduced (mostly < 4‰) in porewaters compared to reported biological isotope effects, whereas model-based estimates provide intermediate fractionations. We attribute the generally low isotope fractionation to high sediment reactivity and insufficient nitrate diffusion to the nitrate-reducing zone, leading to near-complete nitrate consumption at the microbial level (i.e., before the cellular level effect is expressed at the porewater level). Consistent with this interpretation, environments characterized by higher organic matter reactivity exhibited the lowest isotope fractionation. The N and O isotope values in nitrate exhibited partial decoupling, resulting in both negative and positive Δδ18O:Δδ15N deviations from 1:1. Negative deviations may reflect an enhanced contribution of the periplasmatic nitrate reductase, particularly in lacustrine environments with fluctuating O2 concentrations. Positive deviations likely indicate nitrate (re)generation via nitrification or anammox, and tight nitrate-nitrite redox cycling (i.e., nitrate reduction coupled to nitrite oxidation). The spatial overlap of N transformations (e.g., nitrification–denitrification) in our model results increased the coupling of processes through nitrite, which strongly influences nitrate isotope dynamics. Model simulations indicate that nitrite-reducing processes generate 15N-enriched nitrite due to N isotopic fractionation; subsequent nitrite oxidation, associated with an inverse kinetic isotope effect, produces highly 15N-enriched nitrate. Such 15N enrichment of nitrate should therefore not be interpreted as evidence for nitrate reduction and fixed-N loss. Our findings demonstrate that explicit consideration of nitrite dynamics is essential for correctly interpreting nitrate isotope data in sediment porewaters and for avoiding inaccurate estimation of benthic N-transformation pathways and N-loss rates.

title: Oxygen isotope exchange unravels million-year long hydrogeochemical evolution of a deep carbonate aquifer in the Swiss Molasse Basin
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 433 Author(s): Christoph Wanner, Lukas Aschwanden, Mirjam Kiczka, H. Niklaus Waber, Michael Heidinger, Emiliano Stopelli, Daniel Traber
abstract: The stable isotope composition of groundwaters is essential to characterize their origin and processes of their hydrogeochemical evolution. In carbonate aquifers, the interaction between groundwater and carbonates enriched in 18O may shift groundwater δ18O values to the right of the global meteoric water line. Although experimental studies showed that the exchange of oxygen isotopes between groundwater and carbonates may proceed rapidly under ambient conditions, there is little information regarding the kinetics of the exchange under geological conditions. To better quantify the relevance of carbonate-groundwater interaction on oxygen isotope signatures of both groundwater and carbonates, we present an extensive hydrogeochemical characterization of deep groundwaters collected during a deep drilling campaign in the Swiss Molasse Basin. Combining information from chemical and isotopic analyses, groundwater residence time tracers, the geological evolution of the area, as well as geochemical modeling we quantitatively demonstrate that the exchange of oxygen isotopes is mainly relevant for carbonate-dominated aquifers consisting of fractured rock with a low porosity and a large solid to liquid ratio. For such conditions, isotopic equilibrium is reached in more than a few hundred thousand but less than 20 Mio years at temperatures below 70 °C. It follows that the equilibration of groundwater δ18O values may serve as independent proxy for the residence time of very old groundwaters. Moreover, our study shows that for rock buffered systems the oxygen isotope exchange has only minor effects on the oxygen isotope composition of rock-forming calcite. Accordingly, it does not affect the use of the δ18O signature of calcite as environmental proxy.

title: Volcanically driven manganese mineralization mediated by carbonate substrates during the Early Triassic
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 433 Author(s): Li Wang, Ling Gan, Chenchen Yang, Yinqiang Zhao, Hai Xu, Runsheng Yin, Hanjie Wen
abstract: Sedimentary manganese (Mn) deposits are critical Mn resources whose formation is intricately linked to marine redox conditions. This study conducts mineralogical, elemental, and mercury (Hg) isotopic analyses of the Early Triassic Dongping sedimentary Mn deposit (South China) to constrain the drivers of Mn deposition. Manganese ore layers exhibit anomalously high Hg concentrations and Hg/TOC ratios, indicating intense volcanism during Mn mineralization. The temporal coincidence of Mn mineralization (∼250 Ma) with Siberian Traps eruptions points to a causal link. Mn ores, dominated by rhodochrosite with minor Mn calcite and kutnohorite, exhibit core-rim structures, indicating nucleation on pre-existing carbonate (calcite/dolomite) surfaces followed by crystal growth and/or metasomatic replacement. Redox-sensitive elements (Mo, U, V) and Ce/Ce* ratios reveal a transition from oxic to anoxic conditions during mineralization, with a return to oxic conditions post-mineralization. Based on these findings, we propose a three-stage metallogenic model: (1) Volcanic CO2 emission during this period sustained greenhouse warming, enhanced continental weathering, and increased nutrient influx into oceans, promoting primary productivity, ocean stratification and frequent shifts in the oxic-anoxic interface; (2) Redox changes in the oceans drove large-scale Mn deposition in the form of rhodochrosite at basin margins; and (3) Pervasive carbonate grains facilitated rhodochrosite nucleation and growth. This work establishes a genetic link between Siberian Traps volcanism and Early Triassic Mn ore formation, and offers key insights into the genesis of shallow-water sedimentary Mn deposits.

title: Prebiotic organic compounds in asteroid Bennu and Ryugu reflect divergent parent body histories
description: Publication date: 15 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, Volume 433 Author(s): Angel Mojarro, José C. Aponte, Daniel P. Glavin, Jamie E. Elsila, Jason P. Dworkin, Harold C. Connolly
abstract: The return of pristine samples from carbonaceous asteroids Ryugu by JAXA’s Hayabusa2 mission and Bennu by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission has enabled the direct comparative study of prebiotic organic compounds across the two primitive bodies. Using pyrolysis, thermochemolysis, and one-pot derivatization coupled to gas chromatography-triple quadrupole-mass spectrometry, we analyzed free volatile, insoluble, and soluble organic matter in a Ryugu aggregate and compared results to a Bennu aggregate and stones of interest. Pyrolysis of the Ryugu sample revealed polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, their alkylated homologues, and sulfur-, oxygen-, and nitrogen-bearing heterocyclic aromatic compounds consistent with aqueous alteration of the parent body. One-pot derivatization of the Ryugu aggregate yielded only tentative detections of β-alanine and 2,4-diaminopyrimidine. This is in contrast to the 14 proteinogenic α-amino acids and five canonical nucleobases previously detected across Bennu samples using the same technique. Thermochemolysis of the Ryugu sample revealed limited methylated derivatives while Bennu samples did not yield compounds above the procedural blank. The sparse thermochemolysis detections in samples from both asteroids are notable given that diverse methylated derivatives have been reported from the Orguiel (CI1) and Murchison (CM2) meteorites. We interpret these results as most likely originating from reagent-mineral interactions suppressing TMAH yields. Overall, contrasting organic inventories reflect divergent-parent body histories. Results from the Ryugu samples are consistent with a CI1-like classification, displaying increased alkylation of insoluble organic matter alongside depleted soluble organic matter abundances. In contrast, Bennu preserves heterogeneous organic signatures across stones recording multiple distinct alteration episodes. The presence of prebiotic molecules including amino acids and nucleobases across both asteroids further highlights the significance of carbonaceous bodies in contributing the chemical building blocks of life throughout the early Solar System.

title: Dehydration processes of stagnant slab within the mantle transition zone revealed by geochemistry of olivine-hosted melt inclusions
description: Publication date: Available online 4 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Junfu Zhang, Yang Yu, Jie Tang, Feng Wang, Wenliang Xu
abstract: Nearly 50% of subducted plates may stagnate in the mantle transition zone (MTZ), forming the big mantle wedge (BMW) structure. Fluids or melts released by subducted stagnant slab within the MTZ intensively influence the physical–chemical nature and evolution of the upper mantle in a big mantle wedge system. However, dehydration processes of stagnant slab within the MTZ are unclear. Here, we present geochemical and H-B isotopic data of olivine-hosted melt inclusions from Early Oligocene-Miocene basalts in eastern Northeastern China (ENC), with an aim of constraining the dehydration processes of subducted stagnant slab in the MTZ within the BMW system. The olivine-hosted melt inclusions in OIB-like basalts (33–21 Ma) exhibit low water contents in primary melts (545–965 ppm) and mantle sources (116–202 ppm), coupled with low H2O/Ce ratios (7.96–13.6) and low δD values (−406 ‰ to −191 ‰), implying that the water in mantle sources is mainly contributed by ancient sediment-dominated dehydration in the MTZ. The olivine-hosted melt inclusions in weak-arc like basalts (11 Ma) exhibit relatively high water contents in primary melt (5780–6381 ppm) and mantle source (354–390 ppm), with elevated H2O/Ce ratios (135–166) and upper mantle-like δD values (−119 ‰ to −78 ‰), suggesting that the water in mantle source is mainly contributed by the young lower oceanic crust-dominated dehydration in the MTZ. Additionally, the melt inclusions in the ENC basalts also exhibit variable δ11B values (−17.10 ‰ to −0.08 ‰). The heavy B isotopic compositions of a small amount of melt inclusions from 33 Ma and 11 Ma basalts indicate the contribution of subducted serpentinite dehydration. The water contents in mantle sources of 33 Ma and 21 Ma basalts are lower than those in mantle sources of the early Cenozoic basalts, which is consistent with the transition from an active continental margin setting to trench-arc-basin system and formation of the northeastern (NE) Asian BMW, whereas the increase of water contents in mantle sources from 33 Ma to 11 Ma basalts could reflect the initial stagnance of subducted Pacific slab to formation of the NE Asian BMW as well as the transformation from ancient sediment-dominated dehydration to young lower oceanic crust-dominated dehydration, which is closely related to the evolution of the NE Asian BMW.

title: Beyond bulk sediments: extracting salinity signals from Sr/Ba ratios in complex marginal-marine settings
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Xia Zhang, Xiaotian Zhang, Yue Cai, Rong Hu, Guyue Tan
abstract: Sedimentary successions in modern to sub-modern marginal-marine environments are valuable archives of climatic and environmental change. However, paleosalinity reconstruction in these settings is often compromised by lithological heterogeneity, complex sediment sources, hydrodynamic processes, and diagenetic overprinting. Using a well-constrained postglacial succession (∼15 ka to present) from the Qiantang River coastal system, we test and refine Sr/Ba-based salinity proxies, that have been widely used in fine-grained siliciclastic successions. To investigate occurrence modes and interfering factors of Sr and Ba, we analyzed bulk sediments, grain-size fractions, and selective chemical extracts using dilute acetic acid (HAc), ammonium carbonate (AC), sodium acetate (NaAc), and ammonium acetate (AA). Our results show that Sr/Ba ratios in the 1.50) environments. Nevertheless, this ratio tends to overestimate salinity in high-energy settings, where clay winnowing preferentially removes exchangeable Ba. We therefore apply a correction using the relative proportion of the coarse-grained sensitive end-member (FEI). The FEI-normalized SrAC/BaHAc ratio shows enhanced sensitivity to relative sea-level variations and successfully identifies the MFS. This refined multi-proxy framework is well-suited for modern to sub-modern marginal-marine settings where exchangeable fractions are largely preserved, and confounding influences can be corrected through integration with sedimentological analyses. For ancient or diagenetically altered successions, where exchangeable fractions are severely modified but within a closed system, bulk Sr/Ba proxies in fine-grained successions remain a promising alternative, provided that carbonate-rich and/or barite-bearing intervals are treated with caution. This conclusion is supported by the general consistency observed between the Si/Al-normalized Sr/Ba<10μm ratios and the refined exchangeable proxies. Overall, this multi-proxy approach circumvents confounding factors and offers practical utility for paleoenvironmental and relative sea-level reconstruction in complex modern to sub-modern marginal-marine settings. More broadly, the methodological framework might offer a reference point for analogous investigations in other contexts, depending on site-specific preservation conditions of exchangeable fractions.

title: Potassium isotope dichotomy in hydrogenetic ferromanganese crusts: phase-specific archives of seawater signatures or authigenic processes?
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Jiayang Chen, Weiqiang Li, Tianyu Chen, Yang Qu
abstract: Stable potassium (K) isotopes offer valuable insights into K cycles at various scales. Hydrogenetic ferromanganese (Fe-Mn) crusts, precipitated from seawater and enriched in K, could serve as potential marine K isotopic archives. To evaluate this potential, we conducted detailed investigations of the elemental and isotopic characteristics of K in two hydrogenetic Fe-Mn crusts from the northwestern Pacific Ocean floor over the past 80 million years. Sequential extractions reveal two major K-bearing phases: exchangeable K mainly in Mn oxyhydroxides (62.8 ± 8.9%) and structural K in silicates (32.6 ± 9.3%), with other phases contributing less than 5%. The δ41K values of the exchangeable K, ranging from −0.09 ± 0.04‰ to 0.35 ± 0.05‰, are higher than those of silicate K, which range from −0.71 ± 0.06‰ to −0.34 ± 0.05‰. Notably, the δ41K values of exchangeable K in the two crusts exhibit inconsistent temporal variations. This indicates that exchangeable K in Fe-Mn crusts is susceptible to local diagenetic processes, undermining its reliability as a proxy for long-term seawater δ41K changes. In contrast, the δ41K values of silicate K show consistent temporal trends, correlating with changes in distances between the sample sites from the Hawaiian hotspot. This suggests that the isotopic ratios of silicate-bound K in Fe-Mn crusts can record seafloor authigenic processes, and the growth of authigenic minerals in Fe-Mn crusts appears to be mainly influenced by basaltic volcanic detritus from hotspots. This study reveals a fundamental elemental and isotopic dichotomy of K in Fe-Mn crusts, demonstrating that 1) hydrogenetic Fe-Mn crusts are unlikely to be robust recorders of seawater K isotope evolution, and 2) silicate-bound K can be a sensitive tracer for seafloor authigenic processes and hotspot-related volcanism.

title: Nanoscale mechanisms of mesocrystal formation during non-classical heterogeneous growth of manganese (hydr)oxides on ferrihydrite
description: Publication date: Available online 3 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Yixuan Yang, Qingze Chen, Chi Zhang, Haozhe Ma, Jing Liu, Jianxi Zhu, Runliang Zhu, Hongping He
abstract: Crystallization by particle attachment (CPA) is an important non-classical pathway of mineral growth that often produces mesocrystals composed of aligned nanoparticles, whose internal interfaces and defects can impart distinctive geochemical reactivity. Given that mineral nucleation and growth in nature commonly occur on pre-existing substrates, a key yet underexplored question is how CPA-mediated mesocrystal growth operates at such heterogeneous interfaces. Herein, we investigated the heterogeneous oxidation of aqueous Mn(II) on ferrihydrite, with a specific focus on the formation of manganese (Mn) (hydr)oxides mesocrystals via CPA. Our results show that Mn (hydr)oxides formed on ferrihydrite grew via oriented assembly into mesocrystalline nanowires. Specifically, Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles assembled via end-to-end or side-by-side manners to elongate or widen nanowires, respectively. Misorientations among component nanoparticles led to curved nanowires, whereas straight nanowires resulted from well-aligned interfaces. Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles with different crystallographic orientations, and even different mineral phases, can assemble into mesocrystalline nanowires featuring misoriented but crystallographically correlated interfaces. This assembly is rationalized by approximate lattice correspondence at particle junctions and further supported by molecular dynamics simulations revealing energetically favorable interfacial configurations. The assembly of Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles was likely initiated by their detachment from ferrihydrite surfaces, driven by the accumulation and release of stress and strain at mismatched Mn (hydr)oxide-ferrihydrite interfaces. Revealing numerous new atomic details of Mn (hydr)oxide CPA, our study links the assembly behaviors of Mn (hydr)oxide nanoparticles to the development of their mesocrystalline structures. We also integrate our new findings with previous studies and synthesize the mechanisms by which different mineral substrates regulate CPA of Mn (hydr)oxides. These findings advance the understanding of heterogeneous growth of Mn (hydr)oxides on iron (hydr)oxides at the nanoscale and contribute to a more integrated view of coupled Mn-Fe cycling in the environment. Our study also highlights the critical roles of substrate mineral surfaces in non-classical mineral growth.

title: Volcanically driven redox stratification and N–S–C cycling perturbation in a Late Triassic lacustrine system: controls on carbon sequestration efficiency
description: Publication date: Available online 2 November 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Xianxu Fang, Kelai Xi, Yingchang Cao, Xiujuan Wang, Guanghui Yuan, Yuan You, Miruo Lin, Ke Li, Chao Liang, Keyu Liu, Fang Hao
abstract: Water-column redox structure fundamentally governs ecosystem dynamics, biogeochemical cycling, and ultimately sedimentary responses. Redox stratification recorded in deep-time organic-rich lacustrine shales was frequently perturbed by geological events, particularly volcanism, which enhanced deoxygenation and nutrient loading under recurrent volcanic inputs. However, the biogeochemical pathways by which ecological stress developed and persisted remain poorly constrained. Here we investigate the Upper Triassic Chang 73 Member of the Yanchang Formation in the Ordos Basin, a continuous succession of organic-rich lacustrine shales deposited under episodic volcanic influence. Integrating sedimentological, paleontological and multi-proxy geochemical records, we reconstruct the vertical redox structure of the paleolake and assess its response to contrasting volcanic input fluxes. Our results reveal a stable three-layer redox stratification (oxic, suboxic, and euxinic) that couples nitrogen–sulfur–carbon biogeochemical cycling via a cascade of aerobic respiration, denitrification, anammox, Fe–Mn reduction, and sulfate reduction. Positive δ15Norg values provide direct evidence for a chemocline that restricts denitrification and anammox to the suboxic layer without interference from sulfate reduction below. As volcanic input flux increased from low to high, δ13Corg shifted from negative excursions reflecting internal recycling of 12C to positive excursions driven by Rayleigh fractionation. This shift marks the transition from weakened to efficient carbon sequestration. These contrasting redox states demonstrate that volcanic forcing regulated carbon sequestration through nutrient fertilization that elevated primary productivity, but it was the integrity of redox stratification that ultimately determined carbon burial efficiency. Accordingly, we develop an integrated redox‑ecological model that integrates the strength of external volcanic forcing, the feedbacks of internal biogeochemical cycling, and the efficiency of lacustrine carbon sequestration into a coherent system. This model provides a process-based explanation of how this integrity mediates ecological stress and governs carbon sequestration efficiency. Drawing on this deep-time eutrophic lake system, this study identifies critical redox thresholds governing ecosystem responses to nutrient enrichment and deoxygenation in modern lakes.

title: Processes controlling δ 41 K variations in the weathering profile of granite: implications for continental weathering proxies
description: Publication date: Available online 31 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Mei-Li He, Jun-Wen Zhang, Na Wu, Shi-Chao An, Jun-Mu, Dong-Yang Xiong, Liang Guo, Rui Wang, Zhi-Qi Zhao
abstract: Potassium (K) isotopes are significantly fractionated during the chemical weathering of silicate rocks, and therefore represent a potential proxy for the intensity of weathering. However, the processes influencing the fractionation of K isotopes during the weathering of silicate remain unclear. This study analyzes the K isotope composition (δ41K) of a weathering profile that was developed based on granite obtained from southeastern China. The δ41K value exhibited a systematic decrease, from −0.44 ± 0.04‰ in the granite bedrock at the bottom to −0.68 ± 0.03‰ in the most weathered profile near the surface, to indicate significant fractionation of K isotopes during the weathering of the sample. As the degree of weathering increased (CIA: 52.2 ∼ 92.4), the δ41K value of the weathered products decreased, and yielded a strong positive correlation with τK,Ti (R2 = 0.76, p < 0.01), a strong negative correlation with CIA (R2 = 0.79, p < 0.01), and was a proxy for the formation of clay minerals (K/Al; R2 = 0.80, p < 0.01) (excluding the influence of upper-layer plant litter). These observations suggest that the formation of clay minerals leads to the preferential incorporation of isotopically lighter K. Although kaolinite might have adsorbed minor amounts of isotopically heavier K on its surface when pH ≥ 6, this had a limited effect on changes in the δ41K value in the weathering products. The mineralogical composition and 87Sr/86Sr ratios in the profile suggest that the differential weathering of the primary minerals occurred in this weathering profile. While plagioclase had isotopically heavier K compositions than the bedrock, the contribution of its weathering to the total K pool within the weathering profile was relatively limited. Moreover, K-feldspar and biotite yielded similar K isotopic signatures to that of the bedrock, the weathering of which did not significantly influence the δ41K values of the weathering products. Therefore, the differential weathering of the primary minerals had a negligibly small effect on variations in the δ41K values within the weathering profile. Moreover, the total organic carbon (TOC) content in the upper part of the profile (≤100 cm) exhibited a strong positive correlation with τK, Ti (R2 = 0.84, p < 0.01), while the δ41K values of the weathering products showed a significant negative correlation with the TOC (R2 = 0.57, p < 0.01) and K/Rb (R2 = 0.72, p < 0.01). The weathering products near the surface (≤100 cm) were primarily influenced by the input of plant litter with light K isotope compositions, while biogenic processes had a negligibly minor role at deeper depths. These results suggest that the preferential incorporation of isotopically light K is the critical process controlling K isotopic variations within the profile. These results explain the enrichment of light K isotopes as silicate weathering intensifies, and support their use as tracers of the intensity of chemical weathering.

title: Lithospheric mantle derivation and depth-dependent endowment of Neoarchean orogenic gold in the Yilgarn Craton
description: Publication date: Available online 30 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Qingfei Wang, David I. Groves, Runsheng Yin, Shiyu Liu, Carl Brauhart, Lin Yang, Huajian Li, Neal J. McNaughton, Kunfeng Qiu, Yongbo Peng, Jun Deng
abstract: The Yilgarn Craton represents one of the largest Precambrian orogenic gold provinces globally. The Kalgoorlie and Kurnalpi terranes, dominated by mesozonal-epizonal deposits, host the bulk of the gold, whereas the South West and Youanmi terranes, dominated by hypozonal deposits, are far less endowed. The source of auriferous fluids has long been debated between models involving crustal metamorphic devolatilization at mid-crustal levels and magmatic-hydrothermal processes near the crust-mantle boundary, whereas the causes for the marked regional endowment contrast remain poorly understood. Here we present integrated Hg, multiple S, and Sr isotope data to reveal that these four terranes share a common lithospheric mantle source and that their contrasting gold endowment relates to distinct depth-controlled mineralization processes. Non-zero Δ33S values of gold-related sulfides (−0.09 to 0.81 %) are comparable to those of granites across all terranes. This implies that lower-crustal components were involved in the source, arguing against a model involving a mid-crustal metamorphic fluid source. The Δ199Hg values of native gold and sulfides range from negative to positive and center near zero, indicating that lithospheric mantle metasomatized by oceanic sediments with significant input of continental crust is the most plausible source for the auriferous fluid. This is supported by elevated (87Sr/86Sr)i ratios of hydrothermal apatite. Critically, Δ199Hg values are similar between the well-endowed Kurnalpi Terrane and the poorly endowed South West and Youanmi terranes, confirming a common lithospheric mantle source. In striking contrast, δ202Hg values are markedly higher in mesozonal-epizonal deposits (0.11–1.79 %) than in hypozonal deposits. This distinction is attributed to fluid phase separation during mesozonal and epizonal mineralization at middle-upper crustal levels, whereas isotopically light Hg was preferentially partitioned into the vapor phase and lost, leaving the residual fluids enriched in heavy Hg isotopes. In contrast, the greater depths of hypozonal mineralization effectively inhibited such phase separation. Collectively, these interpretations suggest that the primary control on gold endowment is not source heterogeneity but rather the current exposed crustal depths of the terranes.

title: Dissolved organic matter decouples Fe(II) oxidation from arsenic immobilization: radical localization, mineral disorder and colloid stabilization
description: Publication date: Available online 30 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Junhao Niu, Valentina Erastova, Xinghao Wang, Yanwei Wang, Juan Gao
abstract: Arsenic contamination of paddy soils and shallow aquifers threatens drinking-water safety and staple-crop production worldwide, and its severity is set by Fe-As coupling at subsurface oxygenation fronts. Where oxygen periodically infiltrates reduced layers, Fe(II) oxygenation generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) and fresh Fe(III) (oxyhydr)oxides that jointly oxidize mobile As(III) and sequester the resulting As(V). How dissolved organic matter (DOM), a ubiquitous constituent of redox-dynamic environments, disrupts this natural attenuation circuit remains insufficiently resolved at the molecular scale. We examined straw-derived DOM across C/Fe molar ratios of 0–10 during aerobic oxidation of 1 mM Fe(II) in synthetic solutions at pH 5.5–7.5, combining radical quenching, kinetic modelling, XRD, Fe K-edge XAS and STEM-EELS. Converging quenching and modelling evidence indicates that As(III) oxidation proceeded predominantly via hydroxyl radicals generated at the Fe-mineral – water interface (·OHsurf) rather than via the freely dissolved pool. Increasing DOM progressively relocated ·OH generation to aqueous Fe(II)-DOM complexes, where radicals were scavenged before reaching surface-associated As(III); the Fe(II) utilization efficiency for As(III) oxidation accordingly declined from 0.33% to 0.13%. A transition near C/Fe ≈ 5 for rice straw-derived DOM separated two geochemical regimes: below it, micron-scale lepidocrocite aggregates settled and retained arsenic, whereas above it, ferrihydrite–organic nanocolloids of 160–360 nm carrying approximately 40% of total As remained suspended. We identify that DOM controls As fate through coupled effects on the spatial partitioning of radical generation, iron mineral transformation, and colloidal stabilization, and propose C/Fe stoichiometry as a governing chemical parameter for predicting arsenic fate in redox-fluctuating environments.

title: Manganese mineralization driven by dynamic oceanic redox fluctuations: insights from chromium isotopes
description: Publication date: Available online 29 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Qiang Chen, Xuefei Liu, Qingfei Wang, Fangge Chen, Xuefei Sun, Lei Liu, Jun Deng
abstract: Sedimentary manganese (Mn) deposits are valuable archives of paleoceanographic redox conditions and biogeochemical cycles, yet the mechanisms controlling Mn precipitation remain debated. Here, we present mineralogical, geochemical, and Cr isotopic (δ53Cr) data from the Late Carboniferous Ortokarnash Mn deposit (NW China) to constrain its genesis and link redox fluctuations to Mn mineralization. Mn-bearing layers are hosted in organic-rich marlstones with δ53Cr values of 0.46 ± 0.03‰, comparable to those of modern euxinic sediments (Cariaco Basin: 0.53 ± 0.21‰). Together with low redox-sensitive element abundances and abundant fine-grained framboidal pyrite, these signatures indicate wall-rock deposition under euxinic conditions. In contrast, relict primary Mn oxides within Mn carbonates, elevated δ53Cr values (average 1.08‰), and positive Ce anomalies indicate that Mn carbonates formed via diagenetic reduction of Mn oxides originally precipitated in oxic bottom waters. We link these redox oscillations to episodic ventilation and self-regulation of restricted basins during transgressions. Large-scale sea-level rises introduced oxygenated surface waters, transiently oxygenating the basins, while subsequent upwelling of Mn(II)-rich anoxic deep waters drove rapid Mn(II) oxidation. Enhanced nutrient supply during transgressions increased primary productivity and benthic oxygen consumption, promoting diagenetic Mn-oxide reduction and Mn-carbonate formation in anoxic pore waters. This study highlights repeated regional redox fluctuations as a key driver of major Mn carbonate deposits, establishing them as robust archives of local marine redox oscillations throughout Earth’s history.

title: Species-specific strontium distribution and environment in coccolithophores revealed by X-ray fluorescence and spectroscopy
description: Publication date: Available online 28 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): H.J.M. Greene, J.M. Walker, G. Langer
abstract: The Sr/Ca ratio of coccoliths is the most developed coccolithophore-related geochemical proxy; used to reconstruct coccolithophore productivity. A process-based understanding of this proxy is limited, because Sr partitioning models are mostly not independently constrained. It has recently been discovered that the lopadoliths of Scyphosphaera apsteinii display stripes of different Sr concentrations, contrary to model predictions. In this study we use XRF imaging to investigate the distribution of Sr across coccoliths from different coccolithophore families. We measured coccoliths from two Coccolithales species, Coccolithus braarudii and Calcidiscus leptoporus, and two Zygodiscales, Pontosphaera syracusana and Helicosphaera carteri. Only P. syracusana showed Sr stripes akin to the ones in S. apsteinii. Thus, we hypothesize that Sr stripiness is an invention of the Pontosphaeraceae. This family produces high Sr muroliths, whereas the other species investigated here produce comparatively low Sr placoliths. All species investigated so far, however, incorporate Sr into Ca sites of the calcite lattice in coccolith calcite, as opposed to other inorganic or organic phases, as evidenced by XANES. We conclude that the Pontosphaeraceae feature a more complex calcification mechanism than placolith bearing species, including time-dependent Sr partitioning, a process that is not captured by our current models

title: Controls on organic matter fractionation and arsenic sequestration by Fe(III)-clay-humic coprecipitation
description: Publication date: Available online 27 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Hongling Bu, Hanjie Chen, Ziming Xu, Dong Liu, Peng Yuan, Manjia Chen, Shujie Hu, Fangyuan Meng, Chengshuai Liu
abstract: Coprecipitation of iron(III), clay minerals, and organic matter (OM) is a ubiquitous interfacial process in aquatic-terrestrial critical zones including wetlands, riverine sediments, and estuaries, where it governs organic carbon cycling and the subsequent environmental fate of metalloids such as arsenic (As). Molecular fractionation of dissolved organic matter (DOM) during this coprecipitation modulates carbon persistence, and the resulting composites control subsequent As sequestration, yet the mechanisms by which clay minerals shape DOM fractionation and the resulting As sequestration remain unclear. Here we use a ternary model system of Fe(III), montmorillonite (Mnt), and humic substance (HS) to investigate how clay alters Fe–OM coprecipitation and subsequent As uptake. We find that Mnt surfaces promote the heterogeneous nucleation of poorly crystalline ferrihydrite in intimate spatial association with clay edges, producing a defective Fe–OM–Mnt interface that imposes strong molecular selectivity on DOM removal. ESI-FT-ICR-MS shows that CHONS-rich ligands are preferentially scavenged from solution, while aliphatic-like molecules remain in the residual DOM. The same interface that sorts DOM also controls As sequestration. TEM-EDS mapping shows that As is spatially associated with clay-derived Si and Al domains within the composite, rather than segregated as discrete iron oxide particles. We propose that As binds to edge-anchored Fe sites bonded to the Mnt surface through ≡Mnt–O–Fe–OOC–HS linkages, rather than to bulk ferrihydrite. These findings indicate that clay minerals are not inert spectators in Fe–OM coprecipitation but active participants that restructure the interfacial environment and thereby alter the partitioning of both organic carbon and As

title: Thermodynamics of NaCl(aq) from 230 to 2000 K and from 0.1 to 10,000 MPa: Applications to Earth and Other Ocean Worlds
description: Publication date: Available online 23 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): J. Michael Brown, Olivier Bollengier, Ula Jones, Steven D. Vance, Baptiste Journaux
abstract: We present a new Gibbs energy representation for aqueous NaCl, based on new sound speed and phase equilibrium measurements, using local basis functions. Throughout, NaCl(aq) denotes the bulk aqueous component — the sum of NaCl 0 , Na + and Cl − — rather than the neutral complex, with the degree of dissociation implicit in the measurements rather than imposed. This comprehensive equation of state, valid for pressures to 10 000 M P a , temperatures from 230 K to 2000 K , and molality to 7 m o l k g − 1 , allows us to address chemical processes within Earth and interior structure and evolution of large icy moons with possible oceans. The region below 500 M P a at temperatures above 500 K , which contains water’s saturation curve and critical point, is excluded for want of constraining measurements; within the domain represented the fluid is a single phase. In regimes unconstrained by data, it assumes near-gas behavior at high temperatures and volume mixing of water and salt at extreme pressures. Differentiation of the representation yields all equilibrium properties, including volumes, specific heat capacities, and chemical potentials. The model is validated by its accurate prediction of ice Ih and VI melting and brucite dehydration in saline solutions, and by its reproduction of antigorite dehydration in pure water through two changes in reaction product to beyond 6000 M P a . We describe three applications of the Gibbs energy representation. (1) The depth during subduction of the antigorite dehydration reaction in the presence of saline geofluids is estimated to be reduced by 2 k m to 4 k m per mole of NaCl in solution, substantially less than the up to 10 k m per mole implied by previously inferred pressure-dependent water activities. (2) A H 2 O − NaCl phase diagram to 1000 M P a and 230 K to 400 K identifies the pressure-variant eutectics for hydrohalite and disodium chloride decaheptahydrate, and places the cenotectic — the absolute limit of liquid stability — at 205 M P a , 235 K and 3.90 m o l k g − 1 , where the liquid coexists with ice Ih, ice II and disodium chloride decaheptahydrate rather than with hydrohalite. (3) Icy moons: structural models of Ganymede, Callisto, and two Titan cases with 1.90 m o l k g − 1 aqueous NaCl show that melting point suppression stabilizes ices II, III, V, and VI, and that ices II and III can be buoyant in the coexisting fluid, with the sense of the ice II contrast reversing between 50 and 100 g k g − 1 . The resulting co-occurrence of ices II and III, not previously reported, admits multiphase overturning and implies that salinity governs the geodynamics of these > 100 k m lithospheres. Finally, we set out how a bulk Gibbs energy surface interfaces with species-based frameworks such as HKF and the Deep Earth Water model, and propose that the pressure derivative of the surface can be used to constrain the degree of association at high pressure.

title: Lignin degradation products in stemflow dissolved organic matter of three deciduous tree species
description: Publication date: Available online 23 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Dillon Siple, Robyn C. O’Halloran, Samantha Chittakone, Karl Kaiser, Delphis F. Levia, Yu-Ping Chin
abstract: Stemflow is meteoric water flowing down a tree trunk and is a significant yet understudied pathway for mobilizing dissolved organic matter (DOM) from forest canopies to the soil. We studied the role of stemflow as a major source of soluble lignin-derived compounds and their degradation products to forest ecosystems during leafed months. Stemflow samples were taken from three deciduous tree species: Liriodendron tulipifera L. (yellow poplar), Fagus grandifolia Ehrh. (American beech), and Betula lenta L. (sweet birch) for three separate rain events. Stemflow was analyzed for its DOM composition and properties, as well as its lignin degradation products. Lignin degradation product composition of stemflow was determined through oxidation of DOM extracts by cupric sulfate and analyzed using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry. Due to limited sampling, results discussed throughout this paper are preliminary, but show an apparent need for future research of lignin-derived compounds within stemflow. We found dissolved organic carbon-normalized lignin degradation products values 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than in river waters and several times higher than throughfall (rainfall that passes through the canopy). Previous research quantifying lignin in deciduous tree detritus found carbon-normalized lignin degradation values similar to stemflow. Thus, while plant detritus provides useful insights into the compositional nature of unaltered source material, stemflow may offer similar information with respect to lignin degradation products. Stemflow lignin degradation product composition showed high syringyl to vanillyl (S/V) ratios typical of angiosperm origin as well as high vanillyl acid to aldehyde (Ad/Al)V ratios. These high (Ad/Al)V ratios are attributed to the constant cycling of depolymerized lignin by microbial degradation with stemflow dissolving and mobilizing these compounds. Thus, stemflow’s role in transporting soluble lignin-derived compounds to soils warrants further investigation, with important implications for understanding terrestrial carbon cycling.

title: Contrasting sulfide behaviors during mantle silicate and carbonate metasomatism: Evidence from Os isotopes and highly siderophile elements in K-rich and Na-rich basalts
description: Publication date: Available online 23 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Zhao-Xue Wang, Zhu Yin Chu, Tian-Hao Wu, Jingao Liu, Sheng-Ao Liu, Peng Peng
abstract: The oxidative breakdown of sulfides in the mantle is essential for extraction of chalcophile/siderophile elements into basaltic magmas and their potential contribution to the formation of metal ore deposits. This breakdown process is commonly associated with melt/fluid metasomatism, but the nature of special metasomatic agents is not yet well-constrained. Here, we report a comparative analysis of radiogenic Os isotopes, Re and platinum group element (PGE) contents in Cenozoic intraplate basalts from Eastern China, through combining new data for ultrapotassic (K2O/Na2O > 3) and potassic (K2O/Na2O = 1–3) basalts with published data for sodic (K2O/Na2O < 1) basalts. The ultrapotassic basalts have highly radiogenic 187Os/188Os ratios (0.1586–0.2954), in contrast to the sodic basalts with modern mantle-like 187Os/188Os values (0.1221–0.1432). Along with the differences in Sr-Nd-Mg-Zn-Fe isotopic compositions, ultrapotassic basalts were sourced from the lithospheric mantle mainly metasomatized by recycled silicic sediments, while sodic basalts originated from the asthenospheric mantle dominantly hybridized by recycled carbonate sediments. The two types of rocks display strong contrasts in terms of Re-PGE. Ultrapotassic basalts have differentiated PGE patterns and low total PGE contents (e.g., (Pd/Ir)N = 1.76–5.27; Ir = 0.036–0.051 ppb), indicating sulfides as a crucial residual phase during mantle melting. In contrast, sodic basalts exhibit almost undifferentiated PGE patterns and elevated total PGE contents (e.g., (Pd/Ir)N = 0.39–2.62; Ir = 0.045–0.314 ppb), indicative of sulfide breakdown during melting. Potassic basalts exhibit Re-PGE patterns and contents falling between ultrapotassic and sodic basalts, supporting a mixing origin inferred from Sr-Nd-Mg-Zn-Fe isotopes. These observations reveal distinct behaviors of sulfides during mantle silicate versus carbonate metasomatism at different depths. Metasomatism by recycled, reduced silicic sediments causes ineffective sulfide extraction, and instead results in long-term storage of chalcophile/siderophile elements in the subcontinental lithospheric mantle, which are potential to be released during subsequent melting events. In contrast, carbonate metasomatism at deeper mantle is a mechanism by which chalcophile/siderophile elements are extracted into magmas, possibly through oxidation-enhanced sulfide breakdown associated with the reduction of recycled carbonate. Collectively, both types of mantle metasomatism can have contributed to the extraction of highly siderophile elements through distinct ways at different stages.

title: Zinc isotope evidence for intrusive Siberian Traps magmatism during the end-Permian mass extinction
description: Publication date: Available online 22 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Na Li, Mengchun Cao, Guolin Xiong, Yi-Bo Lin, Mohammad N. Gorgji, Dongxun Yuan, Guangyi Wei, Thomas J. Algeo, Quan-feng Zheng, Hua Zhang, Shu-zhong Shen
abstract: The end-Permian mass extinction (EPME) coincided with catastrophic changes in global climate, the carbon cycle, marine redox conditions and nutrient cycling. Volcanism associated with the Siberian Traps Large Igneous Province (STLIP) is widely recognized as a primary driver of these changes. However, the mechanisms by which different modes of magmatism influenced marine biogeochemical cycles remain incompletely resolved. Here, we present high-resolution zinc isotope (δ66Zn) records through the Permian-Triassic transition from two well-preserved marine carbonate successions located on opposite margins of the Paleotethys Ocean: Dajiang (South China) and Abadeh (Iran). Despite marked differences in paleogeographic setting and depositional environment, both sections display comparable δ66Zn ranges and coherent stratigraphic trends. Both records exhibit a pronounced negative δ66Zn excursion of ∼0.5–0.6‰ in the uppermost Permian that is closely associated with the onset of the negative δ13C excursion, indicating a broadly coeval perturbation to the marine zinc and carbon cycles prior to the EPME. Carbonate-hosted δ66Zn values records remained perturbed throughout the lowermost Triassic, suggesting that disruption of the marine Zn cycle in shallow-marine environments extended beyond the initial biotic crisis. Mass-balance constraints indicate that changes in biological utilization alone are insufficient to explain the observed isotopic shift. We suggest that a sustained input of isotopically light Zn to the ocean–atmosphere system is likely to account for the excursion, plausibly linked to large-scale sill-complex intrusions and contact metamorphism associated with STLIP magmatism. Sustained low δ66Zn values following the extinction coincided with an enhanced influx of isotopically light Zn during peak thermogenic devolatilization, whereas reduced deposition of Zn-bearing organic matter likely represented a secondary effect on the marine Zn cycle. Our results demonstrate that shallow-marine carbonates preserve first-order changes in shallow seawater δ66Zn associated with large-scale perturbations of the marine Zn cycle and highlight the role of prolonged, sill-dominated intrusive magmatism in altering marine Zn source-sink balance during the end-Permian environmental crisis.

title: Multi-Stage Carbonatite Magmatism Drives Rare Earth Element Enrichment
description: Publication date: Available online 22 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Lucas Tatnell, Andrea Giuliani, Isra Ezad, Christopher M Fisher, Mohammed Bouabdellah, Stephen Centrella, Laurent Sapor, Marco Fiorentini
abstract: Rare earth elements (REE) are crucial for the green-energy transition, with the largest REE deposits occurring in carbonatites. Either magmatic differentiation or hydrothermal remobilization are considered primary mineralizing mechanisms for ore-grade REE enrichment. Here, we test and quantify the hypothesis that during protracted carbonatite magmatism, late carbonatitic brines/brine-melts from younger magmatic events strip REE from previously crystallized primary calcite (± apatite ± REE phases), progressively concentrating REE in the fluid phase. We demonstrate quantitatively that primary calcite in the Twihinate carbonatite complex, Morocco, loses > 50% of its ∼ 0.1 wt% REE during reaction with late carbonatitic brines/brine-melts. Textures and carbonate chemistry show that removal of REE from calcite by these fluids occurs throughout the complex. Mass balance implies that enough calcite is available to source all required metal for ore formation. Comparable observations across carbonatites worldwide indicate that remobilization of REE from primary calcite (± apatite ± REE phases) by residual magmatic fluids may represent a fundamental mechanism for REE mineralization in carbonatite systems.

title: Electrostatic discharge triggers troilite‑to‑magnetite oxidation in Mars dust activity
description: Publication date: Available online 20 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Xiaojia Zeng, Xiongyao Li
abstract: Electrostatic discharge in Martian dust storms may significantly drive the chemical alteration and cycling of surface materials. Troilite is expected on Mars from magmatic and meteoritic sources but remains undetected by rovers, raising the question of possible electrostatic discharge-driven alteration. However, this hypothesis lacks direct experimental support. In this study, we experimentally simulate electrical discharge under Martian conditions by exposing troilite to such discharge in a CO2 atmosphere at low pressure. We found that electrical discharge rapidly oxidizes troilite to magnetite (Fe3O4), forming a ∼ 100 nm thick, polycrystalline, defect-rich alteration layer on the troilite surface. This oxidation is driven by reactive oxygen species attack Fe-S bonds, displace sulfur, and convert the residual iron framework into magnetite. Such an electrical discharge-driven pathway offers a new water-free mechanism for magnetite formation on Mars, specifically active during the hyper-arid Amazonian epoch. This work also provides an additional explanation for the missing troilite in Martian soils and the widespread occurrence of magnetite in Martian dust. More broadly, this study expands our understanding of Martian surface evolution beyond water-dominated scenarios and highlights oxidative role of ongoing dust activities on present-day Mars.

title: Simultaneous formation of DNA and RNA nucleosides in shock-recovery experiments
description: Publication date: Available online 16 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Jiawen Zhao, Koichi Mimura
abstract: Whether RNA, DNA, or both emerged as the first genetic system remains an important question in origin-of-life research. The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA preceded DNA, whereas alternative scenarios allow for the coexistence of RNA- and DNA-related building blocks during early chemical evolution. A key chemical question is whether deoxyribonucleosides can be generated abiotically from molecular precursors that could have been available under prebiotic conditions. Meteorite impacts generate transient high-pressure and high-temperature conditions that can promote rapid chemical reactions in solid-state environments. Here, we investigate the formation of ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside frameworks from ribose and canonical purine and pyrimidine nucleobases under simulated meteorite impact conditions. Shock compression generated both ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside frameworks during a single shock event. Single- and dual-13C-labeling experiments confirmed the incorporation of carbon from both ribose and nucleobase. Experiments conducted under different reaction conditions showed that nucleoside yields and product distributions varied with mineral composition, organic loading, nucleobase composition, and water content. These results demonstrate that shock compression provides a solid-state reaction regime in which both ribonucleoside and deoxyribonucleoside frameworks can be generated from common molecular precursors. This study provides experimental constraints on nucleoside formation and the environmental factors affecting this process under impact-driven conditions.

title: Bomb- 14 C signals in Santa Barbara Basin sediments and radiocarbon constraints on terrestrial organic carbon
description: Publication date: Available online 16 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Hanyue Xu, Hong-Chun Li, Da-Wei Li, Meng Yu, Hailong Zhang, William M. Berelson, Meixun Zhao
abstract: The anthropogenic bomb-14C signal (produced by nuclear bomb tests in the atmosphere during 1945–1964 yr CE) provides a powerful tracer for quantifying organic carbon (OC) dynamics in marine sediments. This study uses two 210Pb-dated box cores (SBB-190629 and SBB-8-2012) from the Santa Barbara Basin (SBB), and the measured total organic carbon (TOC), total nitrogen, δ 13C and Δ14C of TOC (Δ14CTOC) to track the propagation of bomb-14C signal. Although bulk sedimentary Δ14CTOC values were strongly negative (−384‰ to −64‰), a distinct Δ14CTOC enrichment (up to ∼90‰) was identified in both cores after 1960 yr CE. This enrichment is identified as a bomb-14C event through its temporal synchronicity with the Δ14C records of established atmospheric carbon dioxide and surface seawater dissolved inorganic carbon. To deconvolve this signal, we employed a series of mixing models. A δ 13C-based binary mixing model was used to quantify the marine and terrestrial OC fractions since 1815 yr CE. Subsequently, the time-parallel surface seawater dissolved inorganic carbon radiocarbon record was used as the marine end-member to reconstruct the Δ14C composition of terrestrial OC. Finally, through the application of a petrogenic-biospheric mixing model, we revealed a significant bomb-14C enrichment within the biospheric component of the terrestrial OC and quantified a stable, background contribution of 14C-free petrogenic carbon (∼18%). Our findings demonstrate the attenuation of the bomb-14C signal through a complex terrestrial-marine system can still be recorded on sediment in SBB. This study establishes a framework to disentangle the bomb-14C signal on marine, biospheric-terrestrial, and petrogenic-terrestrial components. It also provides an approach for interpreting radiocarbon data in continental margin sediments and for constraining carbon cycling processes across these dynamic interfaces.

title: Rapid changes to permeable continental shelf sediment pore water geochemistry in response to olivine addition as a marine carbon dioxide removal technique
description: Publication date: Available online 16 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Matthew Quinan, Aaron Celestian, Nick Rollins, Zvi Steiner, William Berelson
abstract: Marine enhanced rock weathering using the silicate mineral olivine has emerged as a promising ocean alkalinity enhancement/marine carbon dioxide removal technique in recent years. However, we lack an understanding of olivine dissolution and the concomitant alkalinity production in a marine sedimentary environment, where much of the dissolution is likely to occur, and the geochemical feedbacks therein. Previous olivine enhanced rock weathering experiments have typically been conducted at high fluid-to-mineral ratios using sediments composed predominantly of olivine, conditions that are not representative of olivine addition to natural sedimentary environments. They have also generally been done over long time periods (i.e. weeks to months) to obtain steady state dissolution/alkalinity production rates, thereby looking past the early, transient impacts of fresh olivine addition to marine sediment. Our uncertainty is compounded by the heterogeneity of continental shelf sediments, where variations in composition, grain size, permeability, diagenetic reactions, and pore water flow are likely to produce spatially variable olivine dissolution and alkalinity production. To help close these knowledge gaps, we conducted experiments to investigate the impacts of olivine dissolution on sediment geochemistry immediately following addition to shelf sands under varying physical conditions, all producing consistent results. Olivine dissolution and/or ion exchange resulted in rapid alkalinity production, even at short fluid:mineral contact time (residence times) and low fluid:mineral ratios. However, the precipitation of secondary minerals (CaCO3, Fe oxides, and potentially phyllosilicates) consumed a substantial portion of the produced alkalinity (28–88%), while increasing pore water pH slowed further olivine dissolution/ion exchange. These saturation effects decreased the efficiency with which alkalinity was durably produced by olivine dissolution in the sediment.

title: Coupled kinetics of Mn(II) oxidation and Cd sequestration on ferrihydrite with varying crystallinity
description: Publication date: Available online 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Lizhu Xu, Meiying Huang, Tongliang Wu, Peixin Cui, Cun Liu, Yujun Wang
abstract: Ferrihydrite (Fh) serves as a crucial geochemical interface for Mn(II) adsorption-oxidation in various soils and sediments, influencing the fate of associated Mn and cadmium (Cd). However, the impact of Fh crystallinity on the coupled kinetics and mechanisms of Mn(II) oxidation and Cd sequestration remains incompletely understood, particularly regarding the kinetic interplay. Here, we systematically investigated these coupled reactions on two-line Fh (2LFh with low crystallinity) and six-line Fh (6LFh with high crystallinity). 2LFh has a lower isoelectric point, a lower conduction band potential (E CB), and more abundant vacancy defects, while 6LFh exhibits higher isoelectric point and E CB but fewer vacancy defects. Kinetic experiments across pH 6.0−8.0 revealed similar trends in Cd and Mn(II) removal, with the most pronounced effects observed at pH 8.0. Based on the most pronounced reaction extents observed at pH 8.0, we developed a kinetic model that quantitatively describes the crystallinity-dependent kinetic coupling in Fh-Mn(II)-Cd ternary system. Dissolved Cd(II) and Mn(II) were rapidly adsorbed onto both 2LFh (k Cd = 5.43 × 106 M−1 s−1, k Mn(II) = 5.28 × 102 M−1 s−1) and 6LFh (k Cd = 2.85 × 105 M−1 s−1, k Mn(II) = 1.37 × 103 M−1 s−1). Subsequently, Mn(II) catalytic oxidation by O2 proceeded preferentially on 6LFh via an electrochemical pathway, driven by its higher E CB. This facilitated the abundant formation of amorphous manganese oxide (AMO) and groutite nanorods. In contrast, Mn(II) oxidation on 2LFh predominantly yielded abundant AMO and moderate amounts of manganite nanowires. Although secondary MnOx formation on Fh surfaces transiently increased dissolved Cd(II) by 1.3−15.8% relative to the Mn-free system, the extractable Cd fraction progressively decreased by 2.1−24.0%, with substantial Cd immobilized in secondary MnOx. Mechanistically, the model captures these Mn(II) oxidation pathways and dynamic redistribution of Cd between Fh and MnOx surfaces. These findings highlight that Fe‑Mn redox cycling and secondary mineralization critically govern the fate of heavy metals in redox‑dynamic soil environments, with crystallinity-dependent reaction pathways providing key mechanistic insights.

title: A new view of Xe and Ne in the Paleoarchean atmosphere from paired noble gas isotopic and trace element analyses of Barberton cherts
description: Publication date: Available online 15 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): K.A. Woody, R. Parai, D.A. Fike, C. Jones, G. Avice, M.H. Barickman, J.B. Rodriguez, X.J. Zhang, A.H. Knoll
abstract: The terrestrial atmosphere governs Earth’s habitability and remains our most accessible analogue to distant planetary atmospheres, making the evolution of its composition over Earth history a topic of great interdisciplinary scientific interest. Many different natural samples are capable of trapping and retaining atmospheric gases on billion-year timescales, providing a geochemical archive of bygone processes. These trapped gases record a progressive depletion in the abundance of xenon (Xe) accompanied by its isotopic fractionation in Earth’s Archean atmosphere. However, the detailed history of this loss and isotopic fractionation of Xe is imperfectly constrained, in part because calculations focus on the non-radiogenic light isotopes of Xe (which are the least abundant isotopes) to determine ancient atmospheric compositions. In this study, we employed the full spectrum of Xe isotopes measured in four cherts from the 3.55–3.26 Ga Onverwacht Group of the Barberton Greenstone Belt, South Africa to quantify Xe isotopic fractionation in the Paleoarchean atmosphere. First, we measured the concentration and spatial distribution of Te, Ba, U, and Th by secondary ion mass spectrometry in subsamples of each chert to estimate the expected composition of Xe produced in situ by nuclear reactions. We then analyzed chips of these subsamples for Ne, Ar, and Xe elemental and isotopic compositions. We find that Xe data from Onverwacht bulk cherts reflect mixing between Paleoarchean atmospheric Xe and modern atmospheric Xe, with minor inputs from Xe produced by U, Ba, and Te decay. A mixing model incorporating these five components and testing a range of possible Archean atmospheric compositions indicates that Xe in the ∼ 3.26–3.28 Ga atmosphere was fractionated by ≥ 19 - 3.2 + 3.1 ‰u−1 relative to modern air. Our results emphasize that even samples with noble gas compositions dominated by trapped ancient fluids may in detail reflect multicomponent mixing, and that estimates of the extent of mass-dependent Xe fractionation reported in previous studies are lower limits. Barberton chert 20Ne/22Ne ratios extend below the modern atmospheric ratio, which could reflect post-entrapment fractionation that preferentially retained heavy Ne isotopes, or may indicate the preservation of a trapped multi-component mixture including paleo-atmospheric 20Ne/22Ne that was subsequently raised by volcanic outgassing.

title: Lead isotopes trace interhemispheric transport of water masses and pollution to the tropical western North Atlantic Ocean
description: Publication date: Available online 12 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Hui Xu, Tina van de Flierdt, Arianna Olivelli, Yee-Lap Leung, Alex Griffiths, Katharina Kreissig, Barry J. Coles, Dominik J. Weiss, Rebekah E.T. Moore, Rob Middag, Mark Rehkämper
abstract: The use of leaded gasoline significantly impacted North Atlantic seawater during the 20th century, leaving a legacy of pollution that remains traceable despite the global ban reached in 2021. This study presents new Pb concentration and isotope data from four depth profiles in the western tropical North Atlantic along Leg 2 of GEOTRACES section GA02 from 31.7°N to 1.2°N. The data capture atmospheric inputs and water masses from both hemispheres, revealing latitudinal variability in Pb isotope signatures in the upper part of the water column. In surface waters, low 206Pb/207Pb ratios (1.166–1.173) indicate South American and North African anthropogenic sources at the southern stations, and higher 206Pb/207Pb ratios (1.174–1.179) reflect anthropogenic North American and natural North African mineral dust inputs at the northern stations. A comparison of North Atlantic surface water data for 1981–1999 and 2010–2014 reveals distinct shifts in Pb concentrations and isotope ratios, confirming the effectiveness of Pb isotopes as tracers for identifying and tracking Pb sources over time in the North Atlantic. The Pb concentrations and isotopic signatures of central water masses (formed 4–15 years ago relative to sampling time) and intermediate water masses (formed 20–50 years ago) are consistent with the expected atmospheric Pb sources at the time and location of their formation, emphasizing the influence of both spatial and temporal variations in atmospheric Pb deposition. However, in the intermediate layer, where northern- and southern-sourced water masses mix, a deviation of the Pb concentration from the expected water mass mixing trend suggests removal of some dissolved Pb by particles. North Atlantic Deep Water exhibits persistent anthropogenic Pb signals from historical US and European emissions (20–30 years ago), while bottom waters within a nepheloid layer show evidence of natural Pb release from sediments. Overall, these findings suggest that Pb isotope ratios predominantly act as conservative tracers of water masses in the strongly advective western tropical North Atlantic Ocean.

title: Halogen behavior during high-grade metamorphism and partial melting in the deep continental crust (Ivrea-Verbano Zone, NW Italy)
description: Publication date: Available online 9 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Peng-Yuan Han, Madison S. Huising, Jaime D. Barnes, Michael A.W. Marks, Tao He, Fernando Bea, Zhao-Chu Hu, Roberta L. Rudnick
abstract: Halogen (F, Cl, Br, and I) concentrations and Cl isotope (δ37Cl) ratios in a suite of well-characterized amphibolite- to granulite-facies metapelites, metabasites, and associated leucosomes from the Ivrea-Verbano Zone (IVZ), Northwest Italy, document halogen behavior during high-grade metamorphism and partial melting of the deep continental crust. With increasing metamorphic grade, metapelites record a progressive decrease in F, I, and possibly Br concentrations, likely due to metamorphic dehydration. By contrast, Cl is slightly elevated in granulite-facies metapelites, suggesting a relatively Cl-rich environment in the lower crust. Together with previously reported high Cl contents (up to 0.3 wt%) in garnet-hosted melt inclusions produced during partial melting of metapelites, this suggests that the elevated Cl was present during peak metamorphism and partial melting. All samples (metapelites, metabasites, and leucosomes) exhibit scattered but relatively narrow δ37Cl values, ranging from −1.3 to + 0.8‰, indicating that minimal Cl isotope fractionation occurs during metamorphic dehydration, partial melting, and fluid infiltration in the deep continental crust. The inferred Cl-rich environment in the IVZ lower crust is consistent with the Cl enrichment observed in many other granulite terranes, suggesting that such fluids may be common. Moreover, halogens present in the lower continental crust, whether released by metamorphic dehydration or introduced from other parts of the crust and/or mantle, may have facilitated partial melting and the generation of granitic magma, playing a vital role in the chemical differentiation of the continental crust.

title: Recycling of terrestrial mercury in modern subduction zones: constraints from Hg-Sr-Nd-B isotope systematics
description: Publication date: Available online 2 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Dian-Bing Wang, Ping-Ping Liu, Runsheng Yin
abstract: Mercury (Hg) isotopes, particularly mass-independent fractionation (MIF; expressed as Δ199Hg), serve as a powerful tracer for tracking the recycling of surficial materials into Earth’s deep interior. However, the contribution of terrestrial Hg to modern subduction zones remains poorly understood. Here we present new Hg–B–Sr–Nd isotopic data for volcanic rocks from eight stratovolcanoes and the Toba super-sized volcanic system, all located along the Sumatra segment of the Sunda arc. Sumatra volcanic rocks have negative Δ199Hg values (from −0.19 to −0.02‰), indicating an input of terrestrial Hg. Their mass-dependent fractionation (MDF; expressed as δ202Hg) ranges from −2.08 to −1.07‰, lower than that of the Mesozoic basement on Sumatra (−0.05‰). Together with Sr-Nd isotope constraints indicating minor crustal contamination, these observations rule out a crustal origin for the negative Δ199Hg anomalies and instead reflect a mantle source modified by recycled terrestrial Hg. The near-zero Δ199Hg values of the Nicobar Fan sediments (−0.01 to 0.03‰) indicate that the recycled terrestrial Hg in the mantle source is unlikely to originate from the Nicobar Fan but more likely reflects locally derived Sumatran terrigenous sediments. Three-endmember mixing models coupling Δ199Hg with Sr–Nd isotopes further indicate that the subducted sediment contribution was dominated by Nicobar Fan sediments but included a smaller proportion of Sumatra terrigenous component carrying the negative Hg-MIF signature, with total sediment additions of <5 wt% beneath the Sumatra stratovolcanoes and ∼5–10 wt% beneath the Toba volcanic system. Boron isotopes indicate slab-derived fluid additions of ∼0.01–1.0 wt% and ∼0.01–0.05 wt% beneath Sumatra stratovolcanoes and Toba volcanic systems, respectively. Mass-balance calculations show that fluids containing ∼20 ppb to 3.3 ppm Hg could reproduce the average Δ199Hg value of the Sumatra volcanic rocks, indicating that slab-derived dehydration fluids are potential carriers transferring terrestrial Hg into the mantle wedge. Near the slab tear zone, sediment melts generated during the diapiric ascent and partial melting of subducted sediments result in the enriched Sr-Nd isotopic compositions of the Toba volcanic rocks. Our results demonstrate that Hg isotopes, when integrated with Sr-Nd-B isotope systematics, serve as a sensitive tracer for distinguishing recycling of various components in subduction zones.

title: The effect of pressure and temperature on the fluid/melt partitioning of porphyry ore metals
description: Publication date: Available online 2 October 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Ivano Gennaro, Alexandra Tsay, Zoltán Zajacz
abstract: A major fraction of the total Cu, Mo, and Au mined worldwide is derived from porphyry ore deposits, with Ag representing an abundant by-product from the exploitation of these deposits. The relative endowment of these metals is linked to deposit depth, with Au-rich deposits forming in the shallowest levels of the crust while Mo-rich deposits form deeper. These deposits are fed by magmatic-hydrothermal fluids derived from magma chambers which likely sit 5–15 km below the surface, but attainment of fluid saturation at greater depths has also been proposed. These deposits display a general depth-dependent metal endowment. To determine the effect of pressure (P) and temperature (T) on the ability of the fluid phase to extract these metals from the melt, experiments were conducted in cold-seal pressure vessels and a piston cylinder apparatus covering a range of P (150–700 MPa) and T (760–950 °C) conditions at which fluid exsolution is most likely to occur in crustal magma reservoir systems. Experimental capsules were composed of a Au-Ag-Cu alloy as the source of metals and contained a synthetic rhyolite glass, fluid of 1 or 12 mol Cl/kg H2O, and natural quartz chip for the entrapment of synthetic fluid inclusions. Metal solubilities in the melt and fluid phases increase roughly linearly with increasing T; Cl concentration only affects the solubility of metals in the fluid phase. Fluid/melt partition coefficients of Cu, Ag, and Au decrease monotonically with increasing T and are generally unaffected by P at a fixed fluid salinity. Chlorine and Mo partitioning into the fluid increase by a factor of 4 with P increasing from 150 to 500 MPa at low fluid salinities but decrease slightly at high fluid salinities. Empirical functions were fit which describe the solubility, fluid/melt partitioning, and metal/Na exchange of Cl, Cu, Ag, Au, and Mo as functions of T and P. A simplified magma degassing model based on these equations reveals that ore metal extraction from magmas is the most effective at upper crustal emplacement depths and relatively high initial water concentrations.

title: Hydrothermal experiments reveal methanol, ammonia, and methylamines as tracers of pH and temperature with potential application to Enceladus, Europa, and other icy ocean worlds
description: Publication date: Available online 13 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Kirtland J. Robinson, Everett L. Shock, Sean P. Sylva, Jeffrey S. Seewald
abstract: Icy ocean worlds in our solar system are prime targets in the search for extraterrestrial life. Enceladus and Europa are icy moons with evidence of global subsurface oceans in contact with rocky interiors, which may provide habitable environments for chemotrophic life. However, the interaction between water and rock and any changes in fluid chemistry are poorly constrained because the icy shells of these moons inhibit direct sampling of subsurface aqueous environments. Characterization of subseafloor processes may depend on chemical signatures in materials that are transported to accessible sampling locations near the surfaces of these icy ocean worlds. Here we present a theoretical framework where organic compounds likely to be present at icy ocean worlds can be utilized as tracers of geochemistry if they approach metastable equilibrium abundances, which we test with laboratory experiments. We use thermodynamic calculations of aqueous solutions to demonstrate that abundances of methanol, ammonia, and methylamines (compounds selected based on Enceladus’ plume data) should approach steady state ratios based on reversible substitution reactions that are systematically controlled by pH and temperature. We test these calculations by performing laboratory hydrothermal experiments ranging in temperature (175-325℃) and pH (∼3.5–7.0), demonstrating that chemical concentration measurements alone can be used in predictive models to accurately constrain the different conditions across experimental systems. As examples, with experiments conducted at 250℃, we demonstrate that the chemical tracers in a pH ∼ 3.5 solution predict a pH ≤ ∼5.0 and a temperature of ∼ 225-250℃, while the tracers in a solution at pH ∼ 7.0 predict a pH of ∼ 6.0–7.5 and a temperature of ∼ 200-275℃. Notably, all of our high-temperature experiments are cooled to room temperature prior to analysis, indicating that the hydrothermal signal (i.e., the ratio of chemical species) is preserved due to the slowing of reaction kinetics at lower temperatures, which may be analogous to hydrothermal fluids that vent into icy oceans. Similarly, we also performed a partial-cooling experiment that shows a tracer signal produced at 325℃ remains largely preserved for a year after the experiment was cooled to 175℃. We compare experimental results from gold reaction vessels to experiments previously conducted in glass vessels to assess the effects of experimental vessel type and find only minor differences in product distributions over time. Overall, our findings provide additional motivation to target small organic molecules for analysis on future missions to icy ocean worlds in order to constrain subsurface geochemical parameters critical to habitability

title: The importance of deep reactions between ascending komatiite and pre-existing protocratonic lithosphere for the chemistry of Archaean peridotites and greenstone belt volcanics: insights from reaction experiments
description: Publication date: Available online 9 September 2026 Source: Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta Author(s): Rodrigo Freitas Rodrigues, Balz S. Kamber, Gregory M. Yaxley, Emma L. Tomlinson, Sandra Piazolo, Nathan R. Daczko
abstract: The cratonic lithospheric mantle is the buoyant 200–250 km deep root that enabled ancient continents (cratons) to survive for billions of years. The root stabilised due to extensive melting, erupting magnesian magmas at surface. However, peridotite xenolith samples from the cratonic mantle exhibit far more variable olivine/orthopyroxene and MgO/SiO2 ratios than expected from residues after melting of fertile mantle, exemplified by enigmatic dunites and orthopyroxene-rich harzburgites. Similarly, Archaean ultramafic lavas (komatiites) also show wider MgO/SiO2 variability than could be expected from shallow olivine fractionation. In addition, many komatiites have unexpectedly complex radiogenic isotope systematics, inconsistent with high-degree melting of refractory mantle. Thermodynamic modelling has suggested that these complexities could arise during deep (2–5 GPa) melt-solid reactions. Here, we present high-pressure layered experiments (3 GPa) involving the reaction between komatiite juxtaposed against harzburgite. The melt-bearing reactions yielded layered charges, wherein the initial komatiite layer (original, unreacted composition) was transformed into orthopyroxene-rich harzburgite following the reaction, and the original harzburgite layer resulted in the formation of dunite, with mineral modes and Mg-number depending on temperature. The solid residues of the reacted layers (orthopyroxene-rich and olivine-rich) are compositionally and mineralogically analogous to natural cratonic harzburgites and dunites, respectively. Thermodynamic modelling indicates that the MgO/SiO2 variability of the residues could be further increased by reacting the komatiite with fertile lherzolite instead of harzburgite.
