We found clear element-specific patterns: Ni was enriched in high-input agricultural regions, whereas Pb and Cr were more concentrated in non-croplands. These differences varied by region. Using extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), we identified fertilization intensity, moisture conditions, and socioeconomic development as key nonlinear predictors. Projections under the SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios suggest that by 2100, these concentration differences may either reverse or intensify, with their spatial evolution accompanied by shifts in potential non-carcinogenic health across cropland soils. Our findings show that agricultural land use is closely associated with spatial patterns of soil heavy metals across global wheat-growing regions and highlight land-use differentials as valuable early indicators of pollution risk, particularly in major wheat-producing regions.

title: Tailored nanofiltration membrane for enhanced performance by surface modification using zwitterionic piperazine
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Jincheng Ding, Chunyu Feng, Zongtang Liu, Zhihao Si, Qieyuan Gao
abstract: Nanofiltration (NF) membranes are indispensable for removing hazardous contaminants such as dyes and salts from industrial wastewater, yet their performance is often bottlenecked by the inherent permeability–selectivity trade-off and membrane fouling. Zwitterionic surface modification offers a means to overcome these limitations by promoting hydrophilicity and introducing charge-mediated transport. Here we synthesized a pre-formed zwitterionic piperazine (ZW-PIP) via a one-pot ring-opening of piperazine with 1,3-propanesultone, and directly grafted it onto polyamide films through residual acyl chloride groups. Combined low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF NMR) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations demonstrated that the grafted zwitterionic moieties stabilized a hydration layer and facilitated water and chloride-ion diffusion (>90%), while sterically excluding sulfate. The resulting membrane exhibited a pure water permeance of 29.2 L∙m−2∙h−1∙bar−1. Crucially, this enhanced permeability was achieved while maintaining the exceptional salt-rejection performance for Na2SO4 (>97.0%). This high selectivity persisted even under challenging conditions of elevated salt concentration (8.0 g/L) and operating pressure (8.0 bar). The membrane exhibited robust rejection of various dyes (>96%), sustained stability, and potent antifouling (BSA, FRR 89%) and antibacterial (>99.97%) properties. Collectively, this work offers a mechanistic basis for designing zwitterionic NF membranes with high permeability, selectivity, and fouling resistance for treating complex hazardous wastewater.

title: Copper valence dynamics link microbial redox functions to humification during composting
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Yongsheng Ma, Zhongsen Ye, Shuai Xu, Zhushan Liu
abstract: Organic-waste composting supports resource recovery, but microbial links between Cu transformation and humification remain insufficiently resolved. We combined XPS–Auger analysis, metagenomics, day-4 metatranscriptomics, and genome-resolved analysis to compare Cu(I), Cu(II), and mixed-valence treatments receiving equal Cu inputs with a control without added Cu (CK) during lignocellulosic composting. By day 30, surface Cu(I) proportions reached 55.63% and 59.04% in Cu(I) and mixed-valence treatments, respectively, whereas the Cu(II) treatment remained Cu(II)-dominated. On day 4, AA1 accounted for 1.331% of the exported CAZy expression total in CK and 2.085–2.931% in Cu treatments, alongside distinct substrate-transformation and redox profiles. Cu treatments showed higher day-4 transcript levels of carbohydrate-associated MAG204 and Cu-homeostasis-associated MAG674. The Cu(I) treatment had the greatest humic acid (HA) concentration gain (60.09 g kg⁻¹), whereas the mixed-valence treatment had the highest final HA concentration (122.45 g kg⁻¹). The findings support a Cu-valence-associated working model of redox-active humification; extracellular electron transfer remains to be verified by direct electrochemical measurements.

title: From environmental gradients to putative intrinsic resistance: Deciphering the soil resistome across Mongolian Plateau grasslands
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Jiangxiao Luo, Shijie Dong, Mengbo Yuan, Wei Wen, Yu Ang Li, Yongchao Li, Renxin Zhao
abstract: Soils are important reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet the ecological differentiation and host associations of grassland resistomes remain poorly understood. We investigated topsoil resistomes across desert steppe, typical steppe, and meadow steppe of the Mongolian Plateau using short- and long-read metagenomics. The resistome comprised 28 ARG types and 819 subtypes, dominated by rifamycin, vancomycin, and multidrug resistance genes. ARG abundance increased from desert steppe to meadow steppe. Soil pH, total organic carbon, total nitrogen, and climatic variables were strongly associated with resistome turnover, whereas grazing showed weaker associations. Mobile genetic element (MGE) abundance correlated positively with ARG abundance, but only 3.37% of ARG-carrying contigs contained detectable MGEs. An operational multi-indicator framework distinguished putative intrinsic and putative acquired ARGs with contrasting host and environmental associations. Both fractions were dominated by Actinomycetota, although Pseudomonadota contributed relatively more to putative acquired ARGs. Putative intrinsic ARGs were associated mainly with nutrient-related soil variables, whereas putative acquired ARGs showed stronger climatic and edaphic associations. Long-read assemblies markedly reduced the unclassified fraction. Among 195 ARG-carrying metagenome-assembled genomes, 65.6% represented reference-poor or previously uncultured lineages. These findings reveal spatially structured and heterogeneous grassland resistomes linked to ARG composition, host affiliation, and genomic context.

title: Deep learning-driven fine-grained classification and traceability of illicit pollution sources in urban stormwater networks using 3D-EEM images
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Haiyue Qi, Zuxin Xu, Wenhai Chu, Cheng Ye, Kaidi Lai, Feiyang Ao, Qing Wei, Qian Guo, Wancheng Cai
abstract: Illicit wastewater discharge into stormwater pipes poses a severe ecological risk to receiving waters, yet conventional parallel factor analysis lacks the requisite precision to distinguish spectrally overlapping domestic wastewaters (e.g., office buildings, hotels) due to their intricate composition and overlapping spectral features. This study introduces an end-to-end deep learning framework integrating three-dimensional excitation–emission matrix fluorescence spectroscopy with a hybrid Swin Transformer–ResNet architecture. Through systematic comparison of eight convolutional neural network architectures and subsequent optimization, the refined model delivers superior classification performance with 98.21% accuracy. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping reveals that the model focuses on diagnostically relevant spectral regions (Ex/Em ≈ 225–375/300–475 nm), suggesting potential for reducing the EEM scanning range, although instrument-level benefits require further validation. Within the studied region, the framework generalizes to complex multi-source mixtures without retraining, achieving exact, partial, and type match accuracies of 79.59%, 88.89%, and 98.41%, respectively. T-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding highlights overlapping category pairs, such as Convenience store and Supermarket, indicating cases requiring additional field verification. This work establishes a robust intelligent screening and progressive tracing tool for narrowing pollution sources in drainage networks, reducing blind field investigation and enabling precision rehabilitation of illicit connections to mitigate hazardous contaminant loads to aquatic ecosystems.

title: Enhanced As(V) removal by a Zr-doped β-FeOOH functionalized PTFE membrane: Interfacial structure, selectivity, and ligand exchange
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Kaige Dong, Zhihao Yi, Sakil Mahmud, Yuhang Cheng, Manyu Deng, Feng Zhang, Xuexia Huang, Gaosheng Zhang, Zhu Xiong, Wei Zhang
abstract: Arsenic (As) contamination poses a critical threat to water safety, yet efficient removal of As(V) remains challenging due to the lack of robust adsorbents with high selectivity and stability. Herein, a Zr-doped β-FeOOH-functionalized PTFE membrane (Zr/β-FeOOH-PDA/PEI-M) has been reported and fabricated via in situ mineralization on a PDA/PEI interlayer. By optimizing the Fe-to-Zr molar ratio to 3:2, an unprecedented balance between abundant Zr–O active sites and the preservation of β-FeOOH lattice integrity was achieved, as evidenced by multi-scale characterization. The optimized membrane delivers a remarkable As(V) removal efficiency of 97% with an adsorption capacity (Q e ) of 442.01 mg/m2 in cross-flow filtration, outperforming most state-of-the-art materials. Notably, it exhibits exceptional tolerance to coexisting ions (Ca2+, Mg2+, Cl–, SO4 2–, CO3 2–, PO4 3–) and natural organic matter, maintaining > 80% removal in real Pearl River water and meeting discharge standards. Mechanistically, we reveal a diffusion–ligand exchange–inner-sphere complexation pathway in which Zr4+ enhances Lewis acidity and coordination affinity, while Fe–O sites play an auxiliary role, collectively accounting for the superior selectivity. This work not only provides a scalable, high-performance membrane for As(V) remediation but also offers insights into the rational design of Zr-based adsorbents for capturing toxic oxyanions.

title: Molecular impairment-guided ecotoxicity assessment: Insights from copper and pH stress in zebrafish
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Wanying Gui, Wen-Xiong Wang
abstract: Copper (Cu) toxicity is governed by the redox transition of Cu(II) to Cu(I), yet its temporal dynamics and modulation by water chemistry remain poorly understood. This study developed an omics-driven toxicokinetic framework evaluating Cu toxicity in zebrafish gills across varying pH levels. By interrogating the expression kinetics of key redox-switch genes (steap family/fdx1), we identified a 9-h molecular peak window serving as a highly sensitive signature for incipient toxicity, preceding macroscopic phenotypic shifts. A relatively high-dose of Cu (30 μg/L) advanced steap2/4 peaks to 6 h, indicating STEAP capacity-constrained reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I). Fluorescent quantification of gill Cu(I) accumulation displayed no significant differences. Nonetheless, transcriptomic profiling established a condition-dependent hierarchical pathway impairment: necroptosis > ferroptosis > apoptosis > inflammatory > immune > stress response > oxidative stress response. Acidic regimes uniquely triggered necroptosis and profound metabolic dysfunction. Interaction with a Cu(I)-specific chelator abolished cell necrosis and reversed global transcriptional phenotypes, validating that intracellular Cu(I) trafficking drives systemic damage. This dual-analytical framework, coupling a "Cu toxic molecular switch" with a "gradation of injury pathways", to some extent, provides a temporally resolved predictive tool and offers a robust mechanistic foundation for risk assessment of metals in dynamic aquatic ecosystems.

title: Insights into heavy metal accumulation and chemical speciation in Huixian Karst Wetland, China: Depositional history, mercury isotope tracing and environmental risk assessment
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): He Xiao, Binru Wu, Asfandyar Shahab, Jieyue Li, Xiaojie Sun, Bin Dong, Dunqiu Wang
abstract: Heavy metal (HM) contamination in wetland sediments has attracted increasing attention because of its persistence and potential ecological impacts. In this study, HMs including Cd, Pb, Zn, Ni, As, and Hg in the surface and core sediments of the Huixian Karst Wetland were investigated in terms of the contamination characteristics, ecological risks, depositional history and possible sources for the first time. The mean concentrations of six metals exceeded their respective background values, with Cd, Pb, and Hg showing high enrichment in Zone 2. Based on the Nemerow Integrated Pollution Index (averaging 3.55), the sediments exhibit a severe level of overall contamination. Sequential extraction revealed that while most HMs predominantly remained in the residual fraction, anthropogenic disturbances increased their reducible and acid-exchangeable forms. Notably, according to the risk assessment code, Pb and Hg exhibited high bioavailability—with highly mobile fractions accounting for approximately 67.34% and 59.95%, respectively—thereby posing significant ecological risks. The depositional history (1925–2020) revealed distinct temporal variations in HM accumulation corresponding to historical and socioeconomic developments, including wartime activities, economic reforms, and industrial expansion. Furthermore, mercury isotope compositions (negative δ202Hg values and a significant Δ199Hg-Δ201Hg relationship) suggested possible anthropogenic contributions to sediment Hg, potentially linked to industrial activities.

title: Cascading effects of nano-biochar mitigate antibiotic resistance via phage–host interactions in the soil–crop ecosystem
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Ting Xie, Da Lin, Shuai Du, Di Wu, Dong Zhu
abstract: Controlling the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in agroecosystems is central to One Health, yet whether nano-biochar-amended organic fertilizers can mitigate phage-mediated ARG dissemination along the fertilizer–soil–crop continuum remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 120 viral metagenomes to examine how biochar-amended organic fertilizers modulate ARG dynamics, phage-associated functions, and phage–host interactions across the fertilizer–soil–lettuce continuum. The lettuce phyllosphere served as a key endpoint for ARG accumulation, exhibiting 4.1–4.9 times the total ARG abundance and 56.8–66.3% higher phage-encoded ARG abundance compared with rhizosphere and non-rhizosphere soils. Source-tracking analysis indicated that manure and soil inputs accounted for 50.8–57.0% of phyllosphere ARGs, while 111 manure-associated viral populations were shared with the phyllosphere at the viral cluster level. Notably, nano-biochar-amended vermicompost exerted a cascading mitigation effect, reducing manure- and soil-derived ARG inputs to the phyllosphere by 20.4–21.6% and manure-associated viral sharing by 51.6%. Meanwhile, nano-biochar-amended vermicompost reduced lysogenic phage–host interactions, phage-encoded ARGs, and auxiliary metabolic genes associated with antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which may contribute to reduced phage-associated ARG dissemination potential. Consequently, total ARG abundance in the phyllosphere decreased by 68.9–76.3%, while lettuce biomass increased by 54.1–61.5%. This work suggests that nano-biochar-amended vermicompost may mitigate antibiotic resistance risks and enhance crop productivity partly by attenuating phage-associated ARG dissemination across the fertilizer–soil–crop continuum, highlighting its potential for One Health-oriented resistance-risk control in agricultural production.

title: Sulfamethoxazole in the environment: Occurrence, fate, risks, and remediation strategies
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Oussama Baaloudj, Miroslav Brumovský, Gianluigi Buttiglieri, Serge Chiron, Laura Scrano, Sabino Aurelio Bufo, Filomena Lelario, Jan Filip, Monica Brienza
abstract: The extensive use of antibiotics in human and veterinary medicine has led to their widespread occurrence in the environment, raising concerns about pseudo-persistence, ecological effects, and their contribution to antimicrobial resistance. Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) is one of the most common sulfonamides and is an environmentally relevant contaminant. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of the environmental behavior and management of SMX, integrating its occurrence, fate, transformation, associated risks, regulatory frameworks, and remediation strategies, while identifying remaining knowledge gaps. The reported concentrations of SMX in aqueous matrices range from ng/L to µg/L and in solid matrices with levels reaching up to 0.18, 12.7, and 0.63 mg/kg in soils, manure, and sewage sludge, respectively. SMX exhibits a low solid-liquid distribution coefficient, suggesting high mobility and the potential for environmental transport, leaching, and plant uptake, with concentrations in plant roots reaching up to 13.8 mg/kg under highly contaminated conditions. Despite the relatively low potential of SMX for bioaccumulation, continuous input may lead to chronic exposure and thus ecotoxicological effects and the development of antimicrobial resistance. Transformation products, recent regulatory advances, and remediation strategies are also reviewed, focusing on the limitations of treatment approaches, including incomplete mineralization and by-product formation. Hybrid treatment systems are proposed as a promising solution to overcome these limitations, but further validation is required to assess their scalability, sustainability, and efficiency under realistic conditions. The review concludes by highlighting the need for integrated monitoring, risk-based regulation, and sustainable remediation strategies to mitigate environmental and health concerns associated with SMX pollution.

title: Amplifying the invisible: Liquid crystal–hydrogel microcavities decode trace Hg ions and aflatoxin B1
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Ziyihui Wang, Ziyu Zhang, Ruijie Wu, Kun Liu, Xiaofang Cui, Jianying Jing, Junfeng Jiang, Li Li, Yu-Cheng Chen, Tiegen Liu
abstract: Chinese herbal medicines (CHMs) have been applied to the prevention and treatment of numerous diseases. Ensuring the safety and pharmacological efficacy of CHMs demands precise detection of trace heavy metal ions and toxins, especially Hg and aflatoxin B1 (AFB1). However, due to subtle chemical signals, current technologies still make it challenging to monitor these quality parameters in a highly sensitive manner. Herein, we introduced a liquid crystal whispering gallery mode microresonator formed by encapsulating liquid crystal droplets in a hydrogel microcavity for monitoring analyte interactions. By employing an aptamer-target assay within the hydrogel, interfacial liquid crystal molecule reorientations and strong light-matter interactions in an optical microresonator can amplify signals. The tuning of resonance wavelength can be converted to improve monitoring of interaction processes. With narrow resonance linewidth, the limit of detection can reach 3.58 nM (Hg²⁺) and 101 fg/ml (aflatoxin B1). This method has been applied to detect the targets in real herbs (relative errors ranging from −2.931–5.572% compared with gold-standard methods) and demonstrated batch-to-batch heterogeneity in herbal analyte content. Further applications in various Chinese herbs evaluation demonstrated the applicability of this method supporting its potential for herbal safety assessment.

title: Silver nanodot embedded waste PET nanofibres for efficient multifunctional air filter
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Bhavesh Thakur, Tulip Biswas, Ajit Kumar, Harun Venkatesan, Sumit Sinha-Ray
abstract: This study focuses on conversion of waste polyethylene terephthalate (PET) into ultrafine nanofibres with silver nanodots (AgND) (diameter 3.49 ± 0.94 nm) embedded within via electrospinning. Ultrafine PET (diameter 74 ± 15 nm) or PET-AgND (diameter 68 ± 17.4 nm) nanofibre-based membranes (basis weight 0.5 ± 0.02 g/m2, thickness 20 ± 1.4 μm), sandwiched between two spun-bond nonwoven layers, achieved a remarkable particle filtration efficiency (PFE) of 99.24–99.93% against 10–1000 nm particles, while maintaining pressure drop (ΔP) of 13 Pa at a face velocity of 5 cm/s. Such 3-ply filters demonstrated PFE > 99.5% against 350 nm particles with ΔP between 13–27 Pa over 28 consecutive filtration cycles. The PET–AgND membranes also demonstrated antibacterial efficacy of 99.78 ± 0.18% against Escherichia coli and 99.92 ± 0.02% against Staphylococcus aureus, respectively. Washability assessments showed reduction of PFE from 99.7% to 57.6% with increment in pressure drop from 13 to 79 Pa, from unwashed till 9 washing-drying trials. The 3-ply filters also exhibited significant air permeability (64.4 ± 0.25 cm3/cm2-s), water vapor transmission rate (82.45 ± 2.7 g3/m2-h) coupled with prominent UV protection (79.5%). This study highlights a sustainable route for converting waste PET into high-performance, multifunctional, filter media.

title: Synergistic drivers of microbial carbon, nitrogen fixation and phosphorus mobilization in mining soils by integrating machine learning with causal analysis
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Yun Zhang, Yalin Yin, Huiling Zhang, Li Tian, Tuantuan Cui, Jia-nan Lu, Yetao Tang, Shizhong Wang, Rongliang Qiu, Yingheng Fei, Yuanqing Chao
abstract: Microbial carbon (C), nitrogen (N) fixation, and phosphorus (P) mobilization are key processes in ecosystem nutrient cycling. However, the key environmental factors driving these microbial functions in heavy metal-contaminated soils of mining areas remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed machine learning and causal analysis models to systematically identify the primary environmental drivers governing the relative abundances of key functional genes associated with C, N fixation and P mobilization in 48 metal mining areas across China. The results revealed that Fe, C/N ratio, and soil pH exert dominant controls on microbial functional genes. Among them, Fe was identified as a shared environmental driver across all functional groups, while C/N balance and soil pH exhibited consistent direct or indirect regulatory effects on microbial functional potential. Furthermore, machine learning-based threshold analysis revealed distinct ecological regulation windows in which microbial functional potential remained at relatively high levels, including Fe contents of 9–30%, C/N ratios of 20.47–50.62, and soil pH values of 5.8–6.30. This study elucidates the key environmental factors shaping microbial functions in mining-affected ecosystems and provides quantitative insights to support precision regulation in ecological restoration of contaminated soils.

title: Scale matching between polyethylene microplastics and soil pores drives nonlinear greenhouse gas emission responses in karst soils
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Jie Xiong, Xiao Wei, Fa Zhou, Xinjun Liu, Dongyi Xie, Dexing Zhang, Yiming Zhou, Yang Liu, Shouyi Wang, Xudong Peng, Xiaojiong Tu, Xiaoyong Bai, Jun You
abstract: A laboratory microcosm experiment evaluated the effects of polyethylene microplastics (PE-MPs) with different particle sizes on the physicochemical properties, enzyme activities, pore structure, bacterial community, and greenhouse gas emissions of karst soil. The effects of PE-MPs on greenhouse gas emissions were nonlinear and depended on the match between microplastic particle size and soil pore scale. Small-sized particles (10–25 μm) may have filled micropores, induced localized anaerobic microsites, and increased microbial attachment interfaces, potentially enhancing CO2 and N2O emissions. Large-sized particles (900–1150 μm) promoted CO2 emissions, potentially by altering soil pore structure and improving aeration. Medium-sized particles (260–300 μm), being close to the characteristic pore size of the soil, may have caused limited disturbance to pore connectivity and microbial habitats and had no significant effect on either gas. Further analyses indicated that the effects of PE-MPs on greenhouse gas emissions were unlikely to result from direct mineralization, decomposition, or chemical release. Instead, PE-MPs may have indirectly affected greenhouse gas emissions by altering soil physical structure, reshaping bacterial community composition, regulating nitrogen forms, and changing enzyme activities. Small-sized particles exhibited the highest short-term integrated warming effect, followed by large-sized particles, whereas medium-sized particles showed the lowest effect.

title: A fluorine-centered framework for energy-normalized evaluation of PFAS destruction technologies
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Seyed Javad Amirfakhri, Jonah Semyonov, Ben Zobel, Maureen Kelley, Xuejun Pan
abstract: Destructive treatment is increasingly recognized as an important long-term strategy for managing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) because it targets irreversible carbon–fluorine (C–F) bond cleavage rather than contaminant transfer or parent-compound disappearance alone. However, comparison of destructive processes remains challenging because defluorination performance and energy demand are not consistently integrated within a common evaluation framework. To address this gap, this study develops an energy-normalized, fluorine-centered framework based on energy-normalized defluorination extent (ENDE) and energy-normalized fluoride production (EFP), which represent fractional defluorination and absolute fluoride production per unit energy input, respectively. Application of the framework to a curated multi-technology dataset of laboratory-scale aqueous PFAS destruction systems revealed substantial variability in energy-normalized defluorination performance. In photocatalytic systems, parent-compound degradation exceeded a median of 99% for several catalyst families, yet ENDE and EFP varied widely. Across technology classes represented in the dataset and at a common 50% defluorination endpoint, electrochemical systems and UV-based advanced reduction processes exhibited higher median ENDE50 and EFP50 values under the reported operating and energy boundaries. Overall, the framework provides a descriptive and diagnostic basis for evaluating energy-normalized C–F bond cleavage across reported PFAS destruction systems and identifying opportunities to improve defluorination performance.

title: From waste to resource: A plasma-flocculation synergistic strategy for flonicamid removal and upcycling of residues into electrocatalysts
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Shaowen Ji, Hongchi Chen, Fang Lu, Yan Yu, Yuxiang Li, Ting An, Denghao Wang, Chao Feng, Yeldana Bakhytzhan, Haojie Li, Kun Yang, Bin Dai, Zongyuan Wang
abstract: Treating fluorinated pesticide wastewater poses dual challenges: efficient decontamination and sustainable management of the generated solid waste. Here, we propose a plasma-assisted flocculation system that simultaneously removes flonicamid (FLO) and upcycles the Cu-containing flocculation residue into a high-performance electrocatalyst for the nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR). By leveraging polyacrylamide (PAM) to promote pollutant-associated aggregation and create localized reaction domains, this strategy enhances interactions between FLO and plasma-generated reactive species, achieving > 95% FLO removal. Mechanistic analyses support a synergistic coupling between PAM-mediated aggregation and plasma oxidation. The recovered solid residue is directly converted into a CuOx-C catalyst rich in mixed-valence Cu0/Cu+/Cu2+ sites and oxygen vacancies. This catalyst delivers an exceptional NH3 yield of 44.53 mg·h−1·mgcat −1 and a Faradaic efficiency of 92.19% at −0.6 V vs. RHE. Residual liquid intermediates are deeply mineralized via anodic oxidation. In-situ spectroscopies further reveal a sequential deoxygenation-hydrogenation pathway for NO3RR, and a 2500 mL continuous-flow system further demonstrates the feasibility of operation at an increased treatment volume. This work integrates pollutant degradation with resource recovery, providing a sustainable “waste-to-catalyst” paradigm for pesticide wastewater valorization.

title: Defect engineering of zero-valent iron promotes interfacial electron transfer for efficient Fenton-like activation at low catalyst dosage
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Ming Lei, Jiaxin Li, Han Wen, Xiaodong Chu, Zhifei Ma, Yu Yang, Linsheng Wei, Jianxin Chen, Lizhi Ran
abstract: Zero-valent iron (ZVI)-activated persulfate systems are limited by sluggish Fe cycling and rapid surface passivation, resulting in inefficient electron utilization and excessive reagent consumption. Here, we develop a NaCl-assisted ball milling strategy to construct a defect-rich ZVI interface (Cl-D-ZVI) with enhanced electron transfer capability. NaCl-assisted ball milling induces local structural disorder and coordination reconstruction at the ZVI interface, facilitating interfacial electron transfer and Fe redox transformation. Cl-D-ZVI enables efficient persulfate activation at a low catalyst dosage (20 mg·L−1), exhibiting consistently higher degradation activity than conventionally ball-milled ZVI. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the defective interface reduces the solid–liquid electron transfer barrier and facilitates Fe redox transformation, thereby promoting the concurrent formation of ·OH and Fe(Ⅳ)=O species. Continuous-flow filtration demonstrates sustained reactivity under different water matrices, while life-cycle assessment indicates reduced environmental impacts of the developed system. This study provides a scalable defect-engineering strategy for improving electron utilization and advancing sustainable iron-based advanced oxidation processes.

title: Old meets new: How emerging contaminants reshape the environmental behavior of legacy contaminants in soils—interaction mechanisms, remediation reassessment, and the regulatory role of soil organic matter
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Jinhang Song, Jianguo Zheng, Fei Liu, Ying Yuan, Kunlong Hui, Wenbin Tan
abstract: Microplastics, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), and antibiotics coexist in soils with legacy metal(loid)s, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and pesticides. These mixtures can alter contaminant fate, microbial selection, and remediation performance, but direct soil evidence remains uneven. This review synthesizes studies mainly from 2015 to 2025, earlier work, and selected early-online papers through June 2026. Soil evidence supports microplastic interactions with metals and PAHs; PFAS-metal evidence remains limited, mainly to retention. Antibiotic-metal evidence primarily concerns resistance co-selection rather than altered metal fate. We organize candidate processes into overlapping diagnostic tiers (physical co-location, interfacial chemical coupling, and biologically mediated feedback) and appraise evidence by study design, environmental relevance, mechanistic support, and risk of bias. A comparative map specifies required observations, alternative explanations, endpoint direction, and direct-evidence confidence. Concentration addition, independent action, and the combination index apply only to commensurable toxicological dose-response endpoints; transport, speciation, accumulation, and resistance require factorial or response-surface analyses. HIX, SUVA254, and PARAFAC components remain conditional dissolved organic matter proxies requiring method controls and independent validation. We classify remediation conclusions as direct mixture evidence, transferred single-contaminant principles, or author recommendations. The synthesis separates established findings from provisional interpretations.

title: Adsorption/desorption processes using palygorskite clay mineral for table olive fermentation brine treatment and phenols recovery
description: Publication date: 1 November 2026 Source: Journal of Hazardous Materials, Volume 518 Author(s): Dimitra Rizopoulou, Christina Vasiliki Lazaratou, Andreas D. Zentelis, Labrini Sygellou, Paraskevas Dimitropoulos, Athanasia G. Tekerlekopoulou, Vasilios Georgakilas, Dimitris V. Vayenas
abstract: Table olive fermentation brine (TOFB) is an acidic, organic-rich agro-industrial effluent containing elevated concentrations of phenolic compounds that pose significant environmental risks due to their toxicity and resistance to biodegradation. Nevertheless, these compounds constitute valuable bioactive molecules exhibiting antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. This study investigates TOFB treatment via adsorption onto palygorskite (Pal), emphasizing simultaneous pollutant removal, recovery of phenolic constituents (TPC) and Pal reusability. Raw Pal exhibited a characteristic fibrous morphology, high specific surface area (233 m²/g), and mesoporous structure, as confirmed by SEM and N₂ physisorption analyses. Adsorption performance was evaluated through batch and continuous-flow experiments under varying operational conditions. In batch systems, decreasing the initial phenolic concentration from 5200 to 40 mg/L increased removal efficiency from 58.5% to 88.3%, while increasing Pal dosage from 2.5 to 100 g/L enhanced removal from 50.6% to 75.6%. Continuous-flow operation achieved 37.5% TPC removal, with column saturation occurring after approximately 20 h. Equilibrium and kinetic analyses indicated that adsorption followed the Freundlich isotherm, whereas fixed-bed performance was adequately described by the Clark model. Desorption experiments enabled phenolic recovery up to 76% using water and a 50% (v/v) ethanol–water solution, with UHPLC–MS/MS–DAD confirming tyrosol and hydroxytyrosol among recovered compounds. Thermal regeneration did not affect the removal efficiency at the initial reusability cycle. However, it was found that the removal efficiency decreased to 30% of the initial capacity at the third time of reusability. Structural evolution throughout adsorption–desorption–regeneration cycles was evaluated using XRD and XPS analysis, supporting an integrated and sustainable TOFB management strategy aligned with circular economy principles.

title: Multi-scale approach to understanding and predicting environmental reactivity in the context of ISR
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Marine Bonnet, Niya Grozeva, Nicolas Seigneur, Sophie Guillon, Bayarmaa Purevsan, Natsagmaa Jadambaa, Mathias Gex, Clémence Besançon, Valentin Robin, Pierre Grizard, Michaël Descostes
abstract: In situ recovery (ISR) is a worldwide mining technique which accounts for more than 52% (in 2024) of global U production, thanks to its cost-effectiveness. However, where an ISR process uses sulfuric acid (H2SO4), local underground exploited aquifers' water quality can be affected by low pH and high concentrations of SO4. Hydrogeochemical processes controlling this groundwater changes are studied here in the context of the planned exploitation of the Zoovch Ovoo deposit in Mongolia, using a multi-scale approach comparing real data with models. At the laboratory scale, experimental data combined with a 1D reactive transport model (RTM) demonstrate that ion-exchange reactions on clay minerals surface are the main geochemical mechanism governing groundwater chemistry (pH and major ions). To consider system heterogeneity and the spatial impact of the ISR process, field data from two pilot cells were combined with a 3D reactive transport model. The model successfully reproduced the field data by considering both ion-exchange and dissolution-precipitation reactions of the mineral phases, especially calcite and gypsum, necessary to explain the water chemistry at larger scale. Vertical and lateral fluid excursions out of the pilot cells were observed depending on the system heterogeneity. This study demonstrated that the relative importance of the various processes investigated depends on the time and distance scales probed. For the short term and U production, heterogeneities and ion-exchange are crucial for explaining the changes in groundwater chemistry. A better understanding and quantification of these processes will help operators optimize production and long-term environmental remediation strategies.

title: Canopy exchange processes enhance acid-neutralizing capacity in subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Shui-Xia Li, Zhi-Yun Jiang, Yi-Hua Xiao, Han-Wen Zhang, Meng-Di Wu, Tong-Zheng Chen, Zhi-Gao Fu, Jing Li, Si-Yi Zhang
abstract: Forest canopy serves as the first interface for atmospheric deposition into ecosystems, thereby playing a crucial role in regulating hydrological processes and associated water chemical cycles by means of canopy exchange processes. However, it remains poorly understood how canopy exchange processes alter chemical processing of rainwater, such as the acid-neutralizing capacity (ANC) in acidic areas. This study examined the hydrological partitioning and associated chemical composition in a typical subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forest in southern China. Hydrological components, including rainfall, throughfall, and stemflow, were measured and sampled from January 2020 to December 2021, and the canopy exchange process was then estimated using a canopy budget model. Results showed that pH and ANC increased in throughfall but decreased in stemflow. During the dry season, throughfall exhibited significantly higher neutralization capacity (ΔpH = 1.11 ± 0.89; ΔANC = 0.11 ± 0.13 meq L−1), whereas in the wet season, the neutralization capacity of throughfall was substantially weaker (ΔpH = 0.07 ± 0.85; ΔANC = 0.03 ± 0.09 meq L−1). In contrast, stemflow showed persistent acidification across both seasons (dry-season ΔpH: −1.29 ± 1.01; wet-season ΔpH: −1.18 ± 0.69), with its ΔANC significantly below zero in the wet season (−0.07 ± 0.09 meq L−1, p = 0.009). The canopy budget model indicated that most solutes (except F−) were leached from the forest canopy, with K+ exhibiting the most pronounced canopy leaching effect. In addition, canopy exchange contributed positively 83% to acid-neutralizing capacity (ANCNTF) of net throughfall flux. Among ions mediating canopy processes, Ca2+, K+, Mg2+, and F− all made positive contributions to the acid neutralizing capacity of canopy exchange (ANCCE) in both dry and wet seasons, with K+ contributing the most (31.43% in the dry season and 25.52% in the wet season). In contrast, NO₃− and Cl− exhibited negative contributions: the negative effect of NO₃− was stronger in the wet season (−20.69%) than in the dry season (−0.63%), whereas Cl− showed the opposite pattern (dry: −12.03%–; wet: −12.03%). Our results suggest that the forest canopy may play a significant role in mitigating the effects of atmospheric acid deposition. This finding contributes to a better understanding of forest eco-hydrological processes and could have important implications for forest management in similar subtropical regions globally.

title: Vadose-zone control of PFOS delivery to groundwater: Explicit unsaturated-zone transport with solid-phase and air–water interfacial sorption
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Vahid Rafiei
abstract: Quantifying PFOS retention in the unsaturated zone beneath contaminated sites requires a model that simulates how much PFOS the unsaturated zone holds and when PFOS first reaches groundwater. Both determine how long a source keeps feeding the aquifer and when watershed and site assessments need an explicit unsaturated zone. We modified the unsaturated-zone transport of MODFLOW 6 to simulate solid-phase and air–water interfacial sorption, each dependent on water content, and drove it at two sites with daily percolation from SWAT+. We applied it at three sites that differ in depth to water, infiltration and water content: two firefighting-foam sites and a tannery legacy source. At the shallow site, the same released mass was run once through the unsaturated zone and once directly to the water table. In a simulated 6.4–6.9 m column (3.0–4.3 m measured nearby), 63–83% of the PFOS released in 1971–1994 was above the water table in 2024, and its median crossing was delayed by at least 42 years; PFOS in the deep aquifer was 70–83% lower in 2017. Without sorption the two runs agreed within 0.2%, so the delay is sorption, not water movement. An advection–dispersion screen shows that 1/10,000 of the source concentration first reaches the water table within a median of 18–38 years at a dispersivity of 10% of the depth, against a median transit of 83–182 years. A single travel time answers neither question: a screen must report when PFOS is first detected and how long the unsaturated zone feeds the aquifer.

title: Machine learning prediction of arsenic natural background level heterogeneity in shallow groundwater: Integrating in-situ hydrochemistry and spatial proxies at the meso-scale
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Laura Landi, Joel Podgorski, Michael Berg, Marco Rotiroti, Chiara Zanotti, Alessandro Amorosi, Enrico Dinelli, Maria Filippini
abstract: Geogenic arsenic (As) contamination poses a major environmental concern, yet mapping its Natural Background Levels (NBLs) remains challenging in data-scarce, human-impacted regions within heterogeneous sedimentary aquifers. NBLs are essential for distinguishing natural from anthropogenic contributions and for establishing threshold values in environmental policy and groundwater management. This study applies a Random Forest (RF) algorithm to predict arsenic NBL exceedance of the WHO guideline (10 μg/L) in shallow groundwater of the Ferrara province (Po Plain, Italy). Three model configurations were tested using: (i) in-situ hydrochemical variables (hydrochemical model), (ii) spatially continuous variables (geospatial model), and (iii) a combination of both (mixed model). The mixed model achieved the highest performance (AUC = 0.88), followed by the hydrochemical model (AUC = 0.86). The geospatial model performed slightly lower (AUC = 0.83) but enabled the generation of a continuous 50 m-resolution probability map, identifying 17% of the area as potentially exceeding 10 μg/L. Iron, redox potential and dissolved oxygen were the dominant hydrochemical predictors, while organic carbon, clay content, and surficial geology were the dominant spatial variables, reflecting geochemical and sedimentary controls on As mobilization through reductive dissolution processes. Elevated exceedance probabilities are identified in the northeastern sector, proximal to the Po River Delta, and in peat-rich central areas. This study demonstrates that spatially continuous variables can effectively complement hydrochemical data for continuous NBL mapping, capturing meso-scale heterogeneity that single, groundwater body-scale values conventionally adopted in European NBL frameworks are unable to resolve, thus offering a useful tool for contamination assessment and groundwater management.

title: A capillary microporosity framework for modeling the fate and transport of PFAS in concrete
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): K. Schmeltzer, C.J. Newell, P. deBlanc, S. Jacob, J. McDade, R. Caird, G. Dooley, J. Gamlin, E. Kainer, C. Leong, J. Scalia, C. Shackelford
abstract: Concrete pads impacted by aqueous film forming foam (AFFF) represent long-term sources of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) to stormwater runoff that require environmental impact assessment. However, existing assessment models have not reproduced field observed PFAS concentration profiles. Accordingly, a new mechanistic model for PFAS assessment (CAPCON) based on a capillary microporosity framework for PFAS transport within concrete is proposed. The proposed CAPCON model includes dual-domain diffusion within water-filled capillary pores together with episodic PFAS release to runoff driven by wetting and drying cycles based on site-specific climatic conditions. Comparison of CAPCON modeled versus measured PFAS concentration profiles from concrete cores recovered from two field sites with contrasting climatic and PFAS loading conditions resulted in good agreement (log-RMSEs of 0.03 to 0.36). The calibrated CAPCON model also captured the characteristic first-flush pattern observed in field-measured sheet-flow runoff tests, although first-flush magnitudes were overpredicted for three of the four site/compound combinations. Results indicate that climate influences PFAS transport in concrete. In wetter climates, deeper water penetration into concrete increases the extent of water-filled capillary pores, enabling faster diffusive transport through the capillary region and deeper PFAS penetration. In drier climates, diffusion is slower within unsaturated, lower-permeability regions of the concrete, resulting in greater near-surface accumulation. The proposed CAPCON framework provides a mechanistic basis for evaluating PFAS transport and release from concrete pads under variable climatic conditions and offers improved capability for assessing long-term environmental impacts of AFFF-impacted concrete pads.

title: Ammonium transport in zeolite and zero-valent iron columns: Experiments and tempered fractional modeling
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Xiaoxiao Hao, HongGuang Sun, Xuantong Fan, Shuai Yang, Yuncong Yan
abstract: Ammonia nitrogen contamination in groundwater poses risks of eutrophication and drinking-water quality deterioration. Understanding ammonium transport in reactive porous media is critical for predicting its subsurface fate. This study utilized batch adsorption experiments, column transport tests, and a tempered one-sided density (TOSD) transport model to investigate the transport behavior of ammonium in two reactive media—zeolite and zero-valent iron (ZVI)—which serve as model systems for in-situ groundwater remediation. The results of the batch adsorption experiments for zeolite and ZVI were consistent with the pseudo-second-order and pseudo-first-order kinetic adsorption models respectively. Both adsorption isotherms conformed the Freundlich model, and the results indicated greater ammonium uptake by zeolite than by ZVI. The column breakthrough curves exhibited anomalous transport behavior, and the TOSD model (a fractional-order modeling framework) accurately described the transport experimental data, proving the applicability of the TOSD method in describing the anomalous transport of ammonium ions. The model fitting parameters suggested that adsorption and rate-limited mass exchange may be the plausible factors influencing ammonium retention. This study provides experimental evidence and modeling tools for ammonium ion transport in reactive media, which is significance for mitigating groundwater pollution.

title: Aquitard-breaching conduits control salinity dynamics and variable-density contaminant transport in coastal aquifer-aquitard systems
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Zihao Zhang, Leyu You, Jiaxu Zhang, Jina Yin, Jie Yang, Alicia Wilson
abstract: Contaminant transport from semi-confined aquifers to coastal waters is an emerging environmental concern, yet its prediction remains challenging due to the complexity of coastal aquifer systems. In coastal environments, aquitards are breached by conduits formed through natural processes or anthropogenic disturbances, enhancing hydraulic connectivity between otherwise isolated aquifers. Despite their widespread occurrence, the impacts of conduits on salinity distributions and land-derived contaminant migration from semi-confined aquifers to coastal waters remain poorly understood. This study systematically investigates the influences of an aquitard-breaching conduit on salinity dynamics and land-derived contaminant transport in coastal aquifer-aquitard systems. The conduit is represented as a high-permeability pathway through the low-permeability aquitard. Results show that a conduit enhances seawater intrusion into semi-confined aquifers relative to no-conduit conditions, irrespective of conduit locations. Notably, a conduit situated near an underlying saltwater wedge induces saltwater up-coning from that wedge, establishing a hydraulic connection between the overlying and underlying wedges. This up-coning redirects both freshwater-density and saltwater-density contaminant plumes from predominantly horizontal migration to vertically oriented pathways toward the ocean. In the absence of up-coning, plume behavior diverges by density contrast: freshwater-density contaminants preferentially discharge through the conduit, whereas saltwater-density plumes partition between upward discharge via the conduit and seaward transport within the semi-confined aquifer. Compared to no-conduit scenarios, conduits consistently facilitate the export of freshwater-density contaminants, whereas a conduit without saltwater up-coning can prolong the residence time and discharge duration of saltwater-density contaminants and reduce their peak efflux. These findings demonstrate a dual role for aquitard-breaching conduits in modulating seawater intrusion and contaminant fate, providing new insights for managing coastal groundwater systems.

title: Contrasting hydrological states are associated with sediment bacterial community variation and micropollutant biodegradation potential in a river-connected floodplain lake
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): You Li, Xue Yin, Jiao He, Yuanyuan Zhao, Changhui Wang, Leilei Bai
abstract: Hydrological contraction is a defining feature of river-connected floodplain lakes, but its association with sediment bacterial communities and contaminant biodegradation potential remains incompletely understood. During one observed wet-to-dry transition in Dongting Lake, China, we combined sediment physicochemical and enzyme measurements, pre-incubation bacterial community analyses, and standardized microcosm assays of 17α-ethinylestradiol biodegradation potential (EBP30) in sediments. As mean local water coverage decreased from 76.4% in the expanded state to 35.2% in the contracted state, dry-period sediments generally exhibited higher TOC, Fe(III), potential dehydrogenase activity, and field estrogen concentrations. Wet-period sediments showed higher bacterial richness, diversity, and community-level niche breadth and lower compositional dissimilarity and dispersion, whereas dry-period communities exhibited greater relative contributions of dispersal limitation and environmental selection, together with a denser, less modular, and more positively cohesive correlation network. Despite reduced alpha diversity, EBP30 increased from 0.76 ± 0.06 μg g−1 during the wet period to 0.93 ± 0.18 μg g−1 during the dry period, with the largest wet-to-dry increase in East Dongting Lake. Partial least-squares path modeling (PLS-PM) and site-blocked cross-validation indicated that EBP30 was more closely associated with bacterial compositional indicators, dry-period-associated taxa, and sample-level network cohesion than with taxonomic richness alone. A sensitivity PLS-PM using site-level water coverage retained similar explanatory power and identified a supported negative total association between water coverage and EBP30. These findings identify hydrological state as an important correlate of sediment microbial functional potential and emerging-contaminant fate in dynamic floodplain lakes.

title: How do stabilized river meanders affect microbial communities and water quality in urban rivers?
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Dantong Zhu, Jiaxing Zeng, Jiajie Su, Shoushu Liu, Zhuoyin Lu, Saiyu Yuan, Xianglong Wei, Hongwu Tang, Xiangju Cheng
abstract: Urban river meanders are frequently stabilized and hardened for flood control, thereby substantially altering their natural hydrodynamics and ecological functions. However, the influence of such engineered bends on sediment microbial communities, key players in nutrient cycling and thus water quality, remains poorly understood. Here, we integrate 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, co-occurrence network analysis, and community assembly modeling to investigate seven stabilized meanders along Guangzhou's Yangmei River during a single summer sampling campaign. We found that bend-position-related habitat differences were associated with the spatial organization of microbial diversity and putative co-occurrence patterns. Mid-bend sections showed ecological patterns consistent with stronger local hydraulic disturbance, while post-bend sections were more consistent with relatively depositional habitat conditions. Mid-bend sediments, associated with relatively high hydraulic energy, exhibited the lowest α-diversity and distinct co-occurrence patterns, consistent with greater local hydraulic disturbance than at pre- and post-bend sites. Within the sampling campaign, spatial differences in water chemistry were more closely associated with external nitrogen and phosphorus inputs, whereas the spatial heterogeneity of benthic microbiota was more strongly linked to localized hydrodynamic conditions. Co-occurrence patterns also varied among bend positions along the meander transition. Neutral-community modeling suggested that stochastic processes played an important role in bacterial community assembly during the sampling period. Complementary βNTI–RCbray null-model analyses identified dispersal limitation as the predominant inferred process, whereas heterogeneous selection contributed relatively more in post-bend depositional sediments. Our findings highlight local heterogeneity in benthic habitats and water–sediment exchange conditions within stabilized meanders, which may influence local nutrient dynamics. These results suggest that bend-scale hydraulic conditions and microbial habitats warrant consideration in urban river restoration.

title: Coupled sediment and microplastic fluxes revealed by check-dam sediment records
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Kazem Nosrati, Fatemeh Lak, Zahra Etminan, Adrian L. Collins
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in terrestrial environments, yet their redistribution through erosion and accumulation within sediment-retention structures remains poorly quantified. This study quantified MPs in sediments retained behind check dams and examined their relationships with sediment storage and erosion-related sediment yield at the catchment scale. Twenty check dams in a semi-arid mountainous catchment in northeastern Iran were investigated. Sediment storage ranged from 531 to 9828 Mg (mean: 2683 Mg), while specific sediment yield ranged from 16.2 to 855.4 Mg km−2 yr−1 (mean: 247.1 Mg km−2 yr−1). MPs were detected in all sediment samples, with concentrations ranging from 800 to 5240 particles kg−1 dry sediment (mean: 2702 particles kg−1). Estimated MP inventories ranged from 9.0 × 108 to 2.4 × 1010 particles per check dam. Strong positive relationships were observed between specific sediment yield and estimated MP yield (r = 0.99, p < 0.01) and between accumulated sediment mass and estimated MP inventory (r = 0.80, p < 0.01), indicating a close association between sediment dynamics and MP redistribution. Fibrous MPs dominated the assemblage (86.6%), and the 500–1000 μm size class accounted for the largest proportion of detected particles (44.7%). Raman spectroscopy confirmed several polymer types within the analyzed subset. Overall, the findings show substantial accumulation of sediment-associated MPs behind check dams and indicate that erosion-driven sediment mobilization may represent an important pathway for MP redistribution in erosion-prone catchments. However, the persistence of this retention may depend on the stability of accumulated sediments, which can potentially be remobilized during high-energy hydrological events.

title: Non-reactive solute transport in coupled macro-meso-micro porous system: experiments and HYDRUS-2D modeling with GSA-PEST integration
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Aman Chandel, Deepak Swami, Nitin Joshi, Jiri Simunek
abstract: This study investigates the processes governing tracer transport in a stratified porous medium, which produces asymmetric breakthrough curves (BTCs) with multiple inflection points. Such complex BTCs are often analyzed using multi-porosity or multi-permeability flow and transport models. However, these models introduce increased parameter complexity and associated sensitivity, necessitating thorough evaluation. In this context, we coupled the Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) and Parameter Estimation (PEST) with the DualPerm (DP) HYDRUS module to quantify parameter sensitivity and enhance BTC representation. A micro-aquifer experiment was conducted on a stratified porous medium using a non-reactive tracer for testing the capabilities of the developed framework. The sensitivity analysis aimed to examine how different model parameters contribute to different segments of the asymmetric BTC. This analysis revealed that the fracture and immobile domain parameters dominate early tracer breakthrough (64% of the total sensitivity). In comparison, the matrix parameters and the porosity of the immobile region contributed 48% of the total sensitivity during the rising limb period. The prolonged tailing limb was primarily influenced by the matrix parameters (porosity and permeability, 91% sensitivity), with the porosity of the immobile region adding only 4%. It was also established that BTC-based parameter estimation emphasizes peak concentration, but often overlooks critical features like mass recovery, solute residence time, and spatial variance. An alternate approach, which is based on cumulative solute mass recovery, showed efficiency in capturing complex features of experimental BTCs such as inflection points, peak timing, and long-tailing behavior. The proposed framework enhances the capability of the HYDRUS (DualPerm) module to investigate various flow and transport processes, improving mass recovery estimation compared to conventional BTC-based methods.

title: Effect of entrapped water on NAPL migration in unsaturated fractures
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Song Xue, Qingteng Fan, Zexiong Zhou, Zhibing Yang, Gang Liu, Biao Li
abstract: The migration of non-aqueous phase liquids (NAPL) in unsaturated fractures involves NAPL-water-air three-phase displacement. Understanding the impact of entrapped water on this migration process is crucial for predicting NAPL flow and solute transport in the fractured vadose zone. This study presents visualized flow experiments to systematically investigate NAPL (n-octane) invasion behaviors in initially dry and water-entrapped unsaturated single fractures by varying fracture inclination angle and injection flow rate. The experimental results reveal that entrapped water fundamentally shifts NAPL flow patterns from fingering flow in dry fractures to film flow propagating along entrapped water droplets in water-entrapped fractures. Compared to fingering flow in dry fractures, film flow in water-entrapped fractures exhibits enhanced lateral expansion, longer fracture penetration time, higher breakthrough saturation, larger perimeter-area ratio, and stronger ability to invade large-aperture channels. The morphology of the film flow is jointly regulated by injection flow rate and fracture inclination angle. Lower flow rates and larger inclination angles result in thinner films, while sufficiently high flow rates at small inclination angles can trigger a transition from film flow to fingering flow in the main flow channels. We also find that the distribution of NAPL-occupied apertures consistently follows a normal distribution, independent of flow rate and fracture inclination angle, and aligns with the statistical properties of the fracture aperture field. These findings elucidate the regulatory role of entrapped water on NAPL migration and advance the mechanistic understanding of NAPL invasion in unsaturated single fractures, thereby informing groundwater contamination risk assessment and remediation design.

title: Environmental fate of ciprofloxacin in agricultural soils under realistic irrigation water matrices: kinetic, column transport, thermodynamic, mechanistic and machine learning insights
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Saurabh Kumar, Lucas Joseph Makuni, Renu Meena, Nitin Khandelwal
abstract: The combined influence of soil properties, irrigation water chemistry, and transport processes on antibiotic fate remains poorly understood. Here, ciprofloxacin (CIP) retention, transport, and remobilization were investigated in three agricultural soil types under four different irrigation water matrices using batch, column, thermodynamic, mechanistic, and machine-learning approaches. At elevated concentrations (10 mg/L), all soils exhibited comparable retention capacities, whereas substantial differences emerged at extremely elevated concentrations (150 mg/L), with maximum adsorption capacities following the order black soil (≈17.6 mg/g) > alluvial soil (≈15.6 mg/g) > red soil (≈10.4 mg/g). Transport behaviour differed markedly among soils, with retardation factors following the order black soil (7.9) > alluvial soil (2.24) > red soil (1.4). After 180 pore volumes, relative breakthrough remained below 0.03 in black soil but reached 0.25 and 0.45 in alluvial and red soils, respectively. Rainfall flushing further revealed contrasting environmental outcomes, with black soil strongly immobilizing CIP, red soil promoting rapid transport, and alluvial soil acting as a persistent contaminant leaching reservoir. Thermodynamic analyses indicated predominantly endothermic adsorption with enhanced spontaneity at elevated temperatures. FTIR and zeta potential analyses identified surface complexation, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and cation bridging as the primary retention mechanisms. Random Forest modelling identified soil type as the dominant control on CIP retention, accounting for ~92% of total feature importance (R2 = 0.96–0.97). These findings demonstrate that soil properties govern CIP fate and determine contrasting pathways of sequestration, persistence, and groundwater contamination risk.

title: Substrate-explicit coupled modeling of organic matter degradation and sulfide production using a generalized kinetic approach
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): P. Trinchero, A. Nordström, M. Calpe, G. Román-Ross, A. Costa-Solé, O. Silva, G. Deissmann
abstract: In natural subsurface systems, Dissolved Organic Matter (DOM) is a potent reducing agent, as it sustains and catalyzes a number of microbially-mediated reactions. One of such reactions, namely the reduction of sulfate to sulfide mediated by sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) is particularly relevant for the evaluation of the long-term stability of deep geological repositories (DGRs) for spent nuclear fuel. Some of these proposed DGRs will be hosted at great depth in fractured crystalline rocks where sulfide, potentially produced by SRB, is practically the only oxidant of relevance for the copper canisters used to safely store and keep isolated the radionuclides from the natural environment. One important limitation to this reaction is substrate availability, as the DOM that typically infiltrates, e.g. from overlying surficial sediments, is typically bound in complex polymeric organic compounds (cellulose, starch, proteins, fats, etc.) that cannot be directly used by SRB. A further intermediate step is therefore needed which consists in the degradation of ’complex’ organic matter into ‘simpler’ organic substrates. This intermediate step is performed by a different microbial group (typically acetogens and/or fermenters) that acts on a substrate characterized by significant heterogeneity. Previous studies have documented that the organic carbon substrate typically comprises thousands of species depending on the type of subsurface environment. In this study we argue that the evaluation of microbially mediated sulfate reduction by means of reactive transport modeling should explicitly account for the substrate heterogeneity. However, explicitly accounting for thousands of chemical species of complex organic matter presents two significant challenges. The first is how to parameterize each individual reaction. The second is how to include this large number of species in the mass balance calculations. The first challenge was addressed through the development of a Generalized Kinetic Model (GKM) that formulates all rates as a function of a universally accepted rate of electron transfer along with the underlying stoichiometry of each individual metabolic reaction. The computational challenge was overcome by using weight-based reaction rates. In practice, we solve transport and mass balance for the equivalent total concentration of complex organic carbon while retaining information on the underlying substrate and associated microbial population through the use of two weighting functions, which are updated on lagged time based on mass balance. The numerical framework is first verified and then applied to simulate sulfide production in a single fracture–matrix system. Important modeling outcomes, such as the dependence of SRB activity on the degradation of a complex organic substrate and the role of the matrix as a temporary storage term for substrates, are derived.

title: Seasonal changes in petroleum NSZD biodegradation rates associated with water table fluctuations within the zone of soil contamination
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Michael J. Donn, John L. Rayner, Kaveh Sookhak Lari, Andrew King, Greg B. Davis
abstract: Natural Source Zone Depletion (NSZD) is widely used to manage petroleum-contaminated sites, but estimating NSZD rates is challenging because most methods rely on short period, averaged or point-in-time measurements. These can be misleading due to seasonal variability in biological activity, moisture and water table fluctuations influencing NSZD rates. Here we utilise continuous inground sensor measurements and light non-aqueous phase liquid (LNAPL) distributions from cores to understand seasonal processes affecting NSZD rates. Linked to multiphase modelling these data are used to test the hypothesis that seasonal NSZD variations result from LNAPL distributions and water table fluctuations. Using ~3.5 years of continuous oxygen and temperature data across four fuel types, NSZD rates were shown to vary by up to an order of magnitude seasonally. Rates ranged from 0.1 to 0.8 kg/m2/y for diesel to ~5 to 13 kg/m2/y for aviation gasoline, with broadly comparable trends between oxygen- and temperature-based methods. Rising water tables generally reduced NSZD rates at the diesel, gasoline, and crude oil sites by inundating the LNAPL depth distribution and disconnecting it from oxygen in the vadose zone. In contrast, at the aviation gasoline site, where LNAPL persisted above the maximum water table, NSZD rates remained high or increased. Modelling reproduced observed trends at the diesel site and showed that NSZD rates are influenced by the exposure of LNAPL to the vadose zone air phase (i.e., oxygen), with inundation suppressing rates, while exposure enhanced it. This is further supported by soil core TPH measurements that show loss of shorter chain TPH ranges at shallower depths above and within the zone of water table fluctuation relative to deeper in the formation. Continuous monitoring and modelling have provided insights into the dynamic NSZD rate estimates, indicating that care is needed to align field measurements with conceptualisation of LNAPL distributions and water table dynamics.

title: Reactive solute transport driven by coupled stress fields affected by injection pressure and permeability during in-situ chemical oxidation remediation of contaminated groundwater
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Guiyao Xiong, Zhiyu Jiao, Xiaobin Zhu, Qi Zhang, Yun Zhang, Yun Yang, Shujun Ye, Jinguo Wang, Jichun Wu, Brent Sleep
abstract: Groundwater contamination at the site is worsening, and in-situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) has been widely adopted for contaminated groundwater remediation due to its low environmental risk and low cost. Through laboratory experiments and field simulations, we optimized the system for TCE degradation using activated sodium persulfate and explored how injection pressure and formation permeability affect TCE remediation. The results show that both sodium citrate (TCD) and citrate (CA) chelating agents can increase TCE oxidation by persulfate, with optimal molar ratios of Na2S2O8:TCD:Fe2+:TCE of 20:10:10:1, and Na2S2O8:CA:Fe2+:TCE of 20:5:10:1, achieving high TCE removal rates of 97% and 98%, respectively. Pressurized injection increases the hydraulic gradient and flow velocity, thereby enhancing advection and mechanical dispersion, especially in high-permeability media. In low-permeability media, pressurization also modifies porosity and tortuosity and increases the effective diffusion coefficient, which is relatively more important for solute transport. Pressure-induced permeability changes were limited under the tested 0.1–1 MPa range and were secondary to advection, mechanical dispersion, and effective diffusion. In layered subsurface systems, placing horizontal wells at the interface between high- and low-permeability layers was more effective in delivering oxidants to contaminated regions than vertical wells. In summary, higher-pressure oxidant injection improved remediation in the simulated low-permeability formations by increasing advection, mechanical dispersion, and effective diffusion. The relative contributions were site-specific, and diffusion enhancement was not the sole controlling mechanism. The numerical model can effectively simulate ISCO of TCE by accounting for the multi-field-coupled stress field. It can provide valuable insights for designing groundwater remediation projects.

title: Diffusion of inert and reactive tracers: Overview of the DIR field experiment in the Callovo-Oxfordian clay rock (France)
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): V. Blin, M. Descostes, J. Radwan, E. Tevissen, T. Grangeon, T. Fierz, C. Frechou, P. Brisset, M. Filippi, C. Landesman, S. Ribet, P. Meier, M. Saint-Jalmes, R.V.H. Dagnelie, S. Dewonck, J.-C. Robinet
abstract: The geological disposal of radioactive waste is under investigation in several countries, especially in Europe. In this field, clay-rich sedimentary rocks are promising natural barriers to limit and delay the release of radionuclides toward the biosphere, due to their diffusion-driven transport and retention properties. In addition to laboratory studies, field studies in Underground Research Laboratories (URL) represent a significant value to strengthen safety demonstrations. In this context, the DIR experiment (Diffusion of Inert and Reactive tracers) was developed and implanted in the Meuse/Haute-Marne URL located in the Callovo-Oxfordian clay-rich formation. Over 6 years, several diffusion experiments were performed with radioactive tracers: HTO (tritiated water), 36Cl−, 125I−, 22Na+, 134Cs+, assessing the behaviour of neutral, anionic and cationic species. The evolution of each radiotracer activity was monitored in the injection borehole, from at least 100 days up to 3 years. Overcoring of the rock at the end of the experiments allowed the accurate characterization of radiotracer profiles. An overview of the DIR experiment is provided here, illustrating the large amount of data gathered in 4 specific boreholes at two different depths: −445 and − 495 m, within the Callovo-Oxfordian geological layer. The modelling of experimental results allowed the quantification of diffusion properties parallel to the bedding of the rock for the studied radionuclides. Diffusion parameters for HTO are in agreement with those determined on samples using the conventional through diffusion method. Anions are partially excluded from porosity with quantified values 0.3 < ε a(anion)/ε(H2O) < 0.6. On contrary, the diffusion of cations is limited by their adsorption on clay surfaces with the evidence of surface diffusion processes. The sensitivity analysis on adjusted parameters provided additional insights on the local properties, such as homogeneity of the diffusion plume and the limited extension of the damaged zone surrounding boreholes: L EDZ ~ 1–3 cm. Still, further field experiments are necessary to measure diffusion in such EDZ and to improve accuracy on the diffusion anisotropy ratio.

title: Oxidative sulfide weathering and weak mineral attenuation controlling arsenic mobility in a crystalline aquifer
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Swati Ganveer, Kamal Lochan Pruseth, David Anand Aind
abstract: This study investigates the source–sink dynamics and hydrogeochemical controls governing arsenic fate and transport within a fractured crystalline aquifer system. The hydrogeologic framework is characterized by spatial heterogeneity in redox conditions and persistent undersaturation with respect to key Fe-, sulfate-, and Ca-bearing mineral phases. Mineralogical characterization identifies arsenopyrite and cobaltite as the primary geogenic sources; oxidative weathering of these sulfide phases drives the continuous release of arsenic. Aqueous speciation modeling reveals a predominance of A s ( V ) and F e ( I I I ) species, with minor A s ( I I I ) occurring within reducing microenvironments. Persistent undersaturation of Fe- and As-bearing minerals, together with other attenuation-controlling phases, suggests limited potential for secondary mineral precipitation, while allowing arsenic to remain predominantly in the dissolved phase. Weak correlations between arsenic and hydrochemical gradients indicate that contaminant distribution is highly heterogeneous and controlled by the occurrence of mineralized zones. The results demonstrate that persistent arsenic mobility in fractured crystalline aquifers can occur under predominantly oxidizing conditions through sustained sulfide weathering combined with limited attenuation capacity within the aquifer system.

title: Hidden contaminants in a coral paradise: fate, transport, source apportionment, and toxicity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the coral reef ecosystems of the Lakshadweep archipelago
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): E.R. Vignesh, T.R. Gireeshkumar, A. Ramzi, A.R. Jithu, Midhun M. Nair, P.S. Rakesh, K.S. Arya, Anjana Jayaprakash, K. Sudheesh, K.R. Muraleedharan, Narayan Panda, K.U. Abdul Jaleel
abstract: This study examined the environmental fate, source apportionment, and associated ecological and human health risks of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in the coral reef ecosystems of four inhabited islands in the Lakshadweep Archipelago (Kadmat, Kiltan, Kalpeni, and Minicoy). Water, suspended particulate matter (SPM), and sediments were collected from reef lagoons during April 2025 and analysed for 16 PAHs congeners designated as priority by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA). PAHs were in the range of 20.9–240 ng/L in the dissolved phase, 146–356 ng/L in the SPM, and 2.05–22.2 ng/g in sediments. PAH transport and sedimentary accumulation differ markedly from those in siliciclastic coastal environments due to the dominance of carbonate-rich, organic-matter-deficient, highly permeable sediments and strong hydrodynamics that promote rapid particle export to adjacent offshore waters. As a result, reef lagoons act as dynamic conduits that promote contaminant exchange with the Arabian Sea, thereby limiting long-term contaminant accumulation in the lagoon sediments. Source apportionment studies indicated mixed petrogenic and pyrogenic PAHs sources, primarily associated with navigational activities, fuel handling, diesel-powered energy generation, and combustion-related activities. Ecological risk assessment indicated negligible risks from sedimentary PAHs, while dissolved and SPM-bound PAHs posed low to moderate ecological risks. Incremental lifetime cancer risk (ILCR) values for all age groups were within the potential low-risk category, with dermal contact identified as the dominant exposure pathway. This study provides critical baseline information on transport behaviour and ecological implications of PAHs in the coral reef ecosystems of Lakshadweep and recommends sustained environmental monitoring and targeted management strategies to protect the ecological integrity of these coral reef systems under mounting anthropogenic perturbations.

title: Experimental investigations into the evolution of reactive fronts under radial injection conditions
description: Publication date: January 2027 Source: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology, Volume 284 Author(s): Zhipeng Du, Xingrun Wang, Jiajun Chen, Kaiyu Shi, Haixu Duan, Xianghua Yan
abstract: Reactive fronts form at interfaces where remediation agents encounter contaminant plumes in subsurface environments. The contaminant degradation is largely confined to this narrow mixing zone, but the transient reaction dynamics within it remain poorly understood. Existing models often assume uniform flow or constant dispersion, failing to capture how the spatial deceleration of radial velocities alters interfacial mixing. To address this, two-dimensional sandbox experiments were conducted by radially injecting potassium permanganate into a Naphthol Green B-dyed perchloroethylene (PCE) plume.
