Material categories exhibiting radioactive equilibrium in both decay segments were ashes and slag from coal combustion plants, samples utilized in cement manufacturing, old building materials, drilling muds, and waste from zircon and zirconia processing. In contrast, sludges, sinters and filter materials from water treatment facilities, along with waste from oil and gas transportation and processing, were identified as materials with disturbed equilibrium in the 238U −234U – 230Th and 232Th – 228Ra – 228Th decay segments.

title: Contact dose rate as an operational screening parameter for NORM oily sludge segregation on offshore oil and gas platforms
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Marcelo Macedo Valinhas, Marco Aurélio dos Santos, Francisco Cesar Augusto da Silva
abstract: On offshore oil and gas platforms, limited space, time and logistics create significant challenges for the characterization and segregation of NORM waste. This raises a practical question: can routine contact dose rate measurements, already incorporated into offshore radiological protection practices, provide sufficient information to support safe waste segregation decisions before oily-sludge drums leave the platform? This study evaluates the use of contact dose rate (CDR) measurements as an operational parameter for NORM oily-sludge drum segregation and risk-informed waste-management decisions. A historical dataset comprising 22,782 drum records from Brazilian offshore production was analyzed, including 8304 drums with offshore CDR measurements subsequently reassessed onshore and characterized by in situ gamma spectrometry. Offshore and onshore dose rates showed a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.827; R 2 = 0.684; p < 0.001). A multiple regression model without an intercept, based on 226Ra and 228Ra activity concentrations, showed a strong fit (R 2 = 0.8353). For drums with CDR ≤ 0.5 μSv·h−1, the statistical assessment quantified the probability of exceeding radionuclide-specific activity concentration criteria, providing a basis for evaluating uncertainties associated with dose-rate-based segregation and exemption decisions. The findings support the use of CDR as an operational waste-management parameter that may also support exemption from regulatory control under the applicable regulatory conditions, reducing reliance on systematic gamma spectrometric characterization. The study provides quantitative evidence that may contribute to discussions on the refinement of risk-informed regulatory approaches for NORM waste management in the oil and gas industry.

title: Review on algae-derived biopolymers to remove radionuclides from aquatic systems: sorption mechanisms, kinetics and stability
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Govindharajan Sattanathan, Selvarajan Ramganesh, Jeyaseelan Aravind, Srinivasan Venkatesh
abstract: The carboxyl, sulfate, phosphate and hydroxyl groups on algal biomass and its polysaccharides bind uranium, caesium, strontium and radium. The reported uranium capacities for brown macroalgae vary greatly depending on pH and pretreatment, ranging from roughly 150 to 560 mg/g. Green macroalgae and immobilized microalgae report much smaller uranium capacities, typically in the range of 75-290 mg/g. Certain microalgae remove 88-95% of dissolved 137Cs within 48 h. However, these values mostly stem from acidic, single-solute batch experiments. When the same material is used to test actual effluents, removal rates drop, often dramatically. This review evaluates algae as a feedstock for functional polymers, combines capture mechanisms with the aqueous chemistry that governs them, and re-evaluates how isotherm, kinetic, and thermodynamic models are interpreted. The review then compares the quantitative and qualitative data regarding engineered hydrogels and composites, including their stability, regeneration, and response to competition from other ions. Finally, the loaded sorbent is viewed as secondary radioactive waste, and column operation, life-cycle burden, and traditional alternative options are placed within this context. Maximum capacity is less important than selectivity in real water and safe end-of-life management as critical evaluation criteria.

title: Natural and technologically enhanced radioactivity (NORM/TENORM) in soils, mining residues and waters of mining areas worldwide: a systematic review and multivariate synthesis of the 1976–2026 literature
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Edmundo Escareño-Juarez
abstract: Mining and mineral processing redistribute naturally occurring radionuclides and can generate technologically enhanced naturally occurring radioactive material (TENORM). A PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review of the 1976–2026 literature was combined with a quantitative, multivariate synthesis of activity concentrations reported in abstracts. Of 60,242 records from seven bibliographic sources, including the IAEA INIS database, and citation searching, 16,689 were eligible and 1308 studies from 103 countries provided 4532 values (4276 study-level records). In mining-impacted soils, geometric means of 226Ra(238U), 232Th and 40K were 56.7, 38.1 and 306 Bq kg−1; medians exceeded the UNSCEAR world medians by 11% and 26% for 226Ra(238U) and 232Th, whereas 40K was 18% lower. Uranium mining showed the highest soil 226Ra(238U) (geometric mean 324 Bq kg−1) and tin/rare-earth/mineral-sand operations the highest 232Th (78.9 Bq kg−1). The 232Th/226Ra(238U) ratio was lowest in phosphate and uranium operations (medians 0.30 and 0.56) and 0.7–1.4 in the other industries. After adjustment for industry, region and publication year, tailings and residues contained 6.6 times more 226Ra(238U) than soils, and 31% of tailings records exceeded 1 Bq g−1. Uranium exceeded the WHO drinking-water guideline (30 μg L−1; a yardstick for mine waters) in 45% of groundwater and 83% of mine-water records, and 53% of mine-water records exceeded 1 Bq L−1 of 226Ra. The median outdoor effective dose from soils was 0.072 mSv y−1. In this abstract-level dataset, the largest enhancements and guideline exceedances occurred in residues and mine waters and differed among industries; harmonised reporting would enable full-text meta-analysis.

title: Measurement intensity and regulatory effectiveness in radon governance: A comparative analysis of the United States and Europe
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Robert Bobkier, Peter Bossew, Petros Koutrakis, Ewa Katarzyna Czech, Konstantin Kovler
abstract: Measurement intensity, understood as the capacity of a regulatory system to generate exposure-relevant data at scale, is a revealing indicator of how legal frameworks translate scientific knowledge into protective action. Radon is a leading environmental carcinogen, yet the U.S. and Euratom Community legal systems have responded to the same body of scientific evidence through structurally different regulatory architectures. These architectures have produced deep asymmetrical levels of measurement intensity, thereby substantively shaping the foundations upon which mitigation, optimization, and enforcement rest. The present study examines the development of radon governance in the U.S. and Europe through a combined doctrinal, empirical, and regulatory lens. Drawing on U.S. national radon datasets, European Indoor Radon Maps and an analysis of epistemic capacity, it demonstrates that regulatory effectiveness is not strictly correlated with legal stringency. The U.S. federal-state-market architecture, combining non-binding federal guidance with state disclosure rules, transaction-driven testing, and private-market incentives, has generated reported measurement volumes more than one order of magnitude above the currently documented European map-based dataset, together with substantially greater reported mitigation activity. These gross outputs do not, by themselves, establish a net reduction in the number of high-radon dwellings or in population risk, but they demonstrate a markedly greater capacity to generate exposure-relevant information and activate remedial pathways. The Euratom Community has developed a codified framework under Directive, 2013/59, but exhibits structurally lower testing rates, largely because mandatory workplace duties are concentrated within Radon Priority Areas and because comparable mechanisms for embedding household testing in ordinary social and economic routines remain limited. The article concludes that measurement intensity can function as a structural diagnostic of epistemic and remedial capacity, revealing how divergent normative designs generate distinct pathways for converting scientific insight into concrete public-health protection.

title: 210 Pb ex in lacustrine sediments: A half-century global synthesis (1977-2024)
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 300 Author(s): Renaldo Gastineau, Floriane Guillevic, Palak Aggarwal, Anthony Foucher, Olivier Evrard, Christine Alewell, Robert Sabatier, Pierre Sabatier
abstract: Unsupported 210Pb (210Pbex) is a naturally occurring radionuclide widely used to establish sediment chronologies spanning the past ∼150 years, thereby providing high-resolution temporal frameworks for palaeolimnological reconstructions. Since the late 1970s, numerous hypotheses have been advanced to explain the environmental and climatic controls on 210Pbex deposition in lakes, yet no comprehensive synthesis of the accumulated empirical evidence is available. Here, we compile a global database of 210Pb measurements from 670 lacustrine sediment cores from studies published between 1977 and 2024 CE, encompassing 530 lakes across 61 countries and all continents except Antarctica. Before 2000 CE, approximately 85% of the sediment cores studied were located in the Northern Hemisphere. This proportion declined to 45% after 2000, reflecting a geographic expansion of 210Pb-based chronologies use toward the Southern Hemisphere. Using this dataset, we first assess the bivariate relationships between the 210Pbex surface activities, depositional fluxes, inventories, and individual environmental covariates, such as mean annual precipitation, land/ocean ratio, latitude and elevation. We then apply ordinary least squares multiple linear regression (OLS) and random forest (RF) models to rank the drivers of spatial variability in 210Pbex deposition at the global scale. The RF models outperform the OLS; the surface activity, flux and inventory models have low to high explanatory power for interpretation (R2 = 0.21, 0.35 and 0.66, respectively). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) indicate that elevation is the dominant predictor of both fluxes and inventories, followed by latitude and mean annual precipitation. These findings demonstrate that large-scale atmospheric processes primarily govern global patterns of lacustrine 210Pbex deposition. This study provides the first quantitative, data-driven global assessment of the environmental controls on lacustrine 210Pb deposition, enhancing the robustness and comparability of 210Pb-based chronologies worldwide.

title: Calibration of the NDUSRM series and further measurements of 236 U/ 238 U isotopic ratios in the Ewing collection
description: Publication date: Available online 9 October 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity Author(s): Thomas L. Bailey, David Lund, Griffin Mulcahy, Alistaer Zhou, Noah Cabanas, John P. McDonaugh, Ruchi Rathod, William Von Seeger, Philippe Collon
abstract: 236U is one of the rarest isotopes of uranium, occurring in ores with an abundance below 1 × 10−9. Due to a wide variety of geological factors, the 236U content in a given uranium ore body is considered to be a unique “fingerprint” like signature, with applications in nuclear forensics and geophysics. Its low abundance though is only detectable via Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS), capable of measuring 236U/238U ratios below 1 × 10−11. Improvements to the AMS setup at the University of Notre Dame’s Nuclear Science Laboratory, have greatly improved its detection limit, enabling measurements across the entire 236U/238U ratio range found in natural ores. A description of the improvements is presented. A survey of the 236U/238U ratio of various ores from North American and African mines was conducted with the improved setup, using in house reference standards to quantify the measurements. A new detection limit of 1 × 1 0 − 12 was established.

title: Reshaping millennial-scale human–water relationships: A multi-disciplinary synthesis of the Yellow River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qiting Zuo, Lu Liu, Junxia Ma
abstract: Study region Yellow River Basin, China, a large sediment-laden river system shaped by millennia of human activities, environmental changes, and river management. Study focus Recent reviews have documented Yellow River flood history and anthropogenic disturbances in considerable detail, yet their relevance to long-term socio-hydrological governance remains insufficiently synthesized. This review integrates historical, archaeological, paleoenvironmental, ecological, hydrological, geomorphological, and governance evidence to re-examine the millennial-scale evolution of human–water relationships in the basin. New hydrological insights for the region The synthesis identifies four broad stages: adaptive coexistence (ca. 2070 BCE–581 CE), agricultural expansion and landscape transformation (581–1368 CE), sediment-driven vulnerability and hydraulic dependence (1368–1949 CE), and engineering regulation and ecological restoration (since 1949 CE). Across these stages, increasing human pressure and changing ecological buffering capacity altered erosion, sediment accumulation, and river-system responses, while increasing hydraulic dependence during periods of heightened vulnerability. Governance correspondingly shifted from localized adaptation toward basin-scale coordinated regulation, water–sediment management, and ecological restoration. These stage transitions reflect changing feedbacks among climatic variability, human interventions, ecological conditions, fluvial processes, and institutional arrangements, offering a long-term socio-hydrological perspective on hydrological vulnerability and sustainable management in the Yellow River Basin.

title: Afghanistan's water security crisis: Coupled hydroclimatic stress, groundwater depletion, water quality risks, and institutional constraints
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sajid Ullah, Rujun Chen
abstract: Study region Afghanistan is an arid to semiarid country where river flow variability, precipitation fluctuations, limited groundwater recharge, irrigation demand, and snow and glacier dynamics constrain water availability. Changes in these processes at the basin scale directly affect national water security. Study focus This review synthesizes peer-reviewed and gray literature published from 2017 to 2025, integrating hydrogeological, water-quality, remote sensing (RS), geographic information system (GIS), and hydroclimatic studies. It evaluates surface-water availability, groundwater quantity and quality, and the impacts of climate variability and water-management practices on Afghanistan’s water resources. New hydrological insights for the region The reviewed studies demonstrate significant spatial variability across Afghanistan’s major river basins. The Kabul River Basin (KRB) is the most well-documented hotspot of groundwater stress, with reported declines of up to 1.5 m yr⁻¹ , reduced storage, excessive abstraction, and deteriorating water quality. In contrast, the Helmand River Basin (HRB) and Panj-Amu River Basin (PARB) are strongly controlled by cryospheric processes, with snowmelt contributing approximately 77% and 74% of annual river flow, respectively. Changes in snow persistence, glacier conditions, runoff timing, and drought patterns threaten surface-water reliability and groundwater recharge. Overall, Afghanistan’s water crisis stems from the combined effects of hydroclimatic variability and anthropogenic pressures. Significant uncertainties persist in poorly monitored basins, underscoring the need for improved monitoring networks, recharge assessments, and integrated water-resource management.

title: Nature-based solutions for coastal flood risk reduction on the Changhua Coast, Taiwan: Modelling the benefits of wetland restoration under climate change
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Chun-Han Lo, Shih-Chun Hsiao
abstract: Study region Changhua, Taiwan Study focus Estuarine wetlands are increasingly recognized as nature-based solutions that complement structural defenses by providing flood-regulation services and co-benefits such as carbon sequestration. Focusing on the Changhua coast at the Jhuoshuei River estuary in Taiwan, designated as a coastal protection zone under the Coastal Zone Management Act, we develop a coupled hydrodynamic and ecosystem-service framework. The framework links two-dimensional storm-surge modelling using SRH-Coast with ecosystem-service assessment using the InVEST Coastal Blue Carbon module to evaluate wetland loss and restoration under sea-level-rise scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region Our results show that sea-level rise and wetland contraction act as compounding drivers of coastal flood risk along the Changhua coast. Under the + 34.5 cm sea-level-rise scenario, intertidal wetland area decreases from 6063 ha to 4619 ha, while storm-surge inundation extent increases by 65%. Wetland restoration produces the strongest hydrodynamic benefit locally, reducing surge levels by up to 37% across coastal cross-sections, whereas the reduction in total inundation area under future conditions is more modest at about 3%. This scale-dependent response indicates that substantial local surge attenuation does not necessarily translate into an equivalent reduction in system-wide inundation. Projected wetland loss also decreases blue-carbon stocks by about 16.4%, while restoration increases storage by about 31.7% relative to present conditions. Together, these results provide region-specific evidence that wetland preservation and restoration can complement existing coastal protection by attenuating local surge propagation while maintaining blue-carbon storage, and offer a transferable framework for evaluating nature-based flood-risk-reduction strategies on other subsiding, wetland-fringed estuarine coasts.

title: Regional-scale assessment of climate change impacts on land use–specific hydrological processes in the Geum River Basin, South Korea
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jaeyoung Kim, Moon-Hwan Lee, Jongho Ahn
abstract: Study region Geum River Basin, South Korea, East Asia Study focus Climate change is expected to substantially modify hydrological processes: however, the mechanisms underlying these changes remain highly dependent on regional characteristics and land use patterns. In this study, we provide a regional-scale assessment of the effects of climate change on land use specifics hydrological processes in the Geum River Basin, South Korea, which is a key water-supply region characterized by rapid urbanization and a mixture of agricultural– and forested landscapes. New hydrological insights for the region Climate change is intensifying hydrological variability across the Geum River Basin, with fast-response components such as surface runoff generally increasing. However, slow-response components, particularly groundwater recharge and baseflow, are projected to decline. Runoff sensitivities to precipitation and temperature exhibit three distinct response patterns corresponding to urban land, agricultural land, and forestland–grassland, demonstrating that climate drivers propagate through hydrological processes in land use–specific ways. Although projected increases in precipitation enhance meteorological resilience, they do not necessarily translate into improved hydrological water availability, especially in highly urbanized sub-basins. These findings highlight the importance of regionally tailored adaptation strategies. For the Geum River Basin, expanding storage capacity, conserving permeable and vegetated surfaces, and improving seasonal water allocation are identified as priority measures for sustaining water and ecosystem resilience under future climate conditions.

title: Seasonal hydrological contrasts in water–sediment microbiome assembly and eutrophication indicators in a low-gradient urban river–lake network
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qiqi Ding, Hongzhe Fang, Jiulu Liu, Ting Wang, Tianhong Li
abstract: Study region Kunshan, a low-gradient urban river-lake network in the central Taihu Basin (Yangtze River Delta), China. Study Focus Seasonal hydrological variability can reorganize microbial communities in connected river–lake systems, but responses may differ between water and sediment and alter the interpretation of water-quality indicators. We analyzed 94 surface-water and surficial-sediment samples collected in May and August 2024, representing pre-monsoon and summer-monsoon conditions, respectively. Bacterial community composition differed strongly by matrix and sampling period (NMDS stress = 0.0763; PERMANOVA R² = 0.665, p = 0.001), with matrix accounting for the largest share of variation. Water communities showed stronger seasonal displacement and lower evenness in August, whereas sediments maintained higher diversity. Indicator taxa also shifted by matrix and period, including Limnohabitans in May water, Cyanobium in August water, Nitrospira in May sediment, and Dechloromonas in August sediment. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Taxonomic turnover accompanied matrix-specific functional shifts and assembly changes. Water lost aerobic chemoheterotrophic potential in August, while sediment gained anaerobic chemoheterotrophic and nutrient-transformation capacity. Neutral models revealed contrasting effective immigration trajectories between water and sediment. August shifted to higher C:N, lower C:P, tightened coupling, and altered WQI/TLI links to stoichiometric gradients. These demonstrate asymmetric seasonal hydrological effects across the water–sediment interface and that C:N:P provides useful biogeochemical context to refine microbial and eutrophication indicator interpretation for regulated river-lake networks.

title: Long-term hydrochemical dynamics and stoichiometric relationships in the boreal peatland-dominated Oulanka River system, Northeast Finland
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Danny Croghan, Hannu Marttila, Torben R. Christensen, Bjørn Kløve, Riku Paavola
abstract: Study Region The Oulanka River system is a semi-natural boreal catchment in Northeast Finland draining to the Arctic Ocean. Boreal catchments are undergoing hydrological and biogeochemical shifts from climate and land-use change, but long-term data are scarce. Study Focus This study aims to quantify long-term (1966–2024), seasonal and spatial trends in water quality, combining a 58-year time series with spatial sampling (2020–2022) in the Oulanka catchment. We analysed concentrations of dissolved organic carbon (DOC), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), nitrite-nitrate (NO₂NO₃), ammonium (NH₄) and phosphate (PO₄), along with seasonal loading, concentration-discharge (C-Q) relationships and carbon:nitrogen:phosphorus (C:N:P) stoichiometry. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Despite significant warming, DOC concentrations did not increase over the time series, unlike in many boreal catchments. TN declined significantly, NO₂NO₃ and NH₄ were stable, and PO₄ increased. Shoulder seasons were identified as key transport periods and contributed higher loading than the winter and growing season. DOC showed mild chemodynamic behaviour, TP had a positive C-Q slope across seasons, and PO₄ varied by season. Over time, C-Q slopes changed significantlyfor TN and NH, and coefficient of variation (CV) ratios decreased, particularly for PO₄. C:N:P stoichiometry was carbon-dominated, with nitrogen becoming increasingly limiting over time. It varied little among seasons or sites. The findings highlight the value of site-specific catchment studies for understanding boreal water quality and informing management.

title: A novel approach to uncertainty-conscious long-term streamflow reconstruction in ungauged basin combining machine learning and dendro-hydrological indicators
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shahriar Mehrvand, Alexandre F. Nolin, Marie-Amélie Boucher, Kurt C. Kornelsen, Jacques C. Tardif
abstract: Study Region: The Abitibi River watershed is a large hydropower-regulated basin located in northeastern Ontario and northwestern Quebec, Canada, where natural streamflow records are unavailable due to long-term flow regulation and reservoir operations. Study Focus: This study presents an uncertainty-aware framework for long-term streamflow reconstruction and trend analysis in a regulated, data-scarce watershed. The framework integrates hydrological modeling, machine-learning-based parameter estimation, and dendrohydrological validation to reconstruct natural streamflow in the Abitibi River watershed. Three machine learning algorithms are used to estimate parameters of the GR4J-CemaNeige model, generating pseudo-observations of natural streamflow. These pseudo-observations are then used to calibrate five conceptual hydrological models within the Raven platform, producing a 15-member ensemble of daily streamflow simulations for 1950–2023. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: The reconstructed ensemble shows strong agreement with flood-ring signature in tree rings of naturally flowing rivers, with significant correlations ranging from 0.35 to 0.72, and is further supported by comparison with scaled natural flows from a nearby watershed (annual CRPS = 49.39 m3/s). A hierarchical Bayesian linear model reveals statistically significant increases in annual and spring streamflow, with estimated trends of 1.91 and 2.67 m3/s/year, respectively. Overall, the framework provides a robust strategy for reconstructing long-term natural streamflow in regulated watersheds.

title: Dual-constraint physics-informed LSTM-XAJ hybrid model for 10-minute flood forecasting in small-to-medium basins: A case of the Xiang River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xinkui Wang, Changbo Jiang, Yuannan Long, Xinyi Song, Xingyi Zhang
abstract: Study region Luolingqiao (326 km²) and Wenjiashi (164 km²), two small-to-medium sub-basins of the Xiang River Basin in Hunan Province, China. Study focus Reliable flash flood forecasting in small-to-medium basins (SMBs) requires both high temporal resolution and physically constrained long-lead prediction. This study develops a dual-constraint physics-informed framework that couples the Xin'anjiang (XAJ) model with an encoder-decoder LSTM to produce 10-minute runoff forecasts at lead times of up to 6 h, forced exclusively by quality-controlled X-band radar quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE). XAJ-derived physical trajectories are supplied to the LSTM decoder, and a dual-constraint loss penalizes deviations from both observed discharge and XAJ-simulated runoff. The framework is evaluated on 28 flood events under blocked chronological cross-validation, in hindcast mode with observed QPE over the forecast horizon. New hydrological insights for the region At the 6-h lead time, the hybrid model significantly outperforms the standalone XAJ model: relative to XAJ, NSE increases by 20%, RMSE decreases by 25%, and peak error decreases by 46%. Continuous evaluation from 1 to 6 h reveals a crossover near 3 h: the LSTM dominates at shorter horizons, whereas the hybrid model becomes optimal beyond 3–4 h, where physical regularization suppresses recursive error accumulation. Coupling process-based constraints with deep learning at 10-minute resolution is therefore feasible and valuable for flash flood early warning in SMBs with concentration times shorter than 3 h.

title: Impact of hydroclimatic extremes on suspended sediment dynamics in a tropical river basin, India
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Vivek Kumar Bind, Vimal Mishra, Vikrant Jain
abstract: Study region Tapi River Basin, a 724 km-long tropical river in India. Study focus: Hydrological and sediment connectivity regulate sediment supply and channel morphology, while intensifying hydroclimatic extremes enhance flood-driven sediment mobilisation. Using observations and hydrological modelling, we investigated flood, sediment, and channel responses to extreme events and a 35-year assessment. We also developed a flood connectivity framework to evaluate hydrological connectivity during floods and infer potential sediment disconnectivity when observed sediment data are unavailable. New hydrological insights Flood-wave connectivity varies spatially due to heterogeneous rainfall and anthropogenic regulation. Extreme events increase sediment loads by ~200–300% relative to average conditions. Channel response is governed by spatial variations in unit stream power (USP) and sediment availability, with high upstream USP promoting erosion and a 3–4-fold reduction downstream favouring deposition, potentially reducing channel conveyance and increasing flood risk. Sediment mobilisation is strongly associated with daily rainfall > 50 mm and seasonal discharge, highlighting the role of extreme rainfall and hydrological conditions. Model simulations indicate a ~36% increase in sediment yield alongside ~8% and ~28% increases in annual mean and maximum rainfall, respectively, over 35 years, under constant land use. Although hydroclimatic variability appears to be a major driver, land-use change, channel processes, and longitudinal barriers may also influence sediment dynamics. These findings highlight the need to incorporate hydroclimatic extremes and connectivity into sediment and flood-risk management.

title: A GI-based framework for designing stormwater response programs in priority urban areas
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ruixuan Wu, Changbo Jiang, Reza Ahmadian
abstract: Study region Kaifu District, Changsha City, Hunan Province, China. Study focus This paper proposes a framework for designing and optimizing flood control solutions for stakeholder-defined priority areas and applying it to a region to assess its application and validate its effectiveness. The area of green infrastructure within each sub-catchment serves as the decision variable, representing the type, size, and optimal placement location. Life cycle cost and runoff control rates are set as the optimization objectives for the NSGA-II algorithm, and the layout of green infrastructure is iteratively updated based on SWMM simulation results. Ultimately, an optimized strategy for flood mitigation in priority areas is derived. New hydrological insights for the region The study found that the number and distribution of areas playing a critical role in flood mitigation within priority zones — referred to in the paper as “main impact zones” — are primarily influenced by node overflow volumes surrounding the priority areas and the runoff control characteristics of green infrastructure; variations in storm intensity may also cause changes to these areas. Given limited available land area, the selection of which sub-catchment area will yield better results is also influenced by these three factors.

title: 3D flow structure responses to water diversion in China’s fifth largest freshwater lake: Lagrangian observations and modeling
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shihao Li, Wanxing Li, Zhaoliang Peng, Gang Liu, Weiping Hu, Yanping Wang, Yihui Zhang, Jinge Zhu, Jing Luo
abstract: Study region Lake Chaohu, the fifth largest freshwater lake in China, lies in the lower Yangtze and connects to it, serving as an ecological barrier and drinking water source within the catchment. Study focus Lake Chaohu has diverted water from the Yangtze since 2017 to optimize water allocation and mitigate eutrophication. In November 2024, the new Pai River diversion channel was commissioned and completed its first diversion. To reveal its impacts on lake hydrodynamics and synergy with existing routes, we integrated Lagrangian drifters and Acoustic Doppler Current Profilers (ADCPs) to track diverted water trajectories and monitor flow fields at 20 stations during diversion. The EcoLake model simulated six diversion scenarios, evaluating how different pathways and flow allocations regulate the lake-wide flow field. New hydrological insights for the region During the diversion, Lagrangian observations revealed vertical velocity stratification (upper: 4.9 cm/s; middle: 4.1 cm/s; bottom: 3.5 cm/s), while ADCP measurements showed a 39% increase in multi-station average velocity. Simulations demonstrated that the new Pai River route activated western lake hydrodynamics (average velocity increased from 0.05 to 0.3 cm/s, peak inflows exceeding 10 cm/s), whereas the Baishitian route enhanced connectivity between eastern and western basins. A trade-off exists in dual-line schemes—increasing Pai River flow improves western water exchange but intensifies backwater effects on northwestern tributaries.

title: A practical drag-equivalent representation method for submerged pile groups in Froude-similar physical models
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xing Yang, Xiangming Wang
abstract: Study region River, estuarine, and tidal-bay systems containing pile-supported structures, where temporally varying flows can be divided into representative hydraulic conditions. Fangchenggang Port, China, is used as a regional engineering application. Study focus Geometric and Froude similarity preserve the scaled geometry and gravity-dominated flow characteristics of hydrodynamic physical models, but do not necessarily preserve the drag exerted by pile groups on the surrounding flow. This drag dissimilarity can distort how the local influence of pile-supported structures is represented within a larger-scale flow field. We therefore develop drag-similarity criteria based on the overall pile-group drag and the accumulated drag contributions of individual piles, together with an empirical framework accounting for Reynolds number, pile spacing and arrangement, and inflow direction. New hydrological insights for the region The study reveals that pile-supported structures can influence local hydrodynamic responses within regional flow systems and that these effects may be misrepresented when pile groups are scaled only geometrically. Geometric scaling produced excessive pile-group drag, whereas drag-similarity representation provided a closer reproduction of the integrated hydraulic influence of the prototype structure. These findings highlight the importance of considering pile-group drag when representing engineering structures in physical models of natural water systems.

title: Long-term evolution of urban water services in Shaanxi Province, China (2000–2023): A coupling coordination analysis perspective
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yi Huo, Jianping Jia, Wenchao Sun, Ming Wang, Jun Xie, Jietong Pei
abstract: Study region Shaanxi Province, China. Study focus Urban water service is essential for sustaining resilient cities. In this study, to explore its evolution in response to rapid socioeconomic development under natural water resources constraints from 2000 to 2023, a composite system (NSUW) consisting of natural water resource endowment (N), socio-economy (S), urban water supply (U), and wastewater collection and treatment (W) subsystems was constructed. The coupling coordination degree model, K-means clustering, and obstacle degree model were applied to assess the NSUW system’s development level and obstacle factors. New hydrological insights for the region The NSUW system maintained a high coupling degree of approximately 0.90 after 2006 and the development degree rose from 0.18 to 0.34, while its coupling coordination degree increased from 0.37 to 0.53, evolving from mild dissonance to coordination. The coupling coordination evolution of ten prefecture-level cities exhibited three patterns including “Economy-led”, “Resource-constrained”, and “Resource-conservation”. The obstacle degrees of S and W subsystems decreased while those of N and U subsystems increased. As for the key obstacles, water scarcity was identified as a prominent constraint in Xi’an, whereas the U or W subsystem was found to be the restrictive factor for remaining cities. These findings improve understandings of how urban water services evolved under different combinations of water resources availability and socioeconomic development in arid and semi-arid regions.

title: Multiscale source-term coupling of site-scale groundwater and watershed models for long-term tritium transport at the Savannah River Site
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Kazuyuki Sakuma, Haruko Wainwright, Zexuan Xu, Angelique Lawrence, Pieter Hazenberg
abstract: Study region The Fourmile Branch Creek catchment at the Savannah River Site (SRS), USA, a watershed historically impacted by tritium (3H) releases from nuclear production facilities. Study focus We developed a sequential multiscale framework that transfers time-dependent 3H discharge calculated by a process-based 2D site-scale groundwater-flow and transport model to a 3D watershed model with internally coupled surface-subsurface hydrology. The framework avoids the computational cost of resolving site-scale contaminant processes throughout the entire watershed while retaining their effects on long-term river concentrations. New hydrological insights The results show that effective precipitation is the dominant control on 3H discharge and river concentrations, influencing both transport timing and dilution processes. The coupled model reproduces the order of magnitude and temporal trends of observed 3H concentrations in river water under a range of parameter conditions. The study highlights the importance of linking site-scale groundwater processes with watershed-scale modeling to evaluate contaminant transport, while also demonstrating limitations associated with simplified source representation and transport pathways.

title: Analysis of the evolution and attenuation attribution of runoff in the LRB based on ESMD and Budyko framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Renjuan Peng, Yan Kang, Huiru Ai, Weihe Hu, Weiran Wu, Xiaoling Su, Liuyue Yang, Dexin Cui, Ruilin Wei
abstract: Study region The Laoha River Basin (LRB) in the typical semi-arid area of northeast China. Study focus Regarding the existing incomplete and unsystematic studies on runoff evolution and attribution analysis and to address the insufficient knowledge of the runoff evolution characteristics and the unclear dominant drivers of runoff attenuation in the LRB, this study proposed a novel framework of "evolution characteristics - sensitivity analysis - attenuation attribution - spatial contribution" integrating ESMD (Extreme-point Symmetric Mode Decomposition), EN (Elastic Net), Budyko theory, and LSTM network and apply it to the LRB (Laoha River basin) of Northeast China to analyze the evolution and attenuation attribution in runoff. New hydrological insights for the region The annual runoff in the LRB showed a significantly fluctuating downward trend, and two abrupt changes occurred in 1979 and 1998. Runoff sensitivity to CC (climate change) and HA (human activities) increased during the HIPs (human impact phases) compared to the BP (baseline period), and it was higher in the middle and lower reaches than in the upper reaches. HA have had the most significant impact on the runoff attenuation, with the contribution rate exceeding 80% across all phases, of which the human water use and the expansion of cropland were the most direct factors. The middle reaches were the key contributions area of runoff attenuation in the whole basin, with a contribution rate of 75% in the human impact phases, and playing a dominant role in runoff attenuation. These results are expected to offer important information for water resource management in the LRB.

title: Cryogenic vacuum extraction bias misleads plant water source estimates: A correction framework based on soil properties
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yong Zhang, Jinzhao Liu, Xinping Zhang, Jiajie Li, Cicheng Zhang, Xiong Xiao, Keshao Liu, Zhu Liu, Shichuan Fu, Zhen Du
abstract: Study region A typical secondary forest in the East Asian monsoon region. Study focus Using an existing empirical correction method based on soil water content (SWC) and soil clay content (SCC), we corrected for the isotopic bias (Δδ) in soil water extracted via cryogenic vacuum extraction (CVE) and quantified the effects on dual-isotope relationships, line-conditioned excess (lc-excess), and inferred plant water source contributions. New hydrological insights These results highlighted the importance of accounting for soil properties when interpreting soil water isotope values (δS) in heterogeneous environments, advancing stable isotope applications in ecohydrological studies. The uncorrected δS (δuncorrected) and corrected δS (δcorrected) differed significantly (p < 0.01) in all soil layers, with SWC accounting for most of the variation in the estimated correction. The estimated CVE-driven Δδ could mimic isotopic patterns associated with non-equilibrium fractionation. The CVE-driven Δδ correction reduced this bias, increasing the average lc-excess values towards zero. Critically, the δcorrected data revealed plant water uptake patterns that differed from those inferred from the δuncorrected data. Estimates based on the δuncorrected data systematically overestimated water uptake from the surface soil layer, while those based on the δcorrected data indicated significant plant reliance on the intermediate layer (p < 0.05). This reveals an adaptable plant drought-resistance strategy. Furthermore, the δcorrected refined the vertical isotopic stratification and improved the reliability of MixSIAR model outputs by narrowing confidence interval widths (CIWs) by 2.8–8.6% in surface and deep layers, highlighting the necessity of correcting CVE-driven Δδ to avoid ecological misinterpretation.

title: Flood water resources utilization in cascade reservoirs considering flood forecast information
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qianning Wang, Yong Peng, Jian Wu, Huicheng Zhou
abstract: Study region The lower Jinsha River reservoir group (Wudongde, Baihetan, Xiluodu and Xiangjiaba) and Three Gorges Reservoir, China. Study focus This study examines floodwater utilization in cascade reservoirs under forecast uncertainty. A framework estimates the upper bound of pre-fill volume (UBFV) from two-stage flood processes linking forecast-period information to subsequent flood characteristics. Forecast errors are incorporated into reservoir operation, with UBFV constrained by the expected maximum reservoir water level not exceeding a specified reference level. New hydrological insights for the region Forecast-period information is significantlycorrelated with subsequent flood characteristics (coefficients of at least 0.67), supporting conditional scenario generation but not independently establishingforecasting skill. Under the investigated 2020 flood conditions, UBFV ranges from 38 to 54 × 10⁸ m³ for Three Gorges and from 116 to 120 × 10⁸ m³ for the lower Jinsha cascade. Simulated flood-season hydropower generation increases by 1.45%–4.86%. For Three Gorges, the highest UBFV occurs at a five-day horizon under current forecast conditions; in the examined error scenarios, errors above approximately 10% can reduce UBFV as the horizon lengthens. The Jinsha cascade is less sensitive to forecast errors. Flood shape and duration also matter: the concentrated 1981 flood allows more pre-filling, whereas the prolonged 1998 basin-wide flood allows less. The findings inform case-specific dynamic flood-limited water-level control.

title: Benchmark-screened temporal transferability for historical gridded precipitation reconstruction and spatial drought assessment in hyper-arid Kuwait
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Bandar S. AlMutairi
abstract: Study region Kuwait Study focus Long-term drought assessment is difficult in data-sparse regions where only one or a few stations have records long enough for historical validation, while the wider gauge network is shorter. This study develops a benchmark-screened temporal transferability (BSTT) framework for gridded precipitation reconstruction. PERSIANN-CDR was evaluated using the Airport station as the temporal benchmark and shorter stations for local method selection. Candidate bias-correction methods were tested across calibration windows using backward and forward validation and robustness tests. Transferable methods were then evaluated locally, and the selected method was calibrated independently for each native grid cell to reconstruct precipitation. New hydrological insights for the region Conventional forward validation alone was insufficient to establish historical transferability. LOCI showed the strongest temporal transferability, while MVS and QM remained stable across all calibration windows. The reconstructed record revealed spatial and timescale differences in drought behavior using the Standardized Precipitation Index at 3- and 12-month scales. Drought occurred during about 12.3% and 18.1% of months, respectively, with moderate drought dominant at both scales. Longer-timescale droughts were more persistent, more severe, and affected a larger mean area. The 2001–2018 period showed greater long-timescale duration and severity than 1983–2000, while mean intensity changed little. Regional patterns in duration, severity, intensity, and affected area demonstrate the value of BSTT-based reconstruction where long gauge records are spatially limited

title: Fractal theory based simplification of complex urban stormwater pipe networks for efficient hydraulic simulation
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haojun Miao, Xiaoyu Chen, Junyu Zhang, Yunfei Wang, Dafang Fu, Zhengzhao Li, Rajendra Prasad Singh
abstract: Study region This study was conducted in Sandringham, Victoria, Australia, including the Melbourne Bay suburbs of Beaumaris, Black Rock, and Sandringham, as well as parts of Cheltenham, Hampton, Highett, and Mentone. This area is a fully residential catchment of about 750 ha, drained by a 46.8 km stormwater pipe network comprising 1480 conduits, 1478 nodes, and five independent outfalls. Study focus The structural complexity of urban drainage networks makes it difficult to balance simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. This study proposes a fractal-based simplification framework for urban stormwater drainage networks to reduce model complexity while preserving the dominant hydraulic response. The framework was applied to the Sandringham stormwater network to evaluate staged reduction criteria and the hydraulic fidelity of the simplified models to the detailed SWMM numerical baseline. New hydrological insights At the intermediate reduction level, simulation time decreased by 52.5%–57.6%, while the maximum absolute errors in outlet peak flow and total outflow volume across six rainfall scenarios were 5.28% and 8.55%, respectively. More aggressive simplification produced non-monotonic responses and larger local discrepancies. These results indicate that fractal characteristics can support structurally interpretable network reduction, but applicability requires evaluation using multiple hydraulic indicators. Without field observations, the comparisons demonstrate agreement with the SWMM baseline rather than predictive accuracy. The framework may support repeated scenario assessment subject to hydraulic-performance constraints.

title: Evolution of water collection, storage, and supply functions and their coupling relationships in the Asian water tower from 2003 to 2023 based on GRACE and multi-source data
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haoying Tang, Gang Liu, Jing He, Huiwu Zhang, Fan Wu, Xiaofei Sun
abstract: Study Region Tibetan Plateau (TP). Study Focus After data validation, this study constructed multi-product ensembles from multiple GRACE terrestrial water storage datasets and multi-source precipitation (P) and evapotranspiration (ET) products. From a functional perspective of the Asian Water Tower, net water input (N), terrestrial water storage change (TWSC), and runoff (R) were used to represent water collection, water storage, and water supply, respectively. Their interannual and seasonal variations and evolving pairwise coupling correlations were systematically analyzed. New Hydrological Insights for the Region During 2003–2023, the Asian Water Tower exhibited stable water collection (Sen’s slope = −0.065 mm yr−1), declining water storage (−0.171 mm yr−1), and enhanced water supply (0.211 mm yr−1). Spatially, water collection weakened in southern monsoon basins but increased slightly in eastern basins, while water storage declined consistently across most basins. Seasonally, the wet season contributed 98.1% of annual water collection and 94.7% of annual water supply, whereas the dry season experienced persistent storage loss (mean TWSC = −8.553 mm). Functional coupling showed pronounced seasonal differences: N–R coupling was strong in the wet season but decoupled in the dry season, indicating that dry-season runoff depended on antecedent water storage release rather than concurrent precipitation. Three change-point tests consistently identified significant shifts during 2008–2018, with the densest concentration around 2015; this transition was especially evident in 3- and 5-year windows.

title: Coupling hydrological simulation and deep learning for real-time flood defense in mountainous cities: A case study of the June 18, 2023 extreme flood in Guiyang Penshuichi
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jiayang Wang, Liangyu Pan, Xiaoling Tang, Rui Wang, Ning Liu
abstract: Study region This study focuses on Penshuichi Metro Station in Guiyang, southwestern China, where steep slopes and a low-lying urban center promote rapid runoff concentration and water accumulation. Study focus A framework coupling hydrological simulation and deep learning was developed for real-time inundation forecasting and graded flood defense. The Xinanjiang model generated 5000 rainfall–inundation scenarios incorporating rainfall, terrain, runoff concentration, and drainage variability. A Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network with Multi-Head Attention was trained to forecast entrance water depth 10–90 min ahead. The forecasts were combined with inundation duration and pedestrian stability to quantify personnel risk and guide barrier selection. At the 10-min lead time, the model achieved a Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.991 and a Mean Absolute Error of 0.012 m; its efficiency remained 0.905 at 90 min, outperforming five benchmarks. New hydrological insights for the region Reconstruction of the June 18 flood revealed an approximately one-hour lag between peak rainfall and peak inundation risk due to rainfall accumulation, slope-driven runoff concentration, and limited drainage capacity. During this delayed response, the personnel risk coefficient continued to rise and ultimately reached 0.943. Scenario analysis further showed that increasing barrier height progressively reduced risk, with a 1.00-m barrier lowering the peak coefficient to 0.150. These findings highlight the value of water-depth forecasting, timely warnings, and early graded-barrier deployment in mountainous cities.

title: Stable isotope variability in drip water and its implications for speleothem-based Indian Summer Monsoon reconstruction
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Kalyani Panchamwar, Naveen Gandhi, Amzad H. Laskar, Piyush Ahire, M.G. Yadava
abstract: Study region Dandak Cave, located in the Core Monsoon Zone of India. Study focus Understanding the transfer of isotopic composition from precipitation through the karst system to cave drip water is essential for interpreting speleothem-based reconstructions of the Indian Summer Monsoon. Drip water was monitored at three sites in Dandak Cave between 2004 and 2006, with measurements of δ18O, δ13C, and drip rate conducted to investigate the hydrological and geochemical controls on drip water isotopic composition. The observed drip-water δ18O was compared with precipitation δ18O estimates from a Rayleigh box model and an isotope-enabled general circulation model ensemble. New hydrological insights for the region Drip water δ18O displayed a seasonal cycle, with lower (higher) values during the monsoon (non-monsoon) months, consistent with the seasonal evolution of the estimated precipitation δ18O. The relatively small amplitude of drip water δ18O compared to that of precipitation suggests attenuation of event-scale variability within the soil–epikarst. Although the three monitoring sites differed in mean drip rate and drip rate variability, their seasonal mean δ18O values varied by only 0.1–0.2‰, indicating that they record a similar integrated seasonal signal. δ13C varied among sites, reflecting the combined influence of drip hydrology, carbon sources, and cave processes. δ13C and radiocarbon analyses yielded limestone-derived carbon contributions of 26 ± 3% and 24 ± 4%, respectively, indicating substantial host-rock carbon input.

title: Agricultural flash drought risk assessment under climate change based on crop growth stages
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Wei Yanqi, Zhou Yuliang, Jin Juliang, Li Haichao, Ming Bo, Wang Zongzhi, Cui Yi, Jin Tao, Zhou Ping
abstract: Study region Bengbu City, located in the middle reaches of the Huai River Basin, China. Study focus Flash droughts develop rapidly and pose serious threats to agricultural production. However, conventional drought indices based on fixed temporal scales are often insufficient to capture crop water supply–demand dynamics during different growth stages. This study proposed a crop-growth-process-based framework for agricultural flash drought (AFD) risk assessment by integrating DSSAT-CERES-Maize simulations, BCC-CSM2-MR climate projections, and growth-stage-specific water deficit identification. The framework was used to quantify AFD duration, severity, joint occurrence risk, and yield impacts under historical and future climate scenarios. New hydrological insights (1) Historical AFD events showed evident stage-dependent variation, with a mean annual cumulative severity of 9.54 (dimensionless, summed across drought-affected DITs) during 1960–2019 and the highest occurrence in the milking stage (S4). Under SSP5–8.5, AFD duration during S3 decreased by 8.33%, while severity increased by 3.44% around 2080. (2) Yield losses differed markedly among AFD types, and events involving the reproductive stages (S3 and S4) produced the highest yield-loss risk, with historical reductions of 13.98%-39.80% and future maximum reductions exceeding 80% under SSP5–8.5. (3) Pathway analysis identified maximum temperature (Tmax) as the main climatic driver of yield reduction, with the duration of S3 and S4 acting as key mediating variables.

title: Temperature trends in Norwegian rivers from 1990 to 2025 are strongly amplified by latitude
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jan-Erik Thrane, Tor Erik Eriksen, Heleen de Wit, James Edward Sample, Leah A. Jackson-Blake
abstract: Study region Mainland Norway Study focus Based on measured water temperatures from 73 Norwegian rivers in near natural catchments from 58°N to 70°N, we analyzed warming trends from 1990 to 2025 and assessed seasonal and latitudinal variation in warming rates using linear mixed effect modelling. Furthermore, we assessed the coupling between river and air temperature trends, and changes in the likelihood of high-temperature events potentially stressful to cold-water adapted salmonids. New hydrological insight for the region River temperatures increased significantly in all months except December–February, with the strongest warming in June and July (0.60 and 0.52°C decade⁻¹). Warming was strongly amplified at higher latitudes in July, August, and September, consistent with Arctic amplification. For example, estimated July warming rates at 70°N (0.72°C decade⁻¹) were more than twice those at 58°N (0.32°C decade⁻¹), equivalent to 2.5°C and 1.1°C of warming over the 35-year period, respectively. Mean summer (June–September) Sen's slopes for water temperature (0.43°C decade⁻¹) were comparable to those for catchment air temperature (0.40°C decade⁻¹), indicating broad thermal coupling, though water and air temperature trends at individual sites were not correlated, suggesting local modulating factors. The probability of high-temperature events more than doubled across the dataset, increasing from ~20% to ~50% at 58°N between 1990 and 2025. The accelerating thermal change in northern rivers has significant implications for cold-water species and freshwater ecosystems.

title: Runoff prediction based on deep learning and interpretability on covariant relationship in the Yarlung Zangbo River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xingtong Chen, Dingzhi Peng, Yuwei Gong, Tao Wang, Yunqing Xuan
abstract: Study region Yarlung Zangbo River Basin (YZRB). Study focus Site-specific LSTM models were developed to predict daily runoff in the YZRB using precipitation, air temperature, and relative humidity. SHAP attributions were compared across four seasons and between flood and non-flood periods to examine how the contributions of the same meteorological variables vary across stations and periods. New hydrological insights At all five stations, precipitation and relative humidity had larger mean absolute SHAP values during the flood season than the non-flood season. Temperature showed the opposite pattern at four stations, whereas Lhasa had larger temperature attributions during the flood season. At Lhasa, higher flood-season temperatures tended to have negative temperature SHAP values, while lower temperatures tended to have positive values. These differences show that temperature attributions cannot be interpreted uniformly across the YZRB and support examining runoff predictions by station and period. The attributions describe statistical associations learned by the models; possible links to meltwater supply and evapotranspiration require independent verification.

title: Integrating waterborne GPR and group-aware machine learning to resolve lakebed hydrostratigraphy and potential groundwater–lake connectivity for Lake Vadkerti, Hungary
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Diaa Sheishah, Enas Abdelsamei, Ahmed Mohsen, Viktória Blanka Végi, Péter Kozák, Károly Fiala, Ahmed M. Ali, Ferenc Kovács, Izabella Babcsányi, György Sipos
abstract: Study Region: Lake Vadkerti is a climate-stressed shallow alkaline lake in the Danube–Tisza Interfluve, Hungary, where lakebed controls on groundwater–lake connectivity remain poorly constrained. Study Focus: We integrated 22 waterborne 200 MHz GPR profiles, 16 upper-lakebed sediment samples, seven interpreted reflectors, processing-aware amplitude analysis and sample-group-aware machine learning to characterize hydrostratigraphic heterogeneity and screen candidate exchange zones. The shallowest consistently traceable sub-lakebed reflector was selected because it provided the closest GPR correspondence to the 20–30 cm sediment samples. Twelve profile-supported sites formed independent validation groups. Five classifiers were evaluated across 48 class-complete leave-three-groups-out combinations. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Processed amplitude at the shallowest traceable sub-lakebed reflector distinguished Mud from Sand and Transitional sediment. Among five classifiers, tree ensembles performed best. At the 5 m along-profile support, Extra Trees achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.736 ± 0.201; Mud was consistently identified, whereas recall was lower for Sand and Transitional sediment. Incorrect classifications had greater uncertainty than correct classifications. Combining reflector discontinuity, thin-mud support, model support for Sand and proximity to Sand samples identified profile-constrained candidate exchange zones, mainly along the southern and eastern margins and locally along the western margin. These zones are priorities for hydrological testing, not evidence of measured seepage, direction or flux. The workflow is transferable to shallow lakes worldwide where lakebed observations are sparse.

title: Spatiotemporal trend and variability of precipitation across Iran: A multi-stage homogeneity adjustment and autocorrelation-corrected framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Hossein Masoomi, Bahram Saghafian, Meysam Salarijazi, Majid Dehghani
abstract: Study Region Iran, an arid and semi-arid country, was assessed using precipitation records from 75 synoptic stations over 1979–2019; 75 stations met the predefined retention criteria after homogeneity screening. Study Focus The study provides an integrated assessment of precipitation homogeneity, serial dependence, variability, and trends at annual and seasonal scales. Four homogeneity tests were combined with lag-1 autocorrelation testing. The Mann–Kendall (MK) test was used for series without significant autocorrelation, and trend-free pre-whitening MK (TFPW-MK) for autocorrelated series. Sen's slope quantified trend magnitude, and the coefficient of variation (CV) characterized relative variability. Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment was additionally applied separately to the 75 station-level tests within each temporal scale. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Annual precipitation CV averaged 35.3% (15.4–73.3%) and increased from northwest to southeast. Summer had the highest mean CV (222%). At the nominal 5% level, 12 stations showed significant annual trends (9 decreases, 3 increases), while winter had 14 significant decreases. Mean Sen's slopes were −0.48 mm/year annually and −0.78 mm/year in winter. Significant winter decreases were concentrated in southwestern and central Iran. After FDR adjustment, only two station–time-scale trends remained significant, indicating more limited evidence for widespread statistical significance under multiple testing. These results provide a structured basis for regional water-resource and climate-adaptation planning.

title: Assessment of whether tree-ring hydroclimate reconstructions are useful for characterising extreme drought in East Anglia (England)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jane Thurgood, Timothy Osborn
abstract: Region East of England Focus Paleoclimate proxies are used here to characterise extreme droughts including those corresponding to a 1:500-year return period. We evaluate four tree-ring hydroclimate (precipitation or drought index) reconstructions representing similar geographical regions across East Anglia and Southern England. New hydrological insights The overall agreement between the reconstructions is found to be weak or moderate, partly due to their differing seasons, regions and methodological differences. Therefore, we used all four reconstructions to quantify the sensitivity of drought to choice of reconstruction. We show that reconstruction errors influence the quantification of extreme dry seasons (here spring/summer seasons) and must be accounted for in the analysis especially if the reconstruction was calibrated using regression. We demonstrate that modelling the reconstruction error as a random term, as well as z-score standardisation, enables the reconstruction to reproduce instrumental climate behaviour such as the rank-order drought curve. Using these approaches, we quantify the occurrence probability of high threshold extreme events and evaluate the differences in severity of droughts across the reconstruction datasets (which vary in length from 800 to 1112 years). We conclude that tree-ring reconstructions can provide valuable long term hydroclimate insight, but they should be used with caution when investigating extreme droughts due to inter-reconstruction differences and the need to represent reconstruction errors.

title: The Southern rain–snow transition zone as a major source of uncertainty in precipitation-phase partitioning across China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Weiping Wang, Yongqiang Liu, Yan Qin, Qiudong Zhao, Yaqian Li, Haojuan Li, Yongnan Liu
abstract: Study region China, encompassing strong climatic and topographic gradients from the cold and arid northwestern and high-elevation regions to the warm and humid rain–snow transition zones of southern China. Study focus Reliable rain–snow partitioning is essential for representing snowfall accumulation, snowmelt, and precipitation inputs in hydrological modelling. Using surface observations from 1951 to 1979, we evaluated 12 conventional (Ta_0, Td_0, Tw_1, Trh, Dai08, KS98, Jenn_Uni, Jenn_Bi, Jenn_Tri, Ding14, NaquSig, and Yamazaki) threshold-based methods and six machine-learning models (RF, XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, ExtraTrees, and HGB) across China using the snowfall F1 score (F1_snow), Heidke skill score (HSS), overall accuracy (OA) and macro-averaged F1 score (F1_macro). Their sensitivities to temperature (−10–10 °C), relative humidity (0–1), and elevation (0–5 km) were examined. Station-network thinning experiments were further conducted to assess sensitivity to uneven observational coverage, and model transferability was independently evaluated against NOAA Global Surface Summary of the Day (GSOD) observations for 1980–2024 without retraining. New hydrological insights for the region Differences among precipitation-phase methods were expressed much more clearly in snowfall identification than in overall accuracy. Nationwide F1_snow ranged from 0.837 to 0.891 for conventional methods and 0.921–0.929 for machine-learning models, whereas OA remained within 0.970–0.982 and 0.987–0.989, respectively. The largest classification uncertainty occurred within the major rain–snow transition belt at approximately 22°–32°N and under three critical environmental conditions: temperatures of 0–5 °C, RH < 0.4, and elevations of 2500–4000 m. Under these conditions, machine-learning models achieved F1_snow values of 0.587–0.619, 0.832–0.890, and 0.940–0.952, compared with conventional-method means of 0.421, 0.753, and 0.750, respectively. Station thinning produced mostly < ±2% bias in F1_snow, indicating limited sensitivity of the main spatial patterns to uneven station coverage. When transferred directly to GSOD for 1980–2024, the machine-learning models retained F1_snow values of approximately 0.90, demonstrating useful cross-period and cross-dataset applicability, although their relative advantage over conventional methods was reduced.

title: Adaptive regional water allocation strategies in the Republic of Korea: A focus on drought damage sensitivity
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Hoyoung Cha, Seo Yun Lee, Hyochan Kim, Jongjin Baik, Do Guen Yoo, Carlo De Michele, Tae-Woong Kim, Changhyun Jun
abstract: Study region Geum, Yeongsan, and Seomjin River basins (Republic of Korea). Study focus The research develops a framework for allocating water usage during severe drought or supply-constrained conditions by assigning differentiated reduction ratios to domestic, agricultural, and industrial sectors. The framework is built on drought damage sensitivity, using relative drought damage estimates to determine specific water usage reductions that optimize equity and efficiency. New hydrological insights from the region The study reveals regional and sectoral differences in drought damage sensitivity, with modeled drought damage being least sensitive to changes in domestic water usage and most sensitive to changes in industrial water usage. The proposed scenarios allow maximum reductions of 30%, 50%, and 60% in domestic, agricultural, and industrial water usage, respectively, under severe drought conditions. These findings suggest that region-specific water supply adjustment criteria could support more adaptive drought responses than uniform national guidelines that do not account for regional characteristics.

title: Asymmetric generalization and failure mechanisms in zero-shot alpine runoff simulation: The role of hydrological memory heterogeneity
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jiahui Wang, Kun Xing, Sihai Liu
abstract: Study region Alpine headwaters of the Kaidu River (central Tianshan) and Keriya River (northern Kunlun), Northwest China. Study focus We evaluated seasonal performance and bidirectional zero-shot transfer of seven data-driven models and an ensemble with validation-optimized weights for current-month runoff simulation. Models used concurrent and antecedent hydrometeorological and land surface inputs without forecast lead time. Analyses covered seasonal diagnostics, a monthly climatology benchmark, lookback tests (3, 6, 9 months) for four deep learning models, and controlled comparisons of mean squared error (MSE) with hydrology-aware loss. Transfer used fixed source-basin configurations. New hydrological insights for the region Input windows varied by basin and architecture: all four Keriya networks favored 3 months versus 6–9 in Kaidu. These preferences reflect input sensitivity, not measured storage timescales. In Keriya, monthly climatology nearly matched the ensemble in Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE: 0.791 versus 0.804). Negative NSE in small, low-variance snowmelt and baseflow subsets coincided with modest absolute errors. Hydrology-aware loss improved NSE for Kaidu LSTM and DLinear but reduced it in six other comparisons. Transfer exposed another limitation: ensemble NSE was 0.722 from Keriya to Kaidu and 0.357 in reverse. During transfer to Kaidu, XGBoost exceeded the ensemble (NSE = 0.750), whereas TCN retained high correlation (r = 0.930) but exaggerated simulated variability (ratio = 2.06; NSE = −0.417).

title: Spatiotemporally adaptive gaussian mixture modelling (ST-GMM) framework for SAR-based long-term surface water monitoring
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Milon Bokshi, Drubo Paul, Md. Munir Mahmud, Md. Nurul Islam
abstract: Study region Bangladesh, located within the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna (GBM) delta, is one of the world’s largest and most hydrologically dynamic monsoonal floodplain systems. Study focus This study develops a Spatiotemporally Adaptive Gaussian Mixture Model (ST-GMM) framework for monthly surface water monitoring using Sentinel-1 SAR imagery. The framework dynamically models land–water backscatter distributions to derive spatially and temporally adaptive classification thresholds under varying hydro-climatic conditions. New hydrological insights for the region The proposed ST-GMM framework provides an adaptive, training-independent approach for nationwide surface water monitoring by combining Sentinel-1 SAR observations with district-specific probabilistic threshold estimation, enabling reliable mapping under persistent monsoon cloud cover. Validation against 4310 verified 2025 ground-truth observations yielded an overall accuracy of 92.55% (κ = 0.85; balanced accuracy = 91.2%). In a separate optical cross-sensor benchmark on a common 10 m grid, ST-GMM achieved 97.9%-pixel agreement and IoU = 0.896 with Sentinel-2 NDWI, while comparison with Otsu showed a statistically significant performance difference (McNemar χ² = 142.76, p < 0.001). Application of the framework revealed a pronounced seasonal hydrological cycle, with surface water extent expanding from approximately 15,900 km² during the dry season to 37,500 km² during the monsoon. Despite substantial inter-annual fluctuations, no significant long-term national trend was detected during 2015–2025. The framework therefore provides a scalable methodology for long-term hydrological monitoring in cloud-prone monsoonal and deltaic environments.

title: A two‑stage deep learning framework for multi‑source precipitation fusion to optimize seasonal, extreme and precipitation event estimation
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shixuan Li, Wei Qi, Yanpeng Cai
abstract: Study region The study is conducted over mainland China (18.0–53.5°N, 73.5–135.0°E), with a focus on the nine major river basins across China. Study focus A two-stage deep learning multi-source precipitation fusion framework (TDL-MSP) is developed to mitigate systematic biases in existing products and overcome limitations of conventional single-stage regression merging. The framework integrates six widely used precipitation datasets and four near-surface meteorological variables from CMFD 2.0, generating daily 0.25° gridded precipitation across China for 2001–2022. It adopts a classification-regression architecture: UNet identifies precipitation events in the first stage, and SegNeXt performs quantitative rainfall regression in the second. Model performance is evaluated against original products using the CHM_PRE ground dataset as reference. New hydrological insights for the region The TDL‑MSP framework outperforms all original multi‑source precipitation products across China. The optimal SegNeXt_11x model achieves a Pearson correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.817, Kling‑Gupta efficiency (KGE) of 0.608, and root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.364 mm/day. Specifically, its CC is 0.267 higher than ERA5, KGE is 0.388 higher than MSWEP, and RMSE is reduced by up to 1.538 mm/day. Overall, the UNet‑SegNeXt framework improves seasonal and extreme precipitation estimation, exhibiting promising prospects for next‑generation high‑resolution gridded precipitation datasets.

title: Improving stochastic dynamic programming for reservoir operation using drought severity and the copula function
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Mohamad Haytham Klaho, Ramtin Moeini, Mohammadali Alijanian
abstract: Study region Marun Dam reservoir, southwestern Iran. Study focus Reservoir operation under droughts remains challenging because traditional Stochastic Dynamic Programming (SDP) estimates inflow transition probabilities using Markov chains, without explicitly considering drought severity or nonlinear dependence between hydrological variables. This study reformulates the transition probability matrix (TPM) of SDP by integrating inflow and drought severity into the TPM using copula functions, specifying more realistic reservoir operation policies under drought conditions. To achieve this, the Copula-Hybrid Drought Index (CHDI) is proposed, based on the predicted rainfall projections acquired from the results of modeled climate-change simulations under the SSP3.70 scenario. New hydrological insights for the region Historical analysis of Marun Dam reservoir shows that the implementation of the proposed SDP, integrating inflow with the drought severity for the previous period using copula-based transition probabilities (TPMC), yields greater sustainability and conserves more water in the reservoir for future ‎droughts‎, compared with the SDP method using the conventional Markov-chain transition probabilities (TPMM). However, this improvement comes with a higher objective ‎function value. The proposed approach is also examined using three suggested scenarios, named S1, S2, and S3, to update the operation policies under droughts, and shows a reduction in drought severity and duration of drought spells by reserving more water for the drought periods, albeit at the cost of lower sustainability and objective function values. This research confirms that incorporating inflow with drought through TPMs enhances the robustness of reservoir operation policies under drought conditions, particularly for arid and semi-arid regions facing increasing climate variability.

title: GRACE-derived groundwater storage anomalies and their lagged responses to climatic and anthropogenic drivers in the West Liaohe River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xuechun Li, Gaoxu Wang, Daiyuan Li, Liyu Quan, Yongxiang Wu, Rui Zou, Siyang Feng
abstract: Study region The West Liaohe River Basin (WLRB), northern China, is a semi-arid mountain–plain system linking mountainous recharge zones to a heavily irrigated downstream plain. Study focus Using GRACE/GRACE-FO and climatic, ecological, and water-use data (2002–2024), we assessed groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) trends, lagged associations with environmental factors, and relative predictor importance using correlation, Bayesian lag analysis, and Random Forest models. New hydrological insights for the region GWSA declined significantly across the WLRB, plain, and mountainous areas at −5.94, −5.96, and −5.91 mm yr⁻¹, respectively (p < 0.001).
