Depletion intensified after 2011 and persisted after 2018 despite increasing precipitation, indicating that wetter conditions did not reverse groundwater losses. Associations with climatic and ecological variables were concentrated mainly within 1–6 months, with stronger and more spatially coherent soil moisture associations in the plain. The negative soil moisture–GWSA relationship may partly reflect the subtraction of soil moisture from GRACE-derived terrestrial water storage. Precipitation associations were weak, consistent with indirect rather than immediate recharge responses. Random Forest analysis identified irrigated area as the strongest negative predictor in the whole basin and plain, whereas groundwater withdrawal showed the strongest negative association in mountainous areas. These contrasts highlight the need for coordinated, regionally differentiated groundwater management.

title: Implications of land-use and climate change for meeting environmental flows and water quality targets in a groundwater-dominated watershed
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Dogil Lee, Wendy Graham, Rob de Rooij, Nathan Reaver, David Kaplan
abstract: Study region This study was conducted in the Santa Fe River Basin (SFRB), a tributary basin of the Suwannee River in the Southeastern USA. The SFRB is an agriculturally important, groundwater-dominated watershed, which overlies the Upper Floridan Aquifer (UFA). Its mixed agricultural, forested and urban land uses, strong surface-groundwater interactions, and sensitive spring and river ecosystems make it ideal for understanding important water-resource responses across the broader region. Study focus This work addressed two specific research questions: How do climate and land-use change affect groundwater recharge, streamflow and nitrate loads in the SFRB; and under what future conditions can existing regulations for minimum streamflow and nitrate loading be achieved? We addressed these questions using SWAT-MODFLOW to simulate five land-use scenarios under historical climate and future climates representing extreme wet and dry projections. New hydrologic insights for the region Climate was the dominant driver of changes in groundwater recharge and streamflow, whereas land use had the greatest influence on nitrate loads. All land-use scenarios met minimum streamflow requirements under historical and wet future climates. However, no land-use scenarios met minimum flows for the RCP8.5 dry future, and only the pre-development scenario met minimum flows for the RCP4.5 dry future. The 65% nitrate load reduction required to meet current nutrient regulations was achieved only under the pre-development scenario and, even then, not under the RCP8.5 wet future.

title: Attribution of the most severe decadal drought in Southwest China during 2003–2014 and its impact on vegetation productivity
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Lu Gao, Tianjiao Ma, Tiantian Yu, Zhikai Wang, Qingyu Cai, Xu Xue, Kexu Zhu, Xinfeng Wu, Yehong Luo, Changhao Wu, Wen Chen
abstract: Study region Southwest China (SWC). Study focus This study identifies the decadal drought background of frequent droughts in SWC since the early 21st century, quantifies the roles of precipitation and potential evapotranspiration (PET), and evaluates vegetation impacts. Monthly precipitation and PET during 1961–2023 were used to calculate the 12-month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI12). An objective change-point test, quantitative attribution, moisture budget analysis, and vegetation productivity indicators were combined. New hydrological insights for the region The most severe decadal drought in SWC occurred during 2003–2014, characterized by a 12-month cumulative precipitation deficit of 49.34 mm and an increase in PET of 32.18 mm. Precipitation decline was the dominant contributor to the decadal drought, accounting for 68.6% of its intensity, while enhanced PET further intensified drought severity, with residual PET and precipitation-associated PET contributing 20.9% and 10.5%, respectively. About 70% of the precipitation deficit occurred during the wet season. Moisture budget analysis reveals a clear hydrological pathway linking wet-season precipitation decline to atmospheric circulation. Anomalous descending motion weakened vertical moisture transport, with dynamic vertical moisture advection reaching −0.35 mm day⁻¹, thereby enhancing moisture divergence and reducing wet-season precipitation over SWC. The persistent water deficit was accompanied by a nonlinear reduction in vegetation productivity under moderate-to-extreme drought conditions, with the strongest impacts in Yunnan, Guangxi, and the Sichuan–Chongqing–Guizhou border region.

title: Quantifying evaporation from a large reservoir in the Yellow River Basin: Based on stable isotope methods
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiaoyu Qi, Guofeng Zhu, Rui Li, Zhijie Zheng, Ziwen Liu, Enwei Huang, Yuhao Wang, Yinying Jiao, Yani Gun, Jiangwei Yang
abstract: Study region Liujiaxia Reservoir, a large and highly regulated reservoir in the upper Yellow River Basin, northwestern China. Study focus Stable water isotopes in precipitation and reservoir surface water were monitored from August 2021 to July 2023. Local evaporation lines (LELs) were used to characterize evaporative enrichment, and the Craig-Gordon isotope mass-balance framework implemented in Hydrocalculator was used to quantify evaporation over inflow ratios (E/I) and their seasonal variability. New hydrological insights for the region Reservoir water became progressively enriched in δ¹⁸O and δ²H from the inlet toward the outlet and open water sections, indicating cumulative evaporative fractionation. The LEL slope decreased from 8.79 in winter to 3.46 in summer, while isotope derived E/I ranged from 0.41% to 7.82%, with the largest relative evaporation losses occurring in summer. Variability in inlet and outlet water isotopic composition dominated the propagated uncertainty in E/I, emphasizing the importance of representative isotope sampling for constraining evaporation estimates. Stable isotope mass balance therefore provides a useful means of identifying periods of relatively high evaporation loss in large regulated reservoirs and can complement conventional water balance monitoring, although E/I should be interpreted as a relative evaporation loss indicator rather than an absolute evaporation flux.

title: Unveiling the synergistic effect of water taxation and virtual water policies on sustainable development: A factorial input-output driven CGE method
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): S.Z. Li, Y.P. Li, G.H. Huang, X.N. Guo, S.M. Peng, J.T. Liu, P.P. Wang
abstract: Study region The Inner-Shaan-Ning is located in the upper reaches of the Yellow River Basin (China), a water-scarce region associated with intensive agriculture, food, tobacco, and chemical industries. Study focus Water scarcity and water pollution are increasingly restricting socioeconomic and environmental sustainability in water-scarce regions. However, the synergistic effects between water taxation and virtual water policies remain inadequately quantified. This study develops a factorial input-output driven computable general equilibrium (CGE) method (abbreviated as FIOC) to identify the key driving sectors, simulate multi-scenario environmental and economic responses, and quantify individual and interactive effects of multiple policies on sustainable development goal (SDG) performance. New hydrological insights for the region Export demand is the dominant driver of both virtual water consumption and virtual wastewater discharge, in which agriculture, food, tobacco and chemical industries are the main export sectors. There are obvious trade-offs with a single policy tool: taxation can save water, but it may increase wastewater discharge; while the virtual water policy is highly dependent on its specifically targeted industries. Results disclose that a combination policy of the moderate water tax and the lowest import price (i.e. TV28 scenario) is more conducive to achieving the SDG; compared with implementing the moderate water tax policy alone, the combined policy (i.e. TV28) can reduce 0.09% of GDP loss, save 5.8% of water usage, and reduce 8.09% of wastewater discharge.

title: Regional groundwater salinization and hydrostratigraphic heterogeneity in the Indus Delta, Pakistan: An integrated hydrochemical, isotopic, and geophysical assessment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ghulam Murtaza Arain, Nazia Sattar, Nabeel Ali Khan, Sumaira Khatoon, Junaid Jabbar Dahar, Ibrahim Zia
abstract: Study Region The arid Indus Delta coastal aquifer in Sindh, Pakistan, faces reduced freshwater inflows, intensive groundwater abstraction, and seawater intrusion (SWI). Study Focus We assessed salinization through hydrochemical, isotopic, geophysical, and quantitative mixing analyses. Groundwater from multilevel wells (6–18 m) was analyzed for major ions, δ¹ ⁸O, δ²H, δ¹ ³C–DIC, δ³ ⁴S–SO₄²⁻, δ¹ ⁸O–SO₄²⁻, and tritium (³H), complemented by electrical resistivity sounding (ERS). The Seawater Mixing Index (SMI) and chloride-based seawater fractions assessed marine influence, providing the first integrated regional dataset. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Groundwater showed isotopic ranges (δ¹⁸O: −11.65 to +1.00‰; δ²H: −86.29 to +58.59‰). Correlations linked δ¹ ⁸O and EC (r = 0.79), Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ and EC (r = 0.98), SMI and EC (r² = 0.999), and chloride-based seawater fraction and SMI (r² = 0.999). Coastal–inland patterns indicate marine mixing modified by evaporation, ion exchange, and water–rock interaction. δ¹ ³C–DIC (−18.88 to −1.30‰) indicates heterogeneous carbon evolution without uniquely identifying sources. Sulfate isotopes, supported locally by low DO, negative ORP, and detectable sulfide, are consistent with localized sulfate reduction. Tritium (0.76–4.55 TU) indicates modern recharge but cannot constrain groundwater age or intrusion timing. ERS reveals heterogeneous multilayered aquifers with conductive formations to approximately 150–250 m, consistent with shallow salinity patterns. SWI is the primary regional salinization influence, with secondary geochemical modification, supporting depth-specific abstraction and long-term monitoring.

title: Groundwater–surface water interactions in major rivers of Henan Province, China: Insights from stable hydrogen and oxygen isotopes and hydrochemistry
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jiju Guo, Wengeng Cao, Deng Pan, Xiangzhi Li, Yu Ren, Chongsheng Lu, Yanyan Wang, Tian Nan, Zeyan Li, Xiaoyue Sun
abstract: Study region Ten major rivers spanning four drainage basins (Hai, Yellow, Huai, and Yangtze) across the alluvial plains of Henan Province, China. Study focus Groundwater–surface water (GW–SW) exchange dynamics across these anthropogenically disturbed river systems were systematically investigated using an integrated approach combining hydrochemical analysis, dual stable isotopes (δD and δ18O), and end-member mixing analysis. The study aimed to quantitatively determine the direction and mixing fraction of GW–SW exchange across different river reaches. New hydrological insights for the region Three distinct exchange regimes were identified: (i) gaining streams (Luo, Yi, Guo, and mainstem Huai Rivers), where groundwater contributes 21.2%–94.1% of river discharge, predominantly in deeply incised mountain valleys and piedmont zones; (ii) losing streams (Yellow and Ying Rivers), with river-to-aquifer recharge proportions of 16.9%–87.8%; and (iii) alternating gaining–losing systems (Wei, Bai, Ru, and Sha Rivers), where exchange direction reverses spatially between reaches or cross-sectionally between banks. The Wei River exemplifies the latter asymmetry, with west-bank groundwater discharge (8.7%–40.8%) contrasting sharply with east-bank river leakage (27.0%–79.5%). Considered alongside previous studies, our results suggest that groundwater abstraction, perched river conditions associated with channel-bed aggradation, and hydraulic structures may contribute to the increasing spatial complexity across the plains. These findings establish a quantitative framework for GW–SW exchange across Henan's major rivers, providing a scientific basis for precise water resource assessment and sustainable allocation strategies.

title: Propagation mechanisms and triggering probabilities of meteorological to hydrological drought in the Poyang Lake Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Chenyang Liu, Wei Yang, Haifei Liu, Shan He, Jizeng Du
abstract: Study region The middle Yangtze River-Poyang Lake-catchment, China. Study focus This study explores the drought propagation process within the river-lake system of the Poyang Lake basin from 1988 to 2017. Using runs theory, we identified the duration and intensity of meteorological and hydrological droughts. The propagation time from meteorological to hydrological drought was determined through the Pearson maximum correlation coefficient. Using Copula functions, we calculated the probability of meteorological drought triggering river hydrological drought and further analyzed the likelihood of river droughts inducing lake droughts. Furthermore, potential teleconnection factors influencing meteorological drought were explored using methods such as wavelet analysis. New hydrological insights for the region The basin’s meteorological wet-dry state followed a ‘normal-drought-wet’ pattern, entered a drought phase in 2003. While meteorological droughts across the basin averaged 1–2 months, hydrological droughts persisted over 3 months. The Xiushui River experienced significantly more severe hydrological droughts. During drought transmission, as meteorological drought intensifies across the sub-basins, the probability of river drought also increases, Seasonally, the transmission probability was relatively higher during winter-spring. For river-lake transmission Under extreme drought conditions, Xiushui River corresponds to the highest probability of lake drought, Moreover, the probability of lake drought increases as the severity of joint drought across multiple rivers intensifies. Furthermore, compared to AO and PDO, the SOI shows a higher correlation with variations in regional meteorological drought.

title: Snow insulation effect exceeds snowmelt in runoff regulation: Evidence from Changbai Mountain Region, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zan Li, Xiaofeng Li, Yanlin Wei, Yingjie Shi, Yijing Li
abstract: Study region Changbai Mountain region (CMR), Northeast China, on the southern fringe of the cryosphere, is a high-precipitation area with prolonged snow cover, where runoff efficiency is particularly high during the snowmelt period. Study focus Using an enhanced Snowmelt Runoff Model (SRM) that integrates ground freeze-thaw indices (GFI/GTI) with dynamic model runoff coefficients (RC), we constructed three scenarios across five watersheds for 1990–2017: real conditions (S₀), no-snowmelt (S₁), and no-snowpack (S₂), to address the still poorly quantified relative contributions of snowpack water storage and insulation effects to runoff. New hydrological insights In the CMR, neglecting snowmelt reduced annual runoff by 2.72%, whereas omitting SIE increased annual runoff by 5.93%. Critically, SIE’s suppression effect (-5.93%) exceeded snowmelt’s positive input (+2.72%) by over twofold, demonstrating its dominant role in regulating runoff. Dramatic monthly amplifications occurred when SIE was omitted (30.05% increase in March and 23.76% in April), while the largest snowmelt-induced runoff reduction (18.46%) occurred in April under the no-snowmelt scenario. Mechanistically, SIE suppressed ground freezing through a 6.3% reduction in the GFI while enhancing thawing via a 14.9% increase in the GTI, thereby improving soil permeability and reducing runoff efficiency. These findings in CMR highlight the previously underestimated role of SIE in hydrological models and suggest that reduced snow cover may amplify runoff under future warming in seasonal frozen regions, requiring revised water resource management strategies.

title: Hydraulic behavior and solute redistribution of saline-alkali black soil: Implications for stormwater source control
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Liangyao Chen, Junchao He, Xiaoduo Hu, Xiang Liu, Zhaohuan Li, Han Li, Ersong Wang
abstract: Study Region Daqing, northeastern China, has saline-alkali soils, strong evaporation, and shallow groundwater that constrain infiltration-based stormwater source control. Study Focus We examined hydraulic behavior and water and solute redistribution in black soil amended with 0, 0.5, and 2.0% Na2CO3. Saturated hydraulic conductivity (K s ) was measured after 0~4 wetting-drying cycles. Soil water retention was determined by the filter paper method, and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity (K u ) was estimated with the van Genuchten-Mualem model. A complementary column experiment applied sequential rainfall depths of 10, 20, 40, and 70 mm to track soil moisture, electrical conductivity (EC), and gravel layer water EC. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Na2CO3 addition reduced initial Kₛ from 3.31 × 10−6 m/s at 0% to 2.49 × 10−7 and 3.02 × 10−8 m/s at 0.5% and 2.0%. Wetting-drying caused further declines, while estimated Kᵤ remained lower in Na2CO3-amended soils over most of the modeled suction range. During sequential rainfall, the 2.0% treatment accumulated more water near the surface and responded more slowly at depth. EC decreased in the upper 20 cm but increased at 20~40 cm, while gravel layer water EC increased by only 8.9%. Low hydraulic conductivity therefore restricted vertical water transmission and promoted solute accumulation within the soil profile.

title: Substantial erosion of underwater topography in inundated area of large lakes using in situ bathymetry and multi-resource remote sensing on the Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Baojin Qiao, Fangfei Zhu, Jianting Ju, Liping Zhu
abstract: Study region nine large lakes on the Tibetan Plateau. Study focus Lake represents a critical component of water resources on the Tibetan Plateau, little attention has been paid to the evolution of underwater topography in inundated area caused by lake expansion. In this study, we integrated models with in situ bathymetric data and Landsat images with multiple machine learning methods across nine lakes, analyzed the changes in underwater topography since 2000. New hydrological insights for the region Significant topographic changes were observed in all inundated areas since 2000, dominated by erosion with an average erosion depth of 3.34 m. Angdaer Co experienced the maximum average erosion depth (5 m), while Ayakekumu Lake exhibited the minimum (1.93 m). The total erosion volume across the nine lakes reached 2.61 × 109 m3, with Ayakekumu Lake and Aqikekule Lake both recording the largest erosion volumes (5.93 ×108 m3), and Dulishi Lake the smallest (1.16 ×108 m3). Due to the limitation of initial topography, only sediment volume of parts lakes was estimated with 7.65 × 108 m3 and distributed in the deep area, and the largest sediment was Aykekumu (4.6 ×108 m3) and Aqikekule (1.6 ×108 m3). Erosion of underwater topography showed a strong positive correlation with runoff and precipitation. This study highlights significant change of underwater topography in inundated areas driven by lake expansion, offering new insights into the dynamics of lake evolution and sediment processes.

title: Water vapor and energy sources of persistent extreme heavy rainfall related to typhoon over the Huaihe River basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Jingwen Yu, Qingquan Li, Zhiping Wen, Xiaoting Sun, Minghao Wang, Zhiqiang Gong, Yihui Ding, Xinyong Shen
abstract: Study region The Huaihe River Basin (HRB), central and eastern China. Study focus To enhance the regional flood control capacity, the characteristics and mechanism of August persistent extreme heavy rainfall (PEHR) events over the HRB during 1961–2022 were revealed. Typhoons play important roles in sudden water vapor transport and unstable energy growth over the HRB. A cluster analysis based on K-means method of typhoon tracks was performed to assess the potential influence of typhoons on the intensity and spatial distribution of PEHR. The comprehensive understanding of the physical mechanisms underlying PEHR—and their interrelationship with typhoons—can provide a reference for the accuracy of extreme rainfall forecasting. New hydrological insights for the region Under the background of global warming, the uncertainty of PEHR events has increased. Typhoon tracks are directly linked to atmospheric circulation patterns, which in turn create more favorable conditions for typhoons to generate additional water vapor and energy transport pathways toward the HRB, thereby intensifying the regional water cycle. Typhoons with different tracks can alter the boundaries of water vapor budget over the HRB, which can determine whether PEHR events occur along the coast or inland. Additionally, this study quantitatively estimated the intensity-distance ratio threshold of typhoon that could trigger PEHR and the sub-seasonal predictability of PEHR events. The results of this study can provide references for the mechanism of regional water cycle.

title: The structure of the water cycle and recharge mechanisms in the groundwater-influenced Hongjiannao Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiangze Gu, Biao Sun, Xiaohong Shi, Mai Cao, Yi Zheng, Jiaqi Pang, Ruli Kang, Shaoyang Niu, Jianglong Yang, Qi Sun
abstract: Study region Hongjiannao Basin, an arid–semi-arid terminal-lake basin on the southeastern margin of the Mu Us Desert, China. Study focus This study investigates seasonal water-cycle structure, recharge relationships, and hydrochemical evolution in the Hongjiannao Basin. Hydrochemistry, stable isotopes (δ¹⁸O and δ²H), mineral saturation indices, and Bayesian isotope mixing analysis using MixSIAR were integrated to quantify water-source contributions and identify groundwater–river–lake connectivity and the effects of evaporation and seasonal freezing. New hydrological insights for the region Groundwater contributed 76.2%, 95.3%, 88.6%, and 59.1% of river water in April, July, October, and January, respectively, demonstrating its key role in sustaining river water across seasons, although winter estimates were more uncertain. The basin exhibits asymmetric hydrological connectivity, characterized by strong groundwater–river interaction, river-mediated transfer toward the terminal lake, spatially restricted direct groundwater–lake exchange, and strong evaporative modification of lake water. Evaporative concentration, coupled with water–rock interactions, drives pronounced solute enrichment in the terminal lake. During seasonal freezing, isotopic fractionation and solute exclusion at the ice–water interface produce relatively low-salinity ice and solute-enriched under-ice water. Together, these processes show that groundwater recharge, evaporation, and freezing jointly regulate the seasonal hydrological and hydrochemical evolution of this arid terminal-lake system.

title: Rainfall partitioning and contrasting local understory runoff and soil loss responses among three vegetation communities in a karst restoration area
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yuanze Xu, Longshan Zhao, Zijing Yang, Ruyi Zi, Zhen Han, Sheng Li
abstract: Study region Puding County, southwestern China, a karst area characterized by severe rocky desertification and long-term ecological restoration. Study focus Vegetation restoration alters canopy structure and rainfall redistribution, but how these changes relate to localized understory runoff and soil loss remains unclear. We monitored 31 rainfall events in three vegetation communities dominated by Platycladus orientalis, Platycarya strobilacea, and Viburnum dilatatum. Community-scale throughfall, stemflow, and canopy interception were quantified, while runoff and soil loss were monitored in subcanopy and stem-base microplots. Mixed-effects models were used to assess rainfall, microsite, and environmental associations. New hydrological insights for the region Throughfall was the largest rainfall-partitioning component and was highest in P. orientalis (86.21%), although this community did not show the strongest erosion response. P. strobilacea had the greatest runoff and soil loss, with mean soil loss of 28.97 and 61.79 g m⁻² in subcanopy and stem-base microsites, respectively. Gross rainfall showed strong nonlinear associations with runoff and soil loss. Slope and bare-soil cover were positively associated with both responses, whereas saturated hydraulic conductivity was negatively associated. After accounting for gross rainfall, community-level throughfall fraction provided no significant additional explanatory information for subcanopy runoff or soil loss. Because stemflow to individual stem-base microplots was not directly measured, stem-base responses were interpreted as integrated microsite responses.

title: A comprehensive suitability assessment framework for low impact development (LID) incorporating life-cycle carbon benefits: A case study in Wuhan, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Siqi Gong, Jun Zhang, Xiangqian Xiao, Guocai Hao, Jingwen Yu, Jun Xia
abstract: Study region The study area is located in Qingshan District, Wuhan, Hubei Province, China. Study focus Under the combined influences of climate change and rapid urbanization, urban pluvial flooding increasingly threatens infrastructure and public safety. Concurrently, accelerated urban development has intensified carbon-related environmental pressures. Low impact development (LID) emerges as an effective strategy for mitigating urbanization impacts through stormwater control and its carbon mitigation potential. However, existing LID suitability assessments for high-performance scheme design mainly focus on hydrological performance, with limited consideration of carbon processes. In this study, we develop an integrated framework that incorporates life-cycle carbon benefits into LID multi-objective optimization and multi-criteria suitability evaluation. The framework is applied in Wuhan, a national Sponge City pilot, using permeable pavements and bioretention cells as representative measures to derive optimal configurations under different planning objectives. New hydrological insights for the region The results indicate that schemes with higher proportions of permeable pavements achieve better runoff regulation performance. All optimized schemes act as net carbon sinks over the life cycle, and increasing total LID area significantly enhances carbon mitigation, with the reduction up to −26.4 Kt CO₂. Moreover, increasing the proportion of bioretention cells produces pronounced non-linear gains in net carbon reduction. The developed suitability assessment method can effectively balance multiple objectives under varying implementation priorities, contributing to flood management and low-carbon development in Sponge City construction.

title: Remotely sensed annual glacier mass balance in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor during 2000–2020: Widespread mass loss and regional contrasts
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yi Liu, Liming Jiang, Hansheng Wang, Xiaoguang Pang, Xiaoen Li, Xi Lu
abstract: Study region The glacier region in the northern China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) mainly comprises the Karakoram, Pamir, and Hindu Kush subregions. Study focus Annual mass balance (AMB) is essential for characterizing rapid changes in glacier meltwater, yet AMB data remain scarce for widely distributed glaciers in the CPEC. This study combined remote sensing albedo and differencing digital elevation model (DEM) data (Diff-DEM-ABM) to reconstruct AMB during 2000–2020 for 1849 glaciers selected according to method applicability. We further quantified correlations between AMB and climate variables and estimated excess glacier meltwater associated with net mass loss (hereafter, excess meltwater runoff) for three major river basins. New hydrological insights for the region The study glaciers in the CPEC experienced mass loss in most years during 2000–2020. Regional AMB reached its maximum in 2010, when all three subregions showed positive mass balance, followed by predominantly negative AMB during 2011–2020. AMB variability was strongly correlated with warm-season temperature (R=-0.83, P < 0.001) and annual snowfall (R = 0.74, P < 0.001), highlighting clear climatic influence at the annual scale. Mean excess meltwater runoff was highest in the Indus basin (2.63 Gt), followed by the Amu Darya (1.24 Gt) and Tarim (0.60 Gt) basins. These results provide improved insights into interannual glacier mass change, its climatic associations, and the long-term dynamics of glacier-derived water resources in the CPEC.

title: Century-scale human land transformation reshapes flood hazards in a tropical catchment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Rei Itsukushima, Soma Matsushima, Kazuaki Ohtsuki, Mohd Shalahuddin Adnan, Tatsuro Sato
abstract: Study region The Masai River catchment (26 km²) in southern Peninsular Malaysia is a rapidly urbanizing tropical catchment that has undergone extensive land transformation over the past century. Study focus This study integrated historical land-use reconstruction, high-frequency hydrological observations, and an observation-constrained Rainfall–Runoff–Inundation model to assess hydrological changes across four reconstructed land-use conditions: 1926, 2002, 2018, and 2024. Identical rainfall forcing was applied to all scenarios to isolate the hydrological effects of urbanization from climatic variability. The model was calibrated against one observed flood event and independently validated against three additional events. New hydrological insights for the region Relative to the 1926 landscape, progressive urbanization increased peak discharge by 3.4–39.6% and total runoff volume by 3.0–54.4%, while maximum inundation depth under the 100-year, 3-h design storm increased from 1.24 to 1.40 m. Urbanization also reorganized flood hazards spatially: inundation expanded from historically vulnerable downstream reaches toward tributary catchments and newly urbanized upstream areas. Remaining grasslands and open spaces within flood-prone areas represent potential locations for nature-based flood mitigation. These findings demonstrate that century-scale land transformation has left a persistent hydrological legacy in the catchment and show that historical land-use trajectories should be incorporated into regional flood-risk assessment and planning.

title: Agent-based simulation of equity-oriented water reallocation under drought: A case study of the Geum River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yeonju Kim, Jiheun Kim, Hee Won Jee, Jaeyoung Kim, Tae-Woong Kim, Seung Beom Seo
abstract: Study region: Geum River Basin, South Korea, a structurally heterogeneous watershed with 14 agricultural, 12 domestic/industrial intake, and 3 hydropower stakeholders. The basin has the highest agricultural water demand among South Korea’s six major river basins, with precipitation concentrated in the summer monsoon season, making dam operations critical for balancing competing water demands during irrigation. Study focus: This study develops an integrated framework to improve equitable water allocation during droughts by coupling a basin-scale allocation model with an Agent-Based Model (ABM). While centralized optimization overlooks decentralized social dynamics, autonomous stakeholder agents make voluntary diversion decisions based on locally perceived reliability deficits, redistributing water to the most vulnerable peers via hypothetical conveyance infrastructure. Streamflow is represented by SWAT-derived daily inflows spanning 39 water years (October 1981–September 2020). New hydrological insights and conclusions: First, agricultural water supply vulnerability in the Geum River Basin is governed less by absolute demand magnitude and more by basin topology and infrastructure configuration. Tributary-dominated subbasins (Agr 7, Agr 11, and Agr 13), which are structurally isolated from the regulated mainstem, exhibited the lowest supply reliability during the severe historical droughts of 1994–1997 and 2014–2017, identifying these locations as priority targets for adaptive drought management in the basin. Second, agent-based simulation of voluntary water donation among Geum River stakeholders demonstrates that equity improvements can emerge as system-level outcomes from repeated decentralized interactions. During drought period, the agricultural Gini coefficient decreased from 0.152 (no ABM) to 0.097–0.117 across three behavioral scenarios, with the largest reliability gains concentrated at the most structurally vulnerable tributary nodes. Third, sensitivity analysis across nine supply–demand combinations confirmed that the simulated equity benefit within the Geum River Basin is robust to variations in inflow magnitude and irrigation demand scaling, with gains increasing proportionally under higher demand pressure. However, the Pro-social scenario yielded diminishing equity returns relative to the Bounded Rational scenario, as excessively frequent donations reduced the reliability of intake donor stakeholders, suggesting that moderate rather than maximum cooperation produces the most balanced outcomes across stakeholder types.

title: Dissecting the drivers of national terrestrial water storage alterations using non-parametric ensemble learning: The case of Iran
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fereshteh Shakeri, Amirhossein Haddadi, Mohammad Danesh-Yazdi
abstract: Study region Iran faces water bankruptcy driven by decades of overuse and mismanagement, threatening both its population and ecosystems. Study focus This study quantifies long-term terrestrial water storage loss (TWSL) dynamics across Iran by integrating GRACE satellite observations, extensive ground-based hydroclimatic records, and an explainable Random Forest model enhanced with Nataf-based data augmentation. We used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify the relative contributions of climatic variability and anthropogenic forcing. New hydrological insights for the region Results show pronounced hydroclimatic change between 1973 and 2023, indicating a significant increase of 2.05°C in air temperature and a 43 mm reduction in average annual precipitation between 1973–2000 and 2001–2019. The average annual streamflow at unregulated stations decreased by 37% during 1998–2018 relative to 1970–1997. Groundwater storage deficit over 2003–2018 was 83 BCM. GRACE data indicate a TWSL of about 370 BCM from 2002 to 2023, with 61% occurring after 2016, reflecting accelerating depletion. SHAP analysis revealed that groundwater dynamics dominate TWSL, explaining 90.5%, 91.9%, and 92.3% of its variability during normal, dry, and wet conditions, respectively, whereas the influence of other factors remains limited under all climatic conditions. This dominance indicates a decoupling of TWSL from short-term climate variability and a transition toward groundwater-controlled storage dynamics. These findings highlight the need for demand management and effective control of groundwater abstraction from aquifers to ensure long-term sustainability.

title: Extreme rainfall erosivity shapes comprehensive soil erosion risk and exposure patterns in the Qinling-Huaihe region, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yingshan Zhao, Feng Sun, Yi Lu, Jiarui Xing, Yaowen Chang, Xia Liu
abstract: Study region The Qinling-Huaihe region lies within the north-south climatic transition zone of China’s East Asian monsoon region and exhibits pronounced regional differences in precipitation, topography, and socioeconomic conditions. Study focus This study developed a framework of extreme rainfall erosivity analysis-comprehensive soil erosion risk assessment-risk-exposure correspondence analysis. It examines spatiotemporal changes in general extreme rainfall erosivity (R95) and strong extreme rainfall erosivity (R99), comprehensive soil erosion risk patterns and contribution structures, and the concentration and spatial correspondence of socioeconomic exposure across risk levels. New hydrological insights for the region The combined average contributions of R95 and R99 to total rainfall erosivity exceeded 50%. During 1960–2024, R99 and its contribution rate increased in all subregions, with R99 increasing 2.3 and 5.7 times faster than R95 in the Huang–Huai Plain and Sichuan Basin, respectively. R95 and R99 hot spots were concentrated in the Huang–Huai Plain, Middle–Lower Yangtze River Plain, Sichuan Basin, and Wushan Mountains, showing clear regional clustering. During 2000–2020, relatively high–high risk areas increased from 16.90% to 31.78% under R95 and from 16.26% to 25.27% under R99. Risk was dominated by H contributions in the Huang–Huai Plain and Middle–Lower Yangtze River Plain, whereas the Qinling–Daba Mountains remained E-dominated. By 2020, relatively high–high risk areas contained 35.83%–46.97% of GDP and 39.81%42.59% of the population, forming high-risk–high-exposure patterns in the Sichuan Basin, Middle–Lower Yangtze River Plain, and Huang–Huai Plain.

title: Resolving the turbidity paradox: Tide-weighted remote sensing reveals how morphodynamic siltation overwhelms flow attenuation in a macro-tidal bay
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sheng Wu, Wankang Yang, Qingying Yang, Bo Li, Zongyu Li
abstract: Study region Sanmen Bay, a macro-tidal embayment, Zhejiang, China. Study focus This study investigates the physical mechanisms driving decadal turbidity escalation under a regime of widespread hydrodynamic attenuation. Decadal GF-1 satellite observations were processed using a tide-weighted compositing method to eliminate tidal phase biases. A 3D hydrodynamic model (MIKE 3 FM) with decoupled scenarios was applied to isolate the individual and cumulative impacts of natural bathymetric shoaling and engineering structures (reclamations, wind farms, photovoltaic arrays) on regional flow and sediment transport. New hydrological insights for the region From 2014–2024, the regional mean suspended sediment concentration (SSC) increased from 311.1 to 348.8 mg/L, concurrent with a basin-wide mean flow velocity reduction of 0.05–0.15 m/s. Decoupled numerical experiments reveal that large-scale bathymetric shoaling dictates this regional hydrodynamic attenuation, while coastal engineering structures generate localized flow diversion. The turbidity escalation under diminished tidal forcing is controlled by cohesive bed-property feedbacks. Persistent offshore sediment importation and subsequent deposition continually renew a highly porous surficial mud layer, reducing the critical erosion shear stress ( τ ce ). Consequently, the attenuated tidal currents maintain sufficient energy to trigger frequent sediment resuspension. This deposition process, mechanically amplified by water column volume reductions over accreted shallow flats and flood-dominant tidal asymmetry, establishes a morphodynamic loop that chronically traps sediments within the bay, offering key insights for sediment management in anthropogenically altered coastal hydrological systems.

title: Deciphering water salinization mechanisms of arid lake-groundwater systems in Inner Mongolia, China: An integration of multi-isotopic models
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shen Qu, Yuanzhen Zhao, Le Qiao, Xiangwei Li, Renpu Wang, Dongchao Huo, Yufei Bai, Heyang Sun, Xu Yang, Zhongli Wang, Ruihong Yu
abstract: Study region Three representative arid lake-groundwater systems in Inner Mongolia, China: Daihai Lake (DL), Ulansuhai Lake (UL), and the Bahannao Lake Group (BL). Study focus Salinization severely threatens water security of arid lake-groundwater systems, yet the coupled mechanisms linking salinity sources, geochemical transformations and groundwater salt transport have not been well understood. This study established an innovative multi-isotope framework integrating the Rayleigh fractionation model (RFM), Bayesian isotope mixing model (MixSIAR), and ²²²Rn mass balance model (RMBM) to decipher dominant drivers of salinity evolution and their environmental implications for typical inland lake-groundwater systems. New hydrological insights for the region Salinization within the studied systems arises from combined natural geochemical processes and anthropogenic solute inputs, where human-derived sources exert a predominant role. Evaporite and silicate weathering supply primary natural salinity loads, while irrigation water, municipal water and sewage constitute major anthropogenic contributors. evaporation and cation exchange further accelerate salinity enrichment. Lacustrine groundwater discharge functions as a pivotal transport pathway delivering large salt fluxes into lakes, with pronounced spatial heterogeneity governed by local hydrogeological conditions. Salinity-related risks to drinking and irrigation proposes are widely identified across the basins. This integrated modeling framework advances the mechanistic understanding of salinization in arid lake-groundwater systems and offers practical support for water resource regulation in analogous endorheic basins.

title: Attribution of climate and anthropogenic controls on terrestrial water storage changes in the cold and arid regions of the Indus River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Muhammad Adnan, Leilei Yong, Qiaojuan Xi, Muhammad Saifullah, Qaisar Saddique, Waqas Ul Hussan, Hongkai Gao
abstract: Study region The Indus River Basin (IRB) is a major transboundary river basin in South Asia. Study focus The study focuses on quantifying the respective roles of climatic variability and anthropogenic water use in driving terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA) decline using a physically informed, decomposition-based attribution framework and spatiotemporal changes in TWSA over the IRB during April 2002–August 2025 using extended GRACE/GRACE-FO data. New hydrological insights for the region Trend analysis shows intensification of TWSA decline in humid (−39.8 mm yr⁻¹), semiarid (−34.9 mm yr⁻¹), and cold (−27.4 mm yr⁻¹) regions, while comparatively weak decline in arid (−4.02 mm yr⁻¹) during 2016–2025 as compared to 2002–2015. Signed covariance decomposition identified GWSA as the dominant positive component of TWSA variability (99.9–105.2%), followed by GMB (15.7–18.6%), whereas RZSM, SWE and reconstruction error provided compensating contributions. Basin-scale analysis further shows accelerated groundwater depletion during 2016–2023 (GWS ≈ −13.9 mm yr⁻¹), accompanied by intensified anthropogenic-associated TWSA decline (≈ −16.5 mm yr⁻¹). During 2016–2023, anthropogenic-associated components accounted for the largest relative magnitude shares in arid (59%) and semiarid (67%) regions and across the basin (51%). The climate-related share was largest in the cold region (55%), whereas climate-related and anthropogenic-associated shares were comparable in the humid region (38% and 36%, respectively). These findings highlight the combined influence of human water use and hydroclimatic variability in shaping recent basin-scale water storage decline.

title: Performance assessment of urban drainage systems using a river–pipe–surface coupled modeling approach
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Chaohui Chen, Yuzhou Zhang, Peng Wu, Luoyang Wang, Yihan Lou, Tangao Hu
abstract: Study Region: The HUA district represents a typical low-lying urbanized floodplain within a coastal megacity, where a high-density municipal pipe network directly intersects a dynamic river system, making it a regional model for studying compound waterlogging under the nonlinear interaction of localized precipitation and fluctuating downstream river boundaries. Study Focus: The research develops an integrated evaluation framework combining a river–pipe–land two-way dynamically coupled hydraulic model with a multi-level Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Remote sensing data is utilized to refine surface parameters, while a newly proposed Drainage Efficiency Indicator (DEI) system evaluates performance across four dimensions: system capacity, drainage impact, overall efficiency, and backwater suppression. The study analyzes 12 distinct scenarios to quantify the sensitivity of urban drainage to varying rainfall intensities, river stages, and outlet configurations. New Hydrological Insights: Analysis of the study area reveals that precipitation intensity is the primary determinant of drainage efficiency, exhibiting a strong non-linear negative correlation with the DEI score. A critical process-based finding is the peak-on-peak interaction, where the synchronization of the river flood peak and the maximum pipe discharge triggers transient backwater suppression, significantly extending the drainage recession time by up to 425% as return periods increase from 5a to 50a. Prescribed-stage experiments show that high receiving-river levels restrict drainage, while low levels enhance performance under the same local rainfall. The results also reveal an “integrated hydraulic limit” in the urban catchment: lowering outlet elevations reduces backflow risk, but marginal efficiency gains diminish during extreme events, indicating that downstream boundary conditions ultimately become the dominant constraint on system recovery.

title: Spatial association network and structural robustness of human-water system resilience in the Yangtze River Economic Belt, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Beinan Guo, Li Zhang, Hongrui Wang, Yiyang Li, Lili Gao, Haoru Li, Lili Mao, Xinyue Kou, Xiaofeng Wang, Daozhi Gong
abstract: Study region The Yangtze River Economic Belt (YREB), China. Study focus This study investigates the spatiotemporal evolution, spatial association network, and structural robustness of human–water system resilience (HWSR) across 110 prefecture-level cities in the YREB from 2006 to 2022. A multidimensional HWSR framework incorporating resistance, recovery, and adaptability was developed. The projection pursuit–genetic algorithm model was used to quantify city-level HWSR, while standard deviational ellipse analysis, a modified gravity model, social network analysis, network attack simulations, and QAP regression were applied to reveal spatial patterns, intercity associations, network robustness, and driving mechanisms. New hydrological insights for the region HWSR in the YREB increased steadily during 2006–2022, with high-resilience clusters concentrated in the Yangtze River Delta, Chengdu–Chongqing region, and provincial capitals. The spatial association network showed low density, high connectedness, and strong hierarchy, indicating that HWSR is shaped not only by local city-level capacity but also by intercity hydrological, socioeconomic, and governance linkages. Network attack simulations revealed that the HWSR network is relatively robust to random node failures but highly vulnerable to the loss of high-centrality cities. QAP regression further showed that geographic proximity and openness promote HWSR associations, while disparities in informatization and technological innovation inhibit early-stage connectivity. These findings suggest that improving regional water resilience in the YREB requires a shift from single-city management toward basin-wide, networked, and differentiated collaborative governance.

title: Shifting water-sediment relationship under the influence of extensive soil conservation in the Yellow River Basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haiyan Yang, Taihua Wang, Dawen Yang, Haidong Gao, Zihan Yan, Chuandong Wu, Min Chen, Lihua Tang, Ping Li
abstract: Study region The Yellow River Basin (YRB), China, a region characterized by a critical imbalance between scarce water resources and high sediment load. Study focus Although massive anthropogenic interventions have significantly altered the long-standing water-sediment relationship in the YRB, the spatiotemporal details of these shifts remain underexplored. To address this gap, this study employs a distributed model to conduct a basin-wide simulation of hydro-sediment processes from 1961 to 2024, aiming to quantify the driving mechanisms of sediment regime changes. New hydrological insights for the region A distinct spatial mismatch exists between runoff and sediment sources. While runoff exhibited a “decrease-then-increase” pattern, soil erosion intensity consistently declined by 48.9% (1981–2000) and 71.8% (2001–2024) from the 1961–1980 baseline. Erosion decreased exponentially with hillslope conservation area, and check dams intercepted 4.52 billion m³ of sediment. Crucially, attribution analysis revealed significant spatial heterogeneity: climate change dominated sediment variations in the source region, large reservoirs in the upper reaches, and soil conservation measures in the middle-lower reaches. At Huayuankou, hillslope measures (-48.1%), check dams (-41.6%), and reservoirs (-23.0%) dominated sediment reduction, overwhelmingly offsetting the climate-induced increase (+12.7%).

title: Regionalization of flow-duration curves for ungauged catchments in southern peninsular Italy
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Fatemeh Moradi, Roberta Padulano, Cristiana Di Cristo, Giuseppe Del Giudice
abstract: Study region The study covers southern peninsular Italy, including Campania, Calabria, Basilicata, Puglia, and marginal parts of Lazio and Molise. The analysis uses 58 hydrometric stations reconstructed from historical SIMN daily discharge records across heterogeneous Mediterranean catchments. Study focus This study develops a regional framework for estimating long-term flow-duration curves in ungauged Mediterranean catchments. Daily discharge is represented by a mixed formulation that separates flow occurrence from non-zero discharge magnitude. The non-zero component is mean-normalized and described with a log-normal model. Flow occurrence, distribution parameters, mean non-zero discharge, and base-flow index are regionalized using climatic, physiographic, land-cover, drainage-network, and hydrogeological descriptors. Principal component analysis supports hydro-physiographic interpretation, partial least squares regression derives prediction equations, and jackknife validation assesses transferability. New hydrological insights for the region Separating zero-flow occurrence from positive-flow magnitude provides a transferable and physically interpretable basis for regional flow-duration curve estimation in heterogeneous Mediterranean basins. Jackknife validation showed high stability for mean non-zero discharge (R² = 0.98), and the perennial-river location parameter (R² = 0.81), while intermittent-flow parameters retained acceptable predictive skill (R² ≈ 0.70). Reconstructed quantiles agreed closely with observations across most exceedance probabilities, highlighting associations between regional flow regimes and climate, catchment scale, drainage connectivity, and subsurface storage.

title: Spatial distribution, origins, and driving mechanisms of groundwater nitrate contamination in a rural-agricultural-mining catchment: Insight from PMF, machine learning and multi-isotopic techniques
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Houyun Sun, Feng Ma, Xiaofeng Wei, Xiaoshu Wei, Ziran Chen
abstract: Study region A rural-agricultural-mining catchment of Chengde city, the critical water conservation area of Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, northern China. Study focus To comprehensively elucidate the sources and fate of nitrate in the shallow aquifer of the study region, this study established an integrated analytical framework combining hydrochemical and soil geochemical multivariate statistics, geostatistics, redundancy analysis, Random Forest-XGBoost-SHapley Additive exPlanations, PMF-MixSIAR source apportionment modeling, and multi-isotope tracers to identify spatial patterns, influencing factors, sources, and driving mechanisms of groundwater nitrate migration and transformation processes in the aquifer. New hydrological insights for the region The most influential drivers of nitrate include Cl⁻, total nitrogen, total dissolved solids (TDS), electrical conductivity (EC), groundwater depth, residential and industrial-mining land use, soil biogenic elements. The average contributions to groundwater nitrate were: manure/sewage (33.94%), soil nitrogen (24.74%), atmospheric deposition (21.91%), chemical fertilizer (19.18%), geological and mining sources (1.06%), and surface water–groundwater exchange (1.03%). Nitrogen biogeochemical cycling in the catchment is jointly governed by groundwater system and pollutant source–sink dynamics. Groundwater discharge zones—the hyporheic zone—serve as denitrification hotspots, where organic matter drives nitrogen biogeochemical cycling. In riparian wetlands of the V-Ti-Fe-P mining area, nitrate contamination and high-intensity organic carbon loading, microbially mediated processes including nitrate-reducing Fe(II) oxidation, sulfur-oxidizing autotrophic denitrification, and heterotrophic denitrification were observed, though their overall effect on nitrate attenuation was limited.

title: Runoff efficiency and seasonal redistribution under warming–wetting in the Pangu River basin: A snow-state-constrained assessment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tingting Wang, Ping Wang, Wenbin Liu, Hong Wang, Ziwei Li, Fubao Sun, Sergey P. Pozdniakov
abstract: Study region The Pangu River basin is a data-scarce, high-latitude mountainous catchment in the northern Greater Khingan Mountains, Northeast China, where runoff is jointly shaped by seasonal snow, freeze-thaw processes, river ice, catchment storage-release, and limited direct human regulation. Study focus We examined annual runoff and seasonal release under warming-wetting using harmonized monthly runoff observations, a cold-region process-diagnostic model (PHY), and targeted tests of total-runoff residual, parameter, and snow-structure sensitivity. Diagnostic pathway allocation was treated as secondary sensitivity analysis. New hydrological insights for the region Within the snow-state-constrained reference model, historical runoff did not increase proportionally to wetting. Between 1961–1990 and 1995–2024, annual precipitation increased by 53.7 mm, whereas PHY annual runoff changed by only −3.0 mm and runoff efficiency declined from 0.265 to 0.228. April–June (AMJ) runoff showed a model-inferred directional decline of 4.8 mm, with a relative shift toward July–October (JASO); bootstrap intervals for AMJ runoff and seasonal-allocation contrasts included zero. In the PHY diagnostic decomposition, the snow-related spring-release index (SAI) declined from 0.312 to 0.278. Runoff directions persisted under local parameter and residual perturbations, and lower SAI persisted within the reference parameter ensemble. Removing ERA5-Land snow-state assimilation reversed the key historical directions. The efficiency contrast reflects a response conditioned by effective-forcing and numerical snow-state adjustments, not an identified fate of additional precipitation. Weaker snow-supported spring release is therefore a conditional model interpretation, not an established climatic mechanism.

title: Groundwater potential mapping using conventional and machine learning approaches with multi-indicator validation of Aflaj systems in Oman
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Saif Al Aamri, Sameh Kantoush, Mahmood Al Mamari, Mohamed Saber, Emad Mabrouk, Ahmed Emara
abstract: Study region The Alaqida Basin in northern Oman is an arid mountainous watershed where groundwater is a critical water resource. Groundwater occurrence varies spatially with rainfall, geology, topography, drainage, structural features, soil properties, and land use, highlighting the need for reliable groundwater-potential assessment. Study focus This study develops a hybrid groundwater-potential zonation framework integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Seven groundwater-conditioning factors—rainfall, geology, soil, slope, drainage density, lineament density, and land use/land cover—were integrated in GIS to generate an AHP-based groundwater-potential map. The resulting classes were used as reference labels to train XGBoost using 40,083 pixel-based samples. Model performance was evaluated using 5-fold spatial block cross-validation and conventional and ordinal classification metrics. New hydrological insights for the region High and moderate groundwater-potential zones occupy 50.7% of the basin, while low and very low zones account for 45.2% and 4.1%, respectively. XGBoost reproduced the AHP-derived classes with cross-validated accuracy of 0.929, macro F1-score of 0.878, Cohen’s kappa of 0.888, quadratic weighted kappa of 0.941, and Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.889. Low-confidence predictions occupy 5.5% of the basin. Favorable zones coincide with major wadis, coarse alluvial deposits, and structurally enhanced areas, while correspondence with wells, recharge dams, and traditional Aflaj systems provides independent support for the hydrogeological plausibility of the mapped groundwater-potential pattern.

title: A multivariate integrated drought characterization framework using GNSS-GRACE terrestrial water storage and precipitation
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiaoxing He, Jing Yang, Shunqiang Hu, Hai Zhu, Gaël Kermarrec, Rui Fernandes, Jean‑Philippe Montillet, Mingjia Li
abstract: Study region The Yangtze River Basin, the largest river basin in China, is vital for regional water resources, ecosystem sustainability, and socioeconomic development. Increasing drought frequency and severity in recent years, particularly during the extreme 2022 event, have intensified the demand for robust hydrological drought monitoring frameworks. Study focus GNSS, GRACE, and GRACE Follow-On observations provide valuable information on terrestrial water storage (TWS) changes for drought assessment. However, drought indicators based on GNSS-only or GRACE-only estimates are limited by sparse observations, leakage effects, and spatial resolution constraints. This study develops a Joint Precipitation and Joint-EWH Multivariate Standardized Drought Index (JP-MSDI), which integrates precipitation and TWS changes derived from a joint GNSS-GRACE inversion framework using a Copula-based probabilistic model. The framework was applied to the Yangtze River Basin during 2011–2024. New hydrological insights for the region Joint GNSS-GRACE inversion reveals spatially heterogeneous TWS variations, with larger amplitudes in the Jinsha River Basin and eastern middle-lower Yangtze plains, but smaller variations in the central basin and around Tai Hu Lake. Compared with GNSS-only estimates, the joint inversion shows higher correlations and lower RMSE values when evaluated against GLDAS. JP-MSDI identified eight drought events during 2011–2024 and reflected the progression from precipitation deficits to TWS anomalies during the 2022 extreme drought.Compared with runoff observations, the Standardized Runoff Index from multiple hydrological stations, and historical drought records indicate that JP-MSDI captures the main temporal patterns of basin-scale drought.

title: A hydrological-year stratified regionalization framework for sediment rating curves in the largest tributary of the Mekong River
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Nantawoot Inseeyong, Pavisorn Chuenchum, Mengzhen Xu, Kwanchai Pakoksung, Jeerapong Laonamsai
abstract: Study region The Mun River Basin in Thailand, the largest tributary of the Mekong River. Study focus Sparse sediment monitoring limits reliable sediment-load estimation across the Mun River Basin. Sediment rating curves (SRCs) provide a practical means of estimating sediment loads from discharge, but conventional static SRCs do not adequately represent interannual variability in sediment–discharge relationships. This study develops an advanced SRC regionalization framework that integrates hydrological-year stratification (flood, normal, and drought years) with regression-based and catchment-similarity approaches to improve estimation under limited sediment observations. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Hydrological-year stratification showed that SRC parameters vary among flood, normal, and drought conditions. Classification using station-specific 2-year and 10-year return-period peak-flow thresholds separates contrasting hydrological regimes and indicates that interannual flow variability exerts a stronger influence on sediment-response behavior than basin-wide land-use change. Regionalization suitability also depends on catchment characteristics. Regression is more appropriate for gentler catchments with S c 0.05, where sediment response is governed mainly by integrated basin-scale attributes. Catchment similarity is more suitable for steeper catchments with S c > 6.0% and K USLE x C USLE < 0.05, where sediment generation and delivery are more spatially heterogeneous. These findings show that both hydrological regime and catchment physiography should be considered when regionalizing sediment–discharge relationships in the Mun River Basin.

title: Intensification of irrigated agriculture and precipitation explain rising evapotranspiration in the Snake River Basin despite declining atmospheric demand
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Meetpal Singh Kukal, Dinesh Gulati, Meng Zhao, Alex Maas, Kendra E. Kaiser
abstract: Evapotranspiration (ET) is the dominant water outflux in irrigated semi-arid basins, yet its long-term trends and drivers remain poorly quantified at management-relevant scales. In intensively irrigated systems operating under prior appropriation, detecting and attributing changes in consumptive water use is essential for sustainable water governance. Here we show, using OpenET ensemble estimates across 53 HUC-8 watersheds of the Snake River Plain over 2000–2023, corroborated by GRACE-derived water balance and Landsat net primary productivity, that ET increased significantly in 25 of 53 watersheds at a basin-wide median rate of 1.7 mm yr⁻¹ , driven primarily by irrigated area expansion (contributing to 54% of ET trend) and secondarily by precipitation (contributing to19% of ET trend), while declining atmospheric evaporative demand partially offset these gains. The region underwent a significant basin-wide shift toward dairy forage production, with alfalfa, other hay, and corn collectively increasing their share of cropland at the expense of small grains, indicating crop compositional intensification. Reliance on individual OpenET models had significant control on attribution inferences, with the irrigated fraction contribution to ET trends ranging from 11% (geeSEBAL) to 60% (SSEBop) across models compared to 54% for the ensemble. These findings demonstrate that land use intensification can override climatically driven declines in atmospheric evaporative demand. Additionally, inter-model uncertainty in remote sensing ET products is sufficiently large to alter water management conclusions.

title: Projection of hydrological droughts in the upper Hanjiang River under the climate change impact based on stacking machine learning model
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xuerui Gao, Jingyuan Chen, Daning Liu, Ziqi Shang, Lingyao Meng, Baoni Li, Gengxi Zhang, Aili Sun, Shuyu Zhang
abstract: Study region The upper Hanjiang River Basin, a crucial water source region for multiple large-scale inter-basin water transfer projects in China, including the South-to-North Water Diversion Project and the Han-to-Wei Water Transfer Project. Study focus This study focuses on hydrological drought in the upper Hanjiang River Basin, a critical water supply region for major inter-basin water transfer projects. With global warming, droughts have intensified and occurred more frequently, posing potential threats to water supply security for both the source and recipient regions. We projected future runoff (2030–2099) at two key hydrological stations by constructing an ensemble machine learning (ML) runoff model driven by 20 CMIP6 GCMs. Future hydrological droughts under global warming were then identified and analyzed. New hydrological insights for the region The ensemble ML model showed improved performance over individual ML models. Future annual runoff is projected to increase overall, albeit with substantial spread among individual climate models. For hydrological drought, duration is projected to shorten while intensity shows an increasing trend, and a higher proportion of extreme droughts is expected under SSP585 than under SSP245. Despite an overall wetting trend, the increasing intensity and severity of hydrological droughts could undermine the stability and reliability of water supply for inter-basin water transfer projects, necessitating enhanced adaptive management strategies in this critical water-source region.

title: Seasonal divergence in dissolved-carbon concentration and export along a cascade-dammed subtropical river continuum: A case study of the Zijiang River, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Wentao Xu, Yu Cui, Zhengmiao Deng, Hao Qu, Lijie Duan, Cicheng Zhang, Zhitao Huo, Yuan Zhao, Feng Li, Liyan Wang, Tao Wang, Changhui Peng, Yonghong Xie
abstract: Study region The Zijiang River is a subtropical monsoonal tributary of the middle Yangtze River, China, characterized by intensive cascade-reservoir regulation along its mainstem. Study focus We focused on four successive cascade dams and the five longitudinal locations they define (D1–D5), with D1 as the upstream reference and D2–D5 as successive dam-regulated reaches. We examined how hydrological seasonality interacts with repeated cascade regulation to shape DOC and DIC sources, concentrations, and export using seasonal observations integrated with isotope, statistical, and discharge-conditioned analyses. New hydrological insights for the region DOC and DIC displayed a seasonal reversal, with higher DOC in flood season and higher DIC in non-flood season. Yet export timing diverged: in 2023/24, flood-season water carried 63.7–77.7% of annual DOC export, whereas non-flood season carried 57.9–69.6% of DIC export. Plankton-associated DOC dominated D1–D3, then shifted towards mixed plankton–soil contributions in D4–D5. DIC retained a carbonate-weathering background, while soil-CO₂ contribution increased from D3 downstream. Cascade damming was associated with both carbon pools through distinct environmental pathways. These results show that carbon budgets in cascade rivers must resolve season, dam sequence, source composition and in-river processing rather than rely on concentration snapshots.

title: Pakistan monsoon rainfall for climate adaptation using generalized linear models
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haris Horani, Muhammad Yousuf Tufail
abstract: Study region Pakistan, where highly variable summer June, July, August, and September (JJAS) monsoon rainfall drives both water security and flood risks across diverse topography. Study focus To support climate adaptation and sustainable water governance, this study develops a transparent Generalized Linear Modeling (GLM) framework for concurrent statistical estimation of JJAS rainfall totals. Using CHIRPS observations (1981–2020), two nested models were evaluated by leave-one-year-out cross-validation across Pakistan and four hydro-climatic subregions. The precipitation-free atmospheric-teleconnection model (M1) uses winds, thermodynamic variables, and climate indices; the full model (M2) additionally includes concurrent ERA5 seasonal precipitation. New hydrological insights for the region At the Pakistan scale, precipitation-free M1 retained cross-validated R² = 0.43 (RMSE = 30.8 mm), whereas M2 with ERA5 precipitation achieved R² = 0.74 (RMSE = 20.9 mm). M1 also retained substantial skill in LIB (R² = 0.76) and BCP (R² = 0.55), but not in NHM or UIB. Raw ERA5–CHIRPS rainfall correlations of 0.62–0.91 demonstrate strong concurrent product agreement and indicate that the two precipitation estimates should not be treated as practically independent. Relative to an ERA5-only model, the remaining predictors produced a statistically resolved RMSE reduction only in LIB (+8.34 mm; 95% CI 1.61–14.33 mm; positive favors M2). M2 is therefore interpreted as a concurrent multi-product reconstruction, while M1 quantifies the stand-alone atmospheric and teleconnection signal. Comparison with ridge regression and random forest showed comparable ridge performance and no consistent random-forest improvement, supporting the GLM as an interpretable regional baseline.

title: Development of empirical regression model for predicting monthly rainfall erosivity factors based on daily rainfall and its application to future rainfall scenarios in South Korea
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Minseok Park, Jinsol Hong, Sangchul Lee, Kijong Cho, Seunghun Hyun
abstract: Study region South Korea, with daily rainfall data retrieved from 58 meteorological stations across the country. Study focus To improve soil erosion risk assessments constrained by data scarcity, this study compares four monthly rainfall erosivity (R-factor) prediction models using time-based walk-forward cross-validation. Spatial non-stationarity, regional erosivity regimes, and future shifts under climate change scenarios are also investigated. New hydrological insights for the region Across the country, effective rainfall amount (rain10) consistently exerts a stronger influence on erosivity than rainfall frequency (days10), indicating that future regional erosivity will be more sensitive to intensified rainfall than to frequency shifts. Spatial distribution of model coefficients reveals five distinct hydroclimatic regimes; inland areas are heavily influenced by rainfall frequency, whereas coastal and island zones are dominated by rainfall amount driven by typhoon activity and orographic enhancement. Climate projections further indicate a warming-induced snow-to-rain transition that increases January-February rainfall erosivity by upto 300% under high-emission scenarios, redistributing erosive rainfall from the traditional summer monsoon toward the winter non-cropping season. These findings indicate that future soil erosion risk in South Korea will be increasingly governed by the intensity and seasonal redistribution of erosive rainfall, rather than changes in annual rainfall alone.

title: Spatiotemporal propagation of recharge-derived isotopic signals in an alluvial fan aquifer using probabilistic endmember mixing analysis
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shao-Yang Huang, Hsiang-Lan Juan, Ming-Che Wu, Jyun-Lin Chen
abstract: Study region Artificial recharge facilities near the apex of the Choushui River alluvial fan, central Taiwan, were examined. Local groundwater was represented by monitoring wells within or adjacent to the recharge area, whereas regional groundwater was represented by irrigation wells distributed across the surrounding fan. Study focus This study investigates how recharge-derived isotopic signals differ between near-field monitoring wells and regional irrigation wells. We integrated multiyear δ18O and δ2H records with probabilistic endmember mixing analysis to estimate contributions from precipitation, surface water, hyporheic flow, and groundwater endmembers. Reciprocal configurations compared the two groundwater observation scales, and we evaluated posterior contributions by distance, recharge-operation period, and lagged correlation with monthly recharge volume. New hydrological insights for the region Local groundwater showed a larger estimated surface-water contribution and greater spatial and temporal variability than regional groundwater. Regional groundwater showed more evenly distributed source contributions and greater overlap among posterior distributions, indicating less isotope-based source discrimination at the broader observation scale. Descriptive differences between operational periods were larger in local groundwater than in regional groundwater. Small phase contrasts and some source rankings were sensitive to the prior specification. Maximum positive correlations occurred at different lags, but their modest magnitudes indicate descriptive temporal correspondence rather than groundwater travel time. Near-field and regional wells therefore provide complementary information on the expression of recharge-derived isotopic signals.

title: Water conservation in arid and semi-arid basins exhibits a nonlinear effect on water quality improvement
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Junde Ming, Rui Xia, Lina Li, Yao Wang, Jinling Tian, Chao Yan, Yan Chen, Kai Zhang, Qi Zhang
abstract: Study region The Weihe River Basin (WRB), a typical arid and semi-arid basin in China. Study focus Water conservation regulates hydrological processes and pollutant transport, yet the response mechanisms of water quality to water conservation remain an interdisciplinary challenge. This study assessed the spatiotemporal dynamics of water conservation and water quality in the WRB, and developed a distributed time-variant gain water conservation model (DTVGM-WC) to quantify the nonlinear responses, identify critical threshold zones, and elucidate the underlying mechanisms linking water conservation and water quality. New hydrological insights for the region The daily-scale hydrological model achieved acceptable performance, with mean NSE values of 0.74 and 0.73 and mean KGE values of 0.77 and 0.70during calibration and validation periods, respectively. The annual mean water conservation during 2008–2019 was 47.6 mm, with a non-significant increasing trend of 1.67 mm·a⁻¹ and a spatial pattern of higher values in the south. Correlation analysis identified total nitrogen (TN) as the monitored water-quality constituent most clearly associated with water conservation at the monthly scale, with pronounced nonlinear sensitivity during seasonal transition periods. Water conservation exhibited a nonlinear effect on TN dynamics. A quantitative response function was developed to characterize this relationship, revealing threshold zones for water conservation regulating TN concentrations at [5 mm, 15 mm] in April and [4 mm, 8 mm] in October. These nonlinear patterns reflect complex ecohydrological regulation and provide insights into water management in arid and semi-arid basins.

title: Three-phase evolution of a proglacial lake and its hydrological impacts on glacier retreat: Insights from Midui Glacier, southeastern Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yanjun Che, Shijin Wang, Zhuotong Nan, Minghu Ding, Xinggang Ma, Shichang Kang
abstract: Study region Guangxie Co proglacial lake and its parent Midui Glacier on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP). Study focus We quantified the lake-glacier evolution from 1986 to 2021 using remote sensing, glacier modeling, and unmanned surface vessel (USV) bathymetry. This study aims to uncover the mechanisms of proglacial lake expansion and its feedback on glacier retreat. New hydrological insights The lake area expanded by 153% (0.19–0.48 km²), with its volume surging to 4.97 × 10⁶ m³ by 2021, exceeding the pre-1988 Glacier Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) level. Bathymetry revealed a "double-funnel" basin. We identified three expansion phases: (I) glacier retreat (1988–2010), (II) supraglacial lake evolution (2011–2017), and (III) enhanced calving and subglacial melting (2017–2021). These processes accelerated ice loss via thermal erosion and calving. Crucially, the recovered volume highlights the need for continued monitoring and further assessment of dam and outlet stability.

title: Retrieving high-resolution terrestrial water storage anomaly estimates in the Pearl River Basin based on GRACE/GRACE-FO data and ConvLSTM
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ange Hu, Shanshan Deng, Wenxi Zhang, Yuxin Liu, Zhiwen Zhao, Anqin Yan
abstract: Study region The Pearl River Basin is characterized by complex land-surface conditions and frequent droughts and floods. The coarse spatial resolution of GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) limits their ability to characterize intrabasin water-storage variations. Study focus A ConvLSTM statistical downscaling model was developed using two-dimensional dynamic image inputs and a six-month sliding window.
