By integrating multisource hydrometeorological predictors, the model generated 0.1° × 0.1° downscaled TWSA estimates for 2002–2025 from 1° × 1° GRACE/GRACE-FO TWSA. The estimates were comprehensively evaluated through spatial aggregation, FLDAS-based water-balance consistency, groundwater-level temporal consistency, and typical drought and flood events. New hydrological insights for the region After spatial aggregation, the downscaled estimates achieved a correlation coefficient (r) of 0.94 and an NSE of 0.88 against the original basin-average series, with a mean spatial similarity coefficient of 0.79. The basin area showing significant positive correlations with groundwater levels increased from 50.0% to 73.2%. Some spatial patterns during typical events were broadly consistent with historical records. Water storage in the Pearl River Basin did not exhibit persistent unidirectional drying but showed long-duration alternations between storage surplus and deficit, with marked spatial asynchrony. Long-term storage-deficit risk was more prominent in the Xijiang River Basin, whereas the other subbasins predominantly exhibited shorter-cycle surplus–deficit transitions in recent years.

title: Urban rainfall heavy metals wet deposition driven by atmospheric moisture transport pathways in plateau city Kunming: Geographic source-oriented flux and reusability assessment
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Wei Yuan, Jie Zeng, Qixin Wu, Zhiheng Ma, Zhong-Jun Wang, Qing Ma, Xinyi He, Jie Zhang, Xin Ge
abstract: Study region A high-altitude plateau city Kunming, the provincial capital of Yunnan in Southwest China. Study focus Urban atmospheric heavy metals (HMs) derived from natural and human sources are efficiently scavenged by wet deposition and subsequently delivered to terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, posing potential ecological and human health risks. Despite growing attention to HMs in rainwater, limited research has focused on high-altitude plateau cities and its atmospheric hydrological driving factor Here, urban rainwater samples were collected in Kunming over one year to quantify HMs concentrations, sources and deposition fluxes, and to elucidate the controlling role of atmospheric moisture transport pathways. New hydrological insights for the region ΣHMs concentrations exhibited pronounced seasonal variability, with significantly higher levels during the dry season than the rainy season, reflecting differences in rainfall scavenging intensity and air mass origin. Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) identified four major sources of HMs: crustal dust (32.3%), industrial emissions (29.9%), traffic emissions (20.4%), and coal combustion (17.4%). The air moisture transport analysis further supported the co-influences of local resuspension and regional anthropogenic emissions. Finally, the volume-weighted mean concentrations of HMs were generally lower than the relevant water quality standards, and irrigation assessment indicators (sodium adsorption ratio and soluble sodium percentage) indicated low salinity and sodium hazard, suggesting the potential for urban rainwater reuse. Overall, this study reveals the moisture-transport- driven HMs dynamics in rainwater in a plateau city, offering scientific support for regional air pollution mitigation and sustainable harvested rainwater resource management.

title: Rainfall threshold-governed landslide susceptibility in the Himalaya
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Kailiang Zhao, Haijun Qiu, Ya Liu, Zijing Liu, Yaru Zhu, Guoqing Yang, Wanqi Luo, Zhuoyang Li
abstract: Study Region The Himalayan range. Study Focus This study develops a coupled modeling approach that integrates I–D thresholds and an optimal model to evaluate landslide susceptibility across different rainfall intensities. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The cumulative antecedent rainfall during the 168 h preceding landslide events exhibits a sublinear power-law relationship with landslide frequency in the Himalaya. The 5%–90% threshold curves show a decreasing trend in intensity with increasing duration. Driven by complex orographic precipitation, the overall pattern of landslide susceptibility in the Himalayas is characterized by higher values in the southern regions and lower values in the northern regions, with spatial variations across the eastern, central, and western sectors. Furthermore, coupled modeling demonstrates that regional landslide event is highly sensitive to rainfall at different quantiles. When the threshold rises from 5% to 90%, the area of very low susceptibility decreases by nearly 50%, while the area of very high susceptibility increases markedly to 17.95% at the 90% threshold. By integrating rainfall thresholds with landslide susceptibility models, this study provides critical hydrological insights into how landslides respond to diverse rainfall conditions across complex terrains, offering a robust scientific basis for regional landslide susceptibility assessment under different rainfall scenarios.

title: Stage–dependent impacts of altered downstream stage–discharge relationships on the hydrological regime of Dongting Lake
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Yizhuang Liu, Changbo Jiang, Mingyu Chen, Zhaohui Xiang, Wengang Zhao, Yang Yang, Bin Deng
abstract: Study region Dongting Lake, China. Study focus This study examines how changes in the downstream stage–discharge relationship affect the lake water levels, outlet discharge, spatial water-level responses, and duration of hydrological states in Dongting Lake. A two-dimensional MIKE 21 FM model was used to simulate the observed 2020 flood-year, 2018 normal-year, and 2023 dry-year hydrographs. Upstream inflows, bathymetry, mesh configuration, and model parameters were held constant, while only the downstream stage–discharge relationship differed between pre- and post-Three Gorges Dam (TGD) conditions. New hydrological insights for the region The post-TGD stage–discharge relationship produced lower downstream water levels at low discharge but higher levels at high discharge. Under the 2020 flood condition, the post-TGD stage–discharge relationship increased the peak water level at Chenglingji, the lake outlet, by 0.54 m and prolonged high-water duration by 17.92 days, while reducing peak outlet discharge by 660.70 m³ s⁻¹ (2.19%) with little change in mean discharge. Under the 2023 dry-year condition, mean water levels decreased by 0.40 m at Chenglingji and 0.20 m at Yingtian in East Dongting Lake. The 2018 normal-year simulation exhibited the same stage-dependent pattern, with lower mean water levels near the outlet but a 0.28 m increase in the annual peak at Chenglingji. Low-water duration at Chenglingji increased by 19.08, 9.88, and 25.75 days under the flood-, dry-, and normal-year conditions, respectively. The response was concentrated near the outlet and East Dongting Lake and attenuated toward the inner lake. These results demonstrate that a changing downstream stage–discharge relationship modifies lake water levels, outlet-discharge responses, and the duration and spatial extent of high- and low-water conditions.

title: Spatiotemporal evolution of urban water bodies and their response to city development: A comparative analysis of northern and Southern China (1990–2023)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Mao Wang, Guoqiang Peng, Min Chen, Yujing Sun, Chengyang Qian, Jiayi Wang, Qijing Shen
abstract: Study region This study focuses on 20 major cities in northern and southern China. The southern cities include Shanghai, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Wuxi, Chengdu, Suzhou, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Nanjing, and Ningbo, while the northern cities are Beijing, Tianjin, Qingdao, Zhengzhou, Jinan, Xi'an, Yantai, Tangshan, Shenyang, and Dalian. The region spans diverse climatic conditions and hydrological settings, providing a representative context for analyzing long-term urban water body dynamics under rapid urbanization. Study focus This study investigates the spatiotemporal evolution of urban water bodies (UWBs) and their relationship with urban development. Multisource Landsat imagery, together with GDP and population data, were integrated using a U-Net deep learning model to extract water areas and conduct comparative analysis between northern and southern cities. This approach improves extraction accuracy over conventional water indices and enables consistent long-term monitoring across large spatial scales. New hydrological insights for the region This study reveals distinct long-term urban water-body trajectories between the northern and southern cities, together with substantial inter-city heterogeneity within both regions. After accounting for city-level heterogeneity and temporal dependence, region, GDP, and population were not statistically significant predictors of urban water-body area, indicating that these variables alone do not adequately explain the observed variation. The results therefore suggest that the observed north–south contrast reflects complex and city-specific water-body evolution rather than a simple socioeconomic gradient.

title: Will mine closures trigger low-flow crises in river systems? Insights from a machine learning approach for the Upper Vistula Basin, Poland
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ewa Szalińska, Kajetan d'Obyrn, Jakub Staszel, Paweł Wilk, Paulina Orlińska-Woźniak
abstract: Study region Upper Silesian Coal Basin and Upper Vistula River system, southern Poland. Study focus This study assesses how the planned phase-out of mine drainage in the Upper Silesian Coal Basin (2020–2049) may interact with climate change to alter streamflow in the Upper Vistula River system, focusing on the Przemsza–Vistula corridor. Future streamflows were simulated using SWAT within the CHASE-PL framework, driven by nine bias-corrected EURO-CORDEX projections under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. A machine-learning Conditional Weighted Regression approach dynamically combined the ensemble outputs into a Weighted Ensemble Streamflow projection. Mine-closure impacts were quantified by removing mine-water discharges according to the closure schedule. New hydrological insights Mine closures primarily affect low-flow conditions. In the Przemsza River system, the probability of flows below the historical 10th percentile increases markedly after closure. Relative to historical conditions, the combined effects of climate change and mine closure may reduce monthly 10th-percentile flows by up to 4.5 m³ /s (~35%) in the Przemsza River and 1.4 m³ /s (~15%) in the Vistula River. Projected flows increase in spring and summer but decrease in autumn, reflecting interacting climatic and anthropogenic pressures. The hybrid SWAT–machine-learning framework improves the robustness of climate-impact assessments and supports evaluation of the hydrological consequences of socio-economic transitions.

title: Effect of a two-stage tandem rain garden in regulating stormwater runoff under climate change scenarios in Xi'an, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shuangcheng Tang, Yongbo Song, Zhonghua Jia, Zhenghan Yu, Na Cheng, Taotao Lu, Jianqiang Lu
abstract: Study region Xi'an, a semi-humid monsoon city in northwestern China, where a field-scale two-stage tandem rain garden receives rooftop runoff from a university office building catchment. Study focus We evaluated whether a modular DRAINMOD model could reproduce monitored inflow and drainage from the tandem system, assessed long-term runoff reduction under contrasting climate projections, and identified implications for storage and drainage management. Continuous simulations used the 1951–2004 historical baseline and bias-corrected daily precipitation and air temperature from 19 CMIP6 GCMs for 2024–2100 under SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, and SSP5–8.5. New hydrological insights Across the modeled 400–1000 mm annual-rainfall gradient, the fitted sensitivities show that a 1 °C increase offsets the effect of 58.3 mm additional rainfall on runoff-reduction rate. Under representative future conditions, mean runoff reduction stayed above 40%, but the least-favorable wet scenarios declined by 1.07–5.54% by late century, indicating uneven resilience across the rainfall spectrum. This divergence arises because rainfall intensification overwhelms the forebay's capture capacity, whereas higher temperatures accelerate evaporative storage recovery between events. These findings quantify, for this study area, the trade-off between greater rainfall input and enhanced evaporative recovery, identifying storm clustering as the decisive factor governing whether the system retains its runoff-reduction function under future climate.

title: Origin of the hot springs along the Arabian Escarpment in Saudi Arabia and Yemen
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Miliausha Petrova, Manojkumar Gudala, Hussein Hoteit, Abdulkader M. Afifi
abstract: Study region The foothills of the Asir-Yemen mountains bordering the eastern margin of the Red Sea in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Study focus The hot springs in the Al Lith and Jizan region were previously considered as potential geothermal resources due to presumed magmatic or fault-controlled origins. Our purpose is to understand their origin, and we present evidence that they represent discharge points of artesian meteoric groundwater originating from the 2–3 km-high Asir-Yemen Plateau. New hydrological insights for the region The hot springs are not related spatially to rift bounding faults or to post-rift magmatism. The hot springs emerge from the fractured basement in the floors of major incised valleys at the base of the foothills. Their low elevations of ~160 m downstream to 288 m upstream corresponds to the top of the underlying groundwater aquifer. The light H-O isotopic composition of the spring waters indicates a meteoric source from high elevations in the mountains, and tritium content (in 1982) indicates < 25 years residence time in the basement. We conclude that meteoric rainfall which infiltrated over the Asir-Yemen mountains are heated to ~100 °C by the continental geothermal gradient as they descend 2.5 vertical kilometers through the fractured Precambrian basement, before discharging along the base of the foothills. A coupled groundwater-flow and heat-transport numerical simulation independently supports this interpretation by reproducing the observed discharge elevations and spring temperatures under non-magmatic boundary conditions. The weight of the evidence, coupled with low discharge rates, indicates that these hot springs are unsuitable for conventional geothermal energy applications.

title: A complex network perspective on spatiotemporal drought evolution in the Dongjiang River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Qiang Huang, Shaofeng Li, Lan Kong, Shuyun Yuan, Liao Ouyang, Xiaoshan Luo, Peng Li
abstract: Study region The Dongjiang River Basin in southeast China, a critical water source region for the Pearl River Delta with a subtropical monsoon climate and frequent dry–wet transitions. Study focus Drought evolves through development, propagation, and recovery, yet few approaches unify temporal state transitions and directed spatial propagation. Using root-zone soil moisture data (1980–2025) from the GLEAM assimilation product, this study developed a complex network framework coupling a temporal state transition network with a spatial transfer entropy network to characterize complete drought life cycles. Drought life cycles were classified into five evolution modes by soil moisture change rate, with directed spatial propagation quantified via transfer entropy. MODIS-derived gross primary productivity and enhanced vegetation index provided independent ecological validation. New hydrological insights for the region Gradual processes dominated drought evolution, with slow development and quasi-stationary modes accounting for 52.5% of life-cycle time steps. A slow-drying, rapid-wetting asymmetry emerged: the median recovery rate was 1.5 times the development rate, formation decelerated, and termination shifted abruptly to rapid recovery. Spatial propagation was highly connected and weakly modular (86.2% single-step edges), with signals converging from peripheral sources toward three core sinks controlled by a few hub cells. Vegetation responses differed distinctly across the five modes, confirming their ecological relevance. These findings improve understanding of drought evolution and spatial propagation, informing drought zonation and water resources management in the basin.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics and driving factors of surface water in the Middle and Lower Yangtze River Basin from 1986 to 2023
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Peng Chen, Hongzhong Pan, Huaming Yao
abstract: Study region Middle and Lower Yangtze River Basin, China. Study focus Natural and anthropogenic drivers synergistically influence the spatiotemporal characteristics of surface water in the Middle and Lower Yangtze River Basin (MLYRB). However, due to the immense challenges in processing long-term time series data, the long-term changes in surface water area (SWA) within the MLYRB remain inadequately revealed. This study utilized all available Landsat imagery, a robust water body mapping algorithm based on spectral indices and thresholds, and the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform to extract MLYRB SWA from 1986 to 2023 and conduct a comprehensive assessment of its dynamics. New hydrological insights for the region SWA exhibits a sustained decreasing trend (-169.75 km²/yr, p < 0.01), permanent surface water area (PSWA) maintains high stability (CV=0.07), while seasonal surface water area (SSWA) accelerates its decline (-152 km²/yr, p < 0.01). Quantitative attribution indicates that precipitation dominates water body replenishment, while vegetation expansion (ecological encroachment) significantly drives the decline in SSWA. Human interventions—particularly post-Three Gorges Reservoir impoundment—reversed the decline in downstream PSWA but accelerated SSWA contraction ( −242.04 km²/yr). This synergistic influence of natural and anthropogenic factors underscores the complexity of surface water evolution in the basin. This study provides updated information on the spatiotemporal dynamics of surface water in the MLYRB, contributing to the advancement of effective regional water resource management.

title: An enhanced method for rainfall pattern recognition and its asymmetrical change in Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Sijing He, Chengguang Lai, Weizhi Gao, Zhaoli Wang
abstract: Study region Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA). Study focus This study investigated whether long-term changes in heavy rainfall differ among rainfall patterns in the GBA. Using hourly rainfall observations from 23 stations during 1971–2020, independent rainfall events were identified and classified with a duration-adaptive rainfall pattern recognition framework to reduce mismatch between the number of identification points and event duration. Rainfall amount, duration, peak and precipitation concentration index (PCI) were analyzed for quantile-specific temporal trends and spatial variation. New hydrological insights for the region Unimodal rainfall patterns dominated the GBA, with Mode I accounting for 36.12% of all classified events. Rainfall pattern recognition was sensitive to mismatch between the number of identification points and event duration, and instability increased markedly when the former was smaller. Rainfall amount, duration and PCI showed clear quantile-dependent asymmetry, with lower quantiles tending to show negative or near-zero trends and upper quantiles tending to show positive trends, while rainfall peak increased across most of the distribution. This asymmetry was strongest for Mode I and much weaker for the bimodal patterns. Spatially, rainfall amount and peak showed broader centroid movement at upper quantiles, whereas duration and PCI were more variable at lower quantiles. These findings indicate that long-term rainfall change in the GBA is not uniform across events, but is strongly conditioned by rainfall pattern and quantile level.

title: Beyond nowcasting: A unified deep learning framework for short-term flood inundation forecasting (Carlisle, NW England)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xuanchi Chen, Chaoqun Li, Guojie Liang, Xie Lian, Dongqing Zhang, Mingkun Sun, Yongyong Zhang
abstract: Study region Carlisle, a flood-prone city in northwestern England within the River Eden catchment. Study focus Flood inundation forecasting with sufficient lead time and spatial detail is essential for proactive flood risk management, existing approaches remain focused on nowcasting or simplified outputs. This study develops a unified deep learning framework that couples upstream flow forecasting with inundation simulation, enabling grid-scale prediction of flood depth up to 4 h ahead. The model integrates a gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based flow forecasting module with a spatiotemporal inundation module combining convolutional layers, recurrent units, and multi-head attention (MHA). Model performance is evaluated based on the LISFLOOD-FP model using leave-one-out cross-validation, event-based analysis, multi-stage forecasting, and stress test. New hydrological insights for the region Results highlight heterogeneous flood responses among three upstream inflows in discharge magnitude, peak timing, and rising-limb characteristics. Performance declines at longer lead times, particularly for the Caldew River inflow. For the 2005 flood event, flow forecasting component reproduces upstream hydrographs with Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values exceeding 0.97 at short lead times, while inundation forecasting achieves mean root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.24 m and NSE of 0.91 against the LISFLOOD-FP reference. Across stages, RMSE ranges from 0.06 to 0.30 m and NSE remains mostly above 0.95, with larger errors in transition and core-flooded areas and along the Eden River during rapid evolution. A 4-hour inundation forecast is generated in approximately 80 s on a GPU, compared with 36 min for the physics-based LISFLOOD-FP.

title: Enhancing process-based hydrological model with embedded residual neural networks: A hybrid modeling approach for hourly flood simulation
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Shuai Gao, Weihao Chen, Yingchun Huang, Laishun Yang, Ting Zhang, Shuo Zhang, Yuefei Huang
abstract: Study region Chenda, Yutan, Yongding, Guanyinqiao and Longmen catchments located in Fujian Province, China. Study focus This study focused on enhancing the physical interpretability and predictive performance of hydrological simulations by proposing a novel hybrid framework based on an Embedded Residual Neural Network (ERNN) integrated within the HBV model structure. The framework was rigorously evaluated using hourly flood data from five catchments, demonstrating superior accuracy and stability compared to conventional embedded neural network approaches. New hydrological insights This study proposes a novel hybrid framework based on an Embedded Residual Neural Network (ERNN) to enhance the HBV model. Instead of directly replacing empirical equations, our method integrates residual connections within the internal modules of the model, allowing the neural network to learn corrective residuals while preserving the physical consistency of the original hydrological structure. The model was evaluated using hourly flood data from five small and medium-sized catchments in Fujian Province, China. Results show that the proposed ERNN-based model significantly outperforms conventional embedded neural network approaches, achieving higher accuracy and more stable simulations. Furthermore, model performance improves progressively as the number of residual modules increases. The approach also maintains physical coherence in key hydrological state variables, and reduces the model outputs uncertainty across multiple training runs.

title: Machine learning integration of Sentinel-1 SAR and ground-based measurements for soil moisture estimation in temperate forested landscape of Somogy County, Hungary
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tondani Sanah Ramabulana, Gift Siphiwe Nxumalo, Szabolcs Czigány
abstract: Study region Somogy County is located in south-western Hungary (45.95°–46.50°N, 17.40°–18.00°E) and covers 6065 km². The region includes temperate forests, intensive agricultural land, and wetlands developed on diverse soils, including Eutric Luvisols, Cambisols, Albeluvisols, Acid Gleysols, and Aquic Gleysols. The climate ranges from subhumid to humid. Study focus This study integrated Sentinel-1 C-band SAR backscatter (VV and VH polarisations), soil hydraulic properties, SRTM-derived terrain variables, and meteorological data to predict soil water content using three machine-learning approaches: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN). In situ SWC observations were collected at 20 cm depth at three forest monitoring stations (Nagybajom, Barcs and Zselic) during the summers of 2024 and 2025 for model calibration and validation. Regional SWC maps were generated at 10 m resolution and further analysed using a Forest Vulnerability Index and a five-level management priority classification. New hydrological insight for the region Station-scale model performance was strong (R² = 0.866–0.913; RMSE = 0.018–0.022 m³ m⁻³; NSE = 0.838–0.891), while regional predictions showed moderate accuracy (R² = 0.532–0.648; RMSE = 0.033–0.041 m³ m⁻³), with KNN providing the best spatial transferability among the three models tested, though absolute spatial transferability remained limited under station-holdout cross-validation. Given the three-station, two-summer observation network, these county-scale maps serve as a pilot regional extrapolation rather than a fully validated product. VV backscatter, antecedent SWC, and saturated water content were the main predictors. Spatial patterns revealed higher drought sensitivity in sandy lowlands and greater moisture retention in silt-loam uplands, with a marked drying trend between 2024 and 2025, particularly in northern forest areas.

title: An interpretable deep learning framework integrating temporal attention and physically constrained dynamic routing for runoff prediction in the Upper Yangtze River basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiao Zhang, Yuting Li, Xiaole Xu, Li Tan, Yiran Peng, Zhiqiang Jiang, Hui Qin
abstract: Study region In the Upper Yangtze River basin of China. Study focus Accurate runoff prediction is crucial for reducing extreme weather impacts and improving water resources management. However, current deep learning algorithms primarily capture statistical correlations, neglecting the guiding role of hydrological processes. Mainstream models often fail to achieve satisfactory accuracy particularly in high-flow segments. To address these challenges, this study proposed a new interpretable deep learning framework for runoff prediction. The framework improves short-term runoff forecasting accuracy and enhances understanding of the prediction process by developing Temporal Attention Routeformer (TA-Routeformer), which incorporates physical mechanisms and temporal attention mechanisms, and by performing interpretability analysis. New hydrological insights for the region The results demonstrated that TA-Routeformer improved runoff prediction at Yichang station for the next 1–3 days. Compared with Transformer, TA-Routeformer achieved average improvements of 0.71%, 0.89%, 8.09%, and 8.50% in the Determination Coefficient (R2), the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE), the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), respectively. Average Flow Duration Curve High Flow Variability (FHV) values for predictions across the two high-flow segments were −2.742% and −3.672%. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified Yichang (t − 1) and Cuntan (t − 1) as the two most influential inputs across forecast horizons, while temperature and longwave radiation became more influential at longer horizons. Meanwhile, high-flow underestimation remains a concern for flood forecasting at Yichang station.

title: Gauge-to-grid rainfall dataset development for hydrological and flood modeling in the Chao Phraya Basin, Thailand
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Wongnarin Kompor, Taweechai Nuntawisuttiwong, Chaiwat Ekkawatpanit, Chai Jaturapitakkul
abstract: Study Region: The Chao Phraya River Basin (CPRB), Thailand, is vulnerable to monsoon-driven floods. Existing gridded rainfall datasets, K10 and T12, end in 2004 and 2011, respectively, limiting their use for evaluating recent flood events. Study Focus: This study developed a 41-year daily gridded rainfall dataset (1981–2021) using observations from 79 rain gauges, inverse distance weighting (IDW), and digital elevation model-based lapse-rate correction. IDW parameters were assessed through leave-one-out cross-validation. The dataset was evaluated using the H08 hydrological model and CaMa-Flood with a 12-month reservoir operation scheme (M12). Simulated discharge and flood extent were compared with observations for the 2011, 2017, and 2021 flood events. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: IDW configurations with similar monthly accuracy differed in their ability to preserve extreme rainfall, highlighting the importance of application-oriented parameter selection. The final IDW dataset achieved a basin-scale monthly rainfall bias of +0.43% relative to Thiessen. H08 simulations achieved Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values of 0.90–0.93, while CaMa-Flood achieved NSE values of 0.76–0.91. Flood-extent validation yielded critical success index (CSI) values of 0.30–0.44. The 2021 discharge bias highlighted uncertainty associated with simplified reservoir operations. The extended dataset supports historical flood evaluation and provides a foundation for future hydrological forecasting applications in the CPRB.

title: Quantifying the contributions of snowmelt and rainfall to alpine debris flow in the eastern Tibetan Plateau using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery and hydrological simulation
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Xiao Hu, Tao Yang, Dong Sun, Jianbo Wu, Xiaohui Luo, Feng Wang
abstract: Study region The Ridi Gully watershed, a typical alpine catchment on the eastern Tibetan Plateau, China, focusing on the catastrophic debris flow event on 3 August 2024. Study focus Accurate quantitative partitioning of water source contributions to alpine debris flows remains a critical challenge for early warning research. This study combines multi-temporal Sentinel-2 remote sensing interpretation, a temperature-corrected snow cover reconstruction model, and HEC-HMS hydrological modelling. Scenario simulations are adopted to quantify the respective contributions of snowmelt and rainfall to debris flow initiation, supplemented by multi-scenario sensitivity analyses. New hydrological insights for the region Anomalously high 2024 spring-summer temperatures accelerated snow ablation, reducing snow cover area to only 7.66% by 1 August. Snowmelt accounted for 32.63% of total flood volume but less than 1% of peak discharge, while rainfall contributed 67.37% of flood volume and 99.32% of peak discharge. Snowmelt establishes a hydrological background field to lower sediment mobilization thresholds, whereas short-duration high-intensity rainfall is identified as the decisive trigger in our model-based estimates. A dual-factor dynamic early warning strategy is proposed for multi-source alpine debris flow risk mitigation.

title: Three-dimensional evolution of hydrological drought and its linkage to meteorological drought in the Ganjiang River Basin, China
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Weilin Liu, Jingrong Zhang, Zhanxiong Zhou, Pengcheng Zhong, Degao Sun, Lina Liu
abstract: Study region Ganjiang River Basin (GRB), China. Study focus This study investigated the spatiotemporal evolution of hydrological drought (HD) and its relationship with meteorological drought (MD) across the GRB within a three-dimensional spatiotemporal framework. A gridded drought index dataset spanning 1961–2019 was constructed using the SWAT model and Inverse Distance Weighting interpolation. A three-dimensional drought identification framework was applied to pinpoint drought events and analyze their spatiotemporal characteristics, while the copula method was used to explore the linkage between HD and MD. New hydrological insights for the region The affected area, frequency, and severity of HD in the GRB generally decreased over time, with the most severe conditions concentrated in the middle stages of HD events; approximately 50% of events exhibited multimodal behavior. A 3-month lag was identified between MD and HD, and their durations and severities were strongly correlated: HD duration increased with MD duration, but HD severity plateaued beyond a certain MD severity threshold. The MD-HD response probability increased with increasing MD return periods, while the dominant matching characteristic changed with return periods: severity-based correspondence was more prominent at shorter return periods, whereas duration-based correspondence became more dominant at longer return periods.

title: Comparative evaluation of the multi-model ensembles of CMIP5 and CMIP6 for simulating temperature and precipitation in Iran
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Ehsan Nikandish, Azadeh Ahmadi, Narges Azad
abstract: Study region This study focuses on Iran, characterized by diverse climatic zones from humid Caspian coasts to hyper-arid central desert and Persian Gulf shores. Study focus This study evaluates twelve general circulation models (GCMs), (six CMIP5, six CMIP6) and their multi-model ensembles for simulating precipitation, minimum temperature, and maximum temperature over Iran. Observational data from 33 synoptic stations for 1961–2005 were used. Model skill was assessed at monthly, seasonal, and annual scales using Taylor diagrams, skill scores, correlation coefficients, and root mean square deviation. New hydrological insights for the region The CMIP6 multi-model ensemble achieves a Taylor skill score of 0.148, higher than 0.084 for CMIP5. For monthly precipitation, correlation coefficients range from 0.127 to 0.372 for CMIP6 and 0.202–0.364 for CMIP5, with MPI-ESM1–2-HR and IPSL-CM5A-MR showing the highest values. IPSL-CM6A-LR provides the most accurate precipitation estimates among individual models. For maximum temperature, Taylor skill scores range from 0.74 (inmcm4) to 0.84 (CMIP6 ensemble), while for minimum temperature they vary from 0.49 (CMIP5 ensemble) to 0.78 (MPI-ESM1–2-HR). Overall, CMIP6 ensemble shows lower errors, higher correlations, and better skill scores than CMIP5, and reproduces spatial and temporal precipitation patterns more faithfully.

title: Spatial differentiation of ecosystem resilience and asymmetric response mechanisms under flash drought stress in Asian Karst Concentration areas
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Haoze Ding, Qi Guo, Yuan Li, Zhengshan Chen, Qiuwen Zhou, Shunfu Yang, Yuluan Zhao
abstract: Study region The Asian Karst Concentration, spanning southwestern China and the Indochina Peninsula. Study focus This study aimed to determine how karst geomorphology regulates ecosystem resistance and recovery under flash drought stress. We integrated satellite-derived gross primary productivity, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, and evaporative stress index datasets from 2000 to 2024, and applied a multidimensional resilience framework, nonlinear threshold detection, and soil moisture–water use efficiency coupling analysis. New hydrological insights for the region The estimated karst–non-karst contrast in GPP-based resistance was sensitive to spatial grouping and uncertainty assumptions, while karst areas exhibited a smaller next-year productivity rebound. Estimated breakpoints in the resistance–severity relationships differed between karst and non-karst areas (52.8 vs. 105.2), with distinct changes in fitted slopes rather than a common physiological collapse pattern. Median soil moisture–water-use efficiency correlations were higher in karst areas within each aridity class, although the direction of the contrast varied among aridity–vegetation combinations. Event composites showed less negative standardized soil-moisture minima but more negative water-use-efficiency minima in karst areas. Together, these findings highlight the importance of considering productivity maintenance, subsequent rebound, and water-related responses jointly when assessing flash-drought vulnerability. Hydrological heterogeneity provides a plausible explanation for these contrasting responses, but the contribution of subsurface buffering requires independent validation.

title: Developing optimal operating rules for a multi-reservoir system with multi-objective water utilization and multi-year carryover storage: A case study of the Upper Yellow River
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zijia Mi, Xiang Li, Baiyinbaoligao, Jiahua Wei, Xiangpeng Mu, Fengran Xu, Juan Bao, Yanqing Shen, Meiying San, Yu Bai
abstract: Study region The multi-reservoir system on the Upper Yellow River, China, comprising Longyangxia, Laxiwa, Lijiaxia, Gongboxia, Jishixia, and Liujiaxia. Study focus To address the difficulty of directly translating optimal operation results under multi-reservoir, multi-objective, and multi-year regulation conditions into operating rules that can guide reservoir operation, this study develops an integrated framework for cascade reservoir operating rule derivation. The framework constructs optimization-based samples considering different scenarios, performs key factor mining, derives operating rules using data-driven methods, and validates their applicability under broader inflow conditions using stochastic runoff preserving multisite temporal and spatial dependence. New hydrological insights for the region (1) An optimization-based framework transformed optimal operation results under multi-reservoir, multi-objective, and multi-year regulation conditions into rule-learning samples while preserving principal cascade operating features. (2) Key factor mining reduced 59 candidate factors to 29–31, decreasing input dimensionality by 48%-51% while maintaining prediction accuracy close to the full factor sets. (3) Under historical runoff conditions, the derived operating rules generated reservoir operation trajectories close to direct optimization results, with energy production reaching at least 87% and water supply reaching at least 94% of the direct optimization results. (4) Under stochastic runoff conditions, the historical-runoff-derived rules remained effective without retraining, generating operation trajectories close to direct optimization results, with energy production reaching at least 85% and water supply exceeding 90% of the direct optimization results for most combinations.

title: Integrated assessment of heavy metal contamination and ecological and human health risks in agricultural soils, groundwater and surface water of an industrialized arid region (Arak Plain, Iran)
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Saeed Sharafi, Fatemeh Salehi, Maryam Sharafi, Zahra Alimohammadi, Zahra Moradi
abstract: Study region Arak Plain, central Iran. Study focus This study evaluated the concentrations and associated ecological and human health risks of Cd, Cu, Zn, Pb, Ni, Cr, and Hg in agricultural soils, groundwater, and surface water of an industrialized wheat-growing plain. Soil contamination was assessed using the geoaccumulation index, contamination factor, Pollution Load Index, and Potential Ecological Risk Index. Human health risks associated with soil and water exposure were evaluated using non-carcinogenic and carcinogenic risk models. The effects of soil texture, farming system, and their interaction on soil metal concentrations were also examined. New hydrological insights for the region Distinct concentration and risk profiles were observed among agricultural soils, groundwater, and surface water. Because soil and water represent different matrices and were reported in different units, these differences are interpreted as compartment-specific signatures rather than direct evidence of retention, attenuation, or transfer. Zn and Cu showed the highest concentrations in agricultural soils, whereas Cd dominated the toxicity-weighted ecological risk. Soil texture significantly affected only Zn concentrations, with a small effect size, while farming system and its interaction with soil texture were non-significant. Mean soil hazard quotients remained below 1, although some individual values for Cd and Cr approached or exceeded this threshold. Groundwater showed greater modeled non-carcinogenic concern than surface water, particularly for Cd, Pb, and Cu, while Pb made the largest contribution to groundwater carcinogenic risk. The results provide a regional screening-level assessment and identify groundwater as the principal water compartment requiring continued risk-based monitoring in the Arak Plain.

title: What controls reliable hourly flood simulation across hydrological regimes in the mountain catchments of central Chile
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Diego Parra-Vargas, Álvaro Ossandón, Joaquin Meza
abstract: Study region: Forty-nine mountain catchments in central Chile (32–39°S), spanning rainfall-, snowmelt-, and mixed-dominated flood regimes across the Andes and Coastal Range. Steep relief and short channels produce short, sub-daily hydrological response times, and floods threaten much of the national population. Study focus: Flood early warning in these catchments requires resolving flood peaks that evolve within hours, yet conceptual models and calibration metrics are still evaluated overwhelmingly at the daily scale. We assess three lumped conceptual models (GR4H, TUW, and SAC-SMA) calibrated at hourly resolution, using seven objective functions under a traditional full-record approach (T) and a flood-hydrograph-centred approach (FHC), with continuous and categorical (event-detection) metrics. New hydrological insights: Among the tested models, model structure, rather than the choice of objective function, governs temporal transferability. SAC-SMA is the most stable across regimes and approaches (NRMSE increases below 33 percentage points under FHC) and GR4H the most sensitive (below 53). High-flow skill deteriorates systematically from rainfall- to snowmelt-dominated basins, with median correlation falling from 0.65 to 0.10 under T. This pluvial-to-nival degradation quantifies a real limitation of Andean snowmelt regimes, whose prolonged, energy-driven flood response is not resolved at sub-daily resolution by conceptual snow routines, although uncertainty in high-elevation reanalysis forcing plausibly contributes. For rainfall- and mixed-dominated basins, a promising operational strategy combines LCE (T) for detection with KGE-K HiLo (FHC) for peak refinement.

title: A hybrid SWAT-LSTM-transformer model for transferable runoff simulation in ungauged basins
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Zhengbo Peng, Dedi Liu, Jiayu Zhang, Yicheng Li
abstract: Runoff simulation in ungauged basins remains a fundamental and challenging issue in hydrological science, with far-reaching implications for water resources management, flood control, and agricultural planning. While previous studies have extensively developed physically-based and data-driven models for runoff simulation in ungauged basins, both models are still constrained by limited cross-basin transferability and inadequate physical interpretability. To address these constrains, we propose a hybrid model for runoff simulations in a target ungauged basin through integrating the physically-based Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model with the data-driven Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Transformer models as a hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model. SWAT model with default parameters simulate runoff generation processes to quantify the relationship between meteorological forcing variables and observed runoff variables. And the bias of the relationship is simulated by the LSTM-Transformer model. Three metrics of R 2, NSE, PBIAS are employed to evaluate the performances of the models. After the proposed SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model has been calibrated in a gauged basin, it is transferred to a target ungauged basin. There are three basins referring to Tao River water diversion project that are taken as case study area. One is the Upper Wei that is taken as the gauged basin for calibrating models while the other two are Tao, and Zuli River basins that are assumed to be target ungauged basins. The means of R 2, NSE, and absolute PBIAS values are 0.897, 0.841, and 13.37% from transferring the hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model while they are 0.206, −4.405, and 106.65% from the transferring calibrated SWAT model and 0.257, −1.244, and 81.74% from the transferring LSTM-Transformer model in Tao, and Zuli River two target ungauged basins. The results demonstrate that the hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model outperforms both the calibrated SWAT model and the trained LSTM-Transformer model when they are transferred to the target ungauged basins. The relationships between the runoff and the runoff generation processes simulated by a physically-based model even with its default parameters can be captured by the data-driven model, which help to transfer the hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model. And the Transformer model was integrated with the LSTM model to improve the stability of model transfer and alleviate the limitation in high runoff simulations in the target ungauged basins. The sensitive parameters of the SWAT model and the contributions of inputs to the LSTM-Transformer are similar in both gauged and ungauged basins. Therefore, the proposed hybrid SWAT-LSTM-Transformer model is not only an effective approach in the case study area but also can be applied in a ungauged basin.

title: Investigation into the transforming mechanism from flash-to-conventional drought in different soil moisture layers in a highly climate-diverse basin
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Tahira Khurshid, Qiongfang Li, Chuanhao Wu, Muhammad Shafeeque
abstract: Study region The Indus Basin, a highly diverse climate basin in South Asia. Study focus The transformation from flash drought to conventional drought (FD-CD) poses significant challenges to drought risk and management systems, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of the dynamics involved. Previous studies focused on the FD-CD process solely through the perspective of the recovery phase, overlooking the persistent phase between drought onset and recovery. This study aims to determine which phase of drought contributes the most to FD-CD and explore the impact of various climate characteristics on this phase. New hydrological insights We found that FD-CD is more likely to occur in deeper soil moisture layers, particularly in semi-arid and arid regions of the Indus Basin, with its peak period from July to October. The persistent phase of drought is most significant contributor to FD-CD development, with an average duration of 13 octads, significantly longer than the recovery phase (~ 5 octads), while the average rate of soil moisture change is relatively low during the persistent phase (0.025%) compared to the recovery phase (0.08%). XGBoost SHAP analysis reveals significant differences in the contribution of meteorological variables to the persistent phase in various climate zones. The contribution of high temperature to the persistent phase is most significant in the arid zone, while precipitation deficit is a dominant associated factor in other climate zones of the study domain. These findings contribute to understanding the FD-CD dynamics, providing new insights into the importance of the persistent phase in the life expectancy of the FD.

title: Assessing groundwater favourability using multi-scale spatial regression techniques within a GIS framework
description: Publication date: December 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 68 Author(s): Imran Ahmad, Mithas Ahmad Dar, Mariya Belete, Mezid Kassa Abebe, Martina Zelenakova, Amare Adane, Milashu Sisay, Zinabie Mekonnen Taye, Shewaye Amakelew, Getanew Sewnet Zewdu
abstract: Study region Raya Azebo Woreda in northern Ethiopia faces increasing groundwater stress due to variable rainfall, heterogeneous lithology, and growing agricultural and domestic water demand, making reliable groundwater-potential assessment essential for sustainable water management. Study focus This study integrates Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) with GIS to map groundwater potential using lithology, rainfall, land cover, distance to lineaments, and distance to rivers. The model achieved an adjusted R² of 0.8796, with RMSE = 0.3412, MAE = 0.2736, and AUC = 0.964. MGWR identified broad-scale effects for lithology, rainfall, lineaments, and rivers (bandwidth = 101,990.79 m), while land cover exhibited a localized influence (bandwidth = 48,037.78 m). New hydrological insights The MGWR–GIS integration advances conventional groundwater mapping by capturing the scale-dependent spatial influence of individual hydrological controls rather than assuming uniform relationships across the landscape. The resulting classification into poor, moderate, high, and very high groundwater-potential zones provides spatially targeted information for groundwater exploration, recharge planning, and sustainable resource management.

title: Re-evaluating coastal salinization in the Mitidja Plain, northern Algeria, using vintage VES data: Statistical clustering and 3D inversion
Correction: How does rewetting propagate through restored peatlands? An integrated surface–subsurface modelling analysis of water–table dynamics
The beginning of groundwater use by hominins and its key to migrations by Homo erectus out of Africa
abstract: Abstract Despite growing acceptance of the importance of groundwater use by hominins, there has been little hydrogeological investigation into the controls on groundwater availability as relevant to their evolution and geographic dispersal. This study integrates available fossil and stone tool data with hydrogeological landscape reconstruction and conceptualisation to develop understanding and constraints on the earliest use of groundwater by hominins and early migrations between Africa and Eurasia. It is proposed that the first bipedal human ancestors, appearing in the fossil record in Central and East Africa between 6 and 7 Ma, learned from other mammals how to find and access shallow groundwater in ephemeral streambeds. The first evidence of hominin associations with groundwater discharge from springs is from around 2–4.5 Ma in the East African Rift System (EARS), these locations likely being critically stable hydro-refugia within the driest parts of precession-dominated climatic cycles. The first migrating hominin species appears to have been Homo erectus , with those in the EARS leaving in waves as small bands from around 1.9 Ma at the end of a humid period in the Arabian Peninsula. It is proposed that the most hydrologically plausible routes linking the EARS to Eurasia are via Red Sea crossings and then through the Arabian Peninsula moving along the strike of regional aquifers which would have provided perennial groundwater even over long climatically arid periods. The paper demonstrates the fundamental importance of groundwater for early hominin communities during a critical period in the evolution of human physiology and consciousness.

title: A two-stage clustering algorithm for generating digital cores for grouting in highly fractured rock foundations
Resolving 3-D aquifer architecture through assimilated lithological and geophysical data: Insights from multilayered alluvial systems of the Ganga–Mahananda floodplain, eastern India
Hydrochemical characteristics, origins, and health risk assessment of fluoride in groundwater in the Biliu River Basin, Liaodong Peninsula, China
Effect of bioturbation–induced riverbed morphological changes on groundwater/surface-water exchange in mountain rivers
Characterization of subsurface groundwater pathways from treated wastewater effluent infiltration along the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, USA
abstract: Abstract Recharge of treated wastewater to the environment is increasingly becoming a component of water resources management, especially in water-limited areas such as the Grand Canyon. Treated wastewater from the Grand Canyon South Rim Wastewater Treatment Plant has been discharged to a dry wash located along the surface expression of a fault for decades, but the fate of the wastewater is unclear. Previous research suggested possible connections between the treated wastewater discharge sites and springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon, particularly Monument spring. Additional investigations presented in this report add further evidence to the connection between the wastewater and Monument spring, utilizing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, artificial sweeteners, and stable isotopes of water. A dye trace established the first direct connection between wastewater and Monument spring where the dye added to treated wastewater took about 4–6 months to move through the subsurface and was detectable for 5 months. The persistence of wastewater tracers over time and the timing of dye movement suggests a fast subsurface flow pathway. On the basis of geologic observations of faults and jointing, groundwater flow follows a possible combination of karst and other structural pathways. The dye and wastewater tracers were monitored at other springs along the South Rim of Grand Canyon and the combination of repeated dye detections and multiple wastewater tracers were only found at Monument spring. Multiple lines of evidence provide a robust tracer suite to support evidence of structural/karst controls on preferential flowpaths; faults alone are unlikely to explain the flow pathway.

title: Numerical simulation of the impact of tunnel drainage on matrix–conduit water exchange in the karst aquifers of Panzhou City, China
Quantifying water origin of a Mediterranean urban karst aquifer using storm event typology and high-frequency physicochemical signatures
Estimating multi-decadal groundwater levels using incomplete well records in confined and unconfined aquifers of the southern San Joaquin Valley, California (USA)
Hydrochemistry of confined aquifers in Friuli Venezia Giulia, Italy: Regional patterns, trends, and drivers
abstract: Abstract Confined aquifers are considered to be protected from surface contamination, yet intensive abstraction and long-term land-use pressures may alter their quality, especially in coastal areas. This study characterises the hydrochemistry of the multilayered confined aquifer system of the lower Friulian Plain (NE Italy), where groundwater is extensively exploited and locally affected by anthropogenic stressors. The study combines hydrochemical data from 1996 to 2025 from the monitoring activity of Regional Environmental Protection Agency of Friuli Venezia Giulia (ARPA FVG) and new samples collected in 2024–2025, compiling 1210 samples from 103 wells. The aim is to determine how recharge sources, residence time, and human activities control groundwater quality. Hydrochemical families were identified using major ions, redox-sensitive species, organic micropollutants, stable oxygen isotopes, and multivariate statistics. Three groundwater families were recognised: submodern waters, with hypoxic conditions, low to absent contaminant load and likely associated with recharge dating back to the late Würmian glacial period; modern-pristine waters, which are characterised by oxidising conditions, are SO 4 2− -rich, and show low to absent NO 3 − and pesticide concentrations; and modern-impacted waters, which are similar to the latter but display elevated NO 3 − concentrations, lower pH values, and detectable anthropogenic contaminants. Long-term trends indicate that although NO 3 − concentrations are overall stable or slightly decreasing in shallow aquifers, slowly increasing trends occur in deeper wells and near the margins of the NO 3 − plume, suggesting downward and lateral migration of impacted modern groundwater. Cl − concentrations show no increasing trends in coastal wells, indicating no evidence of active seawater intrusion.

title: Validating a numerical model for calco-carbonic reactive transport in a laboratory-scale fracture analog
abstract: Abstract Calco-carbonic reactive transport controls the dissolution of limestone by carbonic acid, a key process shaping the hydraulic and geochemical evolution of carbonate aquifers. Quantitative understanding of the coupling between flow, transport, and chemical reactions is essential for predicting karstification under variable hydraulic gradients, $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 partial pressures, and pH. To support model validation, laboratory experiments were conducted in a 1 m $$^2$$ 2 vertical karst-fracture analog with variable aperture, representing a simplified hydrogeologic fracture domain. Numerical simulations reproduced these experiments under controlled discharge, $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 concentration, and acidity. The coupled reactive transport models capture feedbacks between forced convection, diffusion, and density variations, linking reactive interface dynamics with evolving flow fields. Simulated and measured calcium and carbonate ion concentrations showed good agreement, indicating that diffusive transport at the water–limestone interface primarily limited dissolution. Insights from the combined modeling and experimental framework refine laboratory-scale design, improve interpretation of dissolution kinetics, and strengthen the basis for upscaling to field-scale carbonate aquifers. The results enhance prediction of permeability evolution, flow-path development, and $$\text {CO}_{2}$$ CO 2 - $$\text {H}_{2}\text {O}$$ H 2 O -rock interactions in karst systems.

title: Mechanical and chemical rehabilitation of groundwater abstraction wells clogged by iron and manganese precipitates in Finland
abstract: Résumé Le colmatage des puits de captage d'eau souterraine survient généralement lorsque le fer et le manganèse dissous dans l'eau précipitent sur les éléments du puits, entraînant une baisse du débit. En Finlande, ce phénomène est marqué car les sols sont riches en fer et en manganèse, et les aquifères sédimentaires quaternaires recouverts d'argile présentent généralement une carence en oxygène. Une nouvelle approche de réhabilitation des puits, combinant traitements mécaniques et chimiques, a été appliquée à quatre puits de captage d'eau souterraine situés dans des dépôts sédimentaires quaternaires postglaciaires non confinés en Finlande. D'après les analyses par fluorescence X (XRF), les précipités responsables du colmatage étaient composés de Fe₂O₃, SiO₂, MnO et P₂O₅. Les réhabilitations mécaniques et chimiques ont toutes deux permis d'augmenter considérablement les débits (de 68 à 6 692 %) ; même les puits totalement colmatés ont affiché une nette amélioration de leur débit après l'intervention. À l'issue de la réhabilitation mécanique, les crépines des puits présentaient un niveau de propreté modéré. La réhabilitation chimique a permis un nettoyage supplémentaire des crépines, libérant totalement les fentes et réduisant la turbidité. Le traitement chimique a entraîné une augmentation de la conductivité électrique, de la teneur en sulfates ainsi que des concentrations en fer et en manganèse (dissous et totaux) dans l'eau, en raison des réactifs utilisés et de la dissolution du fer et du manganèse contenus dans les précipités. Toutefois, la qualité de l'eau est revenue à ses niveaux initiaux après une journée de pompage suivant le traitement. Cette méthode de réhabilitation est applicable aux puits de captage situés dans des dépôts sédimentaires quaternaires postglaciaires non confinés, au sein d'aquifères constitués de sable et de gravier à forte conductivité hydraulique. Néanmoins, des études complémentaires sont nécessaires pour mieux comprendre le processus de colmatage ainsi que l'applicabilité de ces méthodes de réhabilitation dans des contextes hydrogéologiques et des environnements redox variés.

title: Sustainable groundwater management in coastal areas: Modelling saltwater intrusion dynamics in Muravera, Italy
abstract: Abstract The coastal alluvial aquifer of Muravera, in south-eastern Sardinia (Italy), is affected by intense saltwater intrusion that seriously threatens freshwater supply. As groundwater overexploitation is often the main process controlling saltwater intrusion dynamics, it can strongly exacerbate salinization, making sustainable groundwater management essential to safeguard these resources. Reliable hydrogeological models based on robust datasets are powerful tools to support decision-making. This work develops a variable-density groundwater flow and solute transport model to analyse saltwater intrusion into the coastal aquifer of Muravera. Four simulation scenarios were implemented. The first reconstructs the historical evolution of salinization over the period of 1999–2023, whereas the other three extend the simulations to 2050 to quantify the various effects of different groundwater abstraction practices and to test a mitigation scenario. Two modelling codes were coupled to support the analysis. Groundwater recharge was computed using the Soil–Water-Balance (SWB) code and subsequently used as input to the iMOD-WQ code, which simulates variable-density flow and salt transport using SEAWAT. This coupling explicitly captures temporal and spatial recharge variability, which is often oversimplified in other approaches. The results indicate that groundwater abstractions for rice-field irrigation exerts a stronger influence on salinization dynamics than drinking-water abstractions. The mitigation scenario attenuates groundwater salinization in the plain, providing useful insights for future groundwater-management strategies.

Advancing hydraulic conductivity estimation in the Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group using borehole NMR logging
abstract: Abstract The Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group is an important aquifer in the United Kingdom (UK) for groundwater and geothermal energy applications. Hydraulic conductivity ( K ) is essential for understanding groundwater movement, contaminant and heat transport in aquifers. Pumping test and borehole nuclear magnetic resonance logging (BNMR) were conducted in three boreholes drilled into the Sherwood Sandstone to determine K . BNMR provides information on the water-filled porosity and pore space geometry, and compared to conventional methods, it is an effective way to estimate K at a high vertical resolution. Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) and Timur-Coates (T-C) were used to estimate K using the standard empirical constants initially developed for petroleum reservoir applications. K SDR and K T-C were upscaled to the larger volume represented by K pumping for comparison. Both the standard SDR and T-C equations underestimated K by at least two orders of magnitude because of the limited transferability of their empirical constants to shallow groundwater systems, as they were derived for petroleum reservoir rocks rather than near-surface materials. The fits between the K SDR , K T-C and K pumping were optimised using a semi-constrained least-squares approach to obtain a set of site-specific parameters for the Sherwood Sandstone Group. The new K SDR and K T-C estimates, based on site-specific parameters, are within an order of magnitude of the K pumping . This study presents the first reported SDR and T-C constants for the Sherwood Sandstone Group, which may be used to estimate a more reliable NMR-derived high-resolution hydraulic conductivity in other locations where this formation is present.

Hydrochemical differences and origins of karst waters around the Jinan Pluton, North China
abstract: Abstract The periphery of the Jinan Pluton, North China, contains abundant cold-water and geothermal karst resources, constituting a natural observatory for investigating karst water origins and hydrogeochemical evolution. To advance the understanding of the occurrence pattern and origins of karst waters around the Jinan Pluton, a total of 36 samples of karst groundwater were collected and analyzed for hydrochemical constituents via ion chromatography (IC) and inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), and isotopic composition. The results are as follows: (1) Along the south-to-north regional groundwater flow path, cold-water and geothermal karst groundwaters around the Jinan Pluton exhibit significantly distinct hydrochemical types. From shallow cold-water karst (spring water) to deep geothermal karst systems, the hydrochemical types become progressively more complex, accompanied by a continuous increase in the extent of water–rock interaction. (2) Within the geothermal field north of the Yellow River, the observed gradual increase in total dissolved solids (TDS) of geothermal karst water from west to east can be attributed to two main factors. First, the geothermal karst water in the western segment of the geothermal field receives significant recharge from the Yellow River. Second, the karst water level in the eastern segment of Jinan is the lowest across the study area, making it the convergence center of regional karst groundwater flow, which results in a relatively isolated hydrogeological environment with respect to the surface. This study reveals karst water hydrochemical evolution near the Jinan Pluton to guide water resource utilization and protection.

Old water, rapid responses: Process-based hydrogeological domains reveal hydraulic–age decoupling and implications for recharge assessment in a complex aquifer system of the Heuningnes Catchment, South Africa
abstract: Abstract Groundwater-level fluctuations are commonly used as recharge indicators because groundwater-level rises are often assumed to represent additions of recently recharged water to aquifer storage. In heterogeneous, multilayer aquifer systems, this assumption remains uncertain because groundwater-level variations may also reflect hydraulic connectivity, pressure transmission, storage redistribution, and groundwater mixing. Misinterpretation of groundwater-level behavior may consequently bias recharge estimates and groundwater-resource assessments. This study evaluated relationships among groundwater-level behavior, groundwater residence times, and hydrogeological process domains within the Heuningnes Catchment, South Africa. Groundwater hydrographs, tritium-derived groundwater ages, and a domain-based conceptual framework were integrated to investigate spatial variability in groundwater flow and recharge processes. Piston-flow (PF) apparent ages ranged from 0 to 60 years, whereas exponential–piston flow model (EPM)-derived mean transit times (MTTs) ranged from 2 to 80–100 years across hydrogeological domains. Recharge-dominated systems showed strong seasonal groundwater-level responses despite the coexistence of young and broad groundwater-age distributions and highly variable hydrograph responses, reflecting mixed recharge and storage influences. Structurally controlled systems showed rapid hydraulic responses despite prolonged groundwater residence times, suggesting pressure transmission independent of groundwater transport times. Residence-time-dominated systems were characterized by older groundwater and subdued hydrograph responses associated with prolonged storage. Groundwater-level response rate showed a weak and statistically non-significant relationship with MTT (Pearson's r = − 0.307, p = 0.460), demonstrating hydraulic–age decoupling and indicating that recharge assessments based solely on groundwater-level fluctuations may substantially misrepresent groundwater recharge processes in structurally complex multilayer aquifer systems.

Groundwater potential zoning in the Grande River Basin: A semi-arid region of Northeast Brazil
abstract: Abstract Seasonal water scarcity in western Bahia, Brazil, has led to increased dependence on groundwater resources; however, basin-scale hydrogeological measurements remain insufficient for preliminary assessments. This study presents a geographic information system-based groundwater potential map for the Grande River Hydrographic Basin (GRHB), where groundwater potential is defined as a relative index reflecting conditions favorable for recharge and subsurface storage, rather than a direct measure of aquifer productivity. Ten hydrogeological and terrain proxy layers, derived from existing datasets and remote sensing, were standardized and integrated using an analytic hierarchy process weighting scheme and a weighted linear combination. The resulting index was classified into five groundwater potential categories. The very high- and high-potential classes account for 48.08 and 25.41% of the basin, respectively, while the moderate class accounts for 19.90%, and the low- and very low-potential classes together comprise 6.59%. Spatial association with available well locations was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis and the area under the curve, which yielded a value of 0.821, indicating that wells are more frequently located in areas with higher index values. Additionally, a groundwater abstraction-pressure proxy, derived from wells with reported daily abstraction volumes, was used to identify potential stress areas where high favorability coincides with concentrated abstraction activities. These outputs serve as a first-order screening tool to guide field verification, monitoring, and targeted data acquisition across the basin.

Integrating geophysical and underwater robotic surveys with transport and geochemical modeling to assess the Solotvyno salt mine hazard in the Transcarpathia province of Ukraine
abstract: Abstract The Solotvyno salt mine in West Ukraine presents significant environmental and infrastructural risks due to uncontrolled salt dissolution following mine flooding, causing ground subsidence, sinkhole formation, and transboundary contamination of the Tisza River. This study employs an innovative multidisciplinary approach to characterize subsurface conditions and contamination pathways. The UX-1Neo autonomous underwater robotic platform conducted 14 dives in two flooded mine shafts, revealing intact main shaft structures but worrying blockages in horizontal passages, distinct haloclines at different depths (60 m in ventilation shaft 9, 140 m in shaft 10), and evidence of ongoing salt crystallization. Ground geophysical surveys such as electrical resistivity tomography, very low frequency radio-magnetotellurics and horizontal loop electromagnetics identified compromised protective clay layers (“pallag”) and potential air-filled voids, explaining accelerated dissolution and surface deformation. Hydrodynamic and contaminant transport modeling quantified salt fluxes (~ 2000 m 3 /day through “pallag” zones, ~ 13–15 m 3 /day from direct mine leakage) and confirmed dissolution rates of approximately 5.0–5.5 m 3 /day of rock salt, driven by both anthropogenic influences and natural gradients toward the Tisza River. NETPATH mixing models revealed variable contamination throughout the system, with the Black Moor area showing highest vulnerability (up to 27.4% mine water contribution) while the Tisza River maintains relatively good water quality despite measurable contamination (1.97% mine water). The suggested approach provides critical insights into risk assessment and remediation planning, representing a significant advancement in monitoring and managing complex environmental hazards associated with abandoned salt mines.

title: Ascertaining controls on spring discharge: Implications for the revival of drying springs in the Middle Hills region of Nepal
Groundwater occurrence and quality in a hyper-arid desert: Insights from high-resolution electrical resistivity surveys in Tharparkar, Pakistan
abstract: Abstract The Tharparkar District in Pakistan is among the world’s most water-scarce regions, characterized by its hyper-arid climatic conditions and the absence of perennial surface water resources. Understanding the occurrence of groundwater potential and its quality is therefore critical, particularly in remote regions where hydrogeological information remains limited. This study characterized groundwater resources using 576 high-resolution electrical resistivity survey (ERS) probes up to a depth of 300 m, conducted from 2017 to 2020. Complementary hydrochemical investigations included laboratory analysis of 168 groundwater samples collected from dug wells and 672 soil samples up to a depth of 0.60 m. Results demonstrated that the water table lies at depths of 2–15 m (26% of the area), 16–30 m (23%), and 31–90 m (51%). Interpretation of ERS data revealed that approximately 10% of the groundwater resources, covering the southern parts of Diplo, Islamkot, and Nagarparkar Talukas, are suitable for drinking at a depth of 25 m, with around 3% classified as fresh and 7% as slightly saline. Groundwater salinity increases with depth, as 51% of the area shows high salinity at depths of 26–50 m and very high salinity at depths of 51–200 m. Arsenic and fluoride concentrations exceed permissible limits in 10 and 28% of the groundwater samples, respectively. These findings provide robust geophysical and hydrochemical evidence to guide targeted groundwater development, water quality mitigation strategies and inform policy interventions, aimed at enhancing water security and safeguarding the health of communities living in severely water-stressed desert regions.
